Separating these three links makes it possible to diagnose why characterization factors differ across emission compartments.
claims.scope: The three-step model framework in the retrieved 208-page USEtox 2.0 Documentation (Version 1.1).
caveats: Describing the pathway framework does not imply that individual process equations have been replicated or empirically validated.
The formal documentation citation is 2017; a 2026 file metadata timestamp does not prove a newer methodological edition.

claims.text: Along the human-toxicity pathway, fate and exposure together determine the intake fraction (iF)—the fraction of an emitted mass that enters the modeled human population via a given pathway, with intake mass in the numerator and emitted mass in the denominator. Specific contact routes such as meat, milk, and fish are aggregated by intake route, and inhalation and ingestion then connect separately to route-specific effect factors that convert effect per unit intake into disease-case potential per unit emission. Changing the emission compartment alters fate and intake relationships, whereas replacing toxicological effect data alters the downstream link; even when both changes lower the total score, they call for different explanations.
claims.scope: Meaning of human intake fraction, effect factors, and characterization matrices in USEtox 2.0 Documentation §§2.2 and 2.5.1.
caveats: This explains model relationships without replicating any substance workbook or validating dose–response curves for site-specific populations.
Shared population quantities or units do not make characterization factors from different models, exposure pathways, or health endpoints automatically compatible.

claims.text: Freshwater ecotoxicity follows a distinct exposure-and-effect chain: exposure tracks the bioavailable dissolved fraction in freshwater, while effect relates species sensitivity to concentration. At the midpoint level, the documentation retains the potentially affected fraction (PAF) of species integrated over water volume and time, whereas human toxicity is expressed as cumulative disease-case potential. Because these indicators measure different receptors, they cannot be summed simply because both carry the label "toxicity." Moving to endpoint damage requires introducing severity factors or conversions to potentially disappeared fraction (PDF) of species. Whichever level is reported, "cases" in a comparative model are not observed local illnesses, and toxicity potentials cannot replace site- and population-specific risk assessments.
claims.scope: Indicator definitions and comparative scope in the USEtox 2.0 documentation.
caveats: Additional modeling assumptions separate effect data and severity factors from real-world case prediction; no site-risk calibration is performed.
Distinct protection targets and indicators cannot be summed merely because both are labeled toxicity.

claims.text: Although major international life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) frameworks all connect emissions to receptors via fate, exposure, and effect, they diverge at the outset into two families over category count, protection boundaries, and reference units (Table 1). The 2011 International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Handbook and EU Environmental Footprint (EF 2.0 through EF 3.1) adopt USEtox with three midpoints—human cancer toxicity (comparative toxic unit for humans, CTUh), human non-cancer toxicity (CTUh), and freshwater ecotoxicity (comparative toxic unit for ecosystems, CTUe)—declining to recommend terrestrial or marine ecotoxicity as insufficiently mature and offering only a split rating for cancer disability-adjusted life years (DALY) at the endpoint level. ReCiPe 2016 (RIVM Report 2016-0104, Chapter 9), by contrast, builds on the nested multimedia model Uniform System for the Evaluation of Substances adapted for LCA (USES-LCA 2.0) populated with the USEtox substance database: it defines five midpoints normalized to 1,4-dichlorobenzene (1,4-DCB) emitted to reference compartments, extrapolates terrestrial effects through soil pore-water partitioning while excluding agricultural soil ecotoxicity to avoid double counting with land use, and converts to endpoints using perspective-invariant 1,4-DCB damage factors. The two families thus part ways before calculation even begins on whether marine waters and industrial soils enter the ledger.
claims.scope: Structural divergence between ILCD 2011/EF (three USEtox CTUh/CTUe midpoints excluding terrestrial/marine ecotoxicity and most endpoints) and ReCiPe 2016 (five USES-LCA 2.0 1,4-DCB-referenced midpoints excluding agricultural-soil ecotoxicity with constant endpoint conversions).
caveats: Excluding agricultural soil ecotoxicity in USES-LCA 2.0 avoids double counting with land-use impacts and does not imply that field pesticide applications have no toxicological effects on soil organisms.

ILCD 2011 ratings and ReCiPe 2016 endpoint constants: ILCD rates metals, amphiphilic, and dissociating substances Level III at midpoint, rates the cancer endpoint Level II for non-polar organics and interim for metals/amphiphilic/dissociating substances, and does not recommend non-cancer or ecotoxicity endpoints. ReCiPe 2016 converts cancer and non-cancer at 11.5 and 2.7 DALY per case to 3.32×10⁻⁶ and 6.65×10⁻⁹ DALY/kg 1,4-DCB eq.; assuming acute toxicity approximates field disappearance (additional damage factor = 1) multiplied by species density, Table 9.4 gives 6.95×10⁻¹⁰, 1.05×10⁻¹⁰, and 5.39×10⁻⁸ species·yr/kg 1,4-DCB eq. for freshwater, marine, and terrestrial ecotoxicity (summary Table 1.5 rounds terrestrial to 5.4×10⁻⁸).

claims.text: Even within freshwater ecotoxicity using the exact same CTUe/kg unit, rewriting the effect benchmark and underlying toxicological datasets can completely overturn metal rankings (Table 2). Original USEtox sets the effect slope using the hazardous concentration for 50% of species (0.5/HC50), whereas EU EF 3.0 and EF 3.1 switched to the 20% hazardous concentration (0.2/HC20) and incorporated regulatory dossiers from the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) and the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). EF 3.0 temporarily retained legacy factors for metals; EF 3.1 brought metals onto the new benchmark and merged "organics, inorganics, and metals" into two sub-indicators—"organics" and metal-inclusive "inorganics." Metals lacking EU dossiers that were extrapolated solely via HC20 = 0.34 × HC50 (such as trivalent antimony) increased by only about 18% (20/17 ≈ 1.176), whereas metals backed by new dossiers reordered across orders of magnitude: aluminum (−99%) and copper (falling to 46.5, nearly −100%) plunged by two to three orders of magnitude while cadmium, silver, and mercury rose to the top. Comparing 1 kg of copper against 1 kg of mercury emitted to freshwater, EF 3.0 ranks copper roughly 45 times higher than mercury, whereas EF 3.1 reverses the order to mercury roughly 714 times higher than copper—a relative-weight flip of about 32,000-fold within the same unit.
claims.scope: Divergence within freshwater CTUe/kg between USEtox's 0.5/HC50 and EF 3.0/3.1's 0.2/HC20 effect benchmarks, the 20/17 extrapolation ratio, and order-of-magnitude metal rank reversals triggered by EU regulatory dossiers in EF 3.1.
caveats: The sharp reductions for aluminum and copper in EF 3.1 reflect both the switch to the HC20 benchmark and the replacement of toxicological datasets with EU dossiers; the change cannot be attributed solely to replacing 0.5 with 0.2 in the numerator.

ILCD Handbook Tables 20–21 note that USES-LCA 2.0 (used in ReCiPe) constructs linear concentration–response relationships from acute half-maximal effective concentrations (EC50), whereas Tool for the Reduction and Assessment of Chemical and Other Environmental Impacts (TRACI) uses no-observed-effect concentrations (NOEC). Exact EF 3.1 XML values (CTUe/kg): Sb³⁺ 143.35416561027336, Al 4351.936148782046, Cu 46.47592828149169, Cd 674494.7621301207, Ag 177087.28968187515, Hg 33175.97305971487.

claims.text: Why were these specific relationships assembled into USEtox? The 2008 paper documents a structured inter-model comparison among existing model developers: seven models participated in the modules they could compute across a test set of 45 non-dissociating, non-amphiphilic organic chemicals. Over three workshops, researchers traced discrepancies layer by layer across fate, exposure, effect, and final factors, adjusting models between rounds to eliminate unintended differences. Consensus here carries a concrete, bounded meaning—agreement on which mechanisms are indispensable and which modeling choices account for earlier divergences—not a blanket endorsement across all chemicals, scenarios, or decision contexts.
claims.scope: Participating models, chemical test set, and harmonization process in Rosenbaum et al. (2008) §2.1.
caveats: The 45-chemical test set is not a random sample of all chemicals, and not every participating model covered all endpoints.
The paper's authors were also the model developers and coordinators; documenting the harmonization process does not constitute independent empirical validation.

claims.text: Narrower spread among harmonized models provides a useful yet bounded check. Researchers traced many discrepancies to box architecture, inter-media transfer links, and effect formulations, allowing USEtox outputs to be benchmarked against participating models. Crucially, however, all models ran on shared input data, and the inter-model spread reported in the paper explicitly excludes input-parameter uncertainty. Closer convergence across models therefore supports specific structural explanations, but cannot be translated into "closer to true disease cases" or treated as a universal error bound for subsequent releases.
claims.scope: Inter-model comparison ranges and exclusion of parameter uncertainty in Rosenbaum et al. (2008) §§3.1–4.2 and Table 2.
caveats: Original model outputs and full supplementary tables were not recomputed here, and distinct statistical metrics are not collapsed into a single generic percentage.
These 2008 comparisons do not validate later indoor-exposure, crop-residue, or other added modules.

claims.text: To evaluate emissions worldwide along one consistent chain, USEtox simplifies the physical environment into coupled compartments. The USEtox 2.0 documentation uses nested boxes and mass balance to connect environmental media, models transport over monthly-to-annual timescales, and assumes steady-state media concentrations during exposure. This abstraction strips out fine spatial and temporal variability. Whenever a study asks about short-term concentration spikes, seasonal pulses, or near-source population exposure, whether these simplifications remain adequate must be judged beforehand—a regional label on a score will not restore omitted local detail.
claims.scope: Spatial box structure and temporal applicability conditions in the USEtox 2.0 documentation.
caveats: Describing model architecture does not validate steady-state, dynamic, or field performance.
Indoor and local-scale capabilities must be checked against internal documentation conflicts and specific release packages.

claims.text: Whether a model includes a given pathway must be verified by exact version and module. The USEtox 2.0 documentation explicitly maps the 2011 paper to version 1.01's general exposure model and states that indoor-exposure and crop-residue modules were added later; yet its limitations chapter retains phrasing close to that 2011 paper, still listing indoor inhalation and direct pesticide-application residue exposure as excluded pathways. This textual comparison supports the interpretation that legacy wording carried over, and cautions against dismissing documented new modules solely from an older limitation list. Textual comparison alone cannot establish editorial causes or the behavior of a specific release package, so practitioners must verify version, active modules, and scenario settings directly in the factor table.
claims.scope: Internal textual conflict within the retrieved USEtox 2.0 Documentation (Version 1.1).
caveats: Compares Rosenbaum et al. (2011) p. 725 with manual p. 177; the direct-reuse note in manual §6.1 (p. 125) applies to the general exposure section that follows rather than serving as a formal erratum for §11.4.2.
Model objects described in §§6.5 and 7 do not automatically equate to all default factors, third-party method packages, or local field exposures.
The retrieved manual formally cites 2017; 2026 file metadata does not verify original 2017 bytes or a newer methodological edition.

claims.text: Cross-framework comparisons also hinge on how multimedia models set time integration and exposure eligibility. Dividing every chemical by 1,4-dichlorobenzene in ReCiPe 2016 appears to be a simple rescaling—and indeed preserves rankings when all other settings stay fixed—yet RIVM Report 2016-0104 (§9.2 and Table 9.1) simultaneously flips five structural switches across the Individualist (I), Hierarchist (H), and Egalitarian (E) perspectives. First, the fate residence time horizon shifts across 20 years, 100 years, and infinity. Second, human exposure to metals retains only two pathways (air inhalation and drinking water, excluding seven agricultural, livestock, and aquatic food-chain routes) under Individualist, but includes all nine under Hierarchist and Egalitarian. Third, marine ecotoxicity for five essential metals (cobalt, copper, manganese, molybdenum, and zinc) covers only coastal continental shelves under Individualist, expanding to the open ocean under Hierarchist and Egalitarian. Fourth, carcinogen inclusion is restricted to International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) Groups 1, 2A, and 2B under Individualist, versus all 844 IARC (2004) substances under the other two perspectives. Fifth, the minimum number of tested species for ecotoxicity relaxes from at least four to one. Toggling all five switches together breaks rank preservation across perspectives and precludes any fixed conversion multiplier between 1,4-DCB equivalents and USEtox.
claims.scope: The five linked structural switches across Individualist, Hierarchist, and Egalitarian perspectives in ReCiPe 2016 (USES-LCA 2.0), and the mathematical conditions under which dividing by 1,4-DCB preserves or breaks rankings.
caveats: Zero or missing factors under the Individualist perspective for certain carcinogens or sparsely tested chemicals reflect stricter evidentiary screening thresholds rather than proof of non-toxicity.

claims.text: Pairing volatile, degradable 1,4-dichlorobenzene with persistent metallic nickel (Table 3) demonstrates how time horizons and food-chain switches generate two-way rank reversals. Because 1,4-dichlorobenzene degrades within weeks to months, its urban-air reference remains 1 and its seawater non-cancer factor stays near 0.82–0.83 across perspectives. By contrast, 1 kg of nickel emitted to urban air scores only 36 under Individualist (20 years, no food chain), but jumps to 2,300 under Hierarchist and 5,800 under Egalitarian once all seven food chains open and residence horizons lengthen; emitted directly to seawater, nickel scores exactly 0 under Individualist (no seafood route and seawater is not consumed as drinking water) but rises to 23 under Hierarchist and 7,900 under Egalitarian. Comparing Option A (100 kg of 1,4-dichlorobenzene to urban air) against Option B (1 kg of nickel to urban air) for non-cancer toxicity: ReCiPe Individualist ranks Option A higher (100 versus 36), Hierarchist and Egalitarian flip decisively to Option B (2,300 and 5,800 versus 100), and switching to EF 3.1 (where 1 kg of nickel equals roughly 75.95 times 1,4-dichlorobenzene) flips the verdict back to Option A (1.4795×10⁻⁶ versus 1.1237×10⁻⁶ CTUh). Emitting 1 kg of each to seawater leaves only Individualist ranking 1,4-dichlorobenzene higher, while the other three datasets rank nickel higher.
claims.scope: Controlled two-way rank reversals between degradable 1,4-DCB and persistent nickel across urban air and seawater in ReCiPe 2016 (I/H/E) and EF 3.1 non-cancer toxicity datasets.
caveats: The 100:1 urban-air and 1:1 seawater emission ratios are controlled tests designed to reveal where per-kilogram factor ratios cross thresholds (urban air: 36, 75.95, 2,300, 5,800; seawater: 0, 7.22, 28, 9,634) and do not represent functionally equivalent product processes.

Other nickel toxicity categories in RIVM Report 2016-0104 Table 9.3 (I/H/E, kg 1,4-DCB eq./kg): urban-air cancer 31, 370, 910; marine ecotoxicity via atmospheric deposition 31, 110, 55,000; seawater cancer 0, 3.5, 1,200.

claims.text: Even within the single EF 3.1 method package, three institutional mapping layers stand between inventory flow names and tested chemical species. First, unspecified-valence elemental metals follow asymmetric rules: freshwater copper maps to divalent copper (46.5 CTUe/kg), elemental antimony and arsenic take the arithmetic mean of trivalent and pentavalent species, yet elemental chromium maps directly to highly toxic hexavalent chromium (freshwater ecotoxicity 12,274 versus 952 CTUe/kg for trivalent chromium; cancer 9.9035×10⁻⁵ versus 0 for trivalent chromium). Second, generic pesticide flows were overhauled: EF 3.0 used class medians that underreported generic entries by roughly two orders of magnitude, so EF 3.1 (JRC130796, Table 8) switched both freshwater ecotoxicity and non-cancer toxicity to 2019 EU sales-weighted averages, raising "unspecified insecticides" to 5.73×10⁷ CTUe/kg and 3.77×10⁻⁴ CTUh/kg (approaching chlorpyrifos) and closing the loophole of lowering toxicity scores through vague naming. Third, "emission to unspecified water" receives asymmetric compartment rules: because transfer from seawater to freshwater is nearly zero, EF 3.0's freshwater-seawater average cut ecotoxicity in half, prompting EF 3.1 to assign the full freshwater factor in ecotoxicity (lifting the global per-capita normalization reference by +33%, from 4.27×10⁴ to 5.67×10⁴ CTUe/person) while retaining the freshwater-seawater average in human toxicity.
claims.scope: Three institutional proxy-mapping layers in EF 3.1: elemental metal speciation mapping, 2019 sales-weighted generic pesticide proxies, and asymmetric freshwater/seawater assignment for emissions to unspecified water.
caveats: Where an inventory compiler knows that real emissions consist mainly of trivalent chromium, specific low-toxicity pesticides, or open-ocean discharges, reporting generic elemental chromium, unspecified insecticides, or unspecified water triggers EF 3.1's conservative proxies and substantially overstates potential toxicity.

Exact EF 3.1 XML proxy values: elemental Cu 46.47592828149169; elemental Sb 11236.40165143179 (mean of Sb³⁺ 143.35416561027336 and Sb⁵⁺ 22329.44913725331); elemental As 3263.3274020720564 (mean of As³⁺ 1786.510738350864 and As⁵⁺ 4740.144065793249); elemental Cr and Cr⁶⁺ 12274.013470217462 (Cr³⁺ 952.2972968312423; 2018 JRC109369 §4.3 had mentioned a 50/50 Cr³⁺/Cr⁶⁺ mean); unspecified insecticides ecotoxicity 5.72902829638445×10⁷ (chlorpyrifos 3.9365×10⁸) and non-cancer 3.77412284590839×10⁻⁴ (chlorpyrifos 0.0025928); seawater Cu ecotoxicity 4.33×10⁻²¹; 1,4-DCB unspecified-water ecotoxicity equals freshwater 5541.6, while cancer takes the mean of freshwater 2.194×10⁻⁷ and seawater 1.724×10⁻⁸, yielding 1.1832×10⁻⁷ CTUh/kg.

claims.text: Even when substance and emission compartment align, calculated totals can still mask the underlying status of toxicological evidence. The USEtox 2.0 documentation lists setting human effect factors to zero when toxicological data are missing as a source of input uncertainty; entering such zeros depresses totals without demonstrating that no real effect exists. On the same page, it notes a second case in which ecotoxicity effect factors are excluded for failing minimum data-quality requirements. Comparing two alternatives therefore requires distinguishing evidence-backed low toxicity, zeros assigned for missing data, ecotoxicity factors excluded on quality grounds, and other uncharacterized emissions—treating missing entries as zero never closes an evidence gap.
claims.scope: Treatment of missing toxicological inputs and interpretation of resulting zeros in USEtox 2.0 Documentation §2.4.2.
caveats: This relies on the documentation's statements without independently verifying specific chemical datasets, cancer/non-cancer parameters, or workbook implementations.
Distinguishing information states is an interpretive recommendation rather than an additional requirement of an external standard.

claims.text: The USEtox 2.0 documentation classifies characterization factors as either "recommended" or "indicative" to signal differences in reliability. It first advises combining both tiers, because dropping indicative factors at the outset leaves those emissions uncharacterized—effectively assuming zero contribution in the total. Only when indicative factors dominate the result does the documentation consider a sensitivity analysis temporarily excluding them useful: exclusion will inevitably change toxicity scores, and the test is whether the study's conclusions change. If conclusions remain intact, substantial uncertainty must still be acknowledged; if conclusions shift, excluding dominant emissions governed by indicative factors may be warranted, provided the report states explicitly that those excluded emissions are no longer characterized yet may still contribute significantly, and factors that omission into interpretation. Seeing an indicative flag therefore calls for including the emission first and evaluating exclusion only under those conditions.
claims.scope: The full four-step procedural sequence for recommended versus indicative factors in USEtox 2.0 Documentation §3.3.2.
caveats: Factor applicability and uncertainty require separate justification; rough expert judgment is not a calculated confidence interval.
These recommendations do not automatically override other study purposes, methods, or future release versions.

claims.text: Beyond missing-data zeros and quality-based exclusions, EF 3.1 machine-readable tables embed three classes of institutional explicit 0.0 values. First, long-term truncation zeros assign 0.0 to every "long-term" air and water flow across cancer (2,108 of 13,717 entries), non-cancer (6,748 of 43,816), and freshwater ecotoxicity (12,207 of 79,349), cutting off post-100-year uncertainty from tailings and landfill leachates. Second, literature-reviewed non-toxic zeros assign 0.0 across all compartments to substances such as sulfur and chloride in non-cancer toxicity, and sulfur, calcium, and bentonite in freshwater ecotoxicity. Third, ambient steady-state concentration-boundary zeros (JRC130796, Table 7) set all 13 non-cancer sub-compartments of chlorine gas and all 15 outdoor-air plus 7 water-and-soil flows of carbon monoxide to 0.0, retaining 1.717×10⁻⁶ CTUh/kg only for 3 indoor-air carbon monoxide flows (while chlorine gas retains 11,918.0 CTUe/kg in freshwater ecotoxicity). Driven primarily by zeroing outdoor carbon monoxide, the global per-capita non-cancer normalization reference dropped 44% (from 2.30×10⁻⁴ to 1.29×10⁻⁴ CTUh/person), lowering scores for 94% of official datasets—yet waste-wood incineration and biogas processes relying on avoided-emission negative credits surged by up to +4,438% once those negative credits vanished.
claims.scope: Three classes of institutional explicit 0.0 values in official EF 3.1 XML beyond missing-data zeros (long-term truncation, literature-reviewed non-toxicity, and ambient steady-state boundary zeros) and their opposing impacts on normalization (−44%) and avoided-emission credit datasets (up to +4,438%).
caveats: Zeroing outdoor carbon monoxide in EF 3.1 steady-state non-cancer toxicity neither denies acute poisoning hazards in confined spaces (hence indoor air retains 1.717×10⁻⁶ CTUh/kg) nor alters its precursor contribution to photochemical ozone formation in Particulate Matter and Photochemical Ozone.

The 2018 JRC109369 report (p. 15, Table 5) still retains outdated text describing long-term sub-compartments as estimated from regular air or freshwater; the +4,438% surge occurred among the 2,752 official EF datasets evaluated in JRC130796, notably Spanish waste-treated-wood incineration displacing conventional energy.

claims.text: Inspecting the official EF 3.1 ZIP archive alongside its technical reports uncovers two original-file discrepancies virtually invisible from summaries alone. First, the same official archive stores same-UUID (universally unique identifier) master tables for all three toxicity categories in both the standard directory (ILCD/lciamethods) and the legacy converter directory (other/converter): cancer and non-cancer differ by only 12 bytes in authorship metadata, but the freshwater ecotoxicity master differs by more than 2.3 MB, assigning freshwater "lactic acid" 1,033.8 CTUe/kg in the standard master and organic sub-table versus 0.0 in the same-UUID converter copy; in addition, the non-cancer and ecotoxicity masters each carry 180 extra rows because five ammonia-to-air flows expand across 37 constant-value location entries. Second, newly added carbon tetrachloride synonym flows include only five outdoor-air flows (omitting indoor air, water, and soil) and truncate legacy chlorofluorocarbon-10 (CFC-10) values from five significant digits to three in the cancer and non-cancer masters. Additional typos—including CTUe unit annotations, an inverted equation in JRC130796, and substance counts in RIVM Report 2016-0104—are recorded in full in the accompanying caveats. Software audits must therefore pin both the full internal archive path and the SHA-256 cryptographic hash, never relying on a UUID or report text alone.
claims.scope: Byte-level and lactic-acid (1,033.8 vs. 0.0) divergence between same-UUID copies in EF-v3.1.zip's ILCD/lciamethods and other/converter directories, 37-location ammonia repetition, carbon tetrachloride vs. CFC-10 precision and compartment gaps, CTUe/CTUh flow-property metadata conflicts, and JRC/RIVM report typos.
caveats: Documenting source-internal discrepancies prevents silent bias during software import or automated script parsing and never authorizes modifying official released files.

Complete four-group audit log: (1) EF 3.1 ZIP dual directories (ILCD/lciamethods vs. other/converter): cancer 7,327,813 vs. 7,327,801 bytes and non-cancer 24,163,382 vs. 24,163,370 bytes (12-byte difference from authorship "EC JRC" vs. "EC's JRC-IES", data-entry "JRC, Environmental Footprint Team" vs. "Simone  Fazio", and letter casing); freshwater ecotoxicity 45,631,200 vs. 43,329,918 bytes (2,301,282-byte difference; lactic acid 1,033.8 in standard master and 73,151-row organic sub-table vs. 0.0 in converter copy); non-cancer 43,816 rows / 43,636 unique UUIDs and ecotoxicity 79,349 rows / 79,169 unique UUIDs, each +180 rows from 5 inorganic-sub-table ammonia-air flows expanded across 37 constant-value locations; (2) carbon tetrachloride synonym flows: cancer per-capita normalization rose from 1.69×10⁻⁵ to 1.73×10⁻⁵ CTUh/person (printed as 2.1%); cancer master and organic sub-table carry version 01.01.000 while cancer inorganic sub-table (398 rows) and all non-cancer/ecotoxicity tables carry 01.00.000; urban ground-level air ecotoxicity matches at 92.003 CTUe/kg, while new carbon tetrachloride cancer/non-cancer factors are 4.31×10⁻⁵ and 8.34×10⁻⁶ (vs. legacy CFC-10 4.3094×10⁻⁵ and 8.3428×10⁻⁶; legacy lowercase "cfc-10" indoor air is 2.775×10⁻⁴ and 5.3729×10⁻⁵); (3) unit discrepancies: USEtox manual defines CTUe as PAF·m³·day, 2018 report Table 2 prints m3*a, archive CTUe flow-property XML mixes [m3*a] and [m3*d], references counting unit group Item(s), and embeds a wrong UUID at the end of its permanent URI, while three cancer XMLs contain leading/trailing spaces " CTUh "; (4) report typos: JRC130796 p. 13 Eq. (3) prints upside down as "HC20/(HC20×0.34)" (while still computing 1.176), p. 28 misprints agricultural-soil Cu²⁺ as unchanged "9.92E+04 to 9.92E+04" (XML value 24.53395145313178 CTUe/kg); JRC109369 p. 14 prints nonexistent hexavalent antimony "Sb(+6)"; RIVM 2016-0104 p. 65 states 3,094 substances, whereas p. 159 lists 3,073 organics plus 20 metals collectively labeled "essential metals" (summing to 3,093, while p. 66 states only 5 are essential metals).

claims.text: These boundaries do not strip toxicity comparisons of practical value. The 2008 USEtox paper proposes using characterized inventory contributions first to identify priority substances, then tracing back to the originating life cycle stages or processes to determine whether fate, exposure, or effect drives the score. In this way, the primary output is a prioritized agenda for investigation and improvement rather than fine rank ordering among nearly indistinguishable totals. Returning to the two benzo[a]pyrene records illustrates the diagnostic logic: if the shift stems from emitted mass, inspect process activity and inventory data; if it stems from compartment-specific factors, inspect the modeled pathways; if a dominant contribution rests on weak toxicological data, test data quality and conclusion sensitivity. Where to investigate next follows directly from why the score moved.
claims.scope: Comparative screening purpose in Rosenbaum et al. (2008) §6.1 synthesized with compartment matching, pathway tracing, and data-status checks.
caveats: Illustrative contribution percentages from the original paper are not adopted as universal cutoffs, nor is model uncertainty reduced to a fixed multiplier.
Model contribution clues require verified inventory, coverage, and technical evidence to support concrete improvement actions.

claims.text: When two toxicity assessments conflict or scores swing sharply after a method update, attributing the gap generically to "high toxicity uncertainty" misses the mechanism; a five-step diagnostic pinpoints the root cause. First, check the receptor family and agricultural-soil boundary (three versus five midpoints, and whether agricultural soil is deferred to land use). Second, if freshwater metals drive the gap, verify whether the effect benchmark is 0.5/HC50 or EU 0.2/HC20 and whether regulatory dossiers were substituted. Third, if persistent metals and degradable organics trade places, inspect residence time horizons (20 years, 100 years, or infinite) and food-chain exposure switches. Fourth, audit inventory speciation and institutional proxies (elemental chromium, sales-weighted generic pesticides, and unspecified-water freshwater/seawater rules). Fifth, disentangle missing-data zeros, long-term truncation zeros, indoor/outdoor steady-state zeros, and avoided-emission negative credits—verifying the exact internal archive path and SHA-256 hash of loaded method files and interpreting organic and metal-inclusive inorganic sub-tables separately when warranted.
claims.scope: Five-step diagnostic protocol for tracing toxicity contributions and auditing methods across USEtox/ILCD/EF and ReCiPe 2016 (USES-LCA 2.0).
caveats: This five-step protocol supports LCIA-level method alignment and hotspot tracing; decisions governed by near-facility human health risk, indoor occupational exposure limits, or receiving-water ecological compliance still require site-specific chemical risk assessment and field monitoring.

claims.text: Once chemical identity, emission compartment, model architecture, and data scope are specified, toxicity assessment can compare characterized toxicity potentials, spotlight contributions warranting deeper analysis, and identify which assumptions could overturn a judgment. Reporting those results requires disclosing coverage gaps alongside assumption sensitivity. Climate, water, and toxicity indicators each describe distinct potential consequences; when an alternative scores lower on some indicators and higher on others, resolving the trade-off depends on comparison scales and protection targets.
claims.scope: Author synthesis of conditional comparative findings and transition from impact pathways to cross-category valuation and trade-offs.
caveats: No claim is made to cover all chemicals, environmental pathways, indicators, or decision uses; toxicity LCIA is not product safety certification.
Indicator construction, value choices, and empirical evidence for corrective action retain distinct responsibilities.

claims.text: Consider two processes that deliver the exact same coating service on an identical substrate. Process A emits more solvent vapor, while Process B emits more nitrogen oxides (NOx). Leaving both rows in the inventory lets readers see the trade-off directly; if a buyer demands a single aggregate score, however, the assessment must specify how each emission is scored. That sets up a concrete question: does Process B's lower solvent vapor offset its higher NOx emissions?
claims.scope: Opposing inventory differences within a constructed coating service comparison.

claims.text: The Swiss Ecological Scarcity method (German: Methode der ökologischen Knappheit) assigns each gram of emission a score in environmental impact points (Umweltbelastungspunkt, UBP). Calculating these eco-factors requires both the current environmental burden of a reference region and the protection targets chosen for that region. The 2013 Swiss edition prioritizes politically binding targets established by competent authorities. An eco-factor therefore expresses how an emission is scored under a specific set of policy references.
claims.scope: Evaluation basis of the 2013 Swiss Ecological Scarcity edition.

claims.text: Translating environmental protection goals into national emission targets requires linking pollutant releases to human and ecosystem receptors. The 2009 Swiss Federal Council report on federal air-quality measures distinguishes ambient air concentration limits, critical deposition loads that ecosystems can tolerate, and the national emission reductions needed to approach those limits. Wind, distance, and atmospheric chemistry govern how pollutants reach populated areas; even after national emissions fall, exceedances can persist near major sources, and transboundary transport alters local air quality.
claims.scope: Receptor-side limits, emission-side reductions, and spatial constraints in the 2009 Swiss Federal Council report.

claims.text: Constructing an eco-factor first separates the grams in a product inventory from annual national flows. The current flow F represents how much the reference region actually emits in one year, while the critical flow Fₖ represents the annual emission level permitted by the chosen target. Both quantities must cover the same substance, geographic boundary, and time scale. Their ratio F/Fₖ is dimensionless: values above 1 indicate that annual emissions exceed the target, whereas a value of 1 means emissions match the target.
claims.scope: Scales of current flow, critical flow, and product inventory flows.

claims.text: A third annual quantity is the normalization flow Fₙ. The Swiss method uses the national annual burden as a common scoring scale through the normalization term 1 UBP/Fₙ, multiplies by the squared distance-to-target weight (F/Fₖ)², and—where conversion to a reference substance is required—applies a characterization factor K. Equation (4) of the 2013 report writes the eco-factor as K × (1 UBP/Fₙ) × (F/Fₖ)² × c, where the scaling constant c equals 10¹²/yr. When Fₙ is expressed in g/yr, the year units in 1/Fₙ and c cancel, leaving eco-factors in UBP/g. Product inventory grams enter only when computing the service score.
claims.scope: Role of each quantity in Equation (4) of the 2013 Swiss Ecological Scarcity report.

claims.text: The same annual emission quantity can appear in both the normalization term and the weighting term: the first establishes a common scoring scale, while the second captures the gap between current emissions and the policy target. For a single pollutant assessed at the national scale, Fₙ can equal F. The earlier formulation reviewed in the 2013 report wrote the factor as (1 UBP/Fₖ) × (F/Fₖ) × c. Algebraically, F/Fₖ² equals (1/F) × (F/Fₖ)², so introducing the square reproduces the same numerical value when Fₙ = F. Starting with the 2006 edition, separating the normalization and weighting terms allows practitioners to retain the Swiss normalization reference while computing weights from another region's current and critical flows—in which case Fₙ can no longer be canceled out.
claims.scope: Algebraic equivalence for a shared national flow versus regionalized weighting.

claims.text: Characterization also depends on what the policy target regulates. Although individual volatile organic compounds differ in their ozone-forming potency, the Swiss report treats generic non-methane volatile organic compounds (NMVOC) on the regulatory mass basis rather than applying substance-specific photochemical ozone creation potentials. When a single substance can be scored along multiple pathways, the 2013 method selects the highest eco-factor rather than summing them. For ammonia, the direct target yields 67 UBP/g NH₃ while the acidification pathway yields 40 UBP/g NH₃, so 67 UBP/g is used. Summing both pathways, or applying a separate per-gram-NH₃-N value to 1 g of NH₃, would alter the meaning of the published table.
claims.scope: Policy-target alignment and highest-factor selection rule in the 2013 Swiss method.

claims.text: Verifying published eco-factors requires distinguishing relative percentage reduction targets in policy reports from the absolute annual critical flows actually entered into the formula. The 1999 Swiss Federal Council report used 1995 as its base year and called for an approximately 60% reduction in volatile organic compounds (VOC) to meet ozone standards. Table 2 of the 2009 report shifted the base year to 2005, specifying a 20% to 30% reduction for NMVOC (linked to ozone concentration limits) and roughly 50% for NOx (linked to both ozone limits and critical acid deposition loads). Because both the base year and substance scope changed, subtracting the two percentages does not measure how much policy was relaxed.
claims.scope: Comparison of base years, substance scopes, and relative targets across the 1999 and 2009 Swiss policy reports.

claims.text: The 2013 edition sets the NMVOC critical flow at 81,000 t/yr, carrying forward a value from earlier reports. Eco-factors 2006 (published in 2009) documented two quantitative bases for this figure. One considered a reduction exceeding 75% from the 1980s peak of 324,000 t/yr—an exact 75% cut leaves 81,000 t/yr, whereas a cut strictly above 75% would leave less. The second cited the 1993 Graz Declaration's 70% to 80% reduction range, corresponding to 64,800 to 97,200 t/yr, whose midpoint is likewise 81,000 t/yr. The 2006 edition linked these bases to the selected critical flow, and the 2013 edition retained that number.
claims.scope: Historical quantitative bases for the retained NMVOC critical flow.
caveats: The 1993 Graz Declaration figures and explanation are reported as cited in the 2009 Eco-factors 2006 report.

claims.text: Table 14 of the 2013 edition illustrates the full calculation for 1 g of generic NMVOC emitted to air, excluding methane and chlorofluorocarbons; substances with dedicated eco-factors such as benzene must be matched separately. Both the normalization flow and the current flow equal 89,025 t/yr, while the critical flow is 81,000 t/yr. Converting 89,025 t/yr to 89,025 × 10⁶ g/yr makes 1 UBP/Fₙ carry units of UBP·yr/g; multiplying by c = 10¹²/yr cancels the year unit, and the weighting ratio (89,025/81,000)² is dimensionless. Substituting these values gives 10¹² ÷ (89,025 × 10⁶) × (89,025/81,000)² = 13.568816 UBP/g. The table publishes 14 UBP/g; the extra digits serve only to show the exact recalculation.
claims.scope: Unit handling and unrounded intermediate recalculation for Table 14 of the 2013 Swiss edition.

claims.text: In the 2021 edition, the same generic NMVOC entry retains the 81,000 t/yr critical flow but updates both the current flow and normalization flow to 79,727 t/yr. Substituting both updated flows into the formula yields a weight of roughly 0.97 and a published eco-factor of 12 UBP/g—not the result of multiplying the old 14 UBP/g by 0.97. Even when national annual emissions dip slightly below the target, each additional gram still receives a positive score. In the same passage, the 2021 report notes that summer ozone concentrations continue to exceed limits: meeting an annual national emission target does not guarantee compliance at every location and hour.
claims.scope: Update in Table 16 of the 2021 Swiss edition and interpretation when current emissions fall below target.

claims.text: For NOx, one must first identify which protection goal governs the critical flow. Using 2000 as its base year, Eco-factors 2006 noted that meeting nitrogen dioxide concentration limits required roughly a 40% reduction, whereas meeting ozone limits required about 60%. The authors adopted the stricter ozone goal, listing a critical flow of 45,000 t/yr—the same critical flow shown in the 1997 status column. The 2013 edition linked this retained 45,000 t/yr value to the reduction mandate in the 2009 federal policy report. In calculation, 45,000 t/yr is the absolute quantity actually entered; percentage reductions in policy reports must always be read alongside their base years.
claims.scope: NOx critical flow and baseline conditions across the 2006 and 2013 Swiss editions.

claims.text: Table 15 of the 2013 edition expresses NOx on a nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) mass basis. Both the normalization flow and current flow equal 78,704 t/yr, and the critical flow is 45,000 t/yr. Squaring the ratio 78,704/45,000 yields a weight of about 3.058923. Converting the normalization flow to 78,704 × 10⁶ g/yr, dividing 1 UBP by this annual flow, and multiplying by the scaling constant c = 10¹²/yr cancels the year unit and gives 10¹² ÷ (78,704 × 10⁶) × 3.058923 = 38.866173 UBP/g. The published table value is 39 UBP/g. Expressing NOx as NO₂ specifies the mass-accounting basis of emissions, not the ambient NO₂ concentration inhaled by residents.
claims.scope: Eco-factor recalculation for NOx expressed as NO₂ in Table 15 of the 2013 Swiss edition.

claims.text: The 2021 update for NOx adds a further complication. The report still cites the mandate to cut emissions by roughly half relative to 2005, but adopts a revised 2005 emission estimate of 93,036 t/yr. Halving that revised baseline produces a new critical flow of 46,518 t/yr. Meanwhile, the 2016–2018 annual average of 70,733 t/yr becomes the new current and normalization flow. Together, these updates lower the published eco-factor from 39 to 33 UBP/g. Readers who inspect only the final table row can easily mistake a revised base-year inventory estimate for a loosening of environmental policy.
claims.scope: Base-year emission revision and current-flow update for NOx in the 2021 Swiss edition.
caveats: The 93,036 t/yr figure is the revised 2005 estimate cited in the 2021 edition; the basis for the earlier 45,000 t/yr critical flow must be traced to the earlier editions and their supporting materials.

claims.text: Return now to the opening coating comparison. Assume that Processes A and B each coat 1 m² of the same substrate in Switzerland with identical hiding power, durability, and quality, while all other activities and flows remain identical. Per service delivered, Process A emits 4 g of generic NMVOC and 1 g of NOx (expressed as NO₂), whereas Process B emits 2 g of generic NMVOC and 2 g of NOx. Service equivalence, both emission pairs, and the applicability of Table 14 to generic NMVOC are all explicit pedagogical assumptions of this comparison.
claims.scope: Equivalent coating service and constructed two-flow inventory comparison.

claims.text: Applying the 2013 published eco-factors gives two totals. Process A scores 4 × 14 = 56 UBP from NMVOC plus 1 × 39 = 39 UBP from NOx, totaling 95 UBP. Process B scores 2 × 14 = 28 UBP plus 2 × 39 = 78 UBP, totaling 106 UBP. Decomposing the difference clarifies why Process A wins: emitting 2 g less NMVOC saves 28 UBP, but emitting 1 g more NOx adds 39 UBP, a net increase of 11 UBP. Any identical background burden adds the same points to both options and leaves the 11-point gap unchanged.
claims.scope: Per-service contribution of the two published 2013 eco-factors.

claims.text: If one simply rescales the point system by multiplying both eco-factors by 10, Processes A and B score 950 and 1,060 UBP respectively. The points saved from lower NMVOC and the points added from higher NOx scale by the same proportion, so multiplying both factors by any shared positive constant leaves the ranking unchanged.
claims.scope: Effect of uniform positive rescaling on option ranking.

claims.text: To see what actually reverses the ranking, multiply only the NOx eco-factor by a positive scalar x while holding the inventory and NMVOC factor fixed. Process B's extra NOx adds 39x UBP while its lower NMVOC saves 28 UBP, making the score difference B − A equal to 39x − 28. Setting this difference to zero yields the crossover threshold x = 28/39, where both options score 84 UBP on the differential flows. Process A scores lower whenever x > 28/39, and Process B scores lower whenever x < 28/39. This threshold uses the published integer factors; unrounded recalculations shift the intersection slightly.
claims.scope: Rank-reversal threshold calculated from published 2013 integer eco-factors.

claims.text: At x = 0.5, for example, the NOx eco-factor drops to 19.5 UBP/g. With the inventory unchanged, Process A scores 75.5 UBP and Process B scores 67 UBP, flipping the preference from Process A to Process B. Varying one factor in isolation locates the exact decision boundary; x does not represent an actual Swiss policy shift, nor does it carry a probability.
claims.scope: Constructed sensitivity test of relative weighting.

claims.text: The coating calculation shows that shifting relative weights can flip rankings; when weights are varied across policy targets, an analysis must state which alternative targets exist and which options change rank. Lewerenz et al. (2024) evaluated nine German electricity generation systems per 1 kWh by drawing 10,000 uniform samples between looser and stricter target values, recalculating scores on each draw, and ranking the lowest score first. They varied only impact items for which documented alternative targets existed: water resources retained its baseline target, and among airborne heavy metals, lead had testable alternative targets whereas mercury kept its baseline value.
claims.scope: Target-sensitivity experiment across nine German electricity generation systems.
caveats: Table 3 footnote a of Lewerenz et al. (2024) flags items without documented alternative targets, including airborne mercury, ozone layer depletion, chemical oxygen demand in water, minerals and metals, water resources, and two non-radioactive waste indicators.

claims.text: Within the authors' sampling range, wind power ranked first in every trial, whereas biogas shifted between third and fifth place and geothermal power shifted between second and fourth. Ground-mounted multicrystalline silicon photovoltaics ranked seventh in 32% of trials and ninth in 40%. Two findings hold simultaneously: some options occupy stable positions across target variations, while others depend on which target set is chosen. These percentages measure rank frequencies under a specified uniform sampling design, not the probability that a particular policy will be enacted.
claims.scope: Stable top ranking alongside localized rank swaps within the sampled target envelope.

claims.text: The sampling bounds themselves carry structural consequences. Because the critical flow sits in the denominator, setting Fₖ to zero produces no finite eco-factor. Whenever the German study encountered distant zero-emission targets, it substituted earlier non-zero targets to define the interval. Moreover, the experiment did not simultaneously propagate characterization or external normalization uncertainty. Calling a ranking "robust" therefore requires specifying which options were compared, what range was sampled, and which quantities were held fixed; because the German power study and the Swiss coating example differ in all three respects, rankings cannot be transferred between them.
claims.scope: Exclusion of zero critical flows and unpropagated uncertainties in target-sensitivity testing.

claims.text: Evaluating the same coating inventory (Process A: 4 g generic NMVOC and 1 g NOx; Process B: 2 g generic NMVOC and 2 g NOx) under European Union Environmental Footprint 3.1 (EF 3.1) highlights the contrast between selecting the single strictest target pathway and summing weighted midpoints across categories (Table 1). The crossover threshold occurs when NOx scores twice as much per gram as NMVOC. Swiss Ecological Scarcity exceeds 2 in both 2013 (2.786) and 2021 (2.750) because domestic NOx target exceedance is heavily squared and only the strictest pathway counts. Looking solely at EF 3.1 photochemical ozone formation, both outdoor flows share 1.0 kg NMVOC-eq/kg (ratio 1.000), reversing the preference to Process B. Once all 16 categories enter global per-capita normalization and hybrid weighting (unit: points, pt), outdoor NOx accumulates across five categories—photochemical ozone, acidification, terrestrial and marine eutrophication, and particulate matter—while generic NMVOC enters only ozone and two toxicity categories. For unspecified outdoor air, NOx scores 3.7196×10⁻⁶ pt/g versus 1.1817×10⁻⁶ pt/g for generic NMVOC (ratio ≈ 3.148), so Process A (8.446×10⁻⁶ pt) outperforms Process B (9.802×10⁻⁶ pt). Other outdoor air sub-compartments likewise exceed a ratio of 2: both frameworks favor Process A, but EF 3.1 does so by summing five impact pathways rather than squaring one policy gap.
claims.scope: Fixed coating inventory (Process A: 4 g generic NMVOC + 1 g NOx; Process B: 2 g generic NMVOC + 2 g NOx; crossover ratio = 2) comparing Swiss Ecological Scarcity against EF 3.1 photochemical ozone alone and full 16-category outdoor weighted scores.
caveats: Calculated from exact cached workbook values: for urban close-to-ground air, outdoor generic NMVOC has freshwater ecotoxicity 9.4933 CTUe/kg and human non-cancer toxicity 1.1026×10⁻⁷ CTUh/kg (versus 8.6069 and 6.2186×10⁻⁸ for unspecified air), giving Process A 8.4749×10⁻⁶ pt and Process B 9.8168×10⁻⁶ pt; for non-urban or high-stack air, generic NMVOC factors are 7.7204 and 1.4112×10⁻⁸ (while the NOx particulate matter factor drops from 1.6×10⁻⁶ to 2.1×10⁻⁷ disease incidence/kg), giving Process A 8.2084×10⁻⁶ pt and Process B 9.3698×10⁻⁶ pt.

Generic NMVOC in EF 3.1 is an unspeciated proxy flow; if coating solvents are speciated into styrene, toluene, xylene, or other individual chemicals, both systems require matching substance-specific factors.

EF 3.1 outdoor category factors and weights: NOx enters photochemical ozone (1.0, weight 4.78%), acidification (0.74 mol H⁺-eq/kg, 6.20%), terrestrial eutrophication (4.26 mol N-eq/kg, 3.71%), marine eutrophication (0.389 kg N-eq/kg, 2.96%), and particulate matter (8.96%); generic NMVOC enters photochemical ozone (1.0), freshwater ecotoxicity (comparative toxic units for ecosystems, CTUe, 1.92%), and human non-cancer toxicity (comparative toxic units for human health, CTUh, 1.84%). The NOx/NMVOC ratio is approximately 3.129 for urban close-to-ground air and 2.989 for non-urban or high-stack air; global population is 6,895,889,018.

claims.text: Holding emission masses constant and moving workshop solvent evaporation into EF 3.1's "emission to indoor air" sub-compartment—while NOx remains outdoors—exposes both coverage asymmetry and near-field rank reversal (Table 1). For generic NMVOC, high indoor inhalation raises human non-cancer toxicity by roughly 144-fold (to 8.957×10⁻⁶ comparative toxic units for human health (CTUh)/kg, contributing 1.2802×10⁻⁶ pt/g), yet EF 3.1's photochemical ozone table omits indoor VOC flows, abruptly zeroing out the 1.1699×10⁻⁶ pt/g ozone contribution. Because the gain and loss nearly cancel, the per-gram score edges up to 1.2832×10⁻⁶ pt, the NOx/NMVOC ratio stays above 2, and Process A still leads. Once the solvent is specified as styrene, however, the ranking flips completely: outdoor styrene scores only 9.1508×10⁻⁷ pt/g (NOx/solvent ratio 4.065, Process A preferred), whereas indoor styrene increases both cancer toxicity (1.0787×10⁻⁴ CTUh/kg) and non-cancer toxicity by about 211-fold, catapulting the per-gram total roughly 146-fold to 1.3376×10⁻⁴ pt. The NOx/solvent ratio collapses to 0.0278, reversing the outcome to Process B (2.750×10⁻⁴ pt) over Process A (5.387×10⁻⁴ pt). Swiss Ecological Scarcity does not split out an indoor air compartment, leaving occupational exposure to workplace hygiene regulations.
claims.scope: Indoor-air sub-compartment test on the fixed coating inventory in EF 3.1, contrasting the missing-ozone offset for generic NMVOC against full rank reversal for styrene and Swiss Ecological Scarcity compartment boundaries.
caveats: Indoor-air characterization factors rely on default ventilation and occupancy assumptions; moreover, misclassifying low-toxicity, high-ozone-potential solvents such as toluene as indoor air can cause an anomalous score drop due to missing indoor ozone rows. If a workshop installs closed capture and thermal oxidation, the actual masses emitted indoors and outdoors also change.

Outdoor unspecified-air styrene factors in EF 3.1: photochemical ozone 0.24, freshwater ecotoxicity 0.22706 CTUe/kg, human non-cancer toxicity 1.9325×10⁻⁸ CTUh/kg, and human cancer toxicity 5.1149×10⁻⁷ CTUh/kg (cancer weight 2.13%); indoor styrene non-cancer toxicity is 4.075×10⁻⁶ CTUh/kg. Indoor generic NMVOC freshwater ecotoxicity is 8.8728 CTUe/kg; NOx/NMVOC ratios against outdoor unspecified and non-urban NOx are 2.899 and 2.736, respectively.

claims.text: Why did a 144-fold surge in indoor generic NMVOC non-cancer toxicity barely match outdoor photochemical ozone? Dissecting the Sala et al. (2018) hybrid weighting table used in the European Union Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) framework reveals that societal value preferences and scientific robustness discounts are multiplied into a single percentage. In the raw 50:50 public-and-expert importance panel (Column A), the three toxicity categories together account for 18.80% (compared with 12.9% for climate change and 6.12% for freshwater ecotoxicity). When multiplied by the 0.1–1 robustness score (Column B), climate change and particulate matter receive the highest tier of 0.87, whereas all three USEtox toxicity categories are compressed to the lowest tier of 0.17. After rescaling to 100%, climate change climbs to 21.06% while the three toxicity categories shrink roughly 3.19-fold to 5.89% combined (freshwater ecotoxicity falls to 1.92%). A two-option test in global per-capita normalized "person-years" shows the consequence: let Route C carry 0.10 climate and 0.60 ecotoxicity person-years, and Route D carry 0.25 climate and 0.05 ecotoxicity person-years (crossover weight ratio 11/3 ≈ 3.667). Raw Column A preferences (weight ratio 2.108) favor Route D, but official EF 3.1 weights (ratio 10.97) immediately flip the ranking to Route C—because the 0.17 robustness discount amplifies the climate-to-ecotoxicity weight ratio more than fivefold.
claims.scope: Decomposition of Column A (50:50 public–expert preferences) and Column B (model robustness factors) in PEFCR Guidance v6.3 Appendix A/B.1 and the EF 3.1 weighting workbook (Sala et al., 2018), with a rank-reversal demonstration.
caveats: The C = A × B column printed in PEFCR Guidance v6.3 Appendix A multiplies underlying unrounded robustness scores before rounding to two decimals (for example, climate change prints 11.18 whereas 12.9 × 0.87 = 11.223; cancer toxicity prints 1.13 whereas 6.8 × 0.17 = 1.156). Published table values are cited as printed rather than altered.

Key values in Sala et al. (2018): printed Column A values across 16 categories sum to 100.03 (climate 12.9, water use 9.69, land use 9.04, fossils 7.37, cancer 6.8, minerals/metals 6.68, freshwater ecotoxicity 6.12, non-cancer 5.88, particulate matter 5.49); Column B robustness tiers are 0.87 (climate, particulate matter), 0.67 (acidification, terrestrial eutrophication), 0.6 (ozone depletion, both resource categories), 0.53 (photochemical ozone, marine eutrophication), 0.47 (ionizing radiation, freshwater eutrophication, land, water), and 0.17 (three toxicities). The toxicity-excluded table raised climate to 22.19% and particulate matter to 9.54%. For Routes C and D, Column A weighted sums are 3.531 versus 4.962 (0.03530 versus 0.04961 normalized), and official EF 3.1 scores are 0.03258 versus 0.05361 pt.

claims.text: Tightening or loosening a target within one country is one form of sensitivity; changing which region's targets apply is another. The 2013 Swiss report explains that for multinational product inventories, most emissions are weighted as if they occurred in Switzerland, with separate rules for categories such as freshwater use. Consequently, when generic eco-factors apply and emission quantities stay the same, relocating a factory to another country may leave its score unchanged—even though the affected populations, watersheds, and policy priorities change.
claims.scope: Consumption-region reference and default Swiss evaluation perspective in the 2013 report.

claims.text: Muhl et al. (2021) separated consumption-region and production-region perspectives for metal supply chains, normalizing both to European Union annual flows while changing the region whose targets set the weights. Their analysis combined only climate change, acidification, and water use, so every percentage below uses that three-category eco-point (EP) total as its denominator. Under European consumption-region weights, roughly 83% of aluminum's score comes from acidification; under production-region weights, roughly 83% comes from water use, 15% from acidification, and 2% from climate change. Although both perspectives show an 83% share, the denominators differ in total magnitude and point to completely different dominant burdens.
claims.scope: Regional perspective and category contribution shares in the Muhl et al. (2021) metal supply-chain study.

claims.text: In the production-region aluminum calculation, the United Arab Emirates carries a water weighting factor of 7,293 and accounts for 99.8% of the aluminum supply chain's water eco-points—a share whose denominator narrows further to water use alone. While that weight reflects severe local water stress, the authors allocated global inventories across countries by national production shares, simplifying country-level differences in actual water consumption and emissions per unit of output. Interpreting a production-region score therefore requires examining both the local weight assigned and how much inventory burden was allocated to that jurisdiction.
claims.scope: Water weighting factor, contribution share, and regional inventory allocation assumptions for production-region aluminum.

claims.text: Because aluminum ingot and hot-rolled steel coil were evaluated per kilogram without a shared functional unit, Muhl et al. explicitly note that their results cannot rank the two materials for delivering the same service; they show only how a supply chain's score composition shifts with geographic perspective. By contrast, the 11-point gap in the coating example answers a shared-service question: under 2013 Swiss published weights, cutting 2 g of NMVOC does not offset adding 1 g of NOx, and sensitivity analysis locates the exact relative weight where the ranking flips. Determining what exposures residents near a specific plant actually experience still requires site-specific release, transport, and receptor data; meanwhile, how the choice of time period and region for per-capita normalization references shapes results is examined further in Regionalization of Impact Assessment.
claims.scope: Distinction among score composition, fixed-service ranking, and local exposure assessment.

claims.text: Following the geographic-reference question reveals how normalization denominators couple algebraically with weights. Swiss Ecological Scarcity multiplies 1/Fₙ by the squared target exceedance (F/Fₖ)²: when both use the same domestic current flow (Fₙ = F), one power of F cancels, leaving the unit eco-factor proportional to F/Fₖ², so higher background emissions increase the penalty. By contrast, EU EF 3.1 holds percentage weights WFᵢ fixed and multiplies each midpoint by WFᵢ/NFᵢ: whenever a revision shrinks the global per-capita normalization factor NFᵢ, the implied unit conversion rate rises inversely without any change in weights. European Commission Joint Research Centre report JRC130796 documents this drift empirically. Between EF 3.0 and EF 3.1, zeroing out outdoor carbon monoxide cut the human non-cancer toxicity NF by 44% (from 2.30×10⁻⁴ to 1.29×10⁻⁴ CTUh/(person·yr)), passively raising its per-CTUh scoring rate by roughly 1.79-fold; simultaneously, the freshwater ecotoxicity NF rose 33% and the climate change NF fell 6.7%. Across 2,752 official datasets, 2,751 changed single score; freshwater ecotoxicity—carrying just a 1.92% weight—became the number-one driver of score change in 1,535 datasets (55.8%), ahead of climate change (21.06% weight, 37.9%), and altered the top three most relevant categories in 6% to 13% of datasets.
claims.scope: Algebraic coupling between normalization denominators and weighting factors in Swiss Ecological Scarcity versus EU EF 3.1, with empirical drift from JRC130796.
caveats: In JRC130796 Section 5.2 Table 14 across 49 representative products, 27 single scores decreased and 22 increased (still wine fell up to 15%; food-producing animal feed rose 13% in the main text and 12.8% in Table 14); these shifts combine both characterization-factor updates and NF denominator recalculations.

Detailed JRC130796 updates: exact workbook non-cancer NF is 1.2874×10⁻⁴ CTUh/(person·yr); freshwater ecotoxicity NF rose from 4.27×10⁴ to 5.67×10⁴ CTUe/(person·yr); climate change NF fell from 8.10×10³ to 7.55×10³ kg CO₂-eq/(person·yr). Top driver of single-score change across datasets: freshwater ecotoxicity in 1,535, climate change in 1,043, non-cancer toxicity in 172, and cancer toxicity in 1. Rank changes occurred for 171 (6%), 280 (10%), and 358 (13%) datasets in the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd most relevant positions, respectively.

claims.text: Because a single score fuses value judgments, robustness discounts, and denominator scales, international LCA standards and the European Union Environmental Footprint regime adopt opposing rules on whether weighted totals may back public superiority claims. Under the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 14044 tradition, both normalization and weighting are optional; both the Institute of Environmental Sciences at Leiden University (CML 2001) guide and the International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD 2010 General Guide, Provision 8.4 III) strictly prohibit numerical value-based weighting in comparative assertions intended for public disclosure, since cross-category weights rest on value choices rather than natural laws. Conversely, European Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 makes global per-capita normalization and Sala et al. (2018) weighting mandatory in PEF and Organisation Environmental Footprint (OEF) studies, requires identifying the most relevant impact categories covering at least 80% of the single score (and at least three categories), and allows public comparative assertions when governed by an approved Product Environmental Footprint Category Rules (PEFCR). Even then, it enforces three hard guardrails: unweighted normalized results may never be summed (which hides equal weighting), characterized, normalized, and weighted profiles must be disclosed side by side, and general studies lacking an applicable PEFCR may not invoke a single score to assert public superiority.
claims.scope: Institutional boundaries on normalization, weighting, and public comparative assertions across ISO 14042/14044, CML 2001, ILCD 2010, and Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279.
caveats: The ISO 14044:2006 Section 4.4 prohibition on weighting in public comparative assertions is verified via public citations in the ILCD 2010 General Guide and the CML 2001 operational guide and does not substitute for inspecting the copyrighted ISO text.

claims.text: Synthesizing the parallel analysis of Swiss Ecological Scarcity and EU EF 3.1 hybrid weighting yields four diagnostic checkpoints before citing any single score. First, verify the weighting authority and multi-pathway rule: does the method square domestic policy exceedances and pick the strictest pathway, or sum 16 weighted midpoints discounted for scientific robustness? Second, inspect compartment splits and chemical speciation, watching for missing indoor-air ozone rows and hundredfold indoor toxicity jumps for solvents like styrene. Third, trace the geographic reference and denominator drift—whether scores bind to domestic flows or rescale inversely with global NF revisions—and never subtract single scores across method versions. Fourth, respect the institutional boundary governing public comparisons: the ISO/ILCD prohibition on weighted public assertions versus the EU framework requiring an approved PEFCR and parallel disclosure of unweighted profiles. With these four checkpoints established, Regionalization of Impact Assessment examines spatial resolution and normalization representativeness, while Monetary Valuation of Environmental Damage turns to monetized endpoint trade-offs across human health, ecosystems, and resources.
claims.scope: Four structural diagnostic checkpoints synthesizing midpoint and distance-to-target weighting and bridging to regionalization and endpoint valuation.
caveats: These four checkpoints govern midpoint and distance-to-policy-target weighting; approaches that first model damages to human health, ecosystems, and resources before monetizing trade-offs are examined in Monetary Valuation of Environmental Damage.

claims.text: Swiss eco-factors depend on domestic policy targets; comparing products in China likewise requires deciding which environmental problems matter and whose burdens serve as the reference. In 2001, Jianxin Yang, Rusong Wang, and Jingru Liu—affiliated with the Research Center for Eco-Environmental Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences—published Study on Life Cycle Impact Assessment Method for Chinese Products, adapting the Danish Environmental Design of Industrial Products (EDIP) framework to select impact categories relevant to China and construct normalization references and weights. The paper notes support from a Sino-European cooperative project on the ecological sustainability of primary industrial products. Its stated uses—comparing functionally equivalent products, eco-design, green consumption, and eco-labeling—explain why the authors sought concise aggregate indicators, but stating intended uses does not verify fitness for each application.
claims.scope: Research question, EDIP lineage, and proposed applications in Yang, Wang, and Liu (2001).
caveats: The authors' statement that their framework was established for the first time is not treated as an independently verified national priority claim.

claims.text: The Yang et al. (2001) framework separates environmental impacts from resource consumption. The environmental branch converts emissions into category potentials, normalizes them against a reference, applies target-based weights, and sums them into an Environmental Impact Load (EIL). It covers eight categories: global warming, ozone depletion, acidification, eutrophication, photochemical ozone formation, solid waste, hazardous waste, and soot and dust. The resource branch asks how renewable and non-renewable resource use relates to scarcity, summarized as a Resource Depletion Index (RDI). Listing these categories clarifies what the authors sought to compare, not that every category possessed an equally detailed local damage model.
claims.scope: Dual-branch structure, impact category set, and resource branch in Figure 1 of Yang et al. (2001).
caveats: This claim describes the published framework without running unpublished parameter sets.

claims.text: In a category such as acidification, inventory emissions are first converted into summable equivalents. For substance i with emitted mass Qᵢ and equivalence factor EF(j)ᵢ in category j, summing the products yields the category impact potential EP(j). The paper uses sulfur dioxide (SO₂) as the reference substance for acidification and carbon dioxide (CO₂) for global warming. At this stage, the result represents only the product system's category potential and has not yet been compared with the average burden of a reference population.
claims.scope: Category impact potential in Section 3.1 of Yang et al. (2001) prior to normalization.

claims.text: To gauge how large a product's impact potential is relative to societal burdens, Yang et al. (2001) divide total 1990 impact potential by the corresponding population to obtain a per-capita reference ER(j)₉₀. Global impacts use a global scale, whereas regional and local impacts use China or the relevant regional scale. Here, normalization means dividing a product's characterized result by an external reference value. Switching to a different region's or year's per-capita reference can alter relative scores—though identical numerical references yield identical relative results. Normalization in this sense is an analytical scaling step, completely distinct from promulgating national standards, and it does not alter how emissions cause environmental harm.
claims.scope: Per-capita normalization references and geographic boundaries in Yang et al. (2001).

claims.text: Yang et al. (2001) also embed product lifetime directly into the normalization formula: NEP(j) = EP(j)/(T × ER(j)₉₀), where T is the product service period and NEP(j) is the normalized environmental impact potential. They express NEP in person-equivalents, using notation to distinguish global versus Chinese populations and the 1990 baseline. When EP is accumulated over the full service life and T is in years, EP/T gives the product's annual average potential; dividing by the annual per-capita reference then asks how many reference residents' annual burdens equal one year of the product's impact. This establishes a shared unit without implying equal severity across categories. If EP is already annualized, dividing by T again would double-annualize it—a time-basis nuance that must be checked against the paper's subsequent weighting equations.
claims.scope: Role of product service period T in the published normalization formula of Yang et al. (2001).
caveats: Specific service-period values and the Chinese vehicle trial inventory mentioned in the paper's conclusion are not published in the article.

claims.text: Before comparing per-capita denominators, analysts must verify whether attaching a country or region code to an elementary flow actually changes its characterization factor (Table 1). The 2011 International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) recommendations explicitly scoped their factors to Europe; the successor European Union Environmental Footprint 3.1 (EF 3.1) package divides location tags into three distinct regimes. First is global country differentiation: water use (Available WAter REmaining, AWARE) spans 209 location codes, where Spain (77.7) is 86.62 times Japan (0.897) and China (42.4) is 31.18 times Germany (1.36). Second is a European whitelist: acidification permits 36 European location codes for 25 air flows (SO₂ in Germany is 2.281 versus 0.108 in Spain, a 21.12-fold spread), excluding China, the United States, India, and Japan, which all fall back to European defaults (SO₂ 1.31, nitrogen oxides (NOx) 0.74). Third is nominal-only location tagging: photochemical ozone and particulate matter (PM) precursors list 36 European country rows whose values are strictly identical to the unspecified row, and primary fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅) contains zero country rows. Consequently, a factory emitting 10 kg SO₂ and consuming 10 m³ of water exhibits opposite extremes in Germany (22.81 and 13.6) versus Spain (1.08 and 777.0); relabeling the plant to China switches water use to China's factor (424.0) while locking acidification to the European default (13.10).
claims.scope: European applicability boundary in ILCD 2011 and the three location-code regimes across four official EF 3.1 LCIA method tables.
caveats: The 10 kg SO₂ and 10 m³ freshwater consumption pair is a controlled sensitivity example designed to isolate location-code behavior across four EF 3.1 method tables, not a measured full inventory of a dyeing plant.

The 209 water-use location codes represent non-blank location rows in the AWARE table (excluding the unspecified default), including certain overseas territories and islands rather than matching United Nations member state counts.

EF 3.1 location-regime details: AWARE global default is 42.95 m³ world-eq/m³ (Switzerland 1.34, United States 33.8, India 29.4); acidification NOx is 0.849 in Germany, 0.252 in Switzerland, and 0.052 mol H⁺-eq/kg in Spain (16.33-fold spread), with SO₂ in Switzerland 0.494; photochemical ozone holds NOx constant at 1.0 and SO₂ at 0.0811 kg NMVOC-eq/kg; particulate matter holds SO₂ constant at 8.0×10⁻⁶ and NOx at 1.6×10⁻⁶, with unspecified primary PM₂.₅ at 2.38497×10⁻⁴ disease incidence/kg.

claims.text: Switching normalization references from regional to "global" cannot be taken at face value either. The official EF 3.1 normalization workbook computes global per-capita normalization factors NFᵢ using a 2010 world population of roughly 6.896 billion, yet auditing all 1,803 elementary flows exposes stark disparities in data completeness. Across the entire table, 1,287 flows (71.38%) scale European Union agricultural emissions by dividing by the EU's 0.0384 share of global cropland (a ~26.04-fold extrapolation), 232 flows (12.87%) multiply EU emissions by an economic scaling factor of 14.12, and 11 flows extrapolate from China. By category, acidification, particulate matter, and terrestrial eutrophication draw 100% from global gridded inventories in the Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGAR), and EU extrapolation accounts for only 0.03% of climate change. By contrast, 96.81% of the freshwater ecotoxicity per-capita reference (56,716.59 comparative toxic units for ecosystems, CTUe/person) is extrapolated from EU inventories via cropland or economic multipliers; human non-cancer and cancer toxicity likewise derive 31.19% and 14.05% from EU and Chinese extrapolations. As the LC-IMPACT paper notes, thousands of chemicals lack routine monitoring in most countries, so labeling a denominator "global" does not eliminate completeness bias between combustion emissions and toxicity categories.
claims.scope: Global per-capita normalization rules in EU PEF and regional extrapolation shares across all 1,803 elementary flows in the EF 3.1 calculation workbook.
caveats: Percentages are summed directly from global contribution columns across rows 3–1805 of worksheet NFs EF3.1_calculation; the largest single contributor to human non-cancer toxicity is the upper-bound United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) Global Mercury Assessment estimate (58.59%), which is excluded from the EU and China country-scaling shares above.

Documenting this data-construction dependence does not negate the conceptual advantage of global per-capita references over single-region territorial denominators for maintaining boundary consistency in multinational supply chains.

Exact workbook breakdown: freshwater ecotoxicity consists of 69.25% EU cropland (0.0384) scaling, 27.56% EU economic (14.12×) scaling, and 0.34% China scaling; human non-cancer toxicity (1.2874×10⁻⁴ comparative toxic units for human health, CTUh/person) includes 19.57% EU scaling, 11.62% China scaling, and 58.59% from the UNEP Global Mercury Assessment upper bound; cancer toxicity (1.7253×10⁻⁵ CTUh/person) includes 9.81% EU scaling and 4.24% China scaling. Other per-capita NFs: acidification 55.57 mol H⁺-eq/person, particulate matter 5.9537×10⁻⁴ disease incidence/person, terrestrial eutrophication 176.75 mol N-eq/person, and climate change 7,553.08 kg CO₂-eq/person.

claims.text: Expressing every category in person-equivalents does not make them equally important. Yang et al. (2001) distinguish scientific, policy, and management targets and construct environmental weights from Chinese government reduction targets for the year 2000. Crucially, they divide the year-2000 target potential by the 1990 population to form the target reference ER(j)T2000—it is not year-2000 actual emissions divided by year-2000 population. Moreover, while the normalization section specifies global references for global impacts, the weighting section does not explain category by category how global references pair with Chinese policy targets, so missing parameters cannot be inferred from the formulas alone.
claims.scope: Policy nature and population basis of the target reference ER(j)T2000 in Yang et al. (2001).

claims.text: The environmental weighting factor WF(j) is defined as the ratio of the 1990 reference to the target reference. When both references share the same nonzero population denominator, population cancels out, leaving the ratio of baseline total impact potential to target total impact potential. A weight above 1 indicates a target lower than the baseline; a weight of 1 indicates no change; a weight below 1 permits emissions to rise above the baseline. This ratio measures the stringency of the chosen target relative to the baseline—it neither tracks whether the target was achieved nor proves that one impact is scientifically more severe than another.
claims.scope: Distance-to-target weighting factor under matched population denominators and positive references.
caveats: This interpretation requires matched impact categories, matched geographic scope, and positive nonzero reference quantities.

claims.text: Algebraic inspection shows how normalization references and target weights interact. Let E denote a product's category impact potential, B the 1990 per-capita reference, and G the target per-capita reference. The paper's weighting product is (B/G) × (E/B). Whenever B and G are nonzero and both occurrences of B represent the exact same reference, B cancels out, leaving E/G, which EIL sums across categories. Although only the target reference G remains in the final ratio, G itself was constructed using the 1990 population—so 1990 demographic information does not vanish completely.
claims.scope: Algebraic cancellation in the printed EIL product formula under matched nonzero references.
caveats: B and G from different impact categories or regions must never be treated as interchangeable.
The substance and factor subscripts in the final expanded EIL expression of Yang et al. (2001) do not match Section 3.1; the analysis here uses the preceding product formulation.

claims.text: While the per-capita reference B cancels cleanly, how the service period T enters the weighted score remains ambiguous. In Yang et al.
