(2001), T appears in the normalization formula NEP = EP/(T × ER₉₀), yet disappears from the printed expressions for weighted environmental impact potential (WP) and EIL. Under a consistent EP basis and nonzero denominators, the definition implies EP/ER₉₀ = T × NEP; substituting into WP = WF × EP/ER₉₀ yields WP = T × WF × NEP. Literally read, WP does not equal WF × NEP. Because the four-page paper never states whether the weighting step used an already-annualized potential, omitted T in typesetting, or followed another convention, each printed formula must be read as written, leaving the treatment of service period unresolved.
claims.scope: Conditional algebraic relation between NEP and WP and unresolved time-basis convention in Yang et al. (2001).
caveats: Undisclosed inputs must not be arbitrarily set to T = 1 to claim reproduction of the original model.

claims.text: The resource branch frames a different comparison. Yang et al. (2001) treat non-renewable resources as traded on global markets, evaluating consumption against reserves to gauge scarcity, whereas for renewable resources they insist that extraction and renewal be evaluated within local boundaries. Supply longevity depends on available stock and net depletion—extraction minus renewal. This logic separates how much of a resource is consumed from whether a specific region faces depletion, showing that global renewability cannot substitute for local availability.
claims.scope: Stocks, net flows, and regional conditions in the resource branch of Yang et al. (2001).
caveats: This formulation is specific to Yang et al. (2001) and is not a universal definition of modern water scarcity or abiotic resource depletion methods.

claims.text: The printed equations for non-renewable resources likewise require careful scrutiny. On page 236, the paper writes weighted resource consumption WR both as WF times normalized resource consumption NR and as product consumption divided by 1990 per-capita reserves, while describing WF as years of supply longevity. Meanwhile, NR in Section 3.2 on the same page includes the product service period. Taken at face value, the two WR expressions do not follow directly from one another, nor is the person-equivalent label for WR reconciled with the unit of years given for RDI. While the conceptual rationale for scarcity is clear, the printed formulas alone do not determine how reciprocals or service periods were handled in computation.
claims.scope: Dimensional and algebraic compatibility boundaries of resource expressions in Yang et al. (2001).
caveats: Internal discrepancies in the source text are preserved without attributing their cause or proposing unsupported corrections.

claims.text: The citation chain defines how far this short paper can be taken as evidence. Yang et al. (2001) link their category selection to a 1999 classification study and attribute detailed normalization references and weights to a 1998 EcoBalance conference paper by Yang and Nielsen. The 2001 Chinese article explains the conceptual framework and notation but publishes neither complete parameter tables nor product inventories. Although its conclusion reports that the cooperative project applied the method to a Chinese passenger vehicle and promises a separate publication, the paper records only that project claim without supplying the data needed to replicate the vehicle results.
claims.scope: Citation lineage and evidentiary scope of product-application claims in Yang et al. (2001).
caveats: The 1998 EcoBalance conference paper was not publicly available in full text; later works by the same authors or with similar titles cannot automatically substitute for that edition's parameters.

claims.text: Reading later reviews requires tracking how retrospective labels map onto original publications. In their 2022 review Research Progress on Life Cycle Impact Assessment Methods and Their Localization in China, Minghui Xie and coauthors label the Yang et al. framework the Chinese product life cycle impact assessment method (LCIA-Y) and place it alongside the Energy Conservation and Emission Reduction (ECER) method, which uses a different base year and policy targets. The 2001 original, however, used only life cycle impact assessment (LCIA), EIL, and RDI. Retrospective labels help locate early literature, but because the two parameter sets rely on different baselines and targets, names alone do not establish version continuity.
claims.scope: Comparison of retrospective naming in Xie et al. (2022) with original terminology and baselines in Yang et al. (2001).
caveats: ECER is cited here strictly as described in Xie et al. (2022) regarding its naming and baseline structure, without reconstructing its underlying parameters.
No claim is made regarding when the abbreviation LCIA-Y first appeared in the literature.

claims.text: Mathematical symbols must also stay bound to their branch. Immediately after presenting a weighting equation, the 2022 review defines WF(j) as resource supply longevity. The 2001 original, however, kept environmental and resource branches separate: environmental WF is the ratio of baseline to policy target, whereas resource WF denotes supply longevity. Checking the 2001 paper restores that distinction—though without resolving its internal resource-equation and service-period ambiguities. A resource-branch definition cannot be plugged into an environmental weighting equation, nor should later shorthand replace branch-specific definitions.
claims.scope: Comparison of WF notation in Xie et al. (2022) against the separate environmental and resource branches in Yang et al. (2001).
caveats: This comparison does not speculate on the editorial cause of the phrasing in Xie et al. (2022) and does not propose a revised formula.

claims.text: Placing the algebraic cancellation back into international methodological debates explains why regional normalization cannot be interpreted in isolation from weighting. Section 4.6 of Part 3 of the Institute of Environmental Sciences at Leiden University (CML 2001) operational guide identifies a counterintuitive distortion: if an analyst performs only regional per-capita normalization NEP = E/B—or follows it with fixed weights that ignore local conditions—then the dirtier a region's historical per-capita emissions B, the larger the denominator and the smaller the normalized score for each additional kilogram emitted. Heavy background pollution thus dilutes rather than heightens relative concern. Only when weighting uses a matched distance-to-target factor WF = B/G does the current denominator B cancel in (B/G) × (E/B) = E/G, letting the policy-permitted target capacity G govern the score. China's Tenth Five-Year Plan for National Environmental Protection illustrates why heavily loaded zones require tighter targets: whereas the national 2005 SO₂ cap cut the 2000 baseline by 10% (target ratio ≈ 1.108, or 1.111 as 1/0.9), the designated Acid Rain and SO₂ Control Zones (Two Control Zones) required a 20% cut, raising the weight to 1.250. Swapping in a high-emission region's denominator B without tightening targets or re-anchoring weights actually makes severe pollution look lighter.
claims.scope: Regional normalization "dirty denominator" paradox in CML 2001 Part 3 §4.6 contrasted with Yang et al. (2001) cancellation and Tenth Five-Year Plan Two Control Zones targets.
caveats: Dividing the Tenth Five-Year Plan national baseline of 19.95 million metric tons by the 18.00 million metric ton cap yields 1.1083, while the plan text also states a 10% reduction (1/0.90 = 1.1111); both published figures are retained, and both lie well below the 1.250 weight for the 20% reduction in the Two Control Zones.
Even when B cancels algebraically, the remaining term E/G is directly comparable across regions only if their target capacities G are set under consistent population and protection criteria.

claims.text: Subsequent research raised concrete objections to early policy references. In 2005, Lin, Zhang, and Chen argued that some early targets were rough estimates and constructed new distance-to-target weights from Chinese environmental policies and statistics for 1995–2005. They cited Nielsen and Yang's 1999 project report directly. While this critique confirms that target selection alters weights, it neither audits the 2001 Chinese article equation by equation nor supplies its missing parameters.
claims.scope: Target of critique and citation lineage in Lin, Zhang, and Chen (2005).
caveats: Text and table values from Lin, Zhang, and Chen (2005) are drawn from publicly retrieved derived PDF text rather than a visual layout audit of the original journal print.

claims.text: Sulfur dioxide offers a case traceable directly to official statistics. Table 12 of the 2000 China Environmental Statistics Annual Report lists 1995 actual emissions, the 2000 control plan, and 2000 actual emissions side by side, while the Tenth Five-Year Plan sets a national reduction target anchored to 2000 alongside stricter targets for the Acid Rain and SO₂ Control Zones. Analysts must distinguish each figure's geographic boundary, year, and status (planned cap versus measured actual): national targets and control-zone targets cannot share the same denominator. Moreover, these 1995–2005 national SO₂ statistics belong to a later policy sequence and cannot backfill the 1990 per-capita category potentials or 2000 target references needed by the earlier framework.
claims.scope: Identity boundaries across official Chinese SO₂ statistics and policy targets.
caveats: Official SO₂ records do not provide NOx characterization or allow full reconstruction of the complete acidification table.

claims.text: That distinction also explains why consecutive five-year weighting ratios cannot simply be multiplied together. In Table 3 and its footnotes, Lin, Zhang, and Chen (2005) separate the planned cap at the end of the first five-year period from the measured actual baseline at the start of the next: both carry the year 2000, yet they are different numbers (the 2000 China Environmental Statistics Annual Report records a national SO₂ control plan of 24.60 million metric tons versus actual emissions of 19.951 million metric tons). An intermediate reference cancels across two ratios only when both periods use the exact same quantity. In addition, the table's NOx contribution and total acidification figures incorporate author estimates and conversions rather than pure observed statistics. Chaining two five-year periods into a ten-year comparison requires verifying consistency in statistical estimates, baselines, and target definitions—not merely adjacent calendar years.
claims.scope: Conditions for chaining consecutive distance-to-target ratios when intermediate references differ.
caveats: This verification covers only SO₂ statistics and target linkage and does not reconstruct the estimated NOx sub-items or total acidification in Table 3 of Lin et al. (2005).

claims.text: Deriving weights from policy targets still involves modeling choices. Lin et al. (2005) note that whenever a regulation specifies an ambient concentration limit, dispersion modeling is still required to relate inventory emissions to concentration changes. A clearly documented management target does not automatically furnish equivalence factors for every pollutant. Distance-to-target weights express the policy priorities of a specific planning period; environmental damage pathways, carrying capacities, and post-implementation effectiveness each carry their own distinct evidentiary requirements.
claims.scope: Boundary between policy-target weighting and evidence on environmental mechanisms or implementation outcomes.
caveats: This boundary neither rules out policy weighting as unusable nor equates it with damage-oriented impact models.

claims.text: The 2005 Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) and Life Cycle Costing (LCC) Study of Building Materials and Components commissioned by the Hong Kong Housing Authority (Contract C1169) shows how an engineering project can adopt regional normalization references selectively. Its "Southeast China" reference table attributes several entries, including climate change, to Yang and Nielsen while citing separate sources for other categories. Because the footnote gives 1999 with a title resembling the 1998 conference paper, the exact source carrier remains ambiguous. What the report establishes is partial borrowing of attributed regional references—not institutional adoption of the entire 2001 Chinese framework.
claims.scope: Traceable partial adoption of regional normalization references in the Hong Kong C1169 report.
caveats: The report's "Southeast China" table encompasses regions including Beijing and Liaoning and should not be equated with standard geographic definitions of southeastern China.
Numbered entries (4) through (8) on printed page 72 of the report do not align one-to-one with the category names listed immediately afterward.

claims.text: The same Hong Kong report also constructs a separate local reference set. For climate change it uses Hong Kong's own greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory, while several other categories pair local pollution data with CML characterization factors. In Appendix C, the 1 kg glass worked example applies Hong Kong's annual per-capita climate reference rather than the regional table listed earlier. This demonstrates that a project can mix and match inventory data, characterization methods, and normalization denominators independently—meaning readers must inspect which dataset and method were actually used at each step.
claims.scope: Local Hong Kong normalization references and modular method assembly in Contract C1169.
caveats: Because the main text and appendix describe certain acidification and photochemical ozone sources differently, verification of the climate-change row does not extend to full reproduction of all impact categories.

claims.text: Weighting constitutes yet another independent choice. The C1169 report explains that its software's default weights came from Phase 1 stakeholder opinion workshops, while users remain free to enter custom weights—an approach quite distinct from calculating distance-to-policy-target ratios. Borrowing normalization references from Yang and Nielsen therefore does not imply adopting their policy weights, and the independent consultant review of the project software does not constitute independent validation of the earlier Chinese model.
claims.scope: Separation of reference adoption, weighting choice, and review scope in Contract C1169.

claims.text: By combining CML characterization, local normalization references, and fixed workshop weights, the Hong Kong C1169 study exposes the "territorial denominator mismatch" of open service economies (Table 2). Both the ILCD 2010 General Guide and the United Nations Environment Programme Global Guidance for Life Cycle Impact Assessment Indicators and Methods (UNEP GLAM) warn that service-oriented cities outsource energy-intensive manufacturing, so territorial emission inventories do not match the cross-border supply chains of consumed goods. Hong Kong's 2000 territorial climate reference of 5,922.49 kg CO₂-eq/(person·yr) sits 21.59% below the EF 3.1 global reference of 7,553.08 kg CO₂-eq/(person·yr), inflating the normalized score of 1 kg of glass (1.32 kg CO₂-eq) by 27.53% (from 1.7476×10⁻⁴ to 2.2288×10⁻⁴ person-years). Because fixed weights do not cancel the denominator, swapping only the climate reference can flip product rankings: consider two equivalent facade materials where Option A emits 80 kg CO₂ and 0.40 kg SO₂ and Option B emits 50 kg CO₂ and 0.60 kg SO₂, evaluated with equal weights and a global converted acidification reference of 42.4195 kg SO₂-eq/(person·yr) (crossover denominator ratio = 150). Under the global climate denominator (ratio 178.06), Option A wins (0.02002 versus 0.02076); switching to Hong Kong's territorial denominator (ratio 139.62) reverses the ranking to Option B (0.02259 versus 0.02294).
claims.scope: Territorial denominator mismatch in open service economies and equal-weight rank reversal triggered by Hong Kong's 2000 climate reference.
caveats: The Option A versus Option B facade comparison is a controlled algebraic test built from published denominators (Hong Kong 5,922.49, EF 3.1 global 7,553.08, and 42.4195) to isolate the crossover mechanism, not a run of the unpublished Hong Kong local SO₂ denominator inside the C1169 software.
Using a global per-capita denominator or a consumption-based footprint denominator aligned with transboundary supply chains avoids this outsourcing-induced territorial shrinkage bias.

claims.text: Even when denominators and weights align, methods organized by political boundaries rarely match the native biophysical units of environmental processes (Table 1). LC-IMPACT and UNEP GLAM specify those native units explicitly: 56 atmospheric source regions for particulate matter and ozone, roughly 11,000 watersheds for water stress, and 804 terrestrial and 449 freshwater ecoregions for biodiversity. Checking the ReCiPe 2016 regionalized supplementary tables reveals distortion in both directions. On the atmospheric side, Tables S1.1–S1.2 merge the Chinese mainland, Hong Kong, and Macao into a single homogeneous source region (primary PM₂.₅ endpoint 1.7×10⁻³ disability-adjusted life years, DALY/kg), while listing Taiwan separately (3.5×10⁻⁴ DALY/kg, making the merged region 4.86 times higher). On the watershed side, Tables S6.3–S6.4 for freshwater fish damage from water consumption show that China's national mean (3.91×10⁻¹² species·yr/m³) flattens stark north–south differences: the Pearl River basin is just 1.67×10⁻¹² (57.29% lower), while the Yangtze River reaches 5.52×10⁻¹² (3.31 times the Pearl River). Applying China's national average to a Pearl River factory overstates its freshwater fish damage by 2.34-fold.
claims.scope: Native biophysical spatial units in LC-IMPACT and UNEP GLAM versus sub-national aggregation bias in ReCiPe 2016 across China–Hong Kong–Macao air emissions and Chinese river basins.
caveats: ReCiPe 2016 Table S1.2 prints units as yr/kton; because 1 kton = 10⁶ kg and human-health years equal DALY, 1.7×10³ yr/kton equals 1.7×10⁻³ DALY/kg identically.
Table S6.4 watershed factors cover only freshwater fish species loss from reduced river discharge and exclude human-health malnutrition pathways from agricultural water scarcity.

Additional ReCiPe 2016 values: Table S1.1 primary PM₂.₅ midpoints are 2.90 kg PM₂.₅-eq/kg for China–Hong Kong–Macao and 0.75 for Taiwan (3.87-fold ratio); Table S6.4 freshwater fish water-consumption factors (species·yr/m³) include 1.99×10⁻¹² for the Tarim River and 4.84×10⁻¹² for the Yellow River (2.90 times the Pearl River).

claims.text: Even when two methods are both regionalized by country, whether 1 kg of emission causes greater impact in East Asia or Europe can flip repeatedly depending on dose–response curvature, urban–rural archetypes, baseline mortality, and receptor choice (Table 1). For 1 kg of ground-level primary PM₂.₅, ReCiPe 2016's linear slope ranks China–Hong Kong–Macao (1.7×10⁻³ DALY/kg) above Switzerland (1.5×10⁻³) and Germany (1.3×10⁻³). Switching to UNEP GLAM 2024's concave nonlinear "unspecified urban/rural marginal" factor reverses the order: high ambient background flattens the marginal slope and rural weighting pulls the national figure down, putting Switzerland (6.446×10⁻⁴) and Germany (6.306×10⁻⁴) at roughly three times China (2.146×10⁻⁴). Switching within the very same workbook to the "urban average" slope flips the ranking back, putting China (1.205×10⁻³ DALY/kg) on top again. Similar reversals occur inside ReCiPe 2016 itself: South Korea's PM₂.₅ midpoint (2.15) exceeds Germany and Switzerland, yet its endpoint (7.0×10⁻⁴ DALY/kg) falls below both; for NOx ozone midpoints, China–Hong Kong–Macao (2.07) exceeds Spain/Portugal (1.18) for human health, whereas Spain/Portugal (3.41) is 48.71 times higher than China–Hong Kong–Macao (0.07) for ecosystems. LC-IMPACT adds species vulnerability scores to keep local degradation distinct from global extinction.
claims.scope: Double China–Europe rank reversals for ground-level primary PM₂.₅ across models and archetypes, plus midpoint-to-endpoint, cross-receptor ozone, and vulnerability-score reversals.
caveats: The UNEP GLAM 2024 PM workbook's underlying characterization-factor sheet lists marginal, average, and linear slope derivations for ground-level emissions, whereas its recommended mapping sheet matches air sub-compartments using average slopes; citations must specify the sheet layer, slope derivation, and urban–rural scenario. Unweighted country-level spatial means do not substitute for site-specific plume dispersion modeling.

A lower marginal factor at high background PM₂.₅ reflects only a flatter local tangent on a concave concentration–response curve and never implies a lighter overall population health burden (under the average-slope metric, urban China ranks highest).

In RIVM Report 2016-0104 Table S3.2 (terrestrial acidification endpoint), beginning at the Brazil row on page 144, omitting the Bouvet Island country label and inserting an extra zero in the NOx column shifts subsequent ammonia and SO₂ entries down by one row (printing Chile's 1.40×10⁻⁷ on the China row and Georgia's 4.77×10⁻⁷ on the Germany row); misaligned rows must not be misread as midpoint-to-endpoint reversals.

Detailed UNEP GLAM 2024 and ReCiPe 2016 figures: GLAM China urban marginal (5.5694×10⁻⁴) is 2.65× rural marginal (2.0979×10⁻⁴); global unspecified-height average is 6.6594×10⁻⁴, China unspecified average 4.2217×10⁻⁴, Germany urban average 8.5423×10⁻⁴, and Switzerland urban average 6.9890×10⁻⁴ (China is 1.72× Switzerland). In ReCiPe 2016, South Korea PM₂.₅ midpoint is 2.15 versus Switzerland/Liechtenstein 1.92 and Germany 1.74, yet Germany's endpoint is 1.86× South Korea's; terrestrial acidification SO₂ midpoints are 1.55 for China, 2.43 for Germany, and 2.21 kg SO₂-eq/kg for Switzerland.

claims.text: Institutional adoption requires its own documentary evidence. Official Chinese standard registries record that recommended national standard GB/T 24040-1999 was issued in March 1999 and took effect in November 1999, while GB/T 24041-2000 was issued in February 2000 and took effect in October 2000. The impact assessment standard (GB/T 24042-2002) and life cycle interpretation standard (GB/T 24043-2002) were issued in April 2002 and took effect in October 2002. In his 2002 article The Application Prospect of Life Cycle Assessment in Cleaner Production, Qihong Sun described the first two standards as published and the latter two as expected; official registry dates confirm the actual institutional milestones without altering the contemporaneous expectation recorded in his article.
claims.scope: Bounded comparison between official Chinese GB/T registration dates and contemporaneous expectations in Sun (2002).
caveats: This record checks official standard registry metadata rather than comparing full copyrighted standard texts clause by clause, and original agency documents for the 1998 standard-drafting launch cited by Sun (2002) were not retrieved.

claims.text: These registry records establish standard identities along with publication and effective dates. Even where a registry states identical adoption of the corresponding International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standard, that fact never implies that any particular study's per-capita references, weights, or aggregate indices received national adoption. Determining whether a standard adopted specific research parameters requires inspecting actual standard clauses, adoption notices, or project records; shared authorship, similar terminology, or chronological proximity serve only as leads for further lookup.
claims.scope: Evidentiary boundary between adopting procedural framework standards and adopting research-specific LCIA parameters.

claims.text: In their 2022 review, Xie et al. break localization into inventory databases, environmental and exposure parameters, reference substances, normalization benchmarks, weights, and impact models. Terminology must also be read within its procedural step: characterization maps flows to category indicators, while normalization scales those indicators against external references. Determining whether a study is genuinely localized always requires checking which data, parameters, or models were actually replaced.
claims.scope: Localization layers and methodological terminology in Xie et al. (2022).
caveats: Preserving source terminology does not imply that different methods share identical models, units, or boundaries.
This summarizes the reviewed article rather than imposing a new external standard.

claims.text: Xie et al. (2022) report that roughly 77% of studies explicitly naming an impact assessment method used foreign methods. Searching the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) Chinese-language journal database for "life cycle assessment" from 1995 to 2020 returned 827 records; of these, 243 explicitly specified an impact assessment method, and 186 were classified as foreign methods. The 77% figure uses 243 as its denominator—it does not represent a census of all Chinese LCA research or industrial practice.
claims.scope: Search frame and method-usage denominator in Section 3 of Xie et al. (2022).
caveats: The 77% share reflects the review authors' search and classification without independent re-coding of all 243 articles.
Non-Chinese journals, alternative search terms, unpublished industrial studies, and articles omitting method names fall outside this denominator.

claims.text: In that tally, "foreign method" classifies institutional origin, not whether a calculation is valid for a given decision. A method's name alone does not reveal which version, regional parameters, characterization factors, or defaults were applied; conversely, attaching a domestic label does not automatically make results more accurate. Bibliometric shares can highlight needs for local modeling capacity, but a single percentage cannot replace auditing a study's actual scope and assumptions.
claims.scope: Limits of inference from method-origin counts in Xie et al. (2022).
caveats: No method is judged universally superior or universally inapplicable on the basis of geographic origin.
How articles applying multiple methods were coded would require inspecting the full extraction log.

claims.text: Xie et al. (2022) also cite a photovoltaic-module monetization case suggesting that European willingness-to-pay parameters for human health and ecosystem quality far exceed Chinese levels, and conclude by calling for updated benchmarks, stronger model collaboration, and domestic willingness-to-pay research. These statements represent an ongoing research agenda and applicability concerns, not proof that localized infrastructure is complete. Whose preferences a willingness-to-pay parameter represents depends on primary survey design, protected endpoints, and decision context. Such concerns motivate targeted research without warranting claims that residents of one country inherently value health or ecosystems less, nor requiring every project to use a domestic method.
claims.scope: Boundaries of recommendations and extrapolation in Sections 4–5 of Xie et al. (2022).
caveats: A research agenda does not furnish primary willingness-to-pay survey evidence or cross-national preference comparisons.
Because Qihong Sun coauthored both Sun (2002) and Xie et al. (2022) within a shared institutional lineage, the two articles should not be treated as completely independent historical witnesses.

claims.text: China's national standard registrations and the European Union's EF compliance rules form complementary institutional mirrors (Table 2). China's GB/T 24040 and 24042—and their 2008 replacements GB/T 24040-2008 and 24044-2008—identically adopt the ISO procedural framework, enforcing discipline on classification, characterization, and optional normalization and weighting while deliberately leaving characterization tables, per-capita references, and weights unspecified. Conversely, the November 2022 EF 3.1 data-guide addendum locks in specific country factors alongside mandatory normalization and weighting, yet explicitly instructs compliant datasets to mark multiple ISO 14040/14044 naming, documentation, review, and quality compliance fields as "Not defined". The former preserves general procedure while leaving parameters open; the latter administratively locks a uniform parameter package while acknowledging it is not equivalent to full ISO metadata compliance. Claiming either "GB/T conformance" or "EF 3.1 compliance" therefore never proves that regional parameters were independently validated for local environmental mechanisms.
claims.scope: Institutional mirror between China's procedural GB/T adoption of ISO standards and EU EF 3.1's locked parameter package with ISO 14040/14044 compliance fields set to "Not defined".
caveats: Statements on GB/T 24040 and 24044 are strictly limited to official public registry metadata on identical adoption and version succession, without reproducing copyrighted standard text.
Setting selected ISO 14040/14044 compliance fields to "Not defined" in the EF 3.1 addendum is an ILCD data-format mapping convention and does not negate EF's own internal review procedures.

claims.text: To support side-by-side comparison, Table 2 organizes early Chinese mainland and Hong Kong localization frameworks, European compliance packages, and Chinese standards and bibliometric reviews across four practical audit layers: spatial granularity of inventories and characterization, geographic and extrapolation boundaries of normalization denominators, cancellation between weights and denominators, and the evidentiary status of institutional or project adoption. Reading across these four columns makes immediately clear which component each scheme actually replaced and which boundaries forbid further extrapolation.
claims.scope: Four-layer localization audit synthesizing Chinese mainland and Hong Kong cases, European and UN method packages, and the UNEP GLAM multi-country cooked-rice case.
caveats: This four-layer audit diagnoses methodological fit for specific studies and does not presume that every product comparison requires sub-national foreground coordinates; when contribution analysis shows spatially insensitive pathways dominate, global or unspecified factors can remain decision-relevant.

claims.text: Looking across early Chinese frameworks, Five-Year Plan target ratios, Hong Kong's modular engineering study, and European and United Nations regionalized packages, "localization" is never a single binary switch. It is a layered combination of inventory spatial resolution, normalization denominator boundaries, exposure–response curvature, and institutional weighting rules. Reporting that an assessment uses a local or global method therefore requires stating which data and parameters changed at each layer, alongside the geographic, temporal, and decision boundaries under which they hold. Policy targets and administratively locked weights are not the only ways to weigh trade-offs: Monetary Valuation of Environmental Damage next examines an alternative route that infers stated monetary trade-offs from respondents' choices over concrete policy outcomes and tax payments.
claims.scope: Layered synthesis supported by the historical Chinese cases, international regionalized packages, and review evidence.

claims.text: Three hypothetical policies sit side by side on a single choice card. One asks each household to pay an extra 5,000 Japanese yen (JPY) for the year in exchange for avoiding the listed health losses and halting additional species extinctions, while still leaving some loss of primary production. A second maintains the status quo with no additional household tax. A third recombines the tax level and the four environmental damages. Norihiro Itsubo and colleagues printed this sample card in their 2003 Japanese paper. Respondents simply choose the policy they find most acceptable; no one is asked to name a price tag for a year of healthy life on the spot.
claims.scope: A set of hypothetical environmental policies published in an early Japanese stated-preference study.

claims.text: The choice card uses estimated damage quantities to probe how people weigh competing environmental losses. Japan's endpoint life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) method—the Life-cycle Impact assessment Method based on Endpoint modeling (LIME), whose early 2002–2004 Tokyo survey is commonly referred to as LIME1—first applies damage models to trace emissions through environmental changes to four safeguard subjects: human health, social assets, primary production, and biodiversity. Only at the final integration step do weights combine those heterogeneous units into a single metric. Conjoint analysis infers relative trade-offs from respondents' choices among hypothetical profiles, which means the resulting valuations depend directly on which consequences appear on the card and how large each attribute shift is set to be.
claims.scope: Division of labor between endpoint damage modeling and conjoint analysis in early Japanese LCIA development.

claims.text: The ecological scarcity method examined in Ecological Scarcity Weighting derives its scoring factors from enacted policy targets. By contrast, the policies on this choice card have not been enacted; they serve only to let respondents trade off environmental damages against annual household taxes. Here, the weights depend on how respondents react when attribute levels change, so knowing statutory emission-reduction targets does not allow one to derive this survey's valuations directly.
claims.scope: Contrasting roles of policy in distance-to-target weighting versus stated-preference valuation.

claims.text: Before asking respondents how much they would pay to reduce damage, researchers must first establish the scale of current damage. In the Japanese study, annual environmental loads generated in Japan were multiplied by their respective damage factors and summed separately for each of the four safeguard subjects to obtain annual reference damages (normalization values). The geographic scope of Japan here defines where the environmental loads originate; who suffers the resulting damage, who answers the survey, and how many households are later used as a multiplier must each be specified separately.
claims.scope: Annual reference damages for survey attribute levels and the geographic boundary of environmental loads.

claims.text: The four safeguard subjects are expressed in four distinct units. Human health is measured in disability-adjusted life years (DALY), combining healthy time lost to premature mortality and disability. Social assets are measured in JPY. Primary production is measured in dry metric tons of lost net primary production—the plant matter fixed by photosynthesis minus losses from plant respiration. Biodiversity is measured in numbers of extinct species. In the social-assets row, yen serves as an accounting unit for physical and economic asset loss rather than a household tax payment; likewise, one dry metric ton of primary production cannot be added directly to one DALY.
claims.scope: Endpoint indicators and measurement units for the four LIME safeguard subjects.

claims.text: Damage models available at the time could not trace every individual emission all the way to plant extinctions. To set biodiversity levels for the questionnaire, the authors drew on vascular-plant records in Japan's Red Data Book, amortizing the 25 species classified as extinct or extinct in the wild over an assumed 50-year horizon to establish an annual reference of 0.5 species per year. That fractional species figure is an artifact of multi-year amortization; while useful for letting respondents compare policy scenarios, it cannot be interpreted as an observed annual extinction rate. The original paper itself flags repeating the survey once more complete damage functions are available as a priority for verification.
claims.scope: Proxy construction of the biodiversity survey reference from vascular-plant Red Data Book records.
caveats: The original study constructed this attribute baseline solely from vascular-plant data and cannot be generalized as a species-loss model covering all taxonomic groups.

claims.text: To make health impacts tangible to lay respondents, the national reference of roughly 1.43 million DALY per year in Japanese Table 3 was translated on the questionnaire into about four days per person per year—or several months if that condition persisted for 50 years. Table 4 labels this attribute "lost life expectancy" in everyday terms, with a table note explaining that the wording was chosen for comprehension. When converting back to coefficients and weights, however, a structural question remains: respondents saw days per person, the damage model includes non-fatal disability, and the payment vehicle was framed per household. How those three bases are reconciled is a central point to check in the health weight below.
claims.scope: Translation from national annual health damage to per-person attribute levels shown to survey respondents.

claims.text: Only after attributes and units are fixed can a survey observe how people make trade-offs. The main survey was conducted on January 22–25, 2002, via intercept interviews at four locations in Tokyo with men and women aged 20–59; Table 5 reports 306 valid respondents, each completing eight choice tasks, while an earlier pretest of 108 respondents was used to revise the questionnaire. Asking each participant to evaluate eight choice sets helps identify relative trade-offs, but eight answers from one individual cannot be treated as eight independent respondents drawn from a national population.
claims.scope: Participant sampling and repeated-choice structure of the Tokyo intercept survey.

claims.text: On any single choice card, lower health loss may appear alongside lower species loss; if a respondent selects that policy, that single choice cannot reveal how much each attribute mattered. To separate individual effects, the authors used an orthogonal experimental design that varied attribute-level combinations across cards while keeping the status-quo option on every card, then pooled responses across choice sets to estimate attribute relationships. Because the paper reproduces only an illustrative card and summary coefficients, the published text does not allow a reader to reconstruct the full task-by-task response dataset.
claims.scope: How orthogonal conjoint design separates attribute effects across multi-attribute choice cards.

claims.text: In the conditional logit model applied by the authors, each policy alternative has a systematic utility component V explained by its attributes plus an unobserved random error term. Systematic utility V is the linear sum of the four damage attributes and the tax amount multiplied by their respective coefficients. Assuming a Type I extreme-value error distribution with the scale parameter fixed at 1, the probability of choosing alternative i equals exp(Vᵢ) divided by the sum of exp(Vⱼ) across all alternatives on the same card. Maximum likelihood estimation fits the coefficients to the observed choices. Each coefficient measures the utility change from a one-coded-unit shift in that attribute while holding all others constant; its numerical magnitude therefore changes whenever the coding unit changes.
claims.scope: Systematic utility, error distribution, and choice probability in the conditional logit specification.

claims.text: Converting estimated coefficients into willingness to pay (WTP) holds all other attributes fixed. Let dx denote a change in damage and dt a change in household tax; keeping systematic utility unchanged requires βₑ dx + βₜ dt = 0. In the original Tokyo paper, both the damage and tax coefficients are negative, meaning higher damage requires a lower tax to leave utility intact. Conversely, when damage falls by one coded unit, the positive tax increase that keeps utility constant is the marginal WTP for avoiding that unit of damage. Taking the ratio of the two coefficients cancels out the arbitrary utility scale, leaving household tax per coded unit of damage.
claims.scope: Iso-utility slope and derivation of positive marginal willingness to pay for avoided damage.

claims.text: Two distinct forms of uncertainty arise here. First, Table 6 reports standard errors for each estimated coefficient, which capture parameter estimation error. Marginal WTP, however, is a ratio of two estimated coefficients, and the same tax coefficient sits in the denominator of every damage ratio; estimating the uncertainty of that ratio requires the covariance between numerator and denominator, so dividing one standard error by another does not produce a valid confidence interval. Second, residents themselves may hold genuinely different environmental trade-offs. Even highly precise common coefficients tell us nothing about how widely individual preferences vary across the population.
claims.scope: Distinction between coefficient estimation error, ratio uncertainty, and individual preference heterogeneity.

claims.text: Primary production illustrates the unit mechanics cleanly. In Japanese Table 6, the damage coefficient is −0.0034133 and the tax coefficient is −0.0000891, where the former corresponds to a coding unit of 100 million dry metric tons of lost primary production and the latter to 1 JPY of additional annual tax per household. Dividing the two gives roughly 38.31 JPY per household for avoiding one coded unit. In the model, that household tax corresponds to preventing 100 million dry metric tons of loss; quoting the ratio as "38.31 JPY per metric ton" shrinks the damage denominator by a factor of 100 million.
claims.scope: Ratio of coded primary-production damage to household tax in Japanese Table 6.
caveats: Row 3 of Japanese Table 6 misprints the attribute label as "primary assets," whereas the surrounding text and Table 7 consistently refer to "primary production."

claims.text: Scaling from a per-household figure to a per-metric-ton weight requires multiplying by Japan's 46,607,000 households and dividing by the 100 million dry metric tons represented by one coded unit. Without intermediate rounding of the coefficient ratio, this yields approximately 17.854509 JPY per dry metric ton, whereas Japanese Table 7 publishes 17.8 JPY per dry metric ton. Crucially, the national household count acts purely as a monetary expansion multiplier while the 306 Tokyo interviewees remain the empirical sample; scaling WTP to the national household total does not expand the sample.
claims.scope: Recalculation of the primary-production monetary weight from printed coefficients and national household count.

claims.text: Because the health attribute was coded in days, converting it to DALY requires checking an additional step. Dividing the health coefficient by the tax coefficient yields approximately 1,567.74; multiplying directly by 365 days per year gives roughly 572,200 JPY, closely matching the published 572,000 JPY per DALY within table rounding. Yet the survey presented days lost per person while framing the tax per household, and the original paper does not walk step by step through how household count, affected population, and per-person days were linked. Finding an arithmetic formula that reproduces the table entry still does not prove how the authors actually performed the aggregation.
claims.scope: Numerical coincidence and aggregation boundary between per-person days lost and per-household tax.

claims.text: Other discrepancies cannot be explained by final-digit rounding alone. Social assets were coded per 100 million JPY of damage, yet Japanese Table 7 reports WTP per 1,000 JPY of damage. Multiplying the coefficient ratio by 46,607,000 households, dividing by 100 million, and multiplying by 1,000 yields about 4,479.71 JPY, compared with 4,460 JPY in the published table. For biodiversity, coded per species, multiplying the coefficient ratio by the same household count yields about 7.7058 × 10¹¹ JPY per species, versus 7.68 × 10¹¹ JPY in the published table. Even when the printed damage coefficients, tax coefficient, and published weights are allowed to vary across their standard final-digit rounding bounds, the recalculated and published intervals fail to overlap in either row. Because earlier intermediate inputs and processing steps are not fully disclosed, the worked comparisons below use the authors' published values.
claims.scope: Unreconciled numerical gaps in the social-assets and biodiversity rows of Japanese Table 7.
caveats: For example, holding the printed household count fixed and varying the coefficients within last-digit rounding yields an interval of roughly 4,476.94–4,482.49 for social assets, whereas 4,460 rounded to three significant figures spans roughly 4,455–4,465. This bound test does not identify the underlying cause of the discrepancy.

claims.text: A monetary weight in JPY per DALY and a dimensionless health share answer two different questions. To ask what fraction of Japan's annual monetized environmental damage is attributable to human health, each unit valuation must first be multiplied back by its corresponding annual reference damage. Multiplying 1.43 million DALY by 572,000 JPY per DALY gives approximately 8.18 × 10¹¹ JPY. Social assets are listed as 54,400 in units of million JPY—equivalent to 54,400,000 units of 1,000 JPY—which multiplied by 4,460 JPY yields roughly 2.43 × 10¹¹ JPY. Valuing all four safeguard subjects this way and dividing each by their combined total yields each subject's annual monetary share.
claims.scope: Multiplication of annual reference damages by unit monetary weights to derive annual monetized totals.

claims.text: Applying the same procedure to the remaining two rows of Japanese Table 3, 15.4 billion dry metric tons of lost primary production multiplied by 17.8 JPY per dry metric ton gives roughly 2.74 × 10¹¹ JPY, and 0.5 extinct species multiplied by 7.68 × 10¹¹ JPY per species gives 3.84 × 10¹¹ JPY. Dividing each unrounded product by the four-item sum places human health at about 0.475917—rounded to 0.48—with the remaining three shares at 0.14, 0.16, and 0.22. That 0.48 embeds both the unit valuation of health and the scale of health damage in the chosen national baseline. It does not mean that 48% of respondents prioritized health, nor that 48% of every product's total damage should be assigned to health.
claims.scope: Composition of annual monetized damage shares across the four LIME safeguard subjects.

claims.text: For any specific product, let Dₑ be its damage in safeguard subject e, vₑ the unit monetary weight, and Nₑ the annual reference damage. The first aggregation route sums Dₑvₑ directly to produce a single score in JPY. The second divides each Dₑ by Nₑ and multiplies by the annual share just derived. Provided the unrounded shares Nₑvₑ / ΣNⱼvⱼ are retained, the two routes differ only by the constant positive denominator ΣNⱼvⱼ and therefore produce identical rankings. Multiplying an unnormalized DALY figure directly by 0.48, however, omits the essential normalization denominator Nₑ.
claims.scope: Conditions under which unit monetary weighting and normalized share weighting yield identical rankings.
caveats: Using annual shares already rounded to two decimal places can break exact algebraic equivalence between the two aggregation routes.

claims.text: Readers consulting the 2004 English paper must first verify which published table supplies their weights. While the English abstract and survey flowchart state that the main survey covered 400 respondents, the sample breakdown and regression tables report 306. Moreover, English and Japanese Table 5 carry the identical survey dates and match cell for cell across all eight sex-and-age groups, indicating that both publications analyze the same underlying respondent pool. Published documentation does not explain how the 400 reported main-survey participants relate to the 306 analyzed respondents, and the matching sample tables rule out treating the two articles as two independent surveys.
claims.scope: Sample correspondence between the 2003 Japanese and 2004 English LIME1 publications.

claims.text: Sharing the same sample table does not guarantee identical valuation tables. English Table 3 lists an annual health reference of 543,000 DALY, and its sample card describes the status quo as roughly two months lost over 50 years—substantially smaller than the reference and displayed values in the Japanese paper. The estimated coefficients for health, the other three damage attributes, and tax also differ. Identical sample sizes and log likelihood statistics are therefore insufficient to establish that two papers share the same attribute coding, data processing, or unit valuations.
claims.scope: Published differences in sample cards, annual references, and estimated valuations between the 2003 and 2004 papers.

claims.text: In 2004 English Table 7, for instance, human health is valued at 9,700,000 JPY per DALY and primary production at 20,200 JPY per dry metric ton. Social assets are reported as 10,000 JPY per 10,000 JPY of loss, shifting the denominator from the 1,000 JPY basis used in the Japanese table. Following the English paper's own rule of multiplying Table 3 by Table 7 to obtain annual monetized damage, the 2.29 million units of "million JPY" for social assets should yield 2.29 × 10¹² JPY, yet English Table 8 prints 3.61 × 10¹² JPY. That published discrepancy remains unresolved, underscoring why comparative studies must cite both the exact unit row and the specific publication.
claims.scope: Unit damage valuations and the social-assets annual total discrepancy in the 2004 English paper.

claims.text: Can the English regression coefficients simply be plugged into the earlier Japanese conversion formula? Testing the health row exposes the difficulty. Dividing the health coefficient magnitude (0.645) by the tax coefficient magnitude (0.0000577) and multiplying by 365 gives roughly 4.08 million JPY. Switching the numeraire to the social-assets coefficient magnitude (0.243) and its coded 10,000 JPY unit—computing 0.645 ÷ 0.243 × 10,000 × 365—yields roughly 9.69 million JPY, close to the published 9.70 million JPY. That second calculation identifies an arithmetic relationship consistent with the printed table, but the English paper itself does not document step by step that the authors used this conversion path for the health row.
claims.scope: Two conditional arithmetic checks on the human-health row of 2004 English Table 7.

claims.text: How do these published table differences affect an actual product comparison? Suppose two production routes deliver 1,000 metric tons of the same product grade on the same day at the same Japanese plant. Isolating the final valuation step on a common damage basis, assume Route A causes 0.001 DALY of health loss and 100 dry metric tons of primary-production loss, whereas Route B causes 0.004 DALY and 10 dry metric tons, with all other damages identical. Both the shared functional service and the four damage values are illustrative pedagogical settings rather than outputs modeled from actual emissions.
claims.scope: Fixed functional service and two illustrative endpoint damage profiles for comparing valuation tables.

claims.text: Applying the weights from 2003 Japanese Table 7 first, Route A scores 0.001 × 572,000 = 572 JPY for human health and 100 × 17.8 = 1,780 JPY for primary production, totaling 2,352 JPY. Route B scores 2,288 JPY and 178 JPY respectively, totaling 2,466 JPY. Across these two differing categories, Route B exceeds Route A by 114 JPY. Adding any equal monetary amount for the identical remaining damages leaves that margin unchanged.
claims.scope: Monetary valuation of the two differing damage categories under 2003 Japanese Table 7.

claims.text: Why can switching tables invert the ranking? Moving from Route A to Route B incurs an additional 0.003 DALY of health loss while saving 90 dry metric tons of primary production. Letting h denote the health weight in JPY per DALY and p the primary-production weight in JPY per dry metric ton, the score difference (Route B minus Route A) equals 0.003h − 90p. The two routes break even when h/p = 30,000 dry metric tons per DALY. Japanese Table 7 implies an h/p ratio of roughly 32,135—just above that threshold—so Route A, with lower health damage, achieves the lower total score. Because the break-even threshold is set by the damage difference vector, any new pair of routes requires recomputing it.
claims.scope: Relative valuation break-even threshold for a fixed two-category damage vector.

claims.text: Now apply 2004 English Table 7 to the exact same damage vector. Route A's health and primary-production contributions become 9,700 JPY and 2,020,000 JPY, totaling 2,029,700 JPY; Route B's contributions become 38,800 JPY and 202,000 JPY, totaling 240,800 JPY. Here the ratio h/p is approximately 480 dry metric tons per DALY, falling on the opposite side of the 30,000 threshold and flipping the verdict in favor of Route B. Both rounds evaluate identical illustrative damages and each remains internally consistent with a single published table, yet the choice of table alone dictates which route scores lower. Because both articles' sample tables point to January 2002, this reversal cannot be interpreted as a shift in public preferences over time.
claims.scope: Re-ranking of identical illustrative damages under 2004 English Table 7.
caveats: The two monetary totals belong to the valuation conditions of their respective publications; this example does not harmonize price years, purchasing power, or methodological generations.

claims.text: When two tables produce opposite rankings for the same comparison, the first question is what evidence justifies selecting a weight set. The Tokyo paper reports that all five estimated coefficients are statistically significant at the 1% level with the expected signs; the authors take this as evidence that respondents understood the questionnaire while acknowledging that some annual references rested on assumptions and recommending a repeat survey once damage functions improve. Statistical significance shows that trade-offs are identifiable within the fitted choice model, but knowing whether people would actually pay requires behavioral evidence tied to real financial consequences, such as incentive-compatible experiments.
claims.scope: Distinction between statistical significance in a choice model and real-payment behavioral validity.

claims.text: In a 1999 working paper, Fredrik Carlsson and Peter Martinsson asked 35 Swedish economics undergraduates to complete hypothetical choice tasks followed by binding real-money choices trading off personal payouts against donations to environmental projects, using different choice combinations across the two rounds to curb direct repetition. In their estimated model, marginal WTP for an additional unit of donation was 0.629 units of personal money under hypothetical conditions and 0.559 under actual payment, with an equality test yielding p = 0.403. Notably, the original t-test treated the two rounds as independent even though the same participants answered both. Failing to detect a statistically significant difference does not prove equivalence; claiming that hypothetical bias is small enough to ignore requires specifying an equivalence margin in advance and testing against it.
claims.scope: Within-subject test comparing hypothetical and binding choices among Swedish undergraduates.
caveats: The experimental design and statistics cited here come from the 1999 working paper; the later published journal version of record carries a separate bibliographic identity.

claims.text: Olof Johansson-Stenman and Henrik Svedsäter added a crucial control in their 2007 working paper. They randomly split 70 mostly graduate-student volunteers at the London School of Economics (LSE) into two arms: one completed hypothetical choices before real-money choices, while the other proceeded directly to real-money choices. For an extra unit donated to an elephant conservation project, the male reference group's willingness to forgo personal money fell sequentially from 0.64 (hypothetical) to 0.56 (real after hypothetical) to 0.23 (direct real payment). Comparing only the first two figures confounds real payment with prior exposure to hypothetical questions; the direct-payment arm isolates order effects, with the authors pointing to internal pressure for consistency as a plausible explanation.
claims.scope: Between-subject versus within-subject control for separating prior hypothetical exposure from real payment.

claims.text: While behavioral experiments test whether hypothetical choices track real payments, survey sampling asks whose preferences those choices represent. The subsequent second edition (LIME2) adopted a two-stage national design—first sampling locations, then drawing households from resident registries for in-home interviews. Roughly 2,000 households were sampled to target about 1,000 responses, and the published 2012 analysis used 952 responses across 147 locations. That study also introduced a random-parameters logit model allowing attribute trade-offs to follow a distribution across respondents. Broadening the sampling frame and modeling preference distributions address population representativeness and individual heterogeneity as distinct challenges.
claims.scope: National sampling frame, analytical sample size, and random-parameters logit modeling in the 2012 LIME2 study.

claims.text: The 2012 publication also explicitly specified an alternative monetary numeraire: the authors treated social-asset losses as equivalent economic losses and priced trade-offs across the other safeguard subjects against that benchmark. The national survey updated annual reference damages as well, and in the reported dimensionless weights biodiversity outweighed human health. Compared with the early Tokyo table, therefore, more than sample size changed—the sampled population, attribute levels, econometric specification, and valuation numeraire all shifted simultaneously. Although the authors interpreted higher monetary valuations as a sign of rising environmental awareness in Japan, they acknowledged that direct comparison is difficult; isolating a shift in public awareness would require controlling for those concurrent methodological changes.
claims.scope: Social-asset valuation numeraire and comparability limits between LIME2 and early Tokyo results.

claims.text: Comparative columns in later editions also merit checking back against original sources. The 2012 paper labels the earlier survey "2003," whereas both original articles' sample tables record January 2002. Moreover, all four monetary weights in the 2012 Table 4 column labeled "2003" match 2004 English Table 7 row for row. Establishing where a particular valuation comes from requires naming that edition's exact table and units; retrospective summary tables are useful for tracing connections, but they cannot independently verify the provenance of earlier figures.
claims.scope: Mapping between retrospective comparison labels in LIME2 and original LIME1 publication tables.

claims.text: Even with a national probability sample, practitioners must still clarify where the weights are being transferred. The 2012 paper restricts direct applicability to Japan. Applying those factors elsewhere requires stating explicitly whether the study intends to evaluate impacts through Japanese respondents' trade-offs or to estimate local residents' preferences, and justifying that choice accordingly. Similarly, the two behavioral experiments examined charitable donations and laboratory payouts rather than Tokyo household taxes and four environmental endpoints; they demonstrate how to test behavioral validity, but they do not supply a universal hypothetical-bias multiplier to apply to Japanese weights.
claims.scope: Geographic transferability of Japanese national weights and scope limits of behavioral control experiments.

claims.text: Placing the two early Tokyo LIME1 tables alongside Table 4 of the 2012 national LIME2 study reveals a non-monotonic reversal and re-reversal in the trade-off between human health and biodiversity. The implied species-to-health equivalence ratio jumps back and forth across the three tables: from roughly 1.343 million DALY per species in 2003 Japanese Table 7 (572,000 JPY/DALY versus 7.68 × 10¹¹ JPY/species), down to roughly 495,000 DALY per species in 2004 English Table 7 (9.70 million versus 4.80 × 10¹²), and back up to roughly 966,000 DALY per species in 2012 LIME2 Table 4 (14.70 million versus 1.42 × 10¹³). Consider two equal-service alternatives: Option C loses 0.010 DALY and 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ species, whereas Option D loses 0.002 DALY and 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ species, giving a break-even threshold of 800,000 DALY per species. Evaluating both options across all three tables favors Option C in 2003 (13,400 versus 16,504 JPY), flips to Option D in 2004 (145,000 versus 115,400 JPY), and flips back to Option C in 2012 (289,000 versus 313,400 JPY). Crossing the threshold twice within a single methodological lineage shows that a monetary single score cannot stand as a definitive verdict detached from its specific table edition.
claims.scope: Verification of a non-monotonic reversal and re-reversal across 2003 LIME1, 2004 LIME1, and 2012 LIME2 tables for a fixed health-versus-biodiversity trade-off (Option C: 0.010 DALY and 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ species; Option D: 0.002 DALY and 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ species; threshold 800,000 DALY/species).
caveats: The damage values for Options C and D are illustrative same-basis settings constructed to test behavior on both sides of the 800,000 DALY/species threshold; absolute yen totals belong to each table's numeraire and survey design and cannot be subtracted across tables as real social welfare gains or losses.

In 2012 LIME2 Table 4, the primary-production weight rises to 4.63 × 10⁴ JPY per dry metric ton, yielding a health-to-primary-production ratio of roughly 317.5 dry metric tons per DALY (still below the earlier example's 30,000 threshold); the exact species-to-health ratios across the three tables are 1,342,657, 494,845, and 965,986 DALY per species.

claims.text: If three monetary tables from the same school can flip a ranking back and forth, why not stop at the areas of protection and forgo cross-area monetary weighting altogether? Europe's flagship endpoint framework, ReCiPe 2016, makes exactly that boundary choice (Table 2). In Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) Report 2016-0104 and Huijbregts et al. (2017), ReCiPe 2016 aggregates 17 midpoint categories into three incommensurable areas of protection: human health (DALY), ecosystem quality (species·yr), and resource scarcity (future surplus extraction cost in 2013 US dollars, USD2013—such as 0.46 USD/kg for crude oil, and 0.16 USD/kg short-term or 0.23 USD/kg medium- and long-term for copper). Once those three endpoint indicators are reached, the method stops deliberately without issuing default panel weights for a cross-area single score, requiring any cross-area aggregation to introduce explicit user-supplied weights. Japan's LIME, by contrast, embeds cross-area trade-offs directly inside household choice cards, collapsing four safeguard subjects onto a single yen scale through marginal WTP.
claims.scope: Methodological contrast between ReCiPe 2016 stopping at three incommensurable areas of protection and LIME aggregating four safeguard subjects into a single yen score via stated preferences.
caveats: Some commercial life cycle assessment (LCA) software packages offer optional normalization or legacy panel-weighting sets for ReCiPe in database menus; those are software add-ons rather than components of the original RIVM 2016-0104 report or Huijbregts et al. (2017) publication.

claims.text: Stopping at three areas of protection does not, however, bypass value judgments: even within human health alone, time horizons and evidentiary thresholds can shift relative weights by more than two orders of magnitude. Suppose Option P emits 1,000 kg of fossil carbon dioxide (CO₂) and 0.10 kg of primary fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅), while Option Q emits 500 kg of CO₂ and 0.60 kg of PM₂.₅, setting a break-even threshold of 1,000 kg CO₂ per kg PM₂.₅. In ReCiPe 2016 summary Table 1.5, primary PM₂.₅ takes a constant health factor of 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ DALY/kg across all three cultural perspectives, whereas fossil CO₂ jumps 160.5-fold from 8.1 × 10⁻⁸ DALY/kg under Individualist (I, 20-year horizon) to 9.3 × 10⁻⁷ under Hierarchist (H, 100-year horizon) and 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ under Egalitarian (E, 1,000-year horizon). As a result, the CO₂ equivalence of 1 kg PM₂.₅ plunges from 7,778 kg to 677 kg and 48.5 kg. Compared against the European Union Environmental Footprint (EF 3.1) single score from the preceding discussion, 1 kg PM₂.₅ equates to 1,287 kg CO₂ for urban ground-level releases, 341 kg for high-stack releases, and just 61.4 kg for non-urban releases. Consequently, ReCiPe I and EF 3.1 urban ground-level favor Option P, whereas ReCiPe H and E as well as EF 3.1 high-stack and non-urban releases all reverse to favor Option Q. Endpoint assessment therefore contains two independent value gates: within-area time horizons and cross-area preference weighting.
claims.scope: Demonstration of two-orders-of-magnitude rank reversals for a fixed CO₂-versus-PM₂.₅ trade-off (Option P: 1,000 kg CO₂ and 0.10 kg PM₂.₅; Option Q: 500 kg CO₂ and 0.60 kg PM₂.₅; threshold 1,000 kg CO₂/kg PM₂.₅) across ReCiPe 2016's three cultural perspectives and EF 3.1's three air sub-compartments.
caveats: Chapter 5 of RIVM Report 2016-0104 reports the unrounded global factor for primary PM₂.₅ as 6.29 × 10⁻⁴ DALY/kg (rounded to 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ in summary Table 1.5); substituting 6.29 × 10⁻⁴ yields CO₂ equivalents of roughly 7,765, 676, and 48.4 kg across the three perspectives, leaving the ranking of Options P and Q completely unchanged.

Detailed scores for Options P versus Q: ReCiPe I (1.440 × 10⁻⁴ versus 4.185 × 10⁻⁴ DALY), H (9.930 × 10⁻⁴ versus 8.430 × 10⁻⁴ DALY), and E (1.306 × 10⁻² versus 6.878 × 10⁻³ DALY); under EF 3.1 (where 1 particulate disease incidence equals 5,397,458 kg CO₂-eq), urban ground-level yields 0.03147 versus 0.03548 pt, urban high-stack 0.02883 versus 0.01965 pt, and non-urban ground-level 0.02805 versus 0.01497 pt.

claims.text: Bringing Ecological Scarcity Weighting and this chapter onto a single diagnostic map clarifies the boundaries of four representative weighting and valuation paradigms in current life cycle assessment (LCA) practice (Table 2). First, Switzerland's ecological scarcity method applies distance-to-policy-target weighting, scoring squared exceedances of statutory limits along the single strictest pathway. Second, EU EF 3.1 applies hybrid midpoint weighting, multiplying 16 globally per-capita normalized categories by combined public–expert importance and scientific robustness. Third, ReCiPe 2016 stops at three incommensurable areas of protection while embedding 20-, 100-, and 1,000-year cultural perspectives inside them. Fourth, Japan's LIME uses stated-preference endpoint monetization, translating four safeguard subjects into yen via household marginal WTP—bypassing external normalization when summing unit valuations directly, but reintroducing national annual reference damages into the numerator when rewritten as annual share weights. Table 2 compares the core mechanisms and rank-reversal triggers of all four routes side by side.
claims.scope: Cross-paradigm synthesis of aggregation level, valuation authority, normalization entry, zero-inventory reversal triggers, and public-comparison constraints across four representative weighting routes.
caveats: The four paradigms rest on independent methodological premises; practitioners must not splice EF's 0.17 toxicity robustness multiplier, Switzerland's (F/Fₖ)² target-exceedance ratio, and LIME's household WTP into unvalidated composite factors.

claims.text: When assessment outputs carry yen or dollar signs, practitioners must take special care not to add conceptually distinct monetary metrics simply because they share a currency unit. Section 4.8 of the CML 2001 operational guide (citing Finnveden 1999a) emphasized that monetary valuation spans stated willingness to pay, revealed preferences, and abatement costs—fundamentally different economic dimensions. Across this and neighboring chapters alone, three incompatible monetary quantities appear: household marginal WTP elicited from LIME policy cards (subjective welfare trade-offs), ReCiPe 2016's USD2013 surplus extraction cost for resource scarcity (an integral of future engineering costs), and life cycle costing (LCC) examined in Life Cycle Costing and Integrated Assessment (actual market cash flows). Adding external damage valuations directly onto corporate LCC cash flows conflates financial outlays with hypothetical welfare exchange rates and risks double-counting environmental costs already internalized through carbon taxes or abatement equipment.
claims.scope: Incommensurability and double-counting boundaries among stated WTP, future surplus extraction costs, and market cash flows (LCC), grounded in CML 2001 Part 3 Section 4.8, ReCiPe 2016 Table 1.2, and LIME.
caveats: Even within stated-preference valuation alone, base-year exchange rates, purchasing power parity (PPP), and income-elasticity adjustments alter cross-country values; Japanese yen weights cannot be converted at market exchange rates into US dollars or euros and treated as local preferences.

claims.text: The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) Global Guidance for Life Cycle Impact Assessment Indicators and Methods (GLAM) Phase 3 Scoping Document explicitly acknowledges that no single weighting method is universally valid across all decision contexts, and therefore advances three parallel deliverables—method-selection guidance, a generic deterministic weighting set, and uncertainty probability distributions—while noting non-monetized multi-criteria methods such as the Preference Ranking Organization Method for Enrichment Evaluations (PROMETHEE), Stochastic Multicriteria Acceptability Analysis (SMAA), and LIME3's extension to the Group of Twenty (G20). Synthesizing international consensus, any study presenting a single score or monetary valuation must uphold three minimum reporting rules. First, publish the unweighted midpoint or area-of-protection endpoint profile alongside the single score so opposing trade-offs are never concealed. Second, disclose normalization denominators, robustness multipliers, cultural time horizons, and exact weight-table editions, rejecting undocumented software defaults. Third, whenever making a comparative ranking, compute the break-even ratio at which the verdict flips—such as 2×, 11/3, 1,000 kg CO₂, or 800,000 DALY per species—transparently handing back to decision-makers the boundary between what the model calculates and which value judgment decides the outcome.
claims.scope: Three mandatory transparency and reporting rules for any weighted or monetized LCA result, grounded in the UNEP GLAM Phase 3 Scoping Document and cross-framework guidance.
caveats: Mention of the LIME3 G20 stated-preference survey reflects only the methodological direction documented in the UNEP GLAM Phase 3 Scoping Document's references and expert survey; this chapter does not incorporate LIME3 country factor tables and therefore makes no country-level numerical comparisons.

claims.text: Real procurement decisions also confront a governance question: whose trade-offs should govern? Comparing conjoint analysis, multi-attribute value methods, and decision conferencing, Kiyotada Hayashi notes that who holds the preferences, when they are elicited, and whether they are formed around a specific decision problem all shape what weights can legitimately accomplish. Presenting disaggregated health, primary-production, and biodiversity damages alongside the chosen weight table, sampled population, and rank-reversal threshold allows decision-makers to pinpoint where disagreement actually lies—whether over the underlying damage estimates or over the relative cost assigned to each safeguard subject. Turning next to social topics such as working conditions first requires clarifying which actors bear what consequences and what kinds of evidence can substantiate them.
claims.scope: Relationship between generic valuation weights and context-specific preference formation in decision-making.

claims.text: Consider a hypothetical workwear procurement decision. Beyond comparing fabric mass and energy use across two garment options, a buyer can ask a different question: under what conditions do the people who make these garments work? The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) Guidelines for Social Life Cycle Assessment of Products and Organizations (2020) examine relationships between people and organizations along a product life cycle under the umbrella of social life cycle assessment (S-LCA), spanning both positive and negative potential impacts on multiple stakeholder groups. In this procurement question, workers are the stakeholder category, working conditions are the issue of concern, and the chosen indicators specify what evidence supports a judgment about those conditions. All three elements are indispensable, and issues such as health can also overlap with environmental life cycle assessment.
claims.scope: Assessment objects, stakeholder categories, and indicators in the UNEP 2020 S-LCA Guidelines applied to the illustrative workwear procurement example
caveats: A stakeholder category is not a directly measurable quantity of damage.
The UNEP 2020 Guidelines retain attribution requirements for educational and non-profit reuse as well as commercial licensing restrictions; citing the Guidelines does not alter the original rights.

The workwear procurement scenario, factory context, and protective requirements are illustrative examples created for this monograph; adjacent sections of the UNEP Guidelines use T-shirt and apparel trade examples to explain function and reference.

claims.text: To compare two workwear options fairly, an analyst must first specify the protective performance, use context, and service period, and only then determine how many garments each option requires to cover replacements. The functional unit defines the identical wear service both supply chains must deliver, while the reference flow states how many garments each supply chain must produce to provide that service. Requiring more garments increases material demand, yet it does not follow that a given social consequence scales proportionally with garment count. The UNEP 2020 Guidelines also discuss expressing the study reference in monetary terms for trade-based models; equal procurement expenditure guarantees neither equivalent protective service nor a life cycle costing result.
claims.scope: Product functional unit, monetary trade-model references, and threshold limits in Section 3.2 of the UNEP 2020 S-LCA Guidelines
caveats: Illustrative functional units in the Guidelines do not establish real-world equivalence between specific commercial products.
The suitability of trade data, product lifetimes, and threshold models still requires independent justification.

claims.text: When the question shifts to working conditions at a supplier over a reporting period, the assessment reference moves from a wear service to the organization itself. In the UNEP 2020 Guidelines, social organizational life cycle assessment (SO-LCA) is anchored to a reporting organization (or a defined part of it), its product portfolio, and a reference period—typically one year. A qualitative institutional finding may hold across that reporting period without being expressible as an annual impact rate, and it certainly cannot be divided by the number of workwear garments sold. The 2020 Guidelines explicitly state that SO-LCA is not intended for comparative assertions disclosed to the public; that boundary defines the intended application of the 2020 edition.
claims.scope: Reporting object and intended-use boundaries of social organizational life cycle assessment (SO-LCA) in the UNEP 2020 Guidelines, illustrated with a workwear supplier
caveats: Footnotes in the Guidelines retain discussion of how S-LCA social indicators may relate to a product functional unit.
The intended-use restriction of the 2020 Guidelines does not preempt applicability determinations under subsequent standards, regulations, or specific institutional schemes.
The supplier and garment counts are illustrative; no actual product-level impact is derived from organizational records.

claims.text: Replacing "100 person-years of protective wear service" with "all operating activities of a supplier during one year" changes more than the accounting perimeter—it changes whether indicators can be divided by output (Table 1). Under Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279, the Organisation Environmental Footprint (OEF) illustrates organizational reporting with apparel manufacturer Y Company Ltd. (producing 40,000 T-shirts and 20,000 pairs of trousers annually, totaling 17,000 kg, including canteen and gardening activities) and permits public comparative assertions between organizations in the same sector with similar product portfolios once normalized under sector rules and annual turnover. By contrast, the UNEP 2020 Guidelines define SO-LCA on the same "organization + product portfolio + reference period" triad yet explicitly bar its use for public comparative assertions. The divergence is mathematical: greenhouse gas emissions and water consumption scale additively with garment volume, whereas suppressing collective bargaining, workplace discrimination, or child labor represents an institutional state and a rights floor. Dividing a single union-suppression incident across 60,000 garments (0.0000167 incidents per garment) or across high-margin brand revenue would arithmetically dilute a rights violation through higher volume or higher prices.
claims.scope: Quantitative structure of product functional units versus organizational apparel-portfolio references, and the institutional divergence between UNEP 2020 SO-LCA and Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 OEF on public comparative assertions
caveats: Recital (18) of Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 explicitly states that the Recommendation covers environmental impacts only and that social and labor impacts of EU-consumed products in third-country supply chains are tracked separately; comparing its organizational reporting unit and comparative-assertion rules does not imply that OEF includes social indicators.

The corrigendum text of (EU) 2021/2279 (OJ L 144/215) retains two original printing typos ("fro" and "environemtnal"), and OJ L 144/218 computes weekly 30 °C machine-washing energy (0.4968 MJ) and water (6.9 L) from a single set of 1 T-shirt plus 1 pair of trousers (0.69 kg × 0.72 MJ/kg and 10 L/kg) rather than from the annual portfolio of 40,000 T-shirts and 20,000 pairs of trousers.

claims.text: Even with a fixed product functional unit, not every social indicator fits inside a linear matrix (Table 1). Heijungs et al.
