(2013) envisioned unifying social calculations through a linear social satellite matrix, g_soc = B_soc A_p⁻¹ f, yet comparison with the UNEP 2021 Methodological Sheets shows that this formulation holds only for extensive quantities such as direct worker hours, acute occupational injuries, or linearly accumulating inhalation doses. Ratios to statutory minimum wages, freedom of association, and weekly working-hour caps are intensive properties or threshold states: when factory capacity is slack, doubling an order from 1,000 to 2,000 sets can still keep schedules at 40 h/week with zero overtime, whereas crossing the capacity threshold drives hours to 65 h/week and causes risk to spike abruptly. Multiplying such indicators by a scaling vector would even double a violation score simply by splitting one sewing step into two unit processes. Consequently, the Product Social Impact Life Cycle Assessment (PSILCA v3) database in openLCA adopts two software workarounds: by default, it encodes risk indicators as pseudo-elementary flows multiplied by worker hours per US dollar (USD) of sector output; an alternative script sums raw percentage or Boolean values and divides by the sum of scaled diagonal entries in the technology matrix to obtain a supply-chain output-weighted average. Table 1 places five assessment frameworks side by side on reference basis and scaling boundaries; the paradoxes of back-calculating worker hours from monetary output follow in the next section.
claims.scope: The linear social satellite matrix conjecture (Heijungs et al. 2013), non-additivity of intensive and threshold social indicators, and PSILCA v3's two software encoding schemes in openLCA
caveats: The openLCA Python script in PSILCA v3 Section 5.4 (p. 103) notes in its comments that summing the diagonal denominator assumes all diagonal product flows are commensurable (for example, all expressed in USD); mixing foreground unit processes denominated in kilograms or garment counts without prior currency harmonization produces a dimensionally invalid sum.

The order increase from 1,000 to 2,000 sets and shift from 40 h to 65 h/week are a controlled illustrative example designed to demonstrate threshold nonlinearity rather than records from a specific apparel plant.

claims.text: Across a workwear supply chain, an analyst can track how many worker hours are invested in cutting, sewing, and finishing. The UNEP 2020 Guidelines classify such records as activity variables, which indicate a process's relative share in the system and can assist in aggregating certain results. Worker hours measure how large an activity is; injury records and observations of working conditions answer what actually happened to workers. Even when results are allocated or weighted by worker hours, an independent rationale is still required before claiming that harm scales proportionally with time worked.
claims.scope: Definition and usage boundaries of activity variables in Section 3.2.5 of the UNEP 2020 S-LCA Guidelines
caveats: Describing how activity variables function does not establish their suitability for a particular study.
The Guidelines' use of the term "elementary flow" in this context does not automatically map to biosphere exchange types in environmental inventory data formats.

claims.text: When supplier-specific records are unavailable, country- or sector-level data still serve a useful role in screening social risks. If those background data flag a process as high priority, the sound next step is to investigate the actual facility rather than inferring from a regional label that a practice has or has not occurred there. A single study may combine company-specific data reflecting actual facility performance with coarser background data indicating contextual risk. Reporting the two layers separately lets readers distinguish verified findings from leads for due diligence.
claims.scope: Distinction between contextual risk and facility performance and data-resolution boundaries in Box 11 of the UNEP 2020 S-LCA Guidelines
caveats: Risk proxies do not constitute definitive verdicts on any country, sector, or company.
Country- or sector-level statistics cannot substitute for site-level investigation and do not directly yield accident probabilities.

claims.text: Once facility-level information is collected, the Reference Scale Approach (Type I) asks where observed performance or risk sits relative to chosen benchmarks. Known as Performance Reference Points (PRPs), these benchmarks may draw on international norms, local legislation, industry practice, expert judgment, or peer distributions. For working conditions, comparing an observation against a statutory minimum and comparing it against an industry peer distribution answer two distinct questions. Reference scales ordinarily do not trace long-term causal consequences: scoring favorably neither measures long-term welfare gains nor confers formal compliance certification.
claims.scope: Scope and limits of the Reference Scale Approach (Type I) and Performance Reference Points (PRPs) in the UNEP 2020 S-LCA Guidelines
caveats: Whether a chosen reference point fits a given study requires explicit justification and cannot replace legal or certification audits.
Classifying Type I approaches in the Guidelines does not constitute a full validation of any specific database's scoring scale.

claims.text: Determining what health consequences might follow from a change in working conditions requires linking activities, exposures, and evaluated outcomes. The UNEP 2020 Guidelines define this second family as the Impact Pathway Approach (Type II), which connects activities to midpoints or endpoints through causal mechanisms or directional relationships established by correlation or regression. Although these pathways resemble environmental impact assessment chains, drawing an arrow does not prove causation. When available evidence suffices only to locate performance on a reference scale, Type I assessment remains valuable in its own right; analysts should push claims to downstream consequences only when the underlying models and data can support them.
claims.scope: Definition and evidentiary limits of the Impact Pathway Approach (Type II) in the UNEP 2020 S-LCA Guidelines
caveats: Defining the Type II method family neither validates specific pathway models nor licenses interpreting every statistical correlation as causal.
Methodological maturity documented in 2020 does not represent the state of practice in 2026.

claims.text: To bypass the non-additivity of intensive indicators, major background databases—such as PSILCA v3 (about 15,000 Eora sectors) and the Social Hotspots Database (SHDB; 6,441 country-specific sectors)—commonly bridge monetary purchases to social scores via worker hours per dollar of output (h/USD) or health damage per dollar (disability-adjusted life years per USD, DALY/USD). Yet within same-sector comparisons, that bridge triggers two structural paradoxes. First is the high-wage, high-price penalty paradox: in the same country, Factory A pays a living wage with zero injuries and sells workwear at 40 USD per set (1.0 h), while Factory B suppresses wages and sells at 20 USD per set (1.5 h with overtime); multiplying procurement spend by a sector-average factor assigns Factory A 2.0 times the risk of Factory B. Second is the automation de-employment paradox: multiplying measured worker hours by the same sector risk factor penalizes an artisanal cooperative (4.0 h) at 4.0 times the risk of an automated line (1.0 h). An internal contradiction also surfaces within UNEP's Global Guidance for Life Cycle Impact Assessment Indicators and Methods (GLAM) Work Environment method: whereas the 2026 main paper uses the United States as a global proxy and explicitly warns against cross-country extrapolation via economic ratios, the 2024 released workbook multiplies 411 nonzero US sectors across 52 countries by the inverse of national average annual wages (43,746 / W_c), making Turkey 28.76 times Switzerland while omitting India, Bangladesh, and Vietnam. Conversely, PSILCA v3's "Safety measures" indicator applies US violation rates uniformly worldwide. Neither shortcut can replace facility-level records.
claims.scope: High-wage/high-price and automation paradoxes in h/USD and DALY/USD scaling bridges, and the direct conflict between the GLAM 2026 paper's warning and its 2024 released workbook's cross-country wage-ratio extrapolation
caveats: Three primary GLAM Work Environment sources report different sector counts: the 2026 main paper (Fig. 7 caption) cites 362 sectors (and misprints an example pointer as "Fig. 72"), the electronic supplementary material (p. S23, Eq. 2) cites 397 industrial commodity sectors, and the October 2024 released workbook (lciamethods_CF) contains 420 sectors (row 385, man-made fiber manufacturing, lacks a North American Industry Classification System [NAICS] code; LCIAMethod_location shifts country codes right into column C starting at row 2; and FLOW_class header F1 is misprinted as "Classfied").

The two workwear factories (40 USD vs. 20 USD and 4.0 h vs. 1.0 h) are controlled algebraic counterexamples under fixed background sector factors to isolate price, labor-hour, and actual injury-rate effects; they do not represent measured corporate data.

In the GLAM 2024 Work Environment workbook (V1.0.2024.10), US representative sector factors (DALY/USD) are 6.662550 × 10⁻⁸ for apparel manufacturing (315000), 4.208644 × 10⁻⁸ for fabric mills (313200), 1.664539 × 10⁻⁸ for fiber, yarn, and thread mills (313100), and 4.501886 × 10⁻⁸ for textile finishing and coating mills (313300). Relative wage multipliers across the 52-country sheet versus the United States are 0.65450 (Switzerland), 1.06698 (Germany), 1.85399 (Japan), 3.26110 (China), 7.20452 (Mexico), 8.21826 (Brazil), and 18.82252 (Turkey). Most PSILCA v3 sectors fall between 0.001 and 1 h/USD, with pre-2011 values extrapolated at 3% per year.

claims.text: Because macro sector factors cannot stand in for factory performance, buyers frequently adopt a two-step workflow—screen with a database, then check certifications—yet each step carries blind spots (Table 2). During screening, SHDB omits sectors contributing less than 0.1% of worker hours, and PSILCA v3's cut-off experiment on German textile manufacturing shows child labor risk falling from 0.0868 medium risk hours (no cut-off) to 0.04864 at a 10⁻⁵ monetary cut-off (a 43.96% loss) and to 0.02 at 10⁻³ (a 76.96% loss); low-wage informal subcontracting readily disappears under routine expenditure thresholds. Field certification does not automatically prove improved working conditions either. Meemken et al.'s (2021) empirical review finds that voluntary sustainability standards cover under 2% of global agricultural land and roughly 2% of smallholders in low-income countries; five layers of non-random self-selection confound cross-sectional comparisons—capturing preexisting capability rather than net causal gains—and hired workers on small farms rarely benefit. Moreover, auditee-paid, pre-announced inspections in Ghanaian cocoa left up to 50% (internal) and 79% (external) of certified farmers uninspected, while 30%–70% of certified global production is not sold through certified channels.
claims.scope: Monetary cut-off blind spots in country-sector hotspot screening (PSILCA v3 German textile chain and SHDB 0.1% worker-hour cut-off) and self-selection and inspection-validity limits of voluntary sustainability certifications (Meemken et al. 2021)
caveats: Meemken et al.'s (2021) empirical review synthesizes evidence primarily from global agrifood and cotton-farming supply chains; while industrial garment sewing and dyeing face analogous subcontracting and announced-audit vulnerabilities, specific non-inspection rates in manufacturing require sector-specific empirical verification.

Documenting self-selection bias and inspection gaps in third-party certification does not deny the practical utility of on-site document checks for spotting policy omissions; rather, it establishes why certificates cannot replace unannounced inspections, worker interviews, and before-and-after evidence.

claims.text: Pushing assessment toward actual physical and mental health outcomes places the work environment across a thirty-year boundary between environmental and social LCA (Table 2). CML 2001 recorded that early studies lacked severity weights for non-fatal injuries and therefore counted only unweighted fatalities; the International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Handbook (2010) then drew a technosphere barrier excluding workplace exposures and accidents from standard biosphere inventories. Not until UNEP GLAM (Fantke et al. 2026) did the consensus methodology reintegrate roughly 70 million DALYs (70,000,000 DALYs) of 2019 global occupational burden into human health endpoints across five sub-indicators: non-fatal injuries (averaging 0.72 DALY/case), fatal injuries (33.3 years of life lost [YLL]/case, or 1.41 times the 23.6 DALY/death for fine particulate matter [PM₂.₅]), 235 workplace inhalation chemicals, indoor PM₂.₅, and occupational noise. Even within physiological pathways, contextual boundaries remain critical: the negative-DALY health benefits of leisure and active-transport physical activity (−1 × 10⁻⁴ to −4.8 × 10⁻⁴ DALY/h) cannot be extrapolated to occupational labor. Above all, freedom of association, equal pay for equal work, and prohibitions on child and forced labor are normative floors that cannot be converted into morbidity rates; a zero-injury log never substitutes for a fundamental rights assessment.
claims.scope: Thirty-year boundary evolution of occupational health in LCA (CML 2001, ILCD 2010, and GLAM 2026), the physical-activity health paradox, and the boundary preventing Type II pathways from replacing Type I rights norms
caveats: GLAM 2026 Table 1 reports fatal workplace injuries in years of life lost (33.3 YLL/death) and PM₂.₅ mortality in DALYs including non-fatal disability components (23.6 DALY/death); both figures come from Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2019 global average severities cited in that table.

GLAM supplementary material Section S-6 also notes that US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) injury records do not cover the entire US workforce and are subject to underreporting filters, so model outputs must not be read as a complete global census of occupational illness and injury.

claims.text: An ordinal scale establishes the order of performance levels. Once levels are mapped to numbers, whether consecutive steps are equally spaced depends entirely on the scoring convention chosen. When legal compliance serves as the reference point, a score of 0 means merely meeting the compliance floor—not the absence of social consequences. A second kind of zero arises whenever aggregation rules allow scores from different issues to be summed: an improvement in one category and a deterioration in another can cancel out to zero. Judging whether such a trade-off is acceptable requires keeping disaggregated results alongside their reference points.
claims.scope: Ordinal scoring conventions, compliance zero, and net-offsetting zero in the UNEP 2020 S-LCA Guidelines (pp. 82–87)
caveats: No single universal linear or nonlinear scoring scale is endorsed.
Distinguishing these scoring semantics does not judge whether any specific offsetting arrangement is justified or unjustified.

claims.text: Within Type I reference scales, the numerical spacing assigned to ordered risk levels can invert option rankings without changing a single fact on the factory floor (Table 2). The SHDB Social Hotspots Index assigns linear integers 0, 1, 2, and 3 to Low, Medium, High, and Very High risk and adds step-up bonuses of 10%, 20%, and 30% when worker-hour shares reach 0.1%, 0.2%, and 1% (capped at 100, excluding positive impacts). By contrast, PSILCA v3 Table 3 assigns base-10 exponential factors—0 for No risk and 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, and 100 from Very Low to Very High (with positive opportunities scored separately at 0.1, 1, and 10)—and multiplies them by worker hours to yield "medium risk hours." Compare two 100 h workwear routes: Route A combines 10 h of Very High risk dyeing with 90 h of Low risk sewing, whereas Route B combines 60 h of Medium risk weaving with 40 h of Low risk packaging. Under SHDB linear scores multiplied by hours, Route A (30 points) scores half as high as Route B (60 points; B is 2.00 times A). Under PSILCA exponential factors, Route A surges to 1,009 medium risk hours—15.77 times Route B's 64 medium risk hours. Modest linear spacing lets large blocks of low-risk hours dilute acute abuses, whereas a base-10 exponential scale equates 1 h of Very High risk to 100 h of Medium risk; the two encodings embed sharply different value judgments.
claims.scope: SHDB linear integer scoring with worker-hour share step bonuses versus PSILCA v3 base-10 exponential risk factors producing a 15.77× ranking reversal on an identical 100 h workwear route, plus primary-source errata verification
caveats: The native SHDB Social Hotspots Index sums scores across issues within a single country-specific sector before applying the 10%, 20%, or 30% worker-hour share multiplier, rather than directly summing score × hours across supply-chain sectors; the controlled example holds labor hours inside one weighted structure specifically to isolate the opposing discrimination behavior of 0/1/2/3 linear spacing versus 0.1/1/10/100 exponential spacing on concentrated Very High risk steps.

Inspection of the official PSILCA v3 documentation reveals two grading-table printing errors that must be flagged: on p. 41 ("Insufficient safety measures"), the table header misprints violations per 100,000 employees as "Indicator value y, DALYs" and reverses the Very High inequality to "y ≤ 0.06" (which overlaps all lower risk bands); on p. 55 ("Certified environmental management system"), High risk is printed as 0.0005 ≤ y < 0.005 while Very High risk is misprinted as "y < 0.005" (consistent with the gradient, it should read y < 0.0005). Analysts must verify underlying distributions before citing surface table thresholds verbatim.

claims.text: Numerical scale encoding also introduces three easily conflated kinds of "zero" (Table 2). First is the benchmark-threshold zero: the UNEP 2020 Guidelines assign 0 to meeting a statutory compliance reference point, and SHDB assigns 0 to Low risk—neither implies zero injuries or zero overtime. Second is the net-offsetting zero: Box 12 of the UNEP 2020 Guidelines warns that adding positive performance such as community philanthropy (+2) to forced overtime (−2) yields a net 0 that conceals severe abuse; PSILCA separates opportunities from risks and SHDB excludes positive impacts precisely to prevent philanthropy from canceling violations. Third is the missing-data zero: SHDB removes no-data issues from the denominator (implicitly assuming unknown items equal the average of known ones), whereas PSILCA v3 Table 3 explicitly assigns "no data" a factor of 0.1 (equivalent to Low risk), so 90 h of unrecorded activity automatically generates 9.0 medium risk hours. Before interpreting any "0" in a social score, readers must verify whether it denotes a compliance baseline, positive-negative cancellation, missing-data exclusion, or the relative worst-case zero used in sustainability dashboards.
claims.scope: Three distinct meanings of zero in social assessment (compliance/low-risk threshold zero, net-offsetting zero, and missing-data exclusion or nonzero default 0.1) contrasted with absolute zero harm
caveats: Imputing missing data at the mean of known issues (SHDB denominator reduction) versus assigning a fixed low-risk penalty of 0.1 (PSILCA v3 Table 3) introduces opposite biases when comparing supply chains with uneven data coverage; public reports must therefore disclose the share of no-data worker hours separately.

claims.text: Before handing social results off to Life Cycle Costing and Integrated Assessment, analysts must enforce a four-cell deduplication boundary sorted by affected population, exposure medium, and monetary ledger (Table 2). Cell 1—same label, different populations, never delete: outdoor smokestack particulates and dyeing effluent harm surrounding communities, whereas workshop machinery injuries and overtime harm factory workers; sharing the word "health" is no reason to drop either. Cell 2—same population, same pathway, never double-count: if environmental life cycle assessment (E-LCA) already activates indoor air toxicity (for example, a coating styrene factor roughly 211 times the outdoor factor) or GLAM work-environment DALYs, S-LCA must not add occupational DALYs for the same workers—and PSILCA's built-in environmental management items must be removed before pairing with E-LCA. Cell 3—separate cash flows from residual harm: ventilation upgrades, higher wages, and injury insurance premiums belong in the life cycle costing (LCC) ledger, while uneliminated, uncompensated residual health losses stay in non-monetary damage metrics. Cell 4—retain fundamental rights independently: freedom of association, non-discrimination, and bans on child labor are neither converted into DALYs nor offset against costs; they enter integrated trade-offs intact with their own reference points.
claims.scope: Four-cell anti-omission and anti-double-counting protocol across E-LCA, S-LCA, and LCC for workwear dyeing and coating supply chains
caveats: Applying the four-cell protocol requires auditing the actual inventory compartments and database subcategories enabled in a study, rather than assuming from pillar titles ("environmental," "social," "economic") that pillars are automatically disjoint or automatically redundant.

claims.text: Returning to the workwear procurement decision: a product functional unit and an organizational annual portfolio answer questions defined on different references; macro risk databases and output-to-hour ratios can only prioritize processes for field verification; on-site audits and reference scales locate factory performance against Performance Reference Points; occupational health pathways estimate DALYs for specific exposures or injuries; and fundamental rights such as freedom of association and non-discrimination remain independent floors. None of these social results constitutes the life cycle costing (LCC) of either the buyer or the manufacturer. Before Life Cycle Costing and Integrated Assessment brings environmental, social, and cost outcomes together, the analysis must keep straight who bears working conditions and health consequences, who pays wages and compliance cash flows, and which reference and zero each ledger employs.
claims.scope: Synthesis of multi-dimensional social assessment conclusions for workwear procurement and actor-reference handoff to life cycle costing
caveats: No claims are made regarding the actual conduct, compliance, or health impacts of any real supplier.

claims.text: Continuing the workwear comparison from Social Performance and Impacts, suppose two garment options deliver the same protective wear service. The buyer can then compare expenditures for acquisition, laundering, and replacement. The manufacturer, however, keeps a different ledger of production outlays and sales revenue: the purchase price paid by the buyer appears as income on the manufacturer's side. Finkbeiner et al. (2010) organize life cycle costing (LCC) around monetary flows across a product's lifetime while distinguishing producer, customer, and societal perspectives. Even under a shared functional reference, interpreting total cost requires stating which actor bears each outlay, receives each revenue, and holds each liability.
claims.scope: Actor perspectives, product lifetime, and functional reference in Section 2.2 of Finkbeiner et al. (2010)
caveats: The Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 (CC BY 3.0) license of Finkbeiner et al. (2010) does not extend to all rights or contents of the cited 2008 LCC monograph.
No cost parameters are supplied here; currency year, discounting, taxes, and actual cash flows remain necessary inputs for any concrete calculation.

claims.text: Do consequences not yet borne by buyer or seller enter this cost ledger? Finkbeiner et al. (2010) quote the 2008 definition of environmental life cycle costing (Environmental LCC): it captures life cycle costs directly borne by one or more actors along with decision-relevant externalities anticipated to be internalized in the future. Whether a future emission charge enters the ledger depends on the evidentiary basis for that expectation and on the study scope. Unpriced health damages cannot be entered as zero, nor does this definition claim to convert all environmental and social impacts into a complete social-welfare account.
claims.scope: Quotation of the 2008 Environmental LCC definition and its internalization boundary in Finkbeiner et al. (2010)
caveats: This claim adheres strictly to Finkbeiner et al.'s (2010) quotation of the 2008 monograph's definition; institutional boundaries across the three LCC archetypes and matrix cancellation mechanisms are compared later in this section using the 2011 code-of-practice paper, the UNEP/SETAC 2011 guidelines, and Heijungs et al. (2013), without extending to uninspected chapters of the 2008 monograph.
The definition supplies no external cost figures, prices, or policy outcomes.

claims.text: Placing the buyer's and manufacturer's ledgers side by side shows how monetary burdens are distributed between them. Merging those two ledgers, however, first requires defining the consolidation boundary: the same purchase payment appears as an expense on one side and as revenue on the other, so it cannot be counted as two independent resource outlays. Separating market transactions from unpriced consequences also keeps visible which burdens remain off the books.
claims.scope: Illustrative actor ledgers under a shared protective wear service
caveats: Distinguishes outlays, revenues, and external consequences only; no consolidated accounting or monetary valuation is performed.

claims.text: Before placing "life cycle costing" inside a life cycle sustainability assessment (LCSA), analysts must distinguish three archetypes coexisting in the literature (Table 1). The United Nations Environment Programme and Society of Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry (UNEP/SETAC) 2011 guidelines designate private financial accounting for a single organization—such as a buyer's total cost of ownership (TCO)—as Conventional LCC; they define Environmental LCC as aligned with a shared functional unit, tracking real monetary flows across the supply chain plus taxes and subsidies expected to be internalized within the decision horizon (for example, within two years); and they classify full monetization of both private costs and external damages as Societal LCC. Heijungs et al.'s (2013) matrix derivation proves why physical and monetary chains behave differently: emissions accumulate step by step along a supply chain, whereas product prices already condense all upstream costs and profits. Buying a car for 10,000 € and operating it for 40,000 € gives a buyer LCC of 50,000 €; adding the automaker's 6,000 € parts procurement double-counts costs already embedded in the purchase price. Inside a monetary technology matrix, intermediate sales cancel out (− and +), making end-user LCC equal to the negative value added of the use process; by the exact same formula, a cradle-to-gate intermediate product lacking a use phase yields a negative LCC—that is, positive net profit.
claims.scope: Institutional boundaries of Conventional, Environmental, and Societal LCC, upstream price-chain double counting, and matrix value-added cancellation
caveats: Swarr et al.'s (2011) 3-page open-access journal paper summarizes the methodology of Hunkeler et al. (2008; synthesizing a three-year working group) and the separately published 98-page SETAC code-of-practice booklet (2011; Table 1 lists seven working-group milestones from 2006 to 2011; print edition priced at 5 USD for members and 12 USD for non-members). Heijungs et al. (2013) note that the 2011 booklet contains only 1 equation, the 2008 book contains 5, and Table 3-1a of the 2011 booklet still double-counts R&D, pilot, and production costs alongside selling price. This comparison is strictly bounded to equations and citations verified in the open-access papers, the UNEP/SETAC 2011 guidelines, and Heijungs et al. (2013).

The negative value-added identity assumes that the terminal reference flow is a non-marketed use service (such as wearing garments or sitting on a chair) and that a given commodity trades at one price across actors; where wholesale-retail markups or turnover taxes exist, trade, transport, or tax processes must be modeled explicitly in the matrix.

In Heijungs et al.'s (2013) one-year wooden-chair sitting example, zero-maintenance LCC is 13.5 € and adding 10 € of annual cleaning spray yields 23.5 €. Conventional LCC traces back to 1933 US Government Accountability Office (GAO) tractor procurement.

claims.text: Under a functional unit of "four years of protective wear for one worker," actor ledgers and discount rates alone can reverse which option wins. Suppose durable Option A costs 116 € in Year 0 for one set (manufacturer cost 80 €, net profit 36 €) plus 16 € in laundering over four years (4 €/year), while replacement Option B costs 58 € in Year 0 and 58 € in Year 2 (total manufacturer cost 72 €, net profit 44 €) plus 24 € in laundering (6 €/year). First, actor incentives diverge: the manufacturer prefers higher-turnover Option B (44 € vs. 36 € profit), whereas at a 0% discount rate the buyer prefers durable Option A (132.00 € vs. 140.00 € total spend). Second, consolidating the supply chain cancels the 116 € internal payment: both options consume an identical 96 € in real production factors plus laundering, so the 8 € spread is purely profit redistribution between buyer and seller. Third, discounting alters intertemporal trade-offs: at a 3% social discount rate, buyer net present value (NPV) still favors Option A (130.87 € vs. 134.97 €); at a 10% corporate opportunity cost of capital, however, Option B's Year 2 replacement drops to 47.93 € in present value, flipping total NPV in favor of Option B (124.95 € vs. 128.68 €, with a crossover near 6.49%)—whereas standard 100-year global warming potential (GWP100) sums Year 0 and Year 2 emissions at an equal 1:1 weight.
claims.scope: Split incentives between buyer and manufacturer, internal payment cancellation, and discount-rate-driven NPV ranking reversal in a four-year workwear procurement example
caveats: The four-year workwear cash flows are a controlled teaching example designed to verify actor cancellation and discount-rate reversal exactly, not quotes from a specific textile supplier; the German bus capital and NPV figures below come directly from UNEP/SETAC 2011 Table 3 (citing Rüdenauer et al. 2007).

Discount-rate sensitivity follows UNEP/SETAC 2011 Section 2.3.1 (including a 0% undiscounted baseline) and Swarr et al. (2011) on distinguishing private capital opportunity costs from social discount rates; financial discounting reflects time preference for money and must not be misread as physical emissions vanishing over time.

In the UNEP/SETAC 2011 Table 3 German heavy-duty bus case (10-year holding period, 600,000 km, 2.0% fuel inflation, 4.4% discount rate), a compressed natural gas (CNG) bus carries an 11.26% higher upfront investment than a diesel bus (328,826 USD vs. 295,544 USD), yet gas-tax relief lowers its lifetime NPV by 4.03% (849,029 USD vs. 884,657 USD).

claims.text: Across this monograph, figures denominated in dollars, euros, or yen actually represent five fundamentally different monetary quantities (Table 1): (1) market cash outlays; (2) internalized pollution taxes or carbon allowance fees already recorded in prices; (3) stated or revealed willingness-to-pay (WTP) or abatement-cost valuation weights converting endpoint damages into currency (such as Life-cycle Impact assessment Method based on Endpoint modeling [LIME2] and ISO 14008 in Monetary Valuation of Environmental Damage); (4) future extra extraction costs for resource-depletion endpoints (such as ReCiPe 2016 in USD2013); and (5) sectoral economic output denominators used to back-calculate worker hours or occupational harm (in Social Performance and Impacts). Mixing these five quantities triggers two layers of double counting. Suppose fabric dyeing emits 40 kg CO₂ and the mill already pays a 50 €/t carbon tax (2.00 €) passed into fabric price: if Societal LCC fails to subtract that pure fiscal transfer while adding full climate shadow damage at 150 €/t (6.00 €), total burden is inflated to 8.00 € (true uninternalized net external damage is 4.00 €). And if an integrated assessment retains both environmental life cycle assessment's (E-LCA's) 40 kg CO₂-eq and Societal LCC's 6.00 € climate damage side by side, the same emission is counted twice across pillars.
claims.scope: Distinction among five monetary quantities across the monograph and proof of single-pillar and cross-pillar double counting between environmental taxes and shadow damage valuations
caveats: The 40 kg CO₂ emission paired with a 50 €/t carbon tax and 150 €/t shadow damage is a transparent algebraic example illustrating fiscal-transfer deduction and cross-pillar deduplication, not a statutory carbon price or official social cost of carbon for any jurisdiction.

References to ISO 14008:2019 rely exclusively on the public overview of use-value versus non-use-value scope in the UNEP Global Guidance for Life Cycle Impact Assessment Indicators and Methods (GLAM) Phase 3 Scoping document (p. 110) and do not extend to paywalled clauses.

CML 2001 reviews Finnveden (1999) grouping weighting methods into five classes; UNEP/SETAC 2011 reports a Japanese washing machine case (535 washes/year, 8 kg/wash) in which LIME external costs represent 3.74% of full cost for the older model and 2.56% of baseline full cost after a water-saving redesign.

claims.text: The same workwear procurement decision confronts energy and emissions, factory working conditions, and actor costs simultaneously. Finkbeiner et al. (2010) summarize life cycle sustainability assessment (LCSA) with the conceptual notation "LCSA = LCA + LCC + SLCA," placing life cycle assessment (LCA), life cycle costing (LCC), and social life cycle assessment (SLCA, also written S-LCA) inside one product framework. The plus sign signals that all three dimensions must enter decision-making—not that kilogram equivalents, social performance grades, and currency can be added directly. The UNEP 2020 S-LCA Guidelines further caution that the three pillars touch overlapping topics such as health; sharing a topic label is not the same as double-counting an identical consequence, which depends on what each assessment actually includes.
claims.scope: Shared conceptual scope and cross-pillar overlap cautions in Finkbeiner et al. (2010) and the UNEP 2020 S-LCA Guidelines
caveats: Neither source establishes a single unified cross-pillar accounting boundary or proves the validity of a composite sustainability index.
Because the two publications share overlapping authorship and editorial lineage, they do not constitute independent empirical replications.

claims.text: To obtain workable social data, Finkbeiner et al. (2010) discussed macro and organizational proxies—such as the Human Development Index (HDI), the Gini coefficient, and the United Nations Global Compact—while acknowledging that none maps directly onto a specific product. Just like the regional risk leads discussed in Social Performance and Impacts, regional or corporate statistics can flag priorities for inquiry, yet attributing them to a specific workwear item still requires documenting how those statistics connect to the garment's supply chain. Proxy values must not be treated as properties measured on the garment itself, nor should the indicators listed in 2010 be mistaken for a fixed contemporary checklist.
claims.scope: Social proxy indicators discussed in Finkbeiner et al. (2010) and boundaries on product-level attribution
caveats: Every proxy indicator and its allocation to a product requires independent data and methodological justification.
Regional indicators cannot establish individual behavior, corporate conduct, or inherent national traits.
Workwear is this monograph's teaching example rather than an empirical case from Finkbeiner et al. (2010).

claims.text: Suppose an environmental assessment estimates potential health impacts on nearby residents from factory emissions, while a social assessment records working conditions for sewing-line workers: both involve health, yet the affected populations and evidentiary bases differ. Only when two assessments actually target the same group of people, the same exposure pathway, and the same outcome must analysts inspect each pillar's accounting scope before deciding whether to display them side by side or consolidate them. Deduplicating mechanically by topic title risks erasing burdens borne by distinct populations.
claims.scope: Interpretation rules for comparing overlapping health-related social and environmental outcomes in the workwear example
caveats: No empirical case magnitudes are assumed for either illustrative pathway, and no assumption is made that all health indicators overlap.

claims.text: Requiring "equivalent system boundaries" across three pillars does not mean applying a single mass or monetary cut-off rule to prune the supply chain. Figure 14 of the UNEP/SETAC 2011 guidelines uses three intersecting circles to show that an integrated boundary should take the union of unit processes significant to at least one pillar. Single-dimension cut-offs create asymmetric blind spots: sewing lubricants or trace fluorinated finishes are negligible by expenditure, so a monetary cut-off misses key toxicity (just as a 10⁻³ monetary cut-off erased most child-labor risk in Social Performance and Impacts); conversely, garment R&D, compliance testing, and marketing account for substantial outlays yet almost zero material mass, so copying a mass cut-off understates manufacturer costs. Multifunctionality rules also diverge: International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 14040 prioritizes system expansion to avoid allocation in environmental LCA, whereas corporate LCC routinely allocates joint overheads by revenue or labor hours. Finally, Hellweg and Milà i Canals (2014) warn of cost-induced rebound effects: the 8 € saved by durable Option A vanishes in a static comparison, yet if re-spent on carbon-intensive goods or travel, economy-wide net emission savings can be partially or even more than offset.
claims.scope: Asymmetric union of physical and economic cut-off rules across pillars, multifunctionality allocation divergence, and macroeconomic rebound effects triggered by micro-level cost savings
caveats: Taking the union of pillar-relevant unit processes prevents single-dimension cut-off omissions, yet enterprise-wide shared activities such as R&D still require transparent volume and lifetime assumptions when amortized per functional unit.

Journal copyright for Hellweg and Milà i Canals (2014) rests with the American Association for the Advancement of Science; this discussion draws only on their published arguments regarding financial and time rebound effects and coupled economic-equilibrium uncertainties to bound product-level LCC+LCA inference, without constructing a general-equilibrium rebound elasticity.

claims.text: Moving toward integrated decisions also requires respecting the native mandates of neighboring environmental tools (Table 2). CML 2001 Appendix B differentiates risk assessment (RA), environmental impact assessment (EIA), technology assessment (TA), life cycle assessment (LCA), substance and material flow analysis (SFA/MFA), and environmental management systems (EMS)—a division reaffirmed by Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 and the International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Handbook (2010). For local concentration thresholds, site-specific RA and project EIA test whether the ratio of predicted environmental concentration to predicted no-effect concentration (PEC/PNEC) exceeds 1 to govern discharge permits: if Option 1 releases 10 g of textile auxiliary into a single low-flow stream and breaches local limits, whereas Option 2 disperses 20 g across ten large rivers while staying compliant everywhere, LCA freshwater ecotoxicity (comparative toxic units for ecosystems, CTUe) scores Option 2 at twice Option 1's burden yet cannot justify issuing a discharge permit for Option 1. For macroeconomic stocks, input-output analysis (IOA) carries 1–5-year statistical lags and aggregates heterogeneous goods within sectors, whereas dynamic material flow analysis (dMFA) tracks element-specific source-sink conservation across technosphere stocks, tailings, and the environment. Product-chain functional comparison, site permitting, and regional stock accounting answer three distinct questions.
claims.scope: Native scope boundaries separating product sustainability assessment from site-specific RA, project EIA, MFA/dMFA, and IOA
caveats: The 10 g concentrated versus 20 g dispersed discharge contrast illustrates the structural gap between linear aggregate impact potential and local PEC/PNEC thresholds; even when regionalized LCIA incorporates watershed dilution factors, footnote (54) of Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 explicitly states that it does not replace statutory RA or EIA procedures.

Suh (2004, Chapters I and VI) records Quesnay's 1758 Tableau Économique modeling monetary commodity flows across three citizen classes and demonstrates that certain early physical input-output tables (such as Hubacek and Giljum 2003) violated total mass conservation by omitting waste and direct natural-input closures; the short-term resource dissipation definition cited in the UNEP Global Guidance for Life Cycle Impact Assessment Indicators and Methods (GLAM) Phase 3 Scoping document derives from Beylot et al.'s systematic review of 45 papers.

Suh (2004) traces the lineage from Quesnay's 1758 Tableau Économique, Leontief's 1936 IOA, and the System of National Accounts (SNA) to Ayres and Kneese's 1969 mass-conserving MFA and physical input-output tables (PIOTs); the UNEP GLAM Phase 3 Scoping document summarizes dMFA thresholds distinguishing short-term (25-year) from long-term (> 100-year) resource dissipation.

claims.text: Commercial communication often seeks to replace multi-indicator LCA with single-issue metrics such as carbon or water footprints. Although Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 cross-references ISO 14067 (carbon footprint) and ISO 14046 (water footprint), it still mandates reporting all 16 Environmental Footprint impact categories, and UNEP/SETAC 2011 warns against claiming a product is "more sustainable" on low carbon or low resource use alone. Steinmann et al. (2016) quantified the information ceiling of reduced indicator sets by running principal component analysis (PCA) on 135 non-collinear environmental indicators across 976 ecoinvent 3.1 products: the first four principal components together explain 92.0% of product-ranking variance (83.3% from the first component alone), and an optimal six-indicator subset—climate change, ozone depletion, combined acidification and eutrophication, terrestrial and marine ecotoxicity, and land use—explains 92.3%. By contrast, the four popular resource footprints—fossil energy (62.8%), land (37.9%), materials (54.3%), and water (58.1%, highly collinear and adding just 0.5%)—jointly explain only 84.3%, leaving a 15.7% ranking blind spot. Burden shifts across cotton pesticide toxicity, water demand, and synthetic dyeing—alongside labor rights and cost conflicts—fall squarely inside that blind spot.
claims.scope: Variance coverage and burden-shifting blind spots of single-issue footprint standards versus multi-indicator LCA profiles in a 976-product principal component analysis
caveats: Steinmann et al. (2016, p. 3915) list the four nontrivial principal components individually as 83.3%, 3.9%, 3.1%, and 1.9% (which sum to 92.2% at one decimal place) while reporting their combined total as 92.0% (and rounding to 92% and 84% in the abstract) due to independent rounding; journal copyright rests with the American Chemical Society, and this claim summarizes only their statistical findings and limits.

The PCA rests on cradle-to-gate inventories per kilogram of base commodity without spatially explicit characterization factors; for energy-intensive durable goods in the use phase or fine-grained comparisons among close substitutes, inter-indicator correlations can shift, so the six-indicator set cannot serve as a universal checklist exempt from goal and scope definition.

claims.text: Side-by-side tables sometimes convert heterogeneous indicators into color bands or unified scores. In Finkbeiner et al.'s (2010) dashboard, relative scores are assigned according to the best- and worst-performing options within the compared set, with missing data flagged separately. A score of 0 at the bottom end simply marks the worst position inside that specific candidate set: it signifies neither zero impact nor an absolute sustainability threshold. Changing the reference set can alter every option's score—making this relative zero fundamentally different from both the compliance zero and the net-offsetting zero of social scales.
claims.scope: Semantic distinction between the relative zero of Finkbeiner et al.'s (2010) dashboard and the compliance and net-offsetting zeros of the UNEP 2020 S-LCA Guidelines
caveats: Dashboard examples illustrate scoring mechanics rather than establishing real-world product rankings.
Relative scores do not define absolute sustainability thresholds; interpretation is restricted to the source algorithm.

claims.text: When decision-makers still choose to aggregate environmental, cost, and social indicators, they must disclose both how each metric is transformed onto a comparable scale and what weights are assigned within and across dimensions. Finkbeiner et al. (2010) use a sustainability triangle and utility schemes to show how options compare once scoring rules and weights are fixed. Stating weights explicitly exposes value trade-offs—and equal weighting remains a value choice—yet the paper does not require every assessment to collapse into a single composite score.
claims.scope: Conditional utility aggregation in Section 3 of Finkbeiner et al. (2010) and weighting boundaries in the UNEP 2020 S-LCA Guidelines
caveats: Conditional diagrams do not constitute recommended weights or real-world option rankings.
Transparent presentation cannot substitute for methodological validity checks or ethical review of trade-offs.

claims.text: Feeding environmental, cost, and social pillars into a single multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) algorithm lets normalization scales and compensation assumptions rewrite the winner directly (Table 2). Finkbeiner et al. (2010) proposed the Life Cycle Sustainability Triangle (LCST) and an intra-set min-max 0–1,000 Life Cycle Sustainability Dashboard (LCSD); the UNEP GLAM Phase 3 Scoping document underscores that equal weighting is itself a subjective value choice and contrasts fully compensatory weighted sums and multi-attribute utility theory (MAUT) with non-compensatory outranking methods (ELECTRE and PROMETHEE). Three reversals can be verified on four-year workwear bids (carbon in kg, cost in €, medium risk hours in h, equal pillar weights). First, min-max dashboards violate independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA): Bid A (22, 120, 20) beats Bid B (30, 100, 24; 583.33 points) and Bid C (18, 140, 36) with 722.22 points, yet adding strictly dominated Bid D (58, 140, 28) stretches the carbon range and flips B (816.67) ahead of A (800.00). Second, compensation clashes with veto floors: low-price Bid E with forced-labor risk (16, 95, 80) wins under equal-weight min-max scoring (666.67 points), whereas ELECTRE with a 50 h veto threshold blocks it outright. Third, eco-efficiency ratios obscure absolute totals and diverge or invert as net cost approaches zero or turns negative.
claims.scope: Quantitative comparison of IIA violation in intra-set min-max dashboards, compensatory weighting masking rights violations, and non-compensatory outranking veto rules
caveats: The three-dimensional numbers for workwear bids A through E are exact rational teaching values engineered to expose min-max IIA failure and non-compensatory veto mechanics; real procurement using ELECTRE or PROMETHEE must set indifference, strict preference, and veto thresholds beforehand with stakeholders and compliance floors and test their robustness.

The UNEP GLAM Phase 3 Scoping document reports 20/31 member responses to its weighting subtask survey (8/20 using MCDA, 17/20 stating weighting choices) and notes that clients of the US Environmental Protection Agency Sustainable Materials Management (USEPA SMM) tool mistook equal weights for a value-free scientific method; Finkbeiner et al. (2010) similarly state that the LCST and LCSD aim to make weight trade-offs transparent rather than mandate a single composite score.

In Finkbeiner et al. (2010) LCST Fig. 4, Option A dominates when environmental weight exceeds 53%; when only environmental and social dimensions are evaluated, Option B dominates if social weight exceeds 43%, and B also dominates whenever economic weight exceeds 47%. Across Bids A, B, and E under equal-weight min-max scoring, the scores are E 666.67, B 577.78, and A 523.81.

claims.text: The rankings above answer which option is lighter, not whether the chosen option still fits within Earth's ecological limits (Table 2). The UNEP GLAM Phase 3 Scoping document classifies external normalization against planetary boundaries as absolute environmental sustainability assessment (AESA): a product's impact divided by its allocated share of the safe operating space must be ≤ 1 to remain within budget. O'Neill and Creutzig (2026) note that conventional cost-benefit analysis reflects substitutable weak sustainability, whereas the "doughnut" framework pairing ecological ceilings with social foundations embodies strong sustainability—carbon cuts cannot offset biodiversity loss, and cost savings cannot excuse labor abuse. Downscaling global ecological limits to a single garment still hits two barriers: existing planetary boundaries lack coverage of human health and abiotic resources, and sharing a global budget among products is a highly sensitive ethical choice. Suppose a person's four-year carbon budget is 4,000 kg and total expenditure is 40,000 €, comparing higher-priced durable Option A' (20 kg, 240 €) against lower-priced Option B' (16 kg, 120 €): allocating budget by expenditure share grants A' 24 kg (ratio 0.833, within budget) and B' only 12 kg (ratio 1.333, over budget); switching to an equal protective-service allowance of 18 kg immediately reverses the verdict to A' over budget (1.111) and B' within budget (0.889).
claims.scope: Weak versus strong sustainability paradigms, coverage gaps in planetary-boundary absolute environmental sustainability assessment (AESA), and budget-sharing principle reversals at the product level
caveats: The 4,000 kg four-year personal carbon budget, 40,000 € total expenditure, and 18.0 kg service allowance are a controlled example isolating how final-consumption expenditure-share allocation versus equal-service allocation flips compliance verdicts; they do not represent statutory personal carbon budgets for any country.

Journal copyright for O'Neill and Creutzig (2026) rests with Springer Nature; this claim summarizes only their paradigm distinction between weak-sustainability cost-benefit discounting and strong-sustainability non-compensatory "doughnut" boundaries. A review of product-level planetary-boundary sharing principles also appears in Bjørn et al. (2020), cited in the GLAM Phase 3 Scoping document.

claims.text: Returning to the full workwear procurement decision: purchase cash flows, internalized taxes, stated-preference damage valuations, and social risk hours follow distinct accounting rules; intra-set min-max dashboards, compensatory linear weights, non-compensatory veto thresholds, and planetary-boundary sharing principles each embed different value premises; and local permit compliance and regional material balances remain the domain of risk assessment, environmental impact assessment, and material flow analysis. Even without agreeing on common weights, decision-makers can begin by displaying procurement outlays, supply-chain labor-rights checks, and multi-indicator environmental profiles side by side—marking missing data, relative zeros, and non-compensable compliance floors—and prioritizing verification of the few assumptions capable of flipping the choice. Moving into Data Infrastructure and Evidence next, the immediate question is: which factory, which material, and which time period do the data in hand actually represent?
claims.scope: Synthesis of multi-dimensional value trade-offs in sustainability assessment and handoff to Part VI (Data Infrastructure and Evidence)
caveats: No real-world procurement recommendations, scores, or weights are offered; missing data continue to be reported separately.

claims.text: Suppose a database already contains a coal-electricity dataset—can it represent the electricity consumed by a target product? The 2011 United Nations Environment Programme and Society of Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry (UNEP/SETAC) Global Guidance Principles assign distinct responsibilities to three actors: dataset developers document how the data were compiled, database managers maintain shared conventions and communicate metadata, and users judge whether a dataset fits their specific study goal. Even when a dataset meets every database entry requirement, the user must still verify whether it actually represents the power-supply process needed for the study.
claims.scope: Three-party roles and user responsibility in the data chain as defined by the 2011 UNEP/SETAC database guidance.
caveats: This does not constitute a quality certification of any actual database or dataset.

claims.text: The first check is what kind of process "coal-fired electricity" denotes in the record. A dataset may reflect a single power plant or an industry average. Determining what it represents requires checking its technology, geography, time period, activity boundary, and intended application. The 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance places these specifications in the goal and scope of a unit-process dataset so developers know what evidence to gather and users can compare the represented process against the study's needs. This extends the goal-and-scope discipline of a full life cycle assessment (LCA) to the level of an individual dataset.
claims.scope: Goal and scope of a unit-process dataset in the 2011 UNEP/SETAC database guidance.
caveats: Matching process names do not prove that a database link is appropriate; the guidance's explanations are not independently verified International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standard clauses.

claims.text: The guidance illustrates non-applicability with two concrete examples. A Chinese coal-electricity dataset dominated by pulverized-coal boilers cannot represent circulating fluidized-bed boilers or combined heat and power plants because the underlying technologies differ. A second dataset supports several impact categories yet lacks data on most heavy metals, preventing its use for corresponding human-toxicity and ecotoxicity assessments. Both examples show how a dataset's documented coverage constrains its valid uses, without implying any general verdict on current coal-electricity datasets or contemporary toxicity methods.
claims.scope: Two illustrative dataset examples on printed page 61 of the 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance showing differences in represented object and flow coverage.
caveats: In the source, the second example lists global warming, ozone depletion, acidification, and eutrophication under the 1992 Institute of Environmental Sciences, Leiden University (CML) method; those historical scopes are not promoted here to current methodological applicability.
The guidance examples provide neither recomputable data files nor actual quality measurements.

claims.text: Before linking electricity or material datasets, a practitioner must identify each dataset's structural role in the database and its linking restrictions. The European Commission's International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) 2010 Detailed Guidance classifies process datasets into unit processes, partly terminated systems, and life cycle inventory (LCI) results, and ties applicability to decision contexts (Situations A, B, C1, and C2). By contrast, ecoinvent v3 strictly separates "transforming activities" from "market activities" representing regional consumption mixes with average transport and losses, requiring a global parent process (GLO) to be created first so that the Rest-of-World (RoW) residual is computed by subtracting local production volumes; the v3.0 release documentation also discloses that adding local data without updating GLO in tandem produced negative-exchange artifacts that were zeroed out or replaced by copying GLO. The European Union Environmental Footprint (EF) Guide for EF Compliant Data Sets (Version 2.0) goes further: in partly disaggregated models, the central partly terminated system carries full documentation, while minor supporting subprocesses are exempt from standalone quality rating and review and must never be reused outside their parent system. The TianGong LCA Data System Public Specification (TIDAS v0.3.0) likewise requires documented weighting bases for production and consumption mixes, prevents grid-loss or 1:1 transformer nodes from automatically turning into consumption mixes, and bars green-certificate contractual claims from rewriting physical generation technology.
claims.scope: Comparison of process dataset structural roles, regional residual closure, and mix-market naming across ILCD 2010, ecoinvent v3, the EU EF Compliant Data Sets Guide v2.0, and TIDAS v0.3.0.
caveats: The ecoinvent v3.0 record of zeroing negative residuals or copying GLO when the global parent was not updated in sync is a historical transitional mechanism disclosed in that release's documentation and does not directly represent the current state of subsequent commercial sub-versions.

TIDAS structured process-naming qualifier rules are marked as recommended definitions in the public index; whether downstream toolchains or products enforce them as hard blocks is governed by consumer policy.

claims.text: Why can a dataset rated top-tier in its home database be disqualified immediately in a specific study? Section 12.2 of the ILCD 2010 Handbook distinguishes intrinsic representativeness from external fitness for purpose: the former asks how well data match their own reference scope, whereas the latter asks whether they represent the process required by the study (for example, substituting a low-variance freight average at 80% load factor for a specifically fully loaded or lightly loaded shipment introduces systematic bias rather than random error). The EU Environmental Footprint framework formalizes this split as a two-stage Data Quality Rating (DQR) gate (Table 1). At the supply side, a power plant scored 1 on technological representativeness (TeR), geographical representativeness (GeR), time-related representativeness (TiR), and precision (P) relative to its own reference receives an ex-factory DQR of 1.0 (excellent). Once entered into the Data Needs Matrix (DNM) of Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279, however, company-operated processes (Situation 1) require company-specific primary data (DQR ≤ 1.5) and cannot be replaced by secondary databases. If that same dataset is used as an upstream secondary proxy without access to primary data (Situation 3) to represent a circulating fluidized-bed boiler in another country (GeR = 5) more than a decade removed (TiR = 5) with different technology (TeR = 4), its context-reassessed DQR rises to (4 + 5 + 5 + 1) / 4 = 3.75, exceeding the 3.0 secondary ceiling and disqualifying it. Only under Situation 2 Option 2, after substituting supply-chain-specific electricity and transport distances, may the original GeR be discounted by 30%.
claims.scope: Cross-stage comparison of the ILCD 2010 intrinsic-versus-external representativeness distinction with the Data Needs Matrix and context-reassessment formulas of Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279.
caveats: The ex-factory 1.0 score reassessed to 3.75 and the Situation 2 Option 2 reduction from an undiscounted 3.125 to 2.90 are controlled illustrative examples constructed strictly from Equation 19, Tables 24–25, and Section 4.6.5.6 of the EU Recommendation, not records of any specific commercial power plant.

Detailed Situation 1/2/3 thresholds: Situation 1 and Situation 2 Option 1 require company-specific primary data with DQR ≤ 1.5 (P ≤ 3 and each representativeness indicator ≤ 2). In the Situation 2 Option 2 illustration, with original GeR = 3.0, P = 2.5, and context-reassessed TeR = 4 and TiR = 3, the undiscounted mean is 3.125 (above cap), whereas applying GeR × 0.7 = 2.1 reduces the mean to 2.90 ≤ 3.0.

claims.text: Even if repeated measurements of coal consumption agree closely, the data still fail to represent the study's process if they came from a different boiler type. Table 4.1 of the 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance lists representativeness and precision as separate quality indicators: representativeness asks how closely the data reflect the target population's technology, geography, and time period, whereas precision describes the variability of the reported values. Deciding whether to take more measurements or search for a different data source begins by diagnosing whether the weakness lies in numerical scatter or in the represented process.
claims.scope: Interpretation derived from the data quality dimensions and dataset-scope rules of the 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance.
caveats: The table is the guidance's adapted version and does not substitute for the original ISO annex table; descriptions of quality dimensions do not supply empirical measurements of precision or representativeness.

claims.text: Distinguishing numerical scatter from process mismatch requires knowing whether a figure was measured, calculated, or estimated. What transport load factor or electricity mix went into a calculation? Those assumptions determine how the result may be used. The 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance recommends documenting key modeling choices while balancing transparency against commercial confidentiality and workload. Documentation should enable users to verify essential conditions and limitations; filling every metadata field does not guarantee sufficiency, nor must confidential raw records always be made public.
claims.scope: Documentation recommendations and confidentiality-versus-workload trade-offs in the 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance.
caveats: The guidance neither mandates disclosing restricted commercial raw data nor certifies that any specific dataset's documentation is sufficient.

claims.text: Turning representativeness, completeness, and precision into auditable records has produced four distinct architectures across major frameworks (Table 1). UNEP/SETAC (2011) sets qualitative dimensions side by side with no composite formula. ILCD 2010 scores six indicators on a 1–5 scale—technological, geographical, and time-related representativeness, plus completeness (C), precision (P), and methodological appropriateness (M)—assigning 5 to unknown items and 0 to not-applicable items while reducing the active indicator count. Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 and EF Guide 2.0 strip completeness and methodological appropriateness out of the formula as binary entry prerequisites that high precision cannot offset (fixing their Extensible Markup Language (XML) fields as "Not applicable") and score only TeR, GeR, TiR, and P. Chapter 10 of the ecoinvent v3 guideline takes a fourth path: instead of computing a dataset-level scalar score, it adds basic uncertainty and five pedigree-matrix indicators into an underlying normal variance on the lognormal scale for every individual input/output exchange (summing to 0.21 across the five worst-tier pedigree scores) solely for Monte Carlo propagation—an empirical calibration examined in detail in Data Quality Scores and Probability.
claims.scope: Cross-framework comparison of four data quality architectures and the prerequisite split across UNEP/SETAC 2011, ILCD 2010, the EU Environmental Footprint system, and ecoinvent v3.
caveats: The ecoinvent v3 sum of 0.21 covers only the five pedigree additional variances on the underlying normal scale at score 5; total exchange variance also adds the basic uncertainty variance looked up by substance and exchange category.

At score 5, ecoinvent v3 assigns underlying normal additional variances of 0.04 for reliability, 0.008 for completeness, 0.04 for temporal correlation, 0.002 for geographical correlation, and 0.12 for further technological correlation (total 0.21).

claims.text: When presented with an aggregated dataset, users may be unable to see which unit processes were combined, how they were linked, or how co-product allocation shaped the totals. The 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance recommends documenting what underlying data exist and whether they are accessible, explaining the linking and aggregation procedures, and preserving original flow detail. Totals alone cannot be inverted to recover internal processes, so documentation provides the minimum evidence needed to judge which choices require recalculation.
claims.scope: Documentation recommendations for aggregated process datasets in the 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance.
caveats: Documentation requirements for aggregated datasets do not imply that the dataset has been recomputed, nor do they mean that aggregation inherently degrades data quality.

claims.text: When inspecting inventories for elementary flows such as heavy metals, analysts must distinguish unmeasured flows, unreported flows, and confirmed zeros. Substituting zeros makes a table look complete without supplying evidence for impact categories that could not previously be calculated. The 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance therefore recommends that data formats and software distinguish missing values from true zeros. Partial records can still support correspondingly bounded analyses, but if an omitted flow matters to the conclusion, the analyst must either gather additional data or narrow the study's scope.
claims.scope: Recommendations on life cycle inventory (LCI) data gaps in the 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance.
caveats: This recommendation addresses missing LCI data and does not directly prescribe a four-state data model for life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) characterization factors.

claims.text: Even when candidate secondary datasets satisfy completeness and methodological prerequisites, aggregation formulas, single-indicator caps, and cutoff rules can trigger three distinct reversals (Table 1). First, weakest-link penalization versus arithmetic averaging reverses rankings: ILCD 2010 Equation 3 weights the worst indicator fivefold in the numerator, whereas EU Recommendation Equation 19 takes the unweighted mean of four indicators. Comparing balanced Dataset A (2, 3, 3, 2, with C = M = 2) against high-precision but geographically mismatched Dataset B (1, 5, 2, 1), ILCD rates A (2.60, basic quality) ahead of B (3.30, data estimate), whereas EU context reassessment puts B (2.25) ahead of A (2.50), with both passing the ≤ 3.0 gate. Second, a supply-side per-indicator cap can veto a low mean: secondary Dataset C (1, 4, 1, 1) averages 1.75 yet is rejected under EF Guide 2.0 because no single weighted indicator may exceed 3.0. Third, the 80% single-score cutoff can mask missing flows: EF secondary datasets rescale DQR weights over the most relevant subprocesses and direct flows accounting for at least 80% of the single overall score, and studies may also use ILCD Entry-Level (ILCD-EL) proxies up to 10% of the single overall score without recalculating DQR; if a dataset missing heavy-metal emissions sits inside the non-dominant 20% or the 10% proxy band of a climate-dominated total, it passes compliance while concealing a toxicity omission.
claims.scope: Quantitative demonstration of ranking reversals and blind spots arising from ILCD Equation 3 weakest-link 5× weighting, EU Recommendation Equation 19 arithmetic averaging, EF supply-side 3.0 per-indicator caps, top-80% rescaling, and the 10% ILCD-EL exemption.
caveats: Datasets A, B, and C are controlled comparison vectors constructed to test algebraic properties under fixed identical inputs; in real studies, if an omitted elementary flow breaches minimum completeness, verifiers may still require gap-filling or disclosure independently of the DQR score.

ILCD 2010 Table 7 tiers: ≤ 1.6 high quality, > 1.6 to ≤ 3 basic quality, > 3 to ≤ 4 data estimate (Table 8's example marks geography not applicable as 0, yielding 23 / 9 ≈ 2.56). EF Guide 2.0 rescaling example: 30% and 50% rescale to 37.5% and 62.5%.

claims.text: When reading a review record, check first whether it covers a single dataset or a complete product study, and second whether it applied database entry criteria or the requirements of the intended study. The 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance allows managers of a new database to evaluate whether prior reviews suffice and to commission supplementary reviews when needed. Users can build on work completed against explicit criteria, but a bare "reviewed" label never shows whether the review addressed the questions that matter to the current study.
claims.scope: Review object and review criteria for datasets in the 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance.
caveats: Printed page 90 carries an additional footnote qualification for full public comparative studies; citations in the guidance do not replace the applicable international standard clauses.

claims.text: Beyond stating the reviewers' qualifications, division of roles, and whether the review was internal or external, a review record should specify what materials were actually inspected—raw data, inventory methods, process results, or documentation—along with the checklist items, unmet criteria, and exceptions. To decide whether a dataset represents a given boiler type, a user can then tell whether reviewers verified technical conditions or merely checked record formatting. Documenting what was inspected clarifies the review's scope, though a complete record does not by itself guarantee that the reviewers' judgments were correct.
claims.scope: Review records and exception reporting in the 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance.
caveats: Completeness of a review record does not guarantee judgment accuracy, nor does it confer expert approval on unreviewed content.

claims.text: Even within a single guidance document, identical inspection terms can serve different purposes across chapters. Chapter 2 of the 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance uses "validation" to examine how faithfully a unit-process dataset represents a real process, listing completeness, plausibility, sensitivity, and consistency checks. By contrast, a footnote to Figure 4.1 in Chapter 4 scopes that chapter's terminology explicitly: "validation" may be a manual or automated check against criteria, whereas "review" denotes an independent, systematic, documented human examination. Determining what checks were actually performed therefore requires returning to the specific object and scope discussed in each section.
claims.scope: Two scope-bounded uses of validation and review terminology in the 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance.
caveats: These differing scales of usage are not treated here as a contradiction, nor are their definitions imposed on other documents.

claims.text: Mapping automated software validation against independent expert review across frameworks reveals four ascending institutional gates (Table 2). In ecoinvent v3, online ecoEditor routines perform automated validation—hard-blocking defects such as a missing global parent process (GLO) while issuing warnings for substance anomalies—and human review targets parallel scrutiny by at least three experts before transforming activities enter the database (v3.0 candidly disclosed that automated checks and three-expert review had not yet achieved full coverage). ILCD 2010 Entry-Level (ILCD-EL) accepts either one independent external reviewer without a separate report or one internal reviewer with a report. The EF Compliant Data Sets Guide v2.0 rejects both solo external review and two-person internal review, permitting only joint review by at least two experts including an external member, requiring a signed consensus report, and mandating recomputation of embedded results with Look@LCI (deviations exceeding 1% render a dataset non-compliant). For externally communicated EF studies, Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 requires verifiers to score at least 6 qualification points and mandates on-site verification of company-specific primary data. TIDAS v0.3.0 retains "Not reviewed" in its review enumeration and leaves blocking policy to downstream consumers: passing public schema validation proves that a record is structurally well-formed and honest, not that it has cleared expert review.
claims.scope: Comparison of automated validation, reviewer team thresholds, on-site verification, and schema boundaries across ecoinvent v3, ILCD 2010 and Entry-Level v1.1, EF Guide v2.0, EU Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279, and TIDAS v0.3.0.
caveats: Chapter 8 of the EF Compliant Data Sets Guide governs secondary-dataset entry review, whereas Chapter 8 of EU Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 governs verification of externally communicated EF studies; their rules on solo external verifiers and qualification scoring are distinct and non-interchangeable.

ecoinvent v3 writes validation outcomes to field 3340, and its three-expert target includes at least 1 economic-activity editor plus at least 2 cross-cutting editors (geography, inventory indicators, metadata, language). EF Guide 2.0 Table 4 approves Type 1 (≥ 3 reviewers with ≥ 1 external) and Type 2 (2 reviewers with ≥ 1 external) and requires two-significant-digit DQR reporting. EU Recommendation Sections 8.3.1–8.4.1 require at least 1 point on each of three criteria and a minimum total of 6 points.

claims.text: The 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance distinguishes among strongly recommended, recommended, and suggested practices, noting that "shall" in its text signals a strong recommendation. It also preserves minority viewpoints backed by facts, scientific argument, or practical experience. Because the degree of consensus varies, recommendations carry differing weight. Users can read these gradations as a snapshot of shared practice at the time of publication, but determining binding requirements today requires consulting the relevant standards, and the guidance does not exhaust viable methods.
claims.scope: Recommendation terminology and consensus-strength gradations in the 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance.
caveats: These drafting conventions belong to the guidance itself; they do not confer legal force or establish the complete requirements of EU methods or international standards.
External requirements cited in the guidance must still be verified against their original editions.

claims.text: The peer-review appendix of the 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance itself illustrates why review scope matters. Reviewers evaluated the submitted draft chapters positively overall while requesting more concrete guidance on allocation and cutoffs. Commenting on the dataset-review chapter, they noted that extensive checklists still left a gap in substantive guidance for catching subtle errors. Chapters 0, 1, and 8 did not undergo chapter-level peer review, yet the technical review panel still endorsed the complete document and collaborative process, and the editors stated that criticisms were incorporated wherever feasible. Reading overall endorsements, specific critiques, and actual review coverage separately clarifies both what an approval covers and where known limits remain; listing a critique in an appendix does not imply the editors left it unaddressed.
claims.scope: Evaluations and review coverage documented in Appendix 2 (peer-review report) of the 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance.
caveats: The appendix also records the editors' note that comments were incorporated where possible; it cannot be inferred that all critiques went unaddressed or that all were fully resolved.

claims.text: Official dataset metadata routinely display several "Fully compliant" entries alongside multiple "Not defined" entries; without understanding the five-aspect compliance block, a reader can easily mistake a valid declaration for a quality defect (Table 2). ILCD 2010 divides compliance into five aspects—quality, method, nomenclature, review, and documentation. The 2012 Entry-Level rules (Version 1.1) define 12 situation × quality Universally Unique Identifiers (UUIDs) for full Handbook compliance plus a separate Entry-Level UUID that fixes quality compliance as "Not defined". The EF 3.1 addendum (Valente et al. 2022) requires official EF datasets to carry six parallel compliance blocks (five when no category rules apply): the Recommendation and category-rule blocks mark all five aspects "Fully compliant"; the ILCD Entry-Level block marks only quality as "Not defined"; the ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 blocks mark the nomenclature, documentation, review, or quality aspects that each standard does not specify as "Not defined"; and the EF reference-package flow-list block marks only nomenclature as "Fully compliant". "Not defined" therefore signals an aspect outside an upstream standard's remit rather than a skipped review. When auditing machine-readable rules, practitioners should also note that a red heading on page 5 of the EF 3.1 addendum misprints the original Guide's Section 5.4.2 supporting-subprocess clause as Section 5.4.1.
claims.scope: ILCD 2010 Table 9 five-aspect compliance architecture, ILCD Data Network v1.1 matrix of 12 full-compliance plus Entry-Level UUIDs, EF 3.1 Addendum Table 1 six-block compliance declaration, and source section-number erratum.
caveats: Compliance-system UUIDs reflect only the institutional status signed off by the dataset publisher and review panel under the reference package active at release; migrating across package versions or reusing datasets in a new study still requires re-checking package versions and the Data Needs Matrix.

claims.text: Whenever a dataset is updated to a new version, check first which changes affect the original rationale for using it. The 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance lists technological updates, improved raw data, newly added elementary flows, and recomputed aggregated results after underlying data changes. It recommends reporting both the changes and their consequences, together with the exact review scope performed on the new version. Older records still document what was checked previously, but whenever a revision touches an earlier justification, the evidence supporting the new version must be verified.
claims.scope: Continuity interpretation linking update types and bounded review scopes in the 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance.
