caveats: Content changes must be reconciled with existing evidence, but not every update invalidates all prior review evidence.

claims.text: As background databases, reference packages, or plant operations evolve over time, whether prior applicability rationales and verification statements remain valid depends on three linked mechanisms (Table 2). First, background residual recalculation: adding a new country-specific activity in ecoinvent v3 cascades into recalculated Rest-of-World (RoW) residuals and downstream market shares. Second, reference-package drift and proxy downgrading: European Commission Joint Research Centre (JRC) testing (JRC130796) across 2,752 official EF node datasets showed that without changing a single physical or energy exchange, upgrading from EF 3.0 to EF 3.1 shifted the top-three most relevant impact categories in 6% (171), 10% (280), and 13% (358) of datasets respectively; Annex I Section 4.6.3 of EU Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 likewise downgrades legacy datasets converted without re-review to proxy status. TIDAS v0.3.0 enforces fixed-length version strings (NN.NN or NN.NN.NNN) that must increase strictly monotonically with content edits. Third, verification validity and deterioration triggers: Section 8.5.3 of the EU Recommendation caps verification validity at three years and mandates an update and re-verification during surveillance if any externally communicated impact category worsens by more than 10.0% or the single overall score worsens by more than 5.0%.
claims.scope: Integrated analysis of ecoinvent v3 residual cascades, EF 3.0-to-3.1 rank shifts across 2,752 official datasets and legacy-conversion downgrades, TIDAS monotonic versioning, and the EU Recommendation's 3-year validity cap and 10.0% / 5.0% re-verification thresholds.
caveats: The 6%, 10%, and 13% rank-shift figures in JRC130796 come from single-score testing of 2,752 official EF node datasets; whether a specific product model's dominant processes change rank still depends on foreground recipe weights.

claims.text: When the preferred compliant database lacks a matching secondary dataset, institutional rules replace ad hoc patching with a rigid gap-filling ladder (Table 2). Annex I Sections 4.6.3–4.6.4 of Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 establish a four-tier hierarchy and triple cutoff cap: use an EF-compliant secondary dataset first; if unavailable, use an EF-compliant proxy and record it under limitations; next, use a flow-aligned ILCD Entry-Level proxy, capped at ≤ 10% of the single overall score with DQR recalculation prohibited; if still unavailable, exclude the process and report it as a data gap for verifier confirmation. Cutoff exemptions are permitted only when excluded processes cumulatively account for less than 3.0% of mass, energy, and every individual impact category (including the single overall score) and are demonstrated to be insignificant. Addressing temporary shortages of EF 3.1 secondary datasets, the European Commission's May 2026 transitional guidance permits using ILCD Entry-Level datasets selected by the Technical Secretariat until the next-generation database arrives (projected for 2028)—and, where gaps persist, other secondary datasets subject to verification—while candidly acknowledging that this may reduce cross-study comparability. Table 2 summarizes the review, compliance, migration, and gap-filling boundaries across all five frameworks.
claims.scope: Comparison of UNEP/SETAC 2011 fallback gap filling, the EU Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 four-tier secondary ladder and 3.0% cutoff boundary, and the May 2026 EU transitional guidance.
caveats: The 2028 date in the May 2026 EU transitional guidance reflects that document's projection for the next official EF database release; the actual transition date depends on subsequent formal EU publication.
Relaxing secondary-data sources during the transition preserves operational feasibility without waiving limitation disclosures or automatically conferring strict cross-study comparability.

claims.text: Taken together, dataset representation roles, study-context representativeness, quality aggregation formulas, review and compliance declarations, and version-migration ladders define conditional fitness for purpose. When data are incomplete, the 2011 UNEP/SETAC guidance allows gap filling only if the candidate dataset is sufficiently consistent with the study's goal and scope and no better source exists, requiring item-by-item justification and explicit disclosure of which impact categories are affected by inconsistencies or omissions. The same coal-electricity dataset may therefore be valid under stated conditions for one calculation yet unsuitable for another due to technological mismatch, context-reassessment failure, or missing heavy-metal flows. Selecting a dataset means being able to state what it represents, why it remains acceptable or must be replaced, and which step better data would alter. Variability and Uncertainty next distinguishes how precisely existing observations estimate a parameter from whether the model captures the required mechanisms; Data Quality Scores and Probability examines how pedigree-matrix variances are calibrated against empirical distributions; and Product Footprint Rules examines how category rules govern public comparative claims.
claims.scope: Chapter-ending synthesis of conditional dataset use across representation roles, quality aggregation boundaries, review criteria, and version-migration gap-filling ladders.
caveats: Permitting item-by-item justification does not make every inconsistency or omission acceptable, nor does it replace study-specific rules, sensitivity checks, or uncertainty analysis.

This synthesis compares applicability boundaries across public guidance and methodological specifications; it does not substitute for on-site verification of real datasets or direct inspection of paywalled international standard texts.

claims.text: Several plants manufacture the same material, yet their emissions per kilogram differ. Imagine plotting a distribution. If the plot shows each plant's true emissions, it displays plant-to-plant variability; if it shows the estimation error when using available records to estimate average emissions, it displays uncertainty about the mean. The framework proposed by Huijbregts (1998) separates variability from uncertainty first, then distinguishes errors arising from measurement, data gaps, models, and methodological choices. This chapter draws on the text reprinted in Huijbregts's 2001 doctoral thesis; the taxonomy clarifies the examples that follow, though individual studies use varying labels.
claims.scope: Huijbregts (1998) taxonomy and the monograph's illustrative multi-plant emission distribution.
caveats: Discussions of the taxonomy and contemporary methodological feasibility reflect their historical context and do not rule out subsequent classifications or methods.
The opening multi-plant distribution is an author-constructed illustration rather than empirical plant emissions or a measured population distribution.

claims.text: Identifying which plants most merit improvement requires knowing how widely emissions differ from plant to plant. Building an average inventory for a group of suppliers instead requires defining both the target population and the averaging rule—for instance, weighting every plant equally or weighting by supply volume. Those two rules target different estimands. Even if the average is estimated with high precision, individual plants can still lie far from that mean.
claims.scope: Distinction between source variability and mean estimation based on Huijbregts (1998), illustrated with hypothetical plant weights.
caveats: Target populations, weights, and study objectives must still be defined explicitly in each concrete study.
Equal weighting and supply-volume weighting are author illustrations rather than universal sampling prescriptions from the source paper.

claims.text: Huijbregts illustrates this contrast with five plants assumed to form a representative sample from a normal emission distribution. The standard deviation (SD) measures how widely plant emissions are scattered, whereas the standard error of the mean (SEM) measures how precisely those five plants estimate the average emission; both carry the same units as the emissions themselves. The appendix also traces how plant-to-plant spread and measurement inaccuracy enter combined statistics: under the example's assumptions, dividing the combined SD by √N (where N is sample size) yields the combined SEM. That conversion cannot test whether the sample is representative and should not be applied mechanically to other sampling designs or weighted averages.
claims.scope: Didactic appendix on printed pages 23–24 of the Huijbregts (2001) thesis, preserving its sampling and distributional assumptions.
caveats: The original table values are not reproduced here, and the formula is not generalized to arbitrary sampling schemes, correlated observations, or weighted designs.

claims.text: Once plant-to-plant spread and mean estimation error are separated, a deeper boundary emerges: three sources of variation differ fundamentally in whether more data can reduce them. Groen et al. (2017) define inherent natural, temporal, and geographical variability as intrinsic properties of the system that cannot be eliminated by larger samples and must instead be captured explicitly through regional, technological, or temporal disaggregation; epistemic uncertainty stems from imperfect measurement or knowledge gaps and can be reduced through additional sampling and literature verification. Heijungs (2020) similarly partitions input uncertainty into lack of knowledge, inherent variability (such as lifetime differences across identical light bulbs), and analyst choices (such as mass versus economic allocation). Stuffing normative choices that belong in separate scenarios into a probability distribution—or expecting larger samples to erase real plant-to-plant and regional differences—confuses the statistical estimand from the outset.
claims.scope: Comparison of the tripartite distinction among variability, epistemic uncertainty, and methodological choices across Huijbregts (1998/2001), Groen et al. (2017), and Heijungs (2020).
caveats: In practice, part of what appears as inherent variability can narrow into tighter subpopulation spreads once technological or geographic classes are disaggregated, yet genuine variation within each subpopulation still cannot be driven to zero by repeated sampling.

claims.text: After defining the target estimand, the next question is what uncertainties affect the input data. Where a plant has repeated measurements, the bottleneck may be instrument precision; where no measurements exist and older records must be borrowed, a different kind of evidence is needed. Probabilistic simulations should state which distribution represents each parameter and incorporate parameter correlations whenever estimable. Simulation can propagate only the uncertainties encoded in the model—repeated runs never recover unmeasured emissions, omitted processes, or missing primary records.
claims.scope: Huijbregts (1998) treatment of parameter uncertainty applied to hypothetical plant measurements and proxy records.
caveats: Uncertainty propagation neither selects an appropriate distribution for any real parameter automatically nor certifies software implementation.
The plant instrument and historical-record examples are author illustrations rather than diagnoses of actual measurement quality.

claims.text: If a model retains only the sum of emissions or resource withdrawals across locations while environmental consequences depend on where they occur, the total lacks the information needed to assess impact. Watershed water consumption in Water Consumption and Scarcity Potential illustrates the point: knowing only total consumptive volume makes it impossible to match each flow to its watershed factor. Estimating total water volume more precisely does not restore missing location identity. Analysts must therefore check separately whether the model preserves the relationships needed to represent environmental consequences.
claims.scope: Distinction between model omissions and parameter intervals grounded in the 1998 framework, without attributing those historical simplifications to all modern LCAs.
caveats: This paragraph neither quantifies model omission error nor validates any specific impact-assessment model.

claims.text: Analysts also select the functional reference, multifunctionality handling, characterization model, and weighting scheme. Huijbregts isolates uncertainty due to choices and shows how parallel scenarios reveal their consequences. Evaluating the same emission inventory under two weighting sets, for example, can reverse the ranking of alternatives, demonstrating that weighting choices govern the conclusion. Without a probabilistic basis, two methodological options cannot serve as two random sample draws, and displaying them side by side does not imply equal probability.
claims.scope: Treatment of choice uncertainty in the Huijbregts framework and analytical assessment of probabilistic weighting; the closing sentence is an analytical interpretation.
caveats: This does not claim that no scenario can ever be assigned a probability, nor does this analysis substitute for original standard clauses.

claims.text: Before interpreting any interval plot, try writing its full title. If the plot depicts actual emissions across individual plants, the interval shows dispersion across the defined plant population. If it depicts the distribution of the estimated average under repeated sampling, its width reflects the precision of the mean estimate. If its two endpoints come from two allocation rules, the interval shows how switching conventions alters the result. Even when all three intervals have identical width, they answer three entirely different questions.
claims.scope: How to read distribution plots versus scenario-comparison intervals.
caveats: An interval whose endpoints stem from methodological conventions is a conditional comparison with no attached probability.

claims.text: Major international frameworks operationalize uncertainty and sensitivity analysis in sharply different ways (Table 1). Section 9.3.3 of the International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) 2010 Handbook requires sensitivity checks on key issues alongside stochastic and systematic uncertainty checks: goal and scope, multifunctionality allocation, and alternative life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) methods are tested through parallel scenarios, inventory and impact layers may use Monte Carlo simulation, improvements are prioritized where high impact meets high uncertainty, and Provision I.a warns that calculated uncertainty routinely misses systematic bias from model assumptions and data gaps. By contrast, Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 (384 pages in its OJ L 144 corrigendum) contains not a single mandatory "Monte Carlo" requirement: Annex I Section 6.2 merely recommends completeness, sensitivity, and consistency robustness checks, Section 6.3 mandates deterministic hotspot cutoffs (cumulatively ≥ 80% of the single overall score and at least 3 impact categories, > 80% of life cycle stages and processes, and ≥ 80% of elementary flows, recomputed with absolute values when negative credits occur), and parameter uncertainty is folded into the precision indicator (P) of the Data Quality Rating (DQR). The EU Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) thus trades probabilistic propagation for fixed hotspot cutoffs and semi-quantitative precision scores to secure regulatory auditability.
claims.scope: Institutional comparison of uncertainty, sensitivity, and hotspot rules between ILCD 2010 Section 9.3.3 and EU Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 Annex I Sections 4.6.5.1 and 6.2–6.4.
caveats: The deterministic hotspot cutoffs of EU PEF establish a regulatory reporting floor and do not prohibit academic studies from adding quantitative probabilistic propagation alongside required disclosures.
Section 6.3 of the EU Recommendation stipulates that whenever the use stage contributes more than 50%, hotspot stages must also be recalculated with the use stage excluded.

claims.text: Even after error sources and institutional frameworks are clear, the computational method itself shapes uncertainty conclusions (Table 2). Identifying which parameters truly drive output variance begins by separating local from global sensitivity analysis (GSA). As Groen et al. (2017) show, local methods—such as one-at-a-time (OAT) perturbations or partial derivatives—require only point estimates and measure marginal slopes near the baseline, ignoring wide differences in parameter dispersion and missing multi-parameter interactions. Global sensitivity analysis instead decomposes the total output variance of the matrix model g = B A⁻¹ f via conditional expectations, using the first-order sensitivity index S_j = var(E(g | p_j)) / var(g) to measure the share of output variance explained by parameter j across its full dispersion range; this requires at least central values and dispersions, and most sampling methods require full probability density functions.
claims.scope: Distinction between local point sensitivity and global variance-decomposition sensitivity based on Groen et al. (2017) Sections 1–2.1, Table 1, and Equations 1–3.
caveats: Global variance decomposition defines importance as contribution to output variance; a parameter with a very large point estimate but zero variance scores zero in GSA and must still be tracked through contribution analysis to identify dominant emission sources.

claims.text: In global propagation, first-order Taylor analytical approximation (key issue analysis, KIA) closely matches stochastic sampling at low dispersion but diverges markedly under highly dispersed, right-skewed inputs (Table 2). Using a 6-parameter electricity case and a 115-parameter whitefish fishery case benchmarked against one million Monte Carlo (MC) runs, Groen et al. (2017) compared single-pass analytical KIA against squared standardized regression coefficients (SRC), squared Spearman rank correlation (SCC), random balance design (RBD), and Sobol main-effect and total-effect indices (SME/STE). At a coefficient of variation (CV) of 5%, KIA nearly coincides with the million-run benchmark (electricity mean 128 kg CO₂ in both, variance 80.0 vs. 80.8; whitefish mean 1.95 vs. 1.96). When CV rises to 30%, however, first-order linearization misses both the upward mean shift caused by lognormal right skew (electricity 128 vs. 145 kg CO₂; whitefish 1.95 vs. 2.16 kg CO₂) and underestimates output variance by roughly 20%–33% (electricity 2,880 vs. 4,300; whitefish 0.606 vs. 0.76). When database inputs span wide right-skewed ranges, linear expansion systematically understates upper-tail risk.
claims.scope: Quantitative comparison of mean and variance biases between first-order Taylor KIA and stochastic sampling at CV = 5% and 30% based on Groen et al. (2017) Section 2.5 and Tables 3–5 (pp. 1131–1133).
caveats: These benchmarks assume uncorrelated lognormal inputs sharing a uniform CV; under other distribution families or mixed dispersions, first-order Taylor underestimation varies with model structure.
Groen et al. (2017) used N = 4,096 samples per batch repeated 50 times (Table 3 counts 2N base sample matrices for Sobol); at CV = 5%, whitefish variance is 0.0168 vs. 0.0170 (kg CO₂)².

claims.text: Even among stochastic sampling methods, global sensitivity indices differ sharply in robustness to high dispersion, outliers, and nonlinear interactions (Table 2). In the CV = 30% electricity case of Groen et al. (2017), right-tail outliers pull the explained variance of linear regression (SRC) down to 81.7% and RBD down to 79.7%. Rank-transforming the sample first keeps SCC at 94.0% (and 94.5% in the whitefish case), while Sobol indices yield SME = 91.6% and a sum of total effects STE = 110%—an 18.4 percentage-point gap that directly exposes interactions and nonlinearity induced by matrix inversion. The authors accordingly recommend SRC or KIA under low uncertainty and SCC or Sobol under high uncertainty, while emphasizing that both cases assumed uncorrelated inputs; in real supply chains with correlated parameters or nonlinear characterization models, correlations and nonlinearities must still be modeled explicitly.
claims.scope: Comparison of high-dispersion outlier and interaction robustness across SRC, SCC, RBD, and Sobol SME/STE based on Groen et al. (2017) Sections 3.2–5, retaining correlation and nonlinearity limits.
caveats: The parenthetical labels inside Figure 8 of the source paper swap Case 1 and Case 2; this paragraph follows the body text and Tables 4–5 on pp. 1132–1135 rather than repeating the printing error.

claims.text: Even with an appropriate stochastic propagation method, mistaking the number of Monte Carlo runs (N_run) for the empirical observation sample size (n) manufactures deceptive "spurious precision" (Table 2). Heijungs (2020) shows that running 100,000 simulations is not merely slow—it commits a statistical category error. Suppose the true population follows N(10, 1) under the identity model Y = X, and a researcher measures only n = 16 observations, obtaining a sample mean of 10.31, an empirical standard error of 0.25, and a 95% confidence interval of [9.819, 10.799]: the interval covers the true value 10, and imprecision remains visible. If that biased sample mean is fed as the input center into N_run = 100,000 Monte Carlo draws, the simulated mean stays at 10.31 while the simulation standard error shrinks as 1 / √N_run to 0.0031, collapsing the 95% interval to [10.305, 10.318] and excluding the true value 10. Increasing simulation runs removes only visible simulation noise while leaving input sampling bias untouched—disguising visible imprecision as invisible inaccuracy.
claims.scope: Distinction between simulation convergence error and empirical sample estimation error based on Heijungs (2020) Sections 1 and 2.5–3 and Figure 1 (pp. 395, 397–400).
caveats: This construction targets the misuse of the simulation mean's standard error s_Y / √N_run for population-mean confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; when used solely to stabilize quantiles (such as the 5th and 95th percentiles) of a fixed input distribution, large N_run still reduces Monte Carlo numerical noise without correcting bias in the input distribution itself.

claims.text: Comparing two product systems introduces two additional inferential traps: ignoring shared backgrounds and abusing large-run significance tests (Table 2). On one hand, Section 9.4 of the ILCD 2010 Handbook recommends evaluating the difference between two systems while accounting for shared-process covariance—plotting independent error bars double-counts shared electricity grids or upstream materials and masks real differences—and Provision II.d strictly prohibits interpreting "no significant difference" as "equal performance". On the other hand, Heijungs (2020) demonstrates with two identical N(10, 1) populations (n = 16 empirical observations each) that a two-sample t-test on the actual measurements yields p = 0.67, showing no evidence of a difference, whereas running N_run = 100,000 Monte Carlo draws before applying the t-test drives the p-value down to roughly 10⁻¹⁶, fabricating an "overwhelmingly significant" difference between identical populations. Heijungs therefore proposes capping the number of Monte Carlo runs used in hypothesis testing at the empirical sample size (for example, capping at 9 runs when two inputs have sample sizes of 16 and 9).
claims.scope: Synthesis of ILCD 2010 Section 9.4 (pp. 302–305) difference-covariance advice and Provision II.d misuse ban with Heijungs (2020) Figure 2 and Section 4 (pp. 400–401) on comparative significance distortion and sample-size caps.
caveats: Capping N_run at the empirical sample size is Heijungs's (2020) cautionary bound for Monte Carlo hypothesis testing; pairing simulations with effect-size thresholds or discernibility rates such as P(A < B) instead of relying mechanically on p-values is a parallel alternative in the literature, though it remains constrained by the empirical accuracy of the underlying input data.

claims.text: That sample-size bound strikes directly at the pedigree matrix relied on by mainstream life cycle inventory databases. In his abstract and Section 4, Heijungs (2020) states bluntly that when input distribution parameters come not from empirical sampling but from qualitative or semi-quantitative scoring schemes such as a pedigree matrix, the analyst cannot define an effective empirical sample size n and therefore cannot compute a valid standard error of the mean. Feeding uncalibrated pedigree distributions into tens of thousands of Monte Carlo runs yields results that look ultra-precise while lacking empirical grounding, creating a fundamental conflict between pedigree-derived distributions and large-scale Monte Carlo significance testing. This pointed critique does not negate the screening value of semi-quantitative quality scores, but it warns that converting qualitative ratings into lognormal probability parameters must first face the test of field sampling design and empirical calibration—the subject of Data Quality Scores and Probability.
claims.scope: Boundary between pedigree-matrix distributions and large-scale Monte Carlo significance testing based on Heijungs (2020) Abstract and Section 4 (pp. 394, 401), bridging to Data Quality Scores and Probability.
caveats: This critique targets treating pedigree-derived distributions as empirically calibrated random variables for significance testing; it does not negate the documentation value of recording semi-quantitative quality tiers during exploratory sensitivity screening or when measurements are unavailable.

claims.text: A further class of error lies inside computation itself. For a fixed process model and demand vector, if tiny numerical perturbations trigger large swings in the solution, the solver's numerical stability must be inspected. Section 2.4 of the publicly available sample chapter of The Computational Structure of Life Cycle Assessment (2002) separates numerical stability in matrix inversion from uncertainty in process data: the former asks whether given inputs can be solved reliably, whereas the latter concerns the empirical quality of those inputs. A numerically stable solution can still rest on inapplicable data, and reliable plant records can still produce an unstable linear solve.
claims.scope: Distinction between numerical execution stability and data uncertainty based on the 2002 author-linked sample chapter; does not cover complete numerical algorithms.
caveats: Condition numbers, rounding error, algorithmic stability, and finite-sample simulation error require separate analysis; distinguishing these layers is not a software certification.

claims.text: Before drawing conclusions from any uncertainty distribution or comparison interval, work through a five-step audit. First, identify whether the plot shows irreducible plant-to-plant or regional variability, reducible mean estimation error, or non-probabilistic methodological scenarios. Second, verify whether the model retains critical spatial and mechanistic links and whether the study follows an open scenario-plus-propagation framework (such as ILCD) or a deterministic hotspot-and-precision framework (such as EU PEF). Third, match the propagation and sensitivity method to input dispersion—at high CVs, watch for first-order Taylor mean bias, variance underestimation, and outlier distortion in linear regression. Fourth, in comparative studies, check whether shared-process covariance is captured on the system difference, separate simulation run counts from empirical sample sizes so massive Monte Carlo runs do not manufacture tiny p-values, and never equate "no significant difference" with "equal". Fifth, verify the numerical stability of matrix inversion independently. Data Quality Scores and Probability follows the empirical boundary of pedigree distributions next, using the Berlin yogurt-cup survey and pedigree-calibration experiments to test how sampling design governs standard errors and whether qualitative scores can reliably be translated into lognormal probability parameters.
claims.scope: Chapter-closing five-step audit and bridge to Data Quality Scores and Probability.
caveats: The multi-plant illustration in this chapter is not used to assume normality or representativeness for the empirical Berlin cup-weight survey.

claims.text: How much does an empty plastic cup for 150 g yogurt sold in Berlin shops weigh on average? Ciroth and Srocka (2008) reported a field survey addressing that question. Here 150 g is the yogurt fill mass, while the study weighed empty plastic cups with their labels removed. The authors framed cup weight as a parameter of the functional unit in life cycle assessment (LCA): an average cup weight helps quantify packaging material in the inventory, though the packaging's required function still has to be defined separately. Knowing how precisely that average is estimated requires knowing first which cups are being averaged.
claims.scope: Study objective and weighed object of the 2008 survey; the final two sentences explain its role as an inventory parameter.
caveats: Applies strictly to the plastic cups and sampling day described in the source; 150 g is not container mass.

claims.text: On the sampling day, any cup type present in a shop counted as one element of the population. Even if a shop stocked dozens of identical cups of the same type, that cup type was counted only once in that shop; if another shop carried the same cup type, it counted again. The average cup weight therefore reflects how cup types appear across shops. Footnote 7 on printed page 273 explicitly distinguishes cup-type shares offered to customers in shops from shares weighted by units sold: estimating a sales-weighted mean cup weight would require knowing sales volumes for each cup type.
claims.scope: Population element definition in Section 3.2 and sales-volume qualification in Footnote 7 (p. 273) of Ciroth and Srocka (2008).
caveats: Shop-offering cup-type shares cannot be interchanged directly with unit-sales shares.

claims.text: Sampling began at the shop level. The authors compiled a frame of 1,215 shops and drew a stratified sample by retail brand. Inside the selected shops, the study followed two routes. In the cluster route, 16 shops were subsampled as clusters and every eligible cup type in each shop was recorded. In the stratified route, cup types were stratified by material, transparency, width, and presence of a foot, and sampled within each stratum. Clustering by shop leveraged an existing shop frame, whereas cup-type stratification grouped cups by physical traits likely linked to weight. The paper notes shop closures and replacements and observes that the clustered shops lay outside the city center; if shop location correlates with cup weight, that spatial distribution can affect the estimate.
claims.scope: Two-stage shop-and-cup-type sampling design of Ciroth and Srocka (2008).
caveats: Because the source records shop closures, replacements, and spatial sampling constraints, nominal sampling fractions cannot be cited as proof of unbiasedness or complete coverage.

claims.text: Estimating the population mean cup weight requires accounting for how frequently each cup-type stratum occurs in the population. Let Wₖ denote the population share of cup-type stratum k and ȳₖ the sample mean cup weight within stratum k; the paper's annex writes the stratified mean cup weight as ȳ = Σₖ Wₖ ȳₖ. Larger strata carry greater weight in the overall mean, using stratum shares estimated from the preceding stage of the survey. The annex also gives a parallel weighted expression for the mean number of cup types per shop (in units of cup types), whereas at the cup-weight stage each observation is the weight of one cup type in one shop (in grams).
claims.scope: Stage distinction and weighted mean cup-weight formula from the annex of Ciroth and Srocka (2008).
caveats: Population shares were estimated from first-stage records; full stratum shares are not reconstructed here, nor is it verified that their estimation error was fully propagated.

claims.text: Stratum weights also govern how each stratum's sampling error enters the overall mean. Under Annex Section 3.5.3's cup-weight-stage definition, for fixed stratum weights, the estimator variance of the mean contains Σₖ Wₖ² (1 − nₖ / Nₖ) sₖ² / nₖ, where sₖ² is the sample cup-weight variance in stratum k, nₖ is the stratum sample size, and Nₖ is the stratum population size. Greater within-stratum dispersion increases sₖ²; for fixed Nₖ and sₖ², increasing nₖ reduces (1 − nₖ / Nₖ) / nₖ so that variance term cannot grow, while Wₖ² sets its weight in the sum. The cluster route instead divides total cup weight across sampled shops by total cup-type occurrences, giving shops with more cup types greater weight in the ratio. Knowing only the total number of cups weighed is therefore not enough to evaluate precision—one must know how cups were allocated across strata and clusters. On the results page, the symbol legend beneath the formula still retains first-stage cup-type-count definitions and is not fully harmonized with the annex's cup-weight-stage definitions.
claims.scope: Interpretation of the stratified estimator variance and cluster ratio estimator in the annex and Section 3.6 of Ciroth and Srocka (2008).
caveats: Raw observations and full stratum sample sizes, means, and variances were not published; the reported stage weights and share estimates cannot be treated as a fully audited sampling implementation.

claims.text: For the cluster route, the study reports a mean cup weight of 5.6589 g and an estimator variance of 0.0072 g². Taking the square root returns units from squared grams to grams, giving a standard error of about 0.0849 g. Dividing by the mean cup weight yields a relative standard error of about 1.4995%, matching the roughly 1.5% reported in the paper. That percentage measures how precisely the cluster sampling design estimates the mean cup weight.
claims.scope: Arithmetic verification of reported cluster mean and estimator variance in Ciroth and Srocka (2008).
caveats: The unit g² follows from the gram-denominated mean estimator and variance formula; it does not imply finer raw measurements than those reported.

claims.text: To see how widely individual cup weights vary across the defined Berlin population, one looks instead at the population cup-weight variance. On the same page, the study reports a variance of 0.72 g², whose square root gives a standard deviation of about 0.8485 g. Dividing by the reported stratified mean cup weight of 5.6474 g gives a relative standard deviation of about 15.0251%, matching the roughly 15% stated in the paper. Even when individual cup types vary substantially in weight, the relative standard error of the mean can remain far smaller than the relative standard deviation of the cups. Standard deviation describes how widely the population's cup weights scatter around the mean; standard error describes how precisely that mean is estimated.
claims.scope: Recomputation of reported population variance relative to the reported stratified mean in Ciroth and Srocka (2008).
caveats: The population here follows the study's cup-type × shop definition; it is neither a complete market census nor a sales-weighted spread.

claims.text: Changing how the very same observations are weighted alters both the estimated mean cup weight and its precision. The authors re-stratified the cluster observations by cup-type attributes and weighted them using population shares from the stratified route. After post-stratification, the estimated mean cup weight shifts to 5.7245 g with an estimator variance of 0.0014 g²—a standard error of about 0.0374 g and a relative standard error of about 0.6536%. Taking 1 minus the ratio of the new to the old reported variance gives a variance reduction of about 80.5556%. Both estimates rest on the exact same weighed cups; the difference comes entirely from the estimator and the newly supplied stratum shares.
claims.scope: Reported post-stratified estimates and relative change between reported estimator variances in Ciroth and Srocka (2008).
caveats: The variance-reduction percentage is computed from the two published variance estimates rather than re-estimated as a design effect from raw observations, and it does not prove that post-stratification always reduces error.

claims.text: The stratified route contains an internal numerical discrepancy in the original paper. Taking the square root of the results-page estimator variance (0.0034 g²) and dividing by the reported stratified mean (5.6474 g) gives a relative standard error of about 1.0325%, whereas the discussion section prints 0.07%. The published summary figures suffice to detect this mismatch, but determining which number needs correction is impossible without the underlying stratum statistics and calculation records.
claims.scope: Numerical comparison between printed pages 271 and 273 of Ciroth and Srocka (2008).
caveats: The cause of the discrepancy is undetermined, no original figure is overwritten, and the mismatch does not invalidate the entire study or sampling method.

claims.text: How well an average cup weight represents a target population depends on how cup-type occurrence is defined and how sampling and weighting are carried out. While the annex prints the estimator formulas, it omits individual cup weights, stratum-level statistics, and shop-to-cup-type shares. Published summary figures allow checking square roots and ratios and separating population spread from mean precision, but reproducing means and variances from scratch requires raw weighing records and sampling-design files. When the 2012 pedigree report later reuses these cup-weight data to propose completeness factors, the same audit applies: one must separate steps verifiable from published tables from steps that depend on unpublished raw data.
claims.scope: Hierarchy distinguishing sampling design, published summary estimates, and raw-data reproducibility in Ciroth and Srocka (2008).
caveats: Raw survey files were not obtained; no observations were reconstructed by back-calculation or figure digitization.

claims.text: How complete an inventory record is represents one dimension evaluated by a pedigree matrix. Ciroth's May 2012 Version 7.1 method-development report also lists reliability, temporal, geographical, and technological indicators, allowing records to be tiered according to verification status and distance from the study's target time, geography, or technology. Those tiers describe qualitative attributes of the data; the report supplies separate uncertainty factors and conversion steps. A quality tier alone never tells an analyst what the standard deviation of observations is or how to assign a probability distribution to a parameter.
claims.scope: Pedigree framework presented in the May 2012 Version 7.1 report; not a reconstruction of Weidema and Wesnæs (1996).
caveats: Descriptions in the 2012 follow-up report do not substitute for every original definition in Weidema and Wesnæs (1996).

claims.text: The 2012 report attempts to ground pedigree uncertainty factors empirically using the dispersion of data assigned to each tier. After harmonizing units and scales, it filters or groups records along a given indicator, compares each group's spread against a reference group, and seeks cross-checks across multiple data sources. For completeness, the Berlin cup-weight dataset offered a concrete testbed: taking subsets of the available observations reveals how within-group dispersion changes as data coverage shrinks.
claims.scope: Calibration procedure described in Sections 4.4–4.5 of the May 2012 report; not an independent statistical recomputation.
caveats: Geometric standard deviations, log standard deviations, squared factors, and interval parameters cannot be interchanged by name.

claims.text: In its completeness reanalysis, the 2012 report constructed 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% subsets of the available cup-weight data and compared their variances and geometric standard deviations. Here 100% refers strictly to all data available in the dataset—as the annex notes, even that full set remained only a sample of the Berlin market. Completeness is always relative to a reference: using 100% of an existing sample is not the same as covering the entire Berlin market.
claims.scope: Reference group and subsets used in the 2012 completeness reanalysis.
caveats: Exact subset memberships, full resampling procedures, and raw database files were not obtained.

claims.text: Coverage fractions still have to be mapped onto pedigree score tiers. The 2012 report mapped 100%, 75%, and 50% to scores 1, 2, and 3 respectively, and used a single supermarket's sample to represent score 4, explaining that score 3 was set at 50% to compensate for limited representativeness of the surveyed supermarkets. Because the original pedigree descriptions combine coverage shares with representativeness assumptions, turning a fraction into a score requires judging how well the data represent the target. Moreover, the correspondence between the 25% plot and the text's "one supermarket" description still does not specify which exact observations entered each subset.
claims.scope: Source-internal mapping between completeness subsets and pedigree score thresholds in the 2012 report.
caveats: This operationalization cannot be generalized as an automatic scoring rule for all datasets; the incomplete disclosure linking figures and text constructions is retained as a boundary.

claims.text: Ordinary variance measures spread on an additive scale. To compare multiplicative spread among positive cup weights, one computes the geometric standard deviation (GSD). Writing the i-th value as xᵢ and the geometric mean as x_g, the report defines G = exp{√[Σᵢ (ln(xᵢ / x_g))² / n]}: take logarithms of each observation's ratio to the geometric mean, average their squares, take the square root, and exponentiate. The resulting G is dimensionless with a minimum of 1. Multiplying every value by a positive constant (such as converting grams to kilograms) leaves all ratios—and hence G—unchanged, whereas adding a constant mass to every observation offers no such invariance. With denominator n, G is purely a descriptive statistic of the available sample and by itself does not prove that the data follow a lognormal distribution.
claims.scope: Empirical GSD with denominator n and its positive-scale invariance in the 2012 report and 2016 journal article.
caveats: Requires strictly positive values; denominator n is the source's definition and cannot be changed silently to n − 1.
The journal article's printed claim of arbitrary affine invariance does not hold mathematically; only positive-scale invariance follows from the definition.

claims.text: The completeness reanalysis compares the dispersion of two groups. The 2012 report explicitly divides the GSD of the available population by the GSD of a subsample, displaying results by supermarket chain while noting that the ratio itself varies. That ratio measures the relative multiplicative spread of the available population versus the subsample; using it to infer how far a specific inventory parameter lies from its true value still lacks a bridge linking within-group spread to parameter error. Even as a heuristic for proposing pedigree factors, one must state which reference group was chosen, how subsets were formed, and how chain-level ratios were summarized into a single number.
claims.scope: Interpretive boundary between the 2012 completeness GSD ratio and general uncertainty factors.
caveats: Exact sample and population GSD calculations, replication counts, and aggregation weights cannot be recovered from the published figures alone.

claims.text: The 2012 report compares subsample ratios in Figure 20, groups them by completeness tier in Figure 21, and lists provisional GSD factors of 1.032982251, 1.041623865, and 1.084355355 for scores 2, 3, and 4—values that round to two decimal places as the recommended 1.03, 1.04, and 1.08. The 2016 journal paper retains those recommendations under a GSD header, still listing 1.03 for score 2. Score 5 is marked "not available"; filling it in with 1 would assign a substantive factor with no basis in the table.
claims.scope: Rounding from high-precision provisional values to recommended factors in the 2012 report and table-header alignment with the 2016 journal article.
caveats: This verifies table-level rounding and cross-version consistency without reconstructing the multi-decimal values from raw samples; extra decimal digits do not constitute stronger empirical precision.

claims.text: Published tables let a reader verify how provisional factors round to recommended values, but recomputing the provisional factors from cup-weight observations is impossible without exact subset memberships, selection rules, and the aggregation steps combining supermarket chains. The 2016 journal paper refers readers back to the 2012 report for completeness details; it rests on the exact same Berlin survey rather than an independent cup-weight experiment.
claims.scope: Relationship between the 2012 report and the 2016 journal paper relying on the same empirical material.
caveats: Unobtained raw files do not imply that no data existed, nor does access to the journal article imply access to the raw dataset.

claims.text: The 2012 report also flags two substantive limitations. When estimating reliability factors, different data sources yielded conflicting results, and the authors noted that measured items and estimated items may differ intrinsically—meaning dispersion differences need not stem solely from reliability. Meanwhile, the completeness factors came from a single survey of homogeneous yogurt cups and were presented strictly as provisional. The exercise demonstrates how empirical records can generate candidate factors, but applying those factors to other industrial sectors still requires sector-appropriate evidence.
claims.scope: Analytical conclusions on printed pages 27–31 of the 2012 report; does not cover all subsequent refinements.
caveats: These source-specific and sampling findings do not establish independent cross-sector external validity.

claims.text: To derive candidate factors from group dispersions, the 2016 journal article states a general rule: for a given quality indicator, denote the best-tier group's GSD as G₁ and tier j's GSD as Gⱼ, and set R = max(Gⱼ / G₁, G₁ / Gⱼ). Taking the larger of the ratio and its reciprocal guarantees R ≥ 1, and comparing the best tier to itself yields 1 even when that group still exhibits internal spread. If the best-tier group happens to be more dispersed than tier j, the rule takes the reciprocal and still produces R > 1—preserving only the multiplicative gap, so identifying which group was actually wider requires checking G₁ and Gⱼ directly.
claims.scope: Directionality and reference meaning of the general candidate-ratio rule in Section 2.6 of Ciroth et al. (2016).
caveats: This is the source paper's proposed candidate rule, not a causal estimate of how quality tiers affect error.

claims.text: The paper illustrates the rule using the data quality indicator "temporal correlation"—which measures how close a dataset's reference period is to the study's target period, not time-series autocorrelation. In the authors' hypothetical example, the best-tier group has GSD = 1.3 and another tier has GSD = 3.2; dividing the larger by the smaller gives R ≈ 2.4615. Both inputs are hypothetical illustrations unrelated to the Berlin cup-weight survey. A different dataset would produce a different candidate ratio, and choosing a final factor requires weighing multiple sources. Once a ratio is obtained, inventory modeling still requires one further decision: defining what role that number plays inside a probability distribution.
claims.scope: Ratio recomputation for the hypothetical temporal-correlation illustration in Section 2.6 of Ciroth et al. (2016).
caveats: These illustrative numbers must not be labeled as empirical Berlin cup-weight calibration results.

claims.text: Suppose an inventory parameter X is the product of several multiplicative components whose logarithms are mutually independent and normally distributed. Taking logarithms turns the product into a sum; independence sets all covariances to zero, so the total variance equals the sum of component variances. Letting g_b denote the basic component's GSD and gᵢ the i-th additional component's GSD, the combined GSD g_T satisfies [ln(g_T)]² = [ln(g_b)]² + Σᵢ [ln(gᵢ)]², where each squared log-GSD is a log-scale variance. If components are correlated, log-scale covariances are also required, and individual GSDs alone cannot determine total spread.
claims.scope: Conditional aggregation of independent lognormal multiplicative components.
caveats: Whether empirical data satisfy lognormality, independence, and the chosen center must be evaluated separately; true covariances were not measured.

claims.text: Returning to the hypothetical temporal-correlation numbers, one can ask a different algebraic question: taking GSD = 1.3 as the baseline, how large an independent multiplicative component must be added to reach a total GSD of exactly 3.2? A nonnegative log-variance increment exists only when the target GSD is at least as large as the baseline. Taking the square root of the difference between total and baseline log-variances and exponentiating gives exp{√[[ln(3.2)]² − [ln(1.3)]²]} ≈ 3.1055. By contrast, inserting the paper's candidate ratio R as an independent component yields a combined GSD of about 2.5554, whereas the log-variance residual reproduces 3.2000 exactly. The two formulas answer different questions; setting 1.3 as baseline and 3.2 as target serves purely as an algebraic comparison, not as a recommendation for an alternative default factor.
claims.scope: Algebraic comparison between the direct ratio R and the log-variance residual required to reproduce a target GSD under an added independent component.
caveats: The source paper does not designate the best-tier GSD as a universal basic uncertainty term for real inventories; that baseline choice is a condition of this comparison.
Applies only when the target GSD is at least as large as the baseline; provides neither empirical validation nor an alternative recommended factor.

claims.text: Even after deciding which spread to represent, the numbers entered into a formula must match its parameter convention. While the 2016 journal table reports GSD values (g), its aggregation equation expresses basic, additional, and total uncertainty factors as squared GSDs (U = g², so ln(U) = 2 ln(g)). Converting basic, additional, and total terms consistently leaves the underlying dispersion unchanged and defines the exact same distribution for a fixed center. For instance, the provisional completeness factor g = 1.03 enters a squared-GSD slot as 1.0609; copying g directly into a squared-GSD field alters the specified distribution.
claims.scope: Consistent algebraic transformation among GSD, squared GSD, and log standard deviation.
caveats: Covers only exact algebraic conversion when U = g² is explicitly defined; does not certify software input fields, current database versions, or every source table's convention.

claims.text: The basic uncertainty term rests on its own foundation. Under the 2012 report's extension framework, stripping away all additional pedigree uncertainties returns the parameter to its basic uncertainty—so even a dataset scored 1 on every indicator retains basic uncertainty. The report's summary explicitly states that the project neither empirically calibrated basic uncertainty factors nor analyzed correlations among pedigree indicators. Combining indicator terms as independent components therefore requires documenting independence explicitly as a modeling assumption.
claims.scope: Basic uncertainty component and independence assumptions in the May 2012 report; does not judge current ecoinvent versions.
caveats: Lognormality and center-value conventions in the report are modeling assumptions; neither empirical distribution families nor covariances were tested.

claims.text: A fictional inventory parameter shows step by step how these assumptions generate a distribution. Let X be the material input required by a unit process per unit of product (in kg/unit), modeled as lognormal with median 10 and basic GSD 1.2. Suppose completeness is scored 2—assigning the published provisional additional GSD g = 1.03—while all other additional factors equal 1 and all log-scale components are mutually independent. Here the center, basic term, tier assignment, and independence are all worked-example assumptions; the published completeness factor illustrates the mechanics of propagation without establishing its suitability for any real material input.
claims.scope: Explicitly fictional unit-process material input and independent lognormal assumptions.
caveats: This is neither the sampling distribution of the Berlin cup-weight mean, nor a measured industrial parameter, nor a complete product life cycle model.

claims.text: To combine the components, first convert the basic and completeness GSDs into log standard deviations, sum their squares, and take the square root: σ = √{[ln(1.2)]² + [ln(1.03)]²} ≈ 0.1847. Exponentiating yields a total GSD of g_T ≈ 1.2029, and squaring gives U_T ≈ 1.4469. All remaining factors have GSD = 1 (logarithm zero). If the completeness factor is also set to 1, only the basic term remains and g_T returns to the basic GSD.
claims.scope: Combination of the assumed independent lognormal components in the worked example.
caveats: Uses published factor values under fixed author conditions; neither propagates calibration error in the factors nor validates an empirical distribution.

claims.text: On the log scale, moving one σ from the center corresponds on the original scale to multiplying or dividing the median by g_T. Stepping two σ to either side and exponentiating divides and multiplies the median by exp(2σ) = U_T, giving the interval 10 / U_T to 10 × U_T, or roughly 6.9115 to 14.4687 kg/unit. That central range describes the assumed distribution of the material-input parameter, whereas the Berlin survey's standard error described the sampling precision of an estimated mean cup weight. Propagating parameter uncertainty to an entire LCA result still requires specifying the model and dependency structure for all remaining materials, emissions, and characterization factors.
claims.scope: Central ±2σ log-scale range of the assumed lognormal parameter distribution.
caveats: The two-standard-deviation interval is not an unconditional or exact 95% empirical coverage guarantee, nor is it a confidence interval for an estimated population mean.

claims.text: The material-input distribution is symmetric around its center on the log scale, so back in kg/unit its upper and lower endpoints sit at equal multiplicative multiples of the median. In this example, 10 is both the median and the geometric mean, whereas the arithmetic mean is 10 exp(σ² / 2) ≈ 10.1720 kg/unit. If an inventory instead reports an arithmetic mean while keeping the same σ, the log-scale center must be set to μ = ln(arithmetic mean) − σ² / 2. Once the type of central value changes, reusing the same raw number as a median specifies a different distribution.
claims.scope: Meaning of the central value and derivation of the arithmetic mean under the assumed lognormal model.
caveats: This is a mathematical property of the assumed distribution, not a re-estimation of the original survey mean, and it makes no claim about which center convention specific software adopts.

claims.text: Empirical calibration is not the only path for turning pedigree scores into probabilistic parameters (Table 2). In Chapter 10 of the ecoinvent v3 data quality guideline, Weidema et al. (2013) recast ecoinvent v2's squared geometric standard deviations as log-scale normal additional variances (σ²), assigning 1–5 tier variances across five indicators (at score 5: reliability 0.04, completeness 0.008, temporal 0.04, geographical 0.002, and further technological 0.12) that add linearly to one basic variance under zero-mean and independence assumptions. Crucially, Table 10.5 in 2013 still represented expert judgment—page 77 explicitly notes that empirical calibration was still underway, the very gap Ciroth et al. later addressed. The guideline also excludes model structural uncertainty and human error from pedigree variances and cautions that deterministic calculations use lognormal geometric means that are always smaller than Monte Carlo arithmetic means.
claims.scope: Pedigree variance formula, expert-judgment provenance, and validity boundaries in Chapter 10 of the ecoinvent v3 data quality guideline (Weidema et al. 2013).
caveats: The numerical values in Table 10.5 represent the 2013 expert-judgment baseline and must not be conflated with Ciroth et al.'s subsequent empirically calibrated factors.

claims.text: Unlike ecoinvent's conversion of scores into stochastic variances, the EU Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) in Annex I Section 4.6.5 of Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 uses an ordinal Data Quality Rating (DQR) paired with hard eligibility gates (Table 2). Completeness and methodological appropriateness are treated as unscored prerequisites; only technological representativeness (TeR), geographical representativeness (GeR), time-related representativeness (TiR), and precision (P) are scored on a 1–5 scale and averaged with equal weights into five ordinal tiers. The Data Needs Matrix (DNM) mandates DQR ≤ 1.5 for company-specific primary data (with P ≤ 3 and each representativeness score ≤ 2), DQR ≤ 3.0 for secondary data, and a ≤ 10% cap on International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Entry-Level proxies. Across both the 2021 and 2022 Official Journal texts, PEF never converts DQR into lognormal variances or Monte Carlo distributions: it answers whether data satisfy required collection tiers, not how random parameter error is distributed.
claims.scope: DQR formula, Table 22 tiers, and Table 25 Data Needs Matrix thresholds in Annex I Section 4.6.5 of Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279.
caveats: The 2021 Recommendation sets the company-specific primary-data threshold at DQR ≤ 1.5, differing from the 1.6 threshold common in earlier 2018 PEFCR guidance drafts; verify the applicable edition when citing.

claims.text: Algebraic consistency aligns a factor with its parameter definition, but whether a value is actually recommended depends on how the report evaluates it. In the 2012 report, Global Emission Model for Integrated Systems (GEMIS) records yielded a candidate GSD of 43.55207485 for reliability score 5. On page 27, the authors judged that value implausibly high and declined to recommend it, and Table 24 on page 49 accordingly lists "not available". Yet the conversion table on page 55 still prints 1237.93 under the coefficient of variation (CV)—defined as standard deviation divided by the mean, reported here as a ratio rather than multiplied by 100 as a percentage. The 2016 journal summary table continues to list reliability score 5 as not available.
claims.scope: Cross-check of reliability score 5's candidate GSD, printed CV conversion value, and recommendation status across the 2012 report and 2016 journal article.
caveats: The text does not explain why a rejected candidate remained populated in a later conversion table; this neither invalidates all other factors nor supplies an adoptable parameter.

claims.text: Can the printed CV of 1237.93 be traced back to that rejected candidate GSD? Page 54 of the 2012 report gives the lognormal conversion CV = √{exp([ln(g)]²) − 1}. Rounding the candidate GSD first to 43.55 and applying the formula gives CV ≈ 1237.9312, which rounds to the table's 1237.93; plugging in the unrounded candidate gives CV ≈ 1238.1538. The contrast confirms that prior rounding alters the converted value, yet numerical agreement alone neither proves the exact script behind the original table nor explains why a rejected candidate remained populated there.
claims.scope: Conditional recomputation showing CV conversion from rounded versus unrounded candidate GSD; does not recover the original table's generating script.
caveats: Numerical agreement after rounding does not prove that the original table used that exact sequence; the unrounded candidate yields a different figure.
Does not restore recommendation status, empirical applicability, or raw statistics for the rejected candidate.

claims.text: Even with a factor table in hand, a separate question arises: can practitioners actually assign consistent tiers under the rules? In the electronic supplementary material of Edelen and Ingwersen (2018), 12 United States Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA) staff members and contractors evaluated four input flows from the same dataset and background documentation. Each participant rated the flows twice—once using Weidema et al.'s (2013) five-indicator matrix and once using Cooper and Kahn's (2012) seven-indicator A/B system. No predetermined "correct" scores were set; the test observed how different users interpret rules and apply them to identical evidence.
claims.scope: Single-dataset, named-method multi-user scoring test documented in Electronic Supplementary Material 1 of Edelen and Ingwersen (2018).
caveats: Participants were not a random sample of all LCA practitioners, and planned scoring items do not equal completed valid responses.
The test did not validate the revised US EPA matrix, the Berlin cup-weight factors, or any training intervention.
The dual-system design was assigned to the same participant group; actual omissions and scoring errors are documented separately and do not imply full completion.

claims.text: In actual responses, some participants left indicators blank, scored the reference flow, or entered values outside the defined scale. How tightly ratings clustered varied by both indicator and input flow. The authors judged the A/B system to show higher repeatability, yet substantial disagreement remained even there. Because the two systems also differ in indicator definitions, observed differences cannot be attributed solely to the number of scale categories, and the supplement provides neither respondent-level raw tables nor a recomputable unified inter-rater reliability coefficient.
claims.scope: Observed outcomes and comparative-design boundaries in Electronic Supplementary Material 1 of Edelen and Ingwersen (2018).
caveats: Response frequencies were not digitized from figures, and group-level observations cannot be generalized to all practitioners.
No pre-/post-training experiment was run, so reduced disagreement cannot be attributed to a validated training protocol.

claims.text: Placing that inter-rater test beside the completeness-factor derivation separates three distinct checkpoints. First, can different analysts assign similar tiers to the same dataset under the same rules? Second, do those tiers have empirical uncertainty factors valid for that class of data? Third, if those factors are used to build a parameter's probability distribution, do the population, center value, and dependency assumptions hold? Rater agreement establishes only the first step; rater disagreement signals a need to tighten scoring rules without proving that calibration is impossible; and transparent factor provenance satisfies only part of what probability modeling requires.
claims.scope: Logical separation among scoring repeatability, empirical factor calibration, and probability-model validity.
caveats: This is neither a universal acceptance checklist nor a ranking of methods; cross-sector external validation remains incomplete.

claims.text: In the PubMed Central (PMC) open-access author manuscript of their 2018 journal article, Edelen and Ingwersen propose using data quality assessment alongside quantitative uncertainty analysis rather than collapsing one into the other. Data quality assessment documents what the data are and whether they fit the study's purpose, whereas uncertainty analysis evaluates how data or model uncertainty affects the results. Used in tandem, each highlights what kind of evidence should be strengthened next while preserving independent fitness-for-purpose judgment.
claims.scope: Section 2.4 of the PubMed Central (PMC) author manuscript of Edelen and Ingwersen (2018; published online 2017) presented as an explicit methodological stance.
caveats: This reflects the authors' recommendation rather than universal scholarly consensus or proof that conditional calibration is impossible.

claims.text: Because data quality ratings depend on intended use, the scoring rationale must be stored alongside the study goal. Temporal, geographical, and technological indicators all measure how closely a dataset matches a target context: when the study goal shifts, suitability must be reassessed even if the indicator labels remain unchanged. Edelen and Ingwersen therefore emphasize preserving raw source descriptions, scoring justifications, and original goals so later users can re-evaluate fitness whenever the application changes.
claims.scope: Discussion of context-dependent scoring, raw descriptions, and metadata preservation in the Edelen and Ingwersen (2018) author manuscript.
caveats: Recognizing context dependence neither provides an existing cross-framework mapping nor guarantees that databases or software preserve all required metadata.

claims.text: Tracing the full chain makes every assumption auditable. The Berlin survey defined its population by shop and cup type, applied design-based weighting to estimate mean cup weight, and separated mean precision from population spread. Reusing those data to propose completeness factors required comparing subset and reference dispersions and explaining how coverage mapped to tiers. Turning those factors into an inventory parameter's probability distribution then required specifying parameter conventions, basic uncertainty, center definitions, and independence assumptions. Auditing backward along those steps reveals what sampling, calibration, and modeling each contribute—and shows whether the next priority is collecting more measurements, clarifying scoring rules, or validating the model. Quality scores record fitness-for-purpose judgments; probability distributions require their own empirical and modeling justification.
claims.scope: Analytical framework connecting data documentation, goal-dependent scoring, probabilistic grounding, and uncertainty propagation; not an external standard or automated scoring policy.
caveats: These methodological positions and limited calibration materials do not settle which framework is universally superior.

claims.text: Set beside ecoinvent's pedigree variances and EU PEF's ordinal DQR, the 2011 Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol Product Standard takes a third path of qualitative disclosure (Table 2). Adopting Weidema and Wesnæs's five data quality indicators (DQIs: technological, temporal, geographical, completeness, and reliability), it rates them across four qualitative tiers ("very good", "good", "fair", and "poor"), defines no unified numerical composite DQR, and mandates no conversion into probability distributions. The standard requires narrative disclosure of data quality for significant processes, improvement actions, inventory uncertainty sources, and key methodological choices while treating Monte Carlo simulation or Taylor expansion as optional. Even with nearly identical indicator names, the GHG Protocol chooses "mandatory narrative disclosure + optional quantitative propagation", echoing the position that representativeness metadata should be preserved alongside—not folded into—quantitative error.
claims.scope: Qualitative DQI ratings in Section 8.3 and qualitative/quantitative uncertainty reporting boundaries in Chapter 10 of the GHG Protocol Product Standard (2011).
caveats: Although Section 8.3.7 notes that companies may consult companion tools to help estimate uncertainty using DQIs, the standard itself does not mandate probabilistic conversion.

claims.text: Placing all four frameworks side by side explains why four or five nearly identical data quality terms yield completely non-interchangeable mathematical and governance objects. Both ecoinvent's expert pedigree table and Ciroth et al.'s empirical calibration translate quality gaps into lognormal variance expansion, yet both assume zero-mean, mutually independent additional errors and omit systematic bias. EU PEF instead uses composite DQR as an ordinal gate for data collection and regulatory eligibility: a company-specific dataset passing DQR ≤ 1.5 can still exhibit substantial random parameter scatter, while widening pedigree variances in ecoinvent cannot satisfy PEF's compliance duty to collect primary activity data. The GHG Protocol and US EPA approach keeps qualitative representativeness explicitly separate from quantitative random error, preventing multi-dimensional representativeness deficits and directional biases from being flattened into a single deceptively precise interval width. Reading any study's data quality report therefore begins with asking whether it delivers variance parameters, compliance gates, or qualitative metadata before carrying those scores into propagation or cross-study comparison.
claims.scope: Cross-framework synthesis and non-interchangeability boundaries across four data quality scoring and probability systems.
caveats: This synthesis compares the published design mechanisms of the four frameworks and does not substitute for sector-specific empirical error validation of any individual system.

claims.text: In terms of source provenance, every cross-framework comparison in this chapter rests strictly on directly verified, open-access primary documents: the Berlin cup-weight sampling and pedigree-calibration studies (Ciroth et al. 2008, 2012, 2016), the US EPA data quality framework (Edelen and Ingwersen 2018), the ecoinvent v3 data quality guideline (Weidema et al. 2013), Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279, and the GHG Protocol Product Standard (2011). For the uniform verification boundary covering the paywalled full text of ISO 14044:2006, see Reading Guide.
claims.scope: Primary-source verification boundary for this chapter's cross-framework comparisons and disclosure of the paywalled ISO 14044:2006 full-text boundary.
caveats: The paywalled ISO standard text remains an explicit public-literature boundary pending authorized clause-by-clause verification.

claims.text: Across Part VI's sequence of chapters, Data Quality Scores and Probability sits at the intersection of dataset applicability, uncertainty propagation, and product footprint governance. Data Applicability examines how background databases govern whether a dataset should be used through fitness screening, regionalized parent-child datasets, and multi-role reviews; Variability and Uncertainty clarifies why random parameter error, methodological scenarios, and model structural uncertainty cannot be pooled into one Monte Carlo run; this chapter shows whether quality scores become stochastic variances, ordinal entry gates, or qualitative metadata across frameworks; and Product Footprint Rules next examines how EU PEF's DQR gates and the GHG Protocol's qualitative disclosures embed into category rules and legal compliance regimes that determine whether a result can support public claims or cross-product comparisons.
claims.scope: Conceptual bridge and division of responsibilities linking Data Quality Scores and Probability with adjacent chapters.
caveats: Cross-chapter links clarify conceptual dependencies; specific rules and empirical evidence remain anchored in each chapter's primary citations.

claims.text: After finishing a liter of milk, should washing the drinking glass count toward that milk's environmental footprint? The 2025 Dairy Product Environmental Footprint Category Rules (Dairy PEFCR), published by the European Dairy Association, define a default service for liquid milk consumed at home as a final product without further heating, cooking, or processing, with a reference flow of 1,000 mL. Its use stage includes household refrigeration and dishwashing. Including glass washing in the inventory first requires clarifying which types of studies this rule governs and what share of dishwashing activity is allocated to that single liter of milk.
claims.scope: Specified function and use stage for liquid milk in the 2025 Dairy Product Environmental Footprint Category Rules (Dairy PEFCR)

claims.text: The first step is to identify what kind of study this rule actually binds. Article 288 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) classifies recommendations and opinions as non-binding legal acts. The main text of Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 defines its intended addressees while preserving the scope of mandatory legislation that establishes dedicated calculation methods. Inside the Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) method annexes, however, the word "shall" specifies the technical requirements a study must satisfy to claim conformance with the PEF method. Reading these texts accurately requires separating the legal force of a recommendation from the technical conditions triggered once a practitioner chooses to apply the method.
claims.scope: Distinction between the non-binding legal status under TFEU Article 288 (2016 consolidated text) and the technical conformance requirements of Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279
caveats: This analysis covers only the specified instruments and methodological conditions; how other statutes, contracts, or schemes incorporate the method depends on their own legal or contractual basis.

claims.text: Category rules pin down the modeling choices that the general method leaves open for specific product groups. The PEF method annexes require a category rule to specify the function, reference flow, system boundaries, and data sources, and any compliant study must follow the applicable category rule where one exists. Within the Dairy PEFCR, "shall" denotes a mandatory requirement, "should" denotes a recommendation whose departure must be justified, and "may" denotes an allowed option. Determining whether a given clause applies therefore requires checking which product, intended use, and calculation step it addresses.
claims.scope: Relationship between the general EU PEF method and Dairy PEFCR specifications, including normative wording
caveats: The 2025 Dairy PEFCR summary describes non-comparative external applications as recommended, whereas page 28 treats external communication as requiring conformance; those two formulations cannot be unconditionally merged into a universal legal mandate.

claims.text: Drafting a category rule also requires selecting the product that anchors its requirements and benchmark. Under the PEF method, a "representative product" may be either an actual product or a virtual product constructed by weighting the characteristics of products sold across the covered market. The Dairy PEFCR constructs virtual representative products for five subcategories and treats the resulting benchmarks as indicative references. Those figures are not direct measurements of any single product on store shelves, nor can they stand in for a specific company's production.
claims.scope: Definition of the EU PEF representative product and the status of virtual representative products in the Dairy PEFCR
caveats: Sales-weighted and other justified weighting approaches are detailed in Annex II, Section A.2.3 of the 2022 corrigendum text; historical market-mix shares are not treated here as current market surveys.

claims.text: The Dairy PEFCR notes that its update was organized by the Technical Secretariat and prepared by Blonk on behalf of the European Dairy Association. That makes it a technical rule for a specific product category. The general PEF method separately lays out formal procedures for review, final-draft submission, and approval. Although a document carrying the label "Final" helps identify the release version, confirming which procedural steps a specific model or follow-on study actually completed requires checking the issuer and formal procedural records separately.
claims.scope: Distinction between the authoring and publication identity of the 2025 Dairy PEFCR and general PEF approval procedures
caveats: The "Final" label printed on the category-rule document itself is not treated here as verified proof of formal Commission approval or exact model-review binding.

claims.text: Checking whether technical rules have changed also requires verifying exact document versions. The April 25, 2018 Dairy PEFCR cites the 2013 PEF Guide and Version 6.3 of the PEFCR Guidance as its basis, whereas the February 2025 partial update references Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 and Environmental Footprint (EF) 3.1. Meanwhile, the 2022 corrigendum reprinted the full text of Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279, and reprinting alone does not indicate which technical rules changed. For dishwashing, the 2018 Dairy PEFCR already listed the same default number of glasses and dishwashing-cycle share still used later, so a newer citation year alone does not prove those two defaults originated in a new method.
claims.scope: Historical relationship among the 2018 and 2025 Dairy PEFCR releases and the 2022 corrigendum reprint
caveats: The inspected Joint Research Centre (JRC) Version 6.3 Guidance bears a May 2018 cover date while suggesting a December 2017 citation on the same page; byte-level identity with pre-April 2018 copies is not established.

claims.text: Validity periods for rules and version dates for background datasets must also be verified separately. The May 2026 transitional guidance on reduced availability of EF-compliant datasets links the transitional validity of certain updated or finalized rules to the release of the next database, then projected for 2028. That guidance also sets conditions for selecting, disclosing, and verifying proxy datasets, and advises against recalculating recently finalized or updated representative products on that basis. Publication year, dataset reference year, and rule applicability window must each be confirmed independently, and whether a specific category qualifies for transitional use must be checked against the guidance's stated conditions.
claims.scope: Validity periods, proxy-data selection conditions, and representative-product recalculation boundaries under the 2026 transitional guidance
caveats: The year 2028 is a projected timeline in the guidance rather than a completed database release; this analysis does not certify the current validity or compliance status of any specific study.

claims.text: Whereas Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 (issued under TFEU Article 288) remains a non-binding technical recommendation, writing product footprints into an EU regulation changes their legal character completely.
