Article 96 of the 2023 EU Batteries Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, 117 pages in the Official Journal) establishes direct binding force across all Member States (entering into force on August 17, 2023, and applying generally from February 18, 2024). Its Article 7 imposes three escalating market-access gates on electric vehicle (EV) batteries, rechargeable industrial batteries with a capacity above 2 kilowatt-hours (kWh), and light means of transport (LMT) batteries, assessed per battery model and per manufacturing plant: first, a mandatory carbon footprint declaration (starting February 18, 2025, or 12 months after the relevant delegated act enters into force for EV batteries, and 18 months for the other covered categories); second, a carbon footprint performance class label (reviewed every 3 years); and third, technical documentation demonstrating that the declared footprint falls below a statutory maximum threshold, failing which the battery cannot be placed on the EU market.
claims.scope: Direct legal force, product scope, and three-stage escalating obligations under Articles 7 and 96 of the EU Batteries Regulation (EU) 2023/1542
caveats: Category-specific calculation rules, performance-class thresholds, and maximum limits depend on subsequent Commission delegated acts; each stage's application date is the later of the date written in the regulation or 12 to 18 months after the corresponding delegated act enters into force.

claims.text: Beyond batteries, the EU Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR, Regulation (EU) 2024/1781), published in June 2024, extends this conversion pathway to a broad spectrum of physical goods (Table 1). Directly applicable across all Member States from July 18, 2024, ESPR covers physical goods including components and intermediate products, while explicitly exempting food, feed, medicinal products, living organisms, and dedicated motor vehicles (so the liquid milk example above falls outside its scope). The regulation positions the PEF method of Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 as one candidate option rather than an automatic mandate: only after product-group delegated acts (ordinarily allowing at least an 18-month transition period) adopt or adapt a method does it become a binding disclosure or performance threshold. Covered products must also carry an open, machine-readable Digital Product Passport (DPP), backed by a central registry that the European Commission must establish by July 19, 2026.
claims.scope: Scope, exemptions, conversion from voluntary PEF to binding delegated acts, and Digital Product Passport architecture under EU ESPR (EU) 2024/1781
caveats: As a framework regulation, ESPR sets no uniform numeric footprint thresholds directly; binding values depend on subsequent product-group delegated acts.

claims.text: Returning to glass washing, the first modeling question is whether the inventory should include the activity at all. The general PEF method distinguishes two kinds of use-stage processes: product-dependent processes, which can be influenced by product design, distribution, or producer instructions, and product-independent processes, which remain unchanged when switching among products in the same category. The Dairy PEFCR classifies washing glasses or tableware as product-dependent, in part because product format determines whether a glass, spoon, or knife is needed. Once an activity is placed inside the boundary, the next step is quantifying its associated water, electricity, and detergent inputs.
claims.scope: Use-stage process classification in the general PEF method and the specific choice made in the Dairy PEFCR

claims.text: The general method's default table specifies five 200 mL glasses per liter of cold milk while noting that better data should be used when available. Following that structure, the Dairy PEFCR assigns each glass to one-fifth of the functional unit and then allocates a fraction of a dishwasher cycle to each glass. Default values give studies a common starting point, but how consumers actually use glassware—and whether superior data justify replacing the defaults—still requires separate empirical evidence.
claims.scope: Epistemic status of default use-stage scenarios in the general PEF method and the Dairy PEFCR

claims.text: At 5 glasses per 1,000 mL and 2.5% of a dishwasher cycle per glass, one liter of milk receives 5 × 2.5% = 0.125 dishwasher cycles. The liquid milk flowchart in the public representative-product workbook likewise records 0.125 cycles for this service. That calculation verifies the allocated cycle share under the rule; how many cycles households actually run still requires separate observation.
claims.scope: Independent recomputation from the default service to the dishwashing activity displayed in the flowchart

claims.text: Once the cycle share is known, the inputs of one full dishwasher cycle can be scaled accordingly. The general default assigns 15 L of water, 10 g of soap, and 1.2 kWh of electricity per cycle; multiplying each by 0.125 cycles yields 1.875 L of water, 0.00125 kg of soap, and 0.54 MJ of electricity. The soap quantity matches the flowchart, and both direct electricity-related input nodes—electricity supply and voltage transformation—display the same energy figure. Because the distinct modeling roles of those two nodes have not been established from native records, they must not be summed as two separate electricity demands. Turning these physical inputs into environmental impact results further requires background models for electricity generation, appliances, material production, and waste treatment.
claims.scope: Conditional calculation from per-cycle defaults to water, soap, and electricity inputs
caveats: The flowchart displays water as 0.00187 m³, whereas the nominal default yields 0.001875 m³, preserving a display-precision difference. Both electricity-related nodes connect directly to dishwashing; resolving their exact exchange semantics requires inspecting the underlying datasets and native records.

The general method's Milk default also includes the life cycle of the drinking glass itself. This calculation traces only the dishwashing activity and does not close glass manufacturing and end of life; glass packaging bottles, drinking glasses, and dishwashers are distinct objects.

claims.text: The workbook's results sheet reports pre-characterized stage contributions. Its dishwashing and refrigeration cells look up stored values by process name from a hidden results sheet. A reader can therefore verify the sum of those two climate contributions directly, but recomputing the climate result from water, electricity, and soap quantities requires process linkages and elementary-flow inventories that those two cells alone do not supply.
claims.scope: Formula structure and meaning of stored results in the published representative-product Excel workbook

claims.text: Reading the workbook's climate change results to nine decimal places gives 0.069478624 kg CO₂ eq for dishwashing and 0.012862507 kg CO₂ eq for refrigeration, summing to 0.082341131 kg CO₂ eq. Rounded to the display precision of Table 45 in the final PEFCR, that total matches the published use-stage figure of 0.0823 kg CO₂ eq. This check links the published workbook directly to the printed table; the extra decimal places serve arithmetic verification and do not imply that household behavior or environmental impacts are measured to nine-digit accuracy.
claims.scope: Summation of published LCIA outputs and reconciliation with the printed precision of Table 45

claims.text: How much of the full life cycle result do those two activities represent? In the workbook, total climate change including the use stage is roughly 1.572 kg CO₂ eq, making the use stage about 5.24% of the total. Subtracting the use stage leaves roughly 1.49 kg CO₂ eq, matching the column excluding the use stage in Table 45. The PEF method requires reporting both the full life cycle result and the result excluding the use stage; the gap between those two columns reflects only the reporting boundary, not any change in actual production or household behavior.
claims.scope: Distinction between reporting-boundary conventions for the same representative product and actual environmental change
caveats: The row-by-row climate sum in the workbook differs from the Info sheet total by roughly 1.88 × 10⁻⁹ kg CO₂ eq for an undetermined reason; the display reconciliation here does not constitute a digit-for-digit native reproduction.

claims.text: Even within the same workbook, discrepancies between the results table and the flowchart call for caution. The results table specifies the representative product quantity as 0.001 m³ of liquid milk—volumetrically equal to 1 L—yet its activity-quantity column lists 0.000125 for dishwashing and 0.00792 for refrigeration, whereas the flowchart shows 0.125 and 7.92. Neither sheet contains a formula explaining an additional scaling factor. Unit conversion from cubic meters to liters alone does not account for that mismatch in the activity column, and an auditor must not silently alter published numbers. Because the use-stage total verified above comes from pre-characterized outputs, it cannot prove backward which activity-quantity basis generated those characterized values.
claims.scope: Unexplained scaling discrepancy between the activity-quantity column and the embedded flowchart in the public workbook

claims.text: Published materials also diverge on the allocated share of the dishwasher itself. The general default assumes a dishwasher lifetime of 1,500 cycles, and the separately published life cycle inventory (LCI) annex likewise allocates 1/1,500 of a machine per cycle. Applying the 0.125 cycles derived above and shown in the flowchart yields roughly 0.00008333 dishwashers. The public flowchart node, however, displays 0.00000833 dishwashers—roughly an order of magnitude smaller. Because the flowchart and the LCI annex come from separate files, those two documents alone cannot establish whether the gap stems from a version mismatch, an allocation adjustment, or an export artifact, nor can they justify modifying the published impact results.
claims.scope: Conditional cross-check between default dishwasher capital allocation and the public flowchart node for the same service

claims.text: Household refrigeration cannot be accepted from a single final number either. Combining the rule's stated market mix of 41% pasteurized or microfiltered milk and 59% ultra-high-temperature (UHT) milk with household storage times of 5 days and 2 days respectively, and multiplying by 3 times the product volume, yields 9.69 L·days (volume × days) per liter of reference flow—whereas the flowchart displays 7.92 L·days. The first figure is a conditional calculation combining published defaults rather than a proven recovery of the original model's internal formula; the mismatch simply shows that the public package lacks the documentation needed to reconcile the two quantities.
claims.scope: Conditional reconstruction of household refrigeration from published market-mix and storage defaults
caveats: No hidden parameter, household residence-time assumption, or native modeling error is inferred as the cause of the gap, and the historical market mix is not treated as a current market measurement.

claims.text: Taken together, the rule-derived dishwashing cycle share matches the flowchart, and the two pre-characterized stage contributions sum cleanly to the published use-stage result. Yet the discrepancies in the activity-quantity column, dishwasher capital share, and refrigeration volume-days remain unexplained across the public files. The flowchart, LCI annex, results table, and background-data identifiers each expose only one layer of the model, while the data-requirements tables merely specify what practitioners should collect. Re-running the original model from process activities requires access to the underlying process datasets, parameters, and exact version records.
claims.scope: Layered verifiability of public Dairy PEFCR materials and limits to full native model reconstruction

claims.text: Stepping outside the EU's multi-category footprint framework, the world's most widely adopted single-indicator product rule is the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard (2011, 148 pages), published jointly by the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD). Section 1.7 immediately sets an indicator boundary: a single greenhouse gas inventory must not be used to claim overall environmental performance, because doing so can mask burden shifting into water use, acidification, or toxicity. On units of analysis and system boundaries (Sections 6.2 and 7.2), final products must define a functional unit and cover the full cradle-to-grave life cycle; only intermediate products with unknown final uses may use a reference flow and a partial cradle-to-gate boundary (the 2011 standard never once uses the term "declared unit" common in construction declarations). For process inclusion, the standard classifies capital goods (buildings and machinery), facility overhead such as lighting and heating, research and development, administration, customer travel to retail stores, and employee commuting as "non-attributable processes" excluded by default (and disclosed if included). For attributable processes, it sets no uniform percentage cut-off: excluding a process requires satisfying all three conditions simultaneously—a data gap exists, neither extrapolation nor proxy data can fill it, and the estimated contribution is insignificant—and publicly disclosing the justification.
claims.scope: Single-indicator warning, unit-of-analysis rules, non-attributable processes, and three-condition exclusion rule in the GHG Protocol Product Standard (2011)
caveats: Published before ISO 14067 was finalized, the 2011 edition is a voluntary corporate single-indicator greenhouse gas standard and does not provide multi-category environmental impact assessment.

claims.text: Placing the GHG Protocol Product Standard alongside Annex II of the EU Batteries Regulation reveals why two frameworks both called "product carbon footprint" can draw opposite boundaries (Table 2). The GHG Protocol accounts for the six Kyoto Protocol greenhouse gases using 100-year global warming potentials (GWP100), requires separate reporting of biogenic carbon and direct land-use change (LUC) over 20 years or a single harvest period, and prohibits mixing delayed-emission discounting, carbon offsets, or avoided emissions into the inventory total. Annex II of the EU Batteries Regulation likewise prohibits counting carbon offsets toward the declared carbon footprint, yet makes sharply different choices on boundary and data granularity: it defines the functional unit as 1 kWh of total energy provided over expected service life (1 kilowatt-minute, kWmin, for standby batteries), covers four stages—raw materials, main production, distribution, and end of life—while explicitly excluding the use stage because grid electricity mixes lie outside the manufacturer's direct control, and mandates plant-specific activity data for five core components (cathode, anode, electrolyte, separator, and cell casing), barring default values and cross-plant sampling.
claims.scope: Contrast between GHG Protocol rules on biogenic carbon, land-use change, and offsets and EU Batteries Regulation Annex II rules on 1 kWh functional unit, use-stage exclusion, and plant-specific data
caveats: Although both frameworks prohibit subtracting carbon offsets from declared totals, their opposite rules on use-stage inclusion and plant-level data granularity make their figures non-interchangeable across regimes.

claims.text: How far an audit can go depends on which artifacts are actually accessible—and the same constraint governs formal review. The category rule, the representative-product model, its underlying datasets, and the published results can each be reviewed as distinct objects. While a public model workbook lets readers inspect selected activities and results, confirming whether it contains every process and parameter used in the native modeling software requires checking the exact scope of what was published.
claims.scope: Analytical distinction between general PEF review requirements and what published representative-product files actually allow a reader to verify

claims.text: In the PEF system, development review of a category rule covers the draft PEFCR, the representative-product study, and supporting studies. When a specific product study is intended for external communication, separate study-level verification must cover the study, report, and communication materials. Even though both processes use similar terminology and examine overlapping technical issues, applying a reviewed category rule does not waive study-level verification when a company communicates results externally.
claims.scope: Distinction between PEFCR development review objects and study-level verification requirements

claims.text: The 2018 Dairy PEFCR includes a review statement in which the panel judged the rule and several modeling choices appropriate and noted that the reported results were broadly consistent with existing literature. At the same time, the panel explicitly recorded that because the benchmark authors used proprietary data, it could not evaluate the relevance, representativeness, or reliability of those underlying screening and supporting-study datasets. Agreement with published literature therefore does not prove that the review panel inspected the proprietary data underneath.
claims.scope: Affirmative findings and data-access limitations recorded in the 2018 Dairy PEFCR review statement

claims.text: A review statement dated November 5, 2024 evaluates the final updated draft bearing the same date. The reviewers confirmed consistency between the update and the referenced methodology, the description of the representative products, data appropriateness, and the accompanying Excel model and data-requirements matrix, noting that the Technical Secretariat had addressed the questions raised. The statement also records that several recommendations were not incorporated into this partial update and were deferred as relevant to the next full revision. The annex of the February 2025 final PDF embeds a scan of this exact statement, making it the same evidentiary record as the standalone two-page release.
claims.scope: Exact scope of the November 2024 review statement and its embedded copy in the 2025 Dairy PEFCR

claims.text: Affirmative review of the 2024 update still does not establish that every proprietary dataset inaccessible in 2018 was subsequently audited item by item. Because the two-page statement points to a separately stored comment log without reproducing the full exchange, it cannot link an individual review comment to a specific cell in the final workbook. Readers must also distinguish what the review statement says from what the final rule text says: the statement refers to the European Union plus the European Free Trade Association (EU+EFTA), whereas the corresponding passage in the final rule refers to EU+EFTA+UK. That textual discrepancy alone does not prove that any region was omitted from the underlying calculation.
claims.scope: Why a summary review statement cannot substitute for item-level revision logs or exact file-to-cell binding

claims.text: The institutional rigor of review and verification likewise scales with legal force. Under the Dairy PEFCR, the category rule undergoes panel review while individual studies undergo independent verification. Under Section 12.2 of the GHG Protocol Product Standard, product inventories must undergo conflict-of-interest-free assurance, but the standard allows either first-party (an independent internal corporate unit) or third-party assurance and distinguishes two assurance levels in Table 12.2: limited assurance issues a negative opinion ("nothing has come to our attention suggesting material modification is needed"), whereas only reasonable assurance issues a positive opinion ("fairly stated in all material respects"). Under the legally binding EU Batteries Regulation, Article 17(2) explicitly bars manufacturer self-declaration (Module A) for Article 7 carbon footprints and mandates conformity assessment by a Member State-designated third-party notified body under one of two Annex VIII routes: Module D1 for series production (auditing the production quality-assurance system through periodic audits plus potential unannounced checks) or Module G for non-series unit production (unit-by-unit verification). Seeing "reviewed" or "assured" on a report therefore always requires asking whether it means internal first-party review, limited assurance, study verification, or statutory notified-body conformity assessment.
claims.scope: Institutional divergence between GHG Protocol first/third-party limited and reasonable assurance and mandatory notified-body conformity assessment (Modules D1/G) under the EU Batteries Regulation
caveats: First-party independent assurance, third-party limited assurance, third-party reasonable assurance, and EU notified-body conformity assessment are not equivalent in legal liability or inspection authority.

claims.text: A frequent practical error is assuming that multiplying each sold product's carbon footprint by sales volume and summing across a company's portfolio automatically equals the company's organizational greenhouse gas inventory (Scope 1 plus Scope 2 plus Scope 3). Section 1.6 of the GHG Protocol Product Standard explicitly clarifies that summing the life cycle emissions of all products approximates total corporate emissions only after adding non-attributable Scope 3 categories—such as employee commuting, business travel, and investments—that fall outside individual product boundaries. Although the product and corporate standards were developed together by the same organizations, product rules delineate attributable processes around a specific functional unit or reference flow, whereas corporate Scope 3 inventories track organizational control and full upstream-downstream value-chain categories for a reporting year. Treating one as a simple disaggregation of the other, or substituting corporate Scope 3 spend factors for plant-measured product footprints, conflates incompatible accounting regimes.
claims.scope: Boundary difference between summed product carbon footprints and corporate Scope 1, 2, and 3 greenhouse gas inventories
caveats: Even after adding non-attributable Scope 3 categories, summing product footprints across different companies double-counts overlapping supply-chain stages and cannot serve as a macroeconomic emissions ledger.

claims.text: A separate dairy example clarifies what comparative claims require. Examining only how enteric methane equations respond to identical inputs—without tracing raw-milk data in the workbook above—the 2018 Dairy PEFCR recommends national inventory reports as primary sources for country-specific parameters, sets Tier 2 as the minimum requirement for enteric methane, and permits country-specific approaches such as Tier 3. Crucially, the table footnote requires using the same emission calculation method whenever comparative claims are made, and the 2025 update retains that wording. Even when national parameters are used, comparative dairy PEF studies must therefore hold the emission algorithm constant.
claims.scope: Raw-milk enteric methane method rules and comparative-claim requirements in the 2018 and 2025 Dairy PEFCR

claims.text: Cataloged by the Natural Resources Institute Finland (Luke) in 2023, a Nordic comparison report first lines up national-inventory inputs and annual per-cow emission estimates from Sweden (2018) and Norway, Finland, and Denmark (2020), and then applies eight calculation methods to a common standard ration and several modified rations. Feeding identical diet inputs into each method isolates how the algorithms themselves respond. This is strictly an algorithm comparison: the study ran no new feeding trials, calculated no eight complete milk footprints, and did not validate the 2025 Dairy PEFCR workbook.
claims.scope: Two comparative designs and scope boundaries of the 2023 Nordic PEF food-comparison report
caveats: Two Danish comparison figures in the national-inventory table cannot be recomputed from the listed inputs for an undetermined reason; no product ranking is drawn from that table, and only two explicit branches of the common-ration test are recomputed below.

claims.text: Consider the report's standard and low-fiber scenarios. Both fix milk yield at 30 kg/day and dry matter intake (DMI) at 22 kg/day, while reducing neutral detergent fiber (NDF) from 335 g/kg dry matter to 270 g/kg dry matter. Before entering an equation calibrated in percentage of dry matter, those concentrations must be converted to 33.5% and 27%. Unit conversion determines the exact numerical values the equation receives; grams per kilogram, percentages, and mass fractions cannot be substituted interchangeably.
claims.scope: Fixed scenario inputs in the Nordic report and unit conversion for the Niu et al. equation

claims.text: What the Nordic report labels the working-group option uses an intercontinental prediction equation from Niu et al. (2018). The original paper fit empirical relationships to lactating dairy-cow records and evaluated them via study-grouped cross-validation, using a different sample size for fitting the final equation than for uniform cross-model evaluation on complete records. That validation establishes predictive performance within a specific dataset and design, but it does not turn a regression coefficient into a causal guarantee of how much real-world methane will drop when a farm alters feed composition.
claims.scope: Provenance and evaluation scope of the Niu et al. prediction equation adopted in the Nordic report
caveats: The original equation was fit on 3,116 observations, whereas the intercontinental evaluation table used 2,566 complete observations; those two sample counts must not be conflated. Nor does the Nordic research report substitute for formal working-group minutes or adoption instruments.

claims.text: The Niu et al. equation expresses daily enteric methane in grams as 33.2 + 13.6 × DMI + 2.43 × NDF (in % of dry matter). Under the standard and low-NDF scenarios, it outputs 413.805 g/day and 398.01 g/day, respectively. Extrapolating those fixed daily rates over 365 days gives approximately 151.0 and 145.3 kg CH₄/(cow·year)—an unrounded difference of about 5.8 kg. What changes here is the prediction equation's output, not an empirically observed annual emission reduction.
claims.scope: Independent arithmetic recomputation of the fixed rations using the Niu et al. prediction equation
caveats: Annualization over 365 days does not model actual lactation and dry-period cycles; kg CH₄/(cow·year) is not converted here into a per-kilogram milk footprint, nor are field feasibility or causal mitigation effects claimed.

claims.text: A second branch in Figure 2 of the Nordic report fixes the methane conversion factor—the share of gross energy converted to methane—at 5.7%. At the same DMI of 22 kg/day and a gross energy density of 18.45 MJ/kg dry matter, both diets supply 405.9 MJ/day of gross energy. Multiplying by 5.7%, dividing by methane's energy content of 55.65 MJ/kg, and annualizing over 365 days yields roughly 151.7 kg CH₄/(cow·year) for both scenarios. The output stays flat because both gross energy intake and the fixed conversion factor remained unchanged in that branch—a result that cannot be generalized to claim that all Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) implementations ignore diet composition.
claims.scope: Energy basis and conditional output of the fixed-Ym branch in Figure 2 of the Nordic report

claims.text: Reproducing the factor plotted in a figure is also distinct from independently verifying that the factor fits those rations. Table 10.12 in Volume 4, Chapter 10 of the 2019 Refinement to the 2006 IPCC Guidelines links default dairy-cow methane conversion factors to milk productivity, diet digestibility, and NDF thresholds, yet the Nordic scenario table omits digestibility. The calculation above therefore reproduces the fixed factor explicitly used in the figure rather than re-verifying the IPCC tier classification; clear formula and table provenance cannot stand in for missing applicability inputs.
claims.scope: Distinction between recomputing the plotted IPCC factor and verifying IPCC Table 10.12 class applicability

claims.text: Because the same diet change produces different responses across the two algorithms, the Dairy PEFCR's requirement to use identical emission equations in comparative PEF studies has a direct technical rationale. This comparison cannot determine which model is more accurate across all farming systems. Moreover, the two branches share underlying empirical lineage—the IPCC default table itself cites Niu et al. among its supporting studies—so the two outputs do not serve as independent field evidence, and enteric methane alone cannot decide a product's overall life cycle standing.
claims.scope: Interpretation of the fixed-input model comparison and shared evidence lineage between the two equations

claims.text: Valid product comparison requires more than matching a reference volume. The Dairy PEFCR restricts comparisons across dairy subcategories as well as between dairy and non-dairy products. Even within the same subcategory, a comparative claim requires that all compared products use either primary raw-milk data or secondary raw-milk data, whereas benchmarking against the representative product permits either. Household default services, raw-milk emission equations, and use-stage boundaries must likewise be aligned before a result can support a comparative claim; a single number, category name, or review statement never suffices on its own.
claims.scope: Synthesis of subcategory restrictions, data-tier symmetry, calculation alignment, and review layers governing comparative claims

claims.text: In the one-liter milk audit, the rule-derived dishwashing share matches the flowchart and the two pre-characterized stage contributions sum cleanly to the published use-stage figure, yet reconstructing the original model from activity inputs remains blocked by missing documentation. The methane example answers a different question: applying different equations to the same diet change alters the output, explaining why comparative dairy PEF studies must hold emission algorithms constant.
claims.scope: Tiered evidentiary judgment drawn from the dairy workbook audit and enteric methane comparison

claims.text: The "same method for comparison" principle illustrated by the dairy methane calculation appears across footprint regimes as formal gates on comparative claims. Section 1.5 and Appendix A of the GHG Protocol Product Standard explicitly declare that the standard does not support International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 14044 comparative assertions (claims that one product has superior or equivalent overall environmental performance relative to a competing product). According to Appendix A, Table A.2 (page 116), only one comparative use is supported "as is" without extra rules: tracking the same product's performance over time. Using results for procurement decisions, product labeling, or cross-product performance claims requires additional product rules—such as Product Category Rules (PCR)—to harmonize units of analysis, equivalent system and temporal boundaries, consistent allocation methods, data quality and uncertainty assessment, and preferably third-party assurance (Section 5.3.2 and Appendix A). By contrast, the EU Batteries Regulation locks boundaries, formulas, and notified-body verification into binding delegated acts precisely so that plant- and model-specific declarations can map directly onto cross-model performance classes and statutory maximum thresholds.
claims.scope: Comparison of GHG Protocol comparative-assertion limits and product-rule recommendations with EU Batteries Regulation statutory grading and Dairy PEFCR methane-method parity
caveats: Product carbon footprint figures calculated under different category rules or methodologies are not automatically comparable across products even when expressed in identical units.

claims.text: Beyond the openly accessible EU Official Journal texts and public standards verified page by page above, widely used product carbon footprint standards (ISO 14067:2018 and GB/T 24067-2024), Type III Environmental Product Declaration (EPD) framework rules (ISO 14025:2006), and European core category rules for construction products (EN 15804+A2) are copyright-protected paywalled standards (see the Reading Guide for this monograph's uniform verification boundary). Here we retain only their public institutional coordinates without reverse-engineering internal modules or exemption clauses; practitioners preparing compliance filings, construction EPDs, or mutual-recognition dossiers must verify every requirement directly against current licensed originals and the governing program operator's latest instructions.
claims.scope: Explicit boundary statement for uninspected paywalled texts of ISO 14067:2018, ISO 14025:2006, EN 15804+A2, and GB/T 24067-2024
caveats: This statement defines an epistemic and verification boundary; until licensed full texts are inspected, no unverified clause numbers or internal module rules are inferred or cited.

claims.text: Category rules establish a shared basis for interpreting footprint results by specifying the service, included activities, and reporting format. Comparing specific products still requires checking whether competing options use commensurate processes and data, how results were computed, and what review actually covered. The following chapter uses a fully recomputable wall-assembly example to show how the same service is translated into process requirements for competing options and how changing a single initial assumption can alter a comparative conclusion.
claims.scope: Bounded synthesis of the chapter's worked examples and transition to the wall-assembly comparison

claims.text: How many times must a thicker plastic bag be used before its climate indicator drops below that of a lightweight carrier bag? A study commissioned by the UK Environment Agency (UK EA) calculated that a heavier low-density polyethylene (LDPE) bag must be used for shopping at least five times, counting the first trip. That threshold holds only under the report's specified assumptions for bag capacity, manufacturing, bin-liner substitution, and end-of-life disposal, and only when both bag types deliver the same grocery transport service. Tracing how the figure of five is derived shows which assumptions move the threshold.
claims.scope: Framing the interpretation of the UK Environment Agency carrier-bag study around its conditional reuse threshold

claims.text: Authored by Chris Edwards and Jonna Meyhoff Fry and dated February 2011, the report uses the UK 2006/07 market as its reference period to inform government, supermarkets, and the public. It evaluates carrier bags available at supermarket checkouts with a capacity above 15 L, covering both established market bags and newer materials. If bags subsequently became lighter or shopping and waste-management practices shifted, updated data are required before repeating the comparison.
claims.scope: Reference period, intended audience, and product scope of the 2011 UK Environment Agency report

claims.text: The object of comparison is a transport service rather than an individual bag. The report defines the functional unit as carrying one month's supermarket groceries—483 items—from store to home in the UK. Larger bags hold more items per trip, and the same bag may be reused across trips. Initial reference flows establish how many bags are required based on carrying capacity alone; because independent data on actual primary reuse were lacking, reuse counts were deferred to conditional breakeven comparisons. Comparing one thick bag against one thin bag does not automatically equalize the number of items transported.
claims.scope: Functional unit and initial reference-flow structure in the UK Environment Agency report

claims.text: Carrying capacities also rest on distinct lines of evidence. The shopper survey in Appendix B interviewed 1,149 shoppers and recorded 14,651 items carried in 2,490 lightweight bags and 573 items carried in 72 LDPE bags, giving unrounded ratios of approximately 5.883936 and 7.958333 items per bag. The main table adopts the two-decimal rounded values of 5.88 and 7.96. By contrast, carrying capacities for paper, non-woven polypropylene (PP), and cotton bags were extrapolated from bag volume using the items-per-liter ratio measured for LDPE. Separating those sources lets readers tell direct bag-type survey counts apart from volumetric extrapolations.
claims.scope: Survey counts, adopted carrying capacities, and volumetric extrapolations to other bag types

claims.text: Dividing 483 items by the adopted carrying capacities gives roughly 82.14 lightweight bags and 60.68 LDPE bags, where fractional bags represent the average model requirement for delivering the monthly service. Multiplying those tabulated bag counts by unit bag masses of 8.12 g and 34.94 g yields roughly 667 g of lightweight bag material versus 2,120 g of thicker LDPE bag material. Although fewer thick bags are needed, they require far more polymer mass. Retaining unrounded quotients shifts the trailing digits slightly; at this stage, the calculation determines only the bag mass required, before accounting for raw-material production, energy use, or disposal.
claims.scope: Bag counts and polymer mass required for the same monthly grocery transport service
caveats: Versioned calculation inputs separately document the minor difference between unrounded division and the report's tabulated display values.

claims.text: The report documents separate sources for monthly grocery volume and bag-packing capacity. Page 17 cites a 2007 UK market-research figure from Taylor Nelson Sofres (TNS) of 446 grocery items over four weeks and then sets the one-month functional unit at 483 items without printing the exact conversion step. Appendix B states that Test Research interviewed shoppers in late 2007 to measure bag filling. One sentence in the appendix mistakenly writes 20.7 as items per bag, whereas the accompanying table lists 20.7 as items per shopper and separately reports an average of 6.6 items per bag. Recomputing the figures requires stating which table row is used and preserving each source's exact denominator. Available records do not establish the relationship between the TNS citation and the Test Research survey, so different attributions alone cannot prove they were two independent surveys.
claims.scope: Audit of grocery-volume provenance and Appendix B shopper-survey denominators

claims.text: The comparisons also share a common baseline for end-of-life treatment and impact assessment. The baseline assumes that discarded bags go 86% to landfill and 14% to incineration, leaving polymer recycling and paper or starch-bag composting mainly to sensitivity scenarios. Bags are modeled with zero recycled content, while an avoided-burden approach credits material recycling and energy recovery. Climate change results use the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) 2007 100-year time horizon, and the other eight impact categories use CML 2 baseline 2000. Whenever modern recycling rates or electricity grids differ, any updated comparison must first specify which of these baseline conditions has changed.
claims.scope: Baseline end-of-life split, recycled-content assumption, and impact-assessment methods in the UK Environment Agency report

claims.text: When a lightweight carrier bag is reused as a household bin liner instead of purchasing a dedicated liner, it delivers an extra service. The report uses system expansion to subtract the avoided production burden of that liner: scaling a 29.3 L, 9.3 g dedicated bin liner by the 19.1 L volume of the carrier bag credits roughly 6.1 g of avoided high-density polyethylene (HDPE) liner material per substitution. Granting that credit presupposes both that substitution actually occurs and that the two bags perform equivalently as liners.
claims.scope: System-expansion credit representing avoided bin-liner production

claims.text: The substitution rate itself comes from a separate consumer survey. In March 2005, the UK Waste & Resources Action Programme (WRAP) conducted street interviews with 1,048 respondents across Great Britain. Question Q7 asked roughly how many carrier bags respondents reused (grouped into categories such as all, most, about half, or some), and Q8 asked how reused bags were used, allowing multiple answers. Across all 1,048 respondents, 53% reported using carrier bags to line kitchen bins. The denominator of that 53% figure is respondents—not total carrier bags, and not total reused bags.
claims.scope: Respondent denominator and multiple-response structure of WRAP survey questions Q7 and Q8

claims.text: The UK Environment Agency report first estimates that roughly 76% of carrier bags are reused and then multiplies that figure by the 53% kitchen-liner response rate to obtain 0.4028, or 40.28%. The methodological jump is that the second factor is a share of surveyed people, yet the equation applies it as a share of bags. Someone who keeps dozens of bags and someone who keeps one bag count equally as one respondent in the survey, even though their effects on bin-liner purchases may differ sharply. Verifying that step requires matched household-level records of bag quantities and secondary uses over the same period.
claims.scope: Bridging assumption mapping respondent survey shares onto modeled bag-level secondary-use rates

claims.text: What can be verified directly is how this credit shifts the published climate result. For one month of grocery transport, lightweight HDPE bags generate 2.082 kg CO₂ eq with zero bin-liner substitution and 0.830 kg CO₂ eq with 100% substitution—a span of 1.252 kg CO₂ eq. Writing the linear interpolation as D(r) = 2.082 − 1.252r and substituting r = 0.4028 yields 1.5776944 kg CO₂ eq, matching the tabulated 1.578 kg CO₂ eq to published precision. Reconciling the endpoints with the intermediate value confirms the linear credit relation, though it does not replicate the underlying bag-manufacturing and waste models.
claims.scope: Parametric verification of the bin-liner credit relationship in Table 6.1

claims.text: The reuse threshold for thicker LDPE bags now follows directly. Used once, LDPE bags generate 6.924 kg CO₂ eq per monthly service. If the same batch of bags is used for n shopping trips in total under the report's remaining assumptions, the monthly climate burden scales to 6.924 / n. Falling strictly below the lightweight HDPE baseline of 1.578 kg CO₂ eq requires n > 6.924 / 1.578, whose smallest integer solution is 5. Because n includes the first shopping trip, the bag must be reused at least four additional times. That figure defines what is required to break even, not whether consumers actually achieve it.
claims.scope: Strict integer derivation of the LDPE climate reuse threshold

claims.text: Changing the secondary service provided by the lightweight baseline moves the threshold immediately. Without any bin-liner substitution credit, the required total uses for LDPE drop to 4; if every lightweight HDPE bag replaces a bin liner, the required total rises to 9. The 0% to 100% range represents bounding test conditions rather than a statistical confidence interval from survey data, and nine uses is a model requirement rather than observed consumer behavior.
claims.scope: Sensitivity of the LDPE reuse threshold to changes in baseline secondary-use substitution

claims.text: Allowing lightweight HDPE bags to be used for three shopping trips sets an even stricter bar. Page 57 of the report considers three shopping uses followed by roughly 40% reuse as bin liners. Dividing 1.578 by 3 and comparing against 6.924 / n requires 14 total uses for LDPE, matching the main text's figure of "approximately 14." In Table 8.1, however, the final column header states only that HDPE is used three times, and the LDPE row lists 12 uses. Unstated bin-liner assumptions and calculation order directly alter interpretation; readers should preserve this documented ambiguity rather than treating 12 and 14 as interchangeable answers.
claims.scope: Conditionality when primary reuse (three trips) and secondary bin-liner use coincide

claims.text: Near a threshold boundary, display precision alone can shift the integer answer. Used once for shopping, cotton bags carry a published climate indicator of 271.533 kg CO₂ eq per monthly service, compared with 0.830 kg CO₂ eq for lightweight HDPE bags with 100% bin-liner substitution. Dividing those two printed figures requires 328 uses to fall strictly below the baseline, whereas Table 8.1 prints 327 uses. At 327 uses, the displayed ratio is roughly 0.830376—still marginally above 0.830. Unprinted internal precision could shift that lower bound, but it is not disclosed alongside the table; sound interpretation must state which precision basis is used rather than treating a rounding-edge digit as a physical service-life certainty.
claims.scope: Display-precision boundary at the cotton-bag reuse threshold

claims.text: Crossing the climate threshold does not guarantee lower impacts across every category. At five uses, thick LDPE bags yield 6.924 / 5 = 1.3848 kg CO₂ eq (rounded in the report to 1.385), below the lightweight HDPE baseline of 1.578 kg CO₂ eq. For abiotic resource depletion, however, 82.711 / 5 = 16.5422 g Sb eq remains slightly above the baseline of 16.227 g Sb eq. Row by row, the thicker bag scores lower in 8 of 9 impact categories. That profile shows which categories move together and where trade-offs persist; category counts must not be treated as a simple majority vote.
claims.scope: Nine-category comparison at five LDPE uses and the abiotic-depletion exception

claims.text: The report first back-calculates the required number of uses for each bag type from the climate indicator and then evaluates the other eight impact categories at those same use counts. Its multi-category charts therefore answer a specific conditional question: if a bag is reused often enough to match the climate benchmark, how do its other impact categories look? Those back-calculated counts are not survey observations of actual use. Deciding which option works best today still requires knowing how bags are actually used, how long they last, and how damaged bags are replaced.
claims.scope: How the report's two-stage evaluation sequence frames its multi-category comparisons

claims.text: Contribution analysis traces impact differences back to specific drivers. While the report identifies polymer production and bag-making energy as dominant contributors to many indicators, it highlights a counterintuitive exception: titanium dioxide pigment accounts for only about 2% of HDPE bag mass, yet vanadium emissions from its production drive more than 19% of freshwater aquatic ecotoxicity. Cutting off an input merely because its mass share is small can therefore miss a dominant driver in a specific impact category. Conversely, a large modeled contribution flags a concentrated hotspot within that model; switching to unpigmented bags or different electricity mixes still requires checking functional performance and actual manufacturing conditions.
claims.scope: Identifying impact drivers through contribution analysis and conditions for verifying proposed improvements

claims.text: Comparing multiple impact categories also requires verifying that competing options were modeled on a commensurate footing. The consistency checklist in the 2006 US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) LCA guide lists items to check side by side, including data-source types, technology age and scale, and the time horizons of impact models. Differences between options may reflect genuine production or use conditions, or they may arise from approximations forced by missing data. Documenting the origin of each difference helps distinguish real product differences from modeling artifacts.
claims.scope: Historical guidance context from the 2006 US EPA life cycle assessment (LCA) guide; does not replace current standards or product-level verification
caveats: Not every data asymmetry automatically introduces bias; each difference must be evaluated within the specific study.

claims.text: The UK report represents supply chains by combining bag-manufacturing data from China, LDPE film conversion from Turkey, and European polymer datasets. Mixing geographies may well mirror actual import flows, yet approximating a specific country's electricity mix with generic European generation processes introduces technological simplification. Reference years also vary between raw-material and conversion datasets, and certain bag-making energy figures are confidential. Readers can therefore audit the report's stated sources and scenario applicability, but published summary tables alone cannot prove independent reproduction of the full native model.
claims.scope: Interplay of geographic mix, temporal coverage, technological approximations, and auditability of confidential data

claims.text: Consistency asks whether options were modeled evenly; completeness asks whether the consequences that matter to the decision were captured at all. The UK report explicitly omits printing inks, retail storage, shopper travel, and capital equipment, and places littering, behavioral change, and socioeconomic effects of bag charges outside its goal and scope. Those exclusions may match the study's original remit, yet if a policy decision centers on marine or beach litter, a climate-based ranking omits the decisive consequence.
claims.scope: Alignment between explicitly excluded items and the decision question being asked

claims.text: A 2019 study grounded in Spanish carrier-bag data proposed an explicit littering-potential indicator. It combines the number of bags needed to deliver the service with single-side surface area, then normalizes by bag price, weight, and degradation parameters to form a relative index. Price and weight act as proxies for assumed behavioral and dispersal pathways, while degradation parameters are drawn from composting conditions. Although the indicator makes a set of "likelihood of becoming litter" factors explicit, it does not model marine exposure, affected organisms, or ecological damage. It helps show what evidence the UK study lacks, but it cannot be added directly to kg CO₂ eq.
claims.scope: Purpose, unit structure, and transferability limits of the 2019 littering-potential indicator

claims.text: Receiving environments strongly alter how bag materials degrade. Field experiments by Napper and Thompson exposed different bag formulations to seawater, soil, and open air, tracking visual deterioration and load-bearing strength. One compostable formulation disappeared from the marine rig within three months yet remained intact in soil after 27 months; other tested formulations still carried groceries after more than three years in seawater or soil, whereas all bag types fragmented within nine months in open air. Disappearing from a test rig or fragmenting into pieces still requires tracking breakdown products and ecological fate. While that experiment cannot calibrate every parameter of the Spanish indicator, it clearly shows that substituting composting tests for marine behavior requires dedicated empirical validation.
claims.scope: Environmental transferability of degradation behavior and limits of observed physical endpoints

claims.text: Setting the 2011 UK Environment Agency findings beside a second independent government study shows concretely how functional units and end-of-life baselines move reuse thresholds. The Danish Environmental Protection Agency (Danish EPA, Miljøstyrelsen, 2018, Environmental Project no. 1985, Bisinella et al.) notes that whereas the UK study defined service as carrying a fixed number of items over a set period, the Danish study defines the functional unit as carrying an average 22 L and 12 kg of groceries home from a Danish supermarket in a single trip, rounding bag counts up to whole integers. Six bag types—including kraft paper, biopolymer, and organic cotton bags—fall short of the required volume or load capacity and must therefore be counted as 2 bags, directly raising their reference-flow mass. At the same time, the Danish model adopts an average EU-manufactured virgin LDPE bag reused once as a household waste bag and then incinerated in Denmark (end-of-life scenario 3, EOL3) as its dynamic baseline: whenever that baseline bag is itself reused for shopping, the reuse thresholds required of every alternative bag scale up proportionally.
claims.scope: Comparison with the Danish EPA (2018) 22 L / 12 kg single-trip functional unit, integer bag rounding rule, and dynamic LDPE waste-bag baseline (EOL3)
caveats: The Danish scenario reflects Denmark's waste-to-energy incineration system and local bag dimensions and cannot be transferred directly to landfill-dominated regions or markets without waste-bag reuse habits.

claims.text: An even sharper divergence appears when moving from climate change alone to the full multi-indicator profile. In the unweighted comparison of Table 24 and the conclusions of the Danish EPA (2018) report against the single-use LDPE baseline reused as a waste bag before incineration, a conventional cotton bag requires 52 reuses on climate change alone but leaps to 7,100 reuses if it must match or beat the baseline across all 15 environmental indicators (driven primarily by ozone depletion; excluding ozone depletion still leaves 50 to 1,400 reuses). Because organic cotton has lower agricultural yields and is rounded up to 2 bags per trip, it requires 149 reuses on climate change alone and 20,000 across all 15 indicators (150 to 3,800 excluding ozone depletion, led by water use and eutrophication). Unbleached and bleached kraft paper bags require 0 and 1 reuse respectively on climate change, yet both require 43 reuses across all indicators. The authors candidly record two hard boundaries: domestic littering in Denmark is treated as negligible and left unmodeled, and these figures represent mathematical environmental breakeven lower bounds rather than claims that cotton or paper bags can physically survive thousands of shopping trips.
claims.scope: Verification of the order-of-magnitude split between climate-only and 15-indicator reuse thresholds, ozone-depletion sensitivity, and unmodeled littering in the Danish EPA (2018) report
caveats: The all-indicator maximum threshold is governed by the single most unfavorable category; for cotton bags, that ceiling is highly sensitive to agricultural pesticide modeling and ozone-depletion characterization uncertainty, which is why the report also lists ranges excluding ozone depletion.

claims.text: Generalizing the rounding sensitivity, secondary-use credits, and unmodeled omissions seen in both carrier-bag studies reveals both shared baselines and quantitative divergences across international interpretation rules. Chapter 9 of the EU International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Detailed Guidance (2010) structures interpretation around identifying significant issues, running completeness, sensitivity, and consistency checks, and formulating conclusions and limitations; it requires sensitivity checks to cover inventory parameters, impact factors, and modeling choices, notes that stochastic uncertainty calculations cannot uncover systematic bias, and requires unmodeled out-of-scope effects such as littering to be segregated rather than folded covertly into rankings. Annex I, Section 6.3 of the EU Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) method ((EU) 2021/2279) pairs those three checks with explicit quantitative hotspot thresholds: the most relevant impact categories must cumulatively account for at least 80% of the weighted single overall score (and at least 3 categories); most relevant life cycle stages and processes must exceed 80% (with mandatory recalculation and parallel reporting excluding the use stage if it exceeds 50%); and most relevant elementary flows must reach at least 80%. Under Section 6.3.5, whenever recycling or substitution credits produce negative values for processes or elementary flows, 100% shares must be recalculated using absolute values so that positive and negative terms do not cancel out and conceal major contributors.
claims.scope: Comparison of ILCD 2010 Chapter 9 interpretation checks and out-of-scope segregation with EU PEF Annex I Sections 6.2–6.3 quantitative 80% hotspot thresholds, 50% use-stage recalculation, and Section 6.3.5 absolute-value credit rules
caveats: The EU PEF 80% category screen relies on global normalization and a weighted single score, which cannot be transplanted directly into ILCD public comparative-assertion contexts where weighting is prohibited.

claims.text: Uncovering limitations does not merely qualify the final text; interpretation also feeds back into the study itself. ILCD 2010 treats interpretation as an iterative phase whose checks can send analysts back to revise the goal, model, or data before fixing how far conclusions may reach. The review comments and author responses preserved in the UK carrier-bag report display one such iteration in practice: some reviewer challenges sharpened the final text, while others exposed data gaps that remained unfilled.
claims.scope: Historical guidance context from ILCD 2010 on iterative interpretation; does not replace current standards or product-level verification

claims.text: Appendix E of the UK report preserves the review comments alongside the authors' responses. Chair Mark Goedkoop participated from the goal-and-scope stage, while Keith Elstob and Jane Bickerstaffe joined later as co-reviewers; the final statement looks back across a late-2009 initial draft and a summer-2010 revised draft. Recording these roles and dates matters: it lets readers trace which draft prompted each critique and prevents reading "critically reviewed" as proof that every input was independently measured.
claims.scope: Reviewer roles, draft versions, and review timeline documented in Appendix E of the UK report

claims.text: One review comment challenged the "five uses" logic directly, asking whether back-calculated climate reuse counts provide a fair comparison of real bag function. The authors accepted the critique. Pages 17, 32, and 57 of the final report acknowledge the absence of actual reuse data by bag type and note that some back-calculated counts are unrealistic; page 57 states explicitly that the study did not compare true function. Review thus tightened the stated boundary of the conclusions, even though real-world usage data remained missing.
claims.scope: Author response and final text revisions addressing the reviewer critique on function and reuse

claims.text: Another review comment requested documentation of how carrying capacities were obtained for paper and starch bags. The authors pointed to supplementary methods, and the final Appendix B indeed details the sampling, measurements, bag-type counts, and volumetric extrapolations. Adding that documentation did not turn extrapolated figures into direct observations, but it made the extrapolation transparent and inspectable: if newer evidence shows different packing or tearing behavior for paper bags, analysts know exactly which reference-flow link to revise.
claims.scope: How review turned undocumented capacity assumptions into an inspectable volumetric extrapolation in Appendix B

claims.text: Checking whether commitments made in review responses were carried through consistently across the final report is equally necessary. For oxo-degradable HDPE recycling, the final scope description and sensitivity table exclude that scenario, yet a later summary still lists it among recycling benefits. Similarly, the authors agreed to drop ozone depletion and presented the main results across nine categories, yet several sensitivity figures retain the ozone-depletion label. Readers can verify these internal inconsistencies directly in the published report, whereas confirming how the native software actually computed those runs requires inspecting the original model.
claims.scope: Audit of residual inconsistencies between review commitments and final tables, figures, and text

claims.text: The review panel ultimately accepted the revised study and endorsed its adjustments to recycling treatment, while explicitly retaining reservations regarding real-world function and missing land-use and water indicators. Using the report responsibly therefore means reading the panel's acceptance together with its recorded reservations: passing critical review neither proves that all environmental consequences were covered nor establishes that shoppers will achieve the calculated reuse counts.
claims.scope: Coexistence of final panel acceptance and retained reservations in Appendix E

claims.text: Some studies cannot support a defensible overall ranking. As the 2006 US EPA guide notes, uncertainty may prevent an unqualified recommendation while the study still clarifies where environmental burdens concentrate and what trade-offs separate the options. How strong a recommendation results can support depends on whether the evidence actually answers the questions that recommendation presupposes.
claims.scope: Historical guidance context from the 2006 US EPA guide; does not replace current standards or product-level verification

claims.text: Failing to resolve a difference and proving that two options differ negligibly are distinct conclusions. The 2010 ILCD Handbook cautions that high uncertainty can mask genuinely meaningful differences, and that missing key data or limited study resources never justify claiming no significant difference exists. Summaries and figures should state explicitly why a study is inconclusive so that insufficient evidence is not misread as environmental equivalence.
claims.scope: Historical guidance context from ILCD 2010; does not replace current standards or product-level verification

claims.text: Under the UK report's stated assumptions for carrying capacity, supply chain, substitution, and disposal, one can accurately state that thick LDPE bags used five times for shopping achieve a lower monthly climate indicator than the lightweight HDPE baseline and score lower in 8 of 9 evaluated categories. Turning that statement into practical advice for shoppers or supermarkets further requires confirming that thicker bags deliver the same transport service, actually reach the required reuse count, and displace lightweight bags used in the assumed way—and back-calculated thresholds must never be cited as proof that those conditions hold.
claims.scope: Conditions required to translate calculated breakeven thresholds into practical consumer or retailer recommendations

claims.text: Later surveys can expand the evidence base, provided their measurement constructs are checked first. A 2016 Welsh government post-implementation review surveyed consumers in 2015 on how many times they typically reused a bag type before discarding it. Heavy-duty plastic bags and cloth or jute bag groups had different respondent bases, and mean reuse calculations capped the highest response category ("more than 50 times") at 50. Such self-reported averages carry explicit temporal, grouping, and top-coding boundaries, and the question did not restrict reuse solely to grocery shopping. They therefore cannot serve directly as the actual grocery-shopping lifespan of every UK cotton bag in 2006 without bridging those definitions first.
claims.scope: Temporal, categorical, usage-scope, and top-coding boundaries of subsequent self-reported reuse survey data

claims.text: Redesigning a carrier-bag study for current decisions would begin by filling the behavioral evidence gap: tracking actual fill rates, cumulative shopping trips, tearing or loss rates, and whether reusing carrier bags truly reduces bin-liner purchases at the household, trip, and bag level. Next, the inventory would be updated for current sourcing regions, bag materials, and waste-treatment mixes, while judging whether previously omitted impact categories must now be added to match today's decision goals. Comparing observed reuse behavior against the recomputed thresholds then shows for which populations and settings the earlier conclusions still hold.
claims.scope: Study redesign priorities derived directly from documented evidence gaps

claims.text: Alongside empirical behavioral data, critical-review governance and reporting transparency determine what evidentiary force a study's conclusions can carry. ILCD 2010 Sections 6.11–6.12 and Chapter 11 distinguish independent internal review, independent external review, and external review panels, advocate interactive concurrent review starting at goal and scope definition, and set five assurance criteria—methodological consistency, scientific validity, data appropriateness, interpretation of limitations, and reporting transparency—while permitting confidential business data to sit in a restricted supplement accessible to reviewers. The two government cases illustrate those boundaries directly: the UK Environment Agency (2011) report underwent a three-member external panel review that preserved unresolved disagreements in Appendix E, whereas the Danish EPA (2018) report underwent external peer review by two experts from COWI and candidly declared that, lacking a full stakeholder panel across all phases, it does not strictly conform to ISO 14044 public comparative-assertion procedures and serves internal decision support only. EU PEF (Annex I, Sections 7.1 and 8.1) further standardizes six report components (standalone executive summary, compliant dataset, main report, verification statement, technical annex with review report, and optional confidential report) and defines any error shifting a single impact category by more than 5% or altering the hotspot list as a major error requiring correction.
claims.scope: Comparison of ILCD 2010 Sections 6.11–6.12 and Chapter 11, the UK EA 2011 three-member panel, the Danish EPA 2018 internal-support boundary, and EU PEF Annex I Sections 7.1/8.1 reporting and 5% major-error rules
caveats: ILCD 2010 Chapter 11 sets out the five overarching assurance criteria while referring detailed review schemes and reviewer-qualification rules to a separate volume; mandatory enforcement of EU PEF verification depends on adoption into specific binding legislation.

claims.text: When findings reach external communication, the most commonly neglected safeguard in international guidance is that limitations must travel with conclusions and undetected differences never prove equivalence. ILCD 2010 Section 9.4 requires all recommendations to follow conservatively from verified significant findings, bars hiding key limitations in appendices by requiring them in core conclusions and executive summaries, and forbids claiming "equivalence" when no statistically significant difference is demonstrated—an inconclusive calculation shows only that current evidence cannot separate the options. EU PEF Annex I, Section 6.4 similarly requires explicit reporting of robustness and validity domains and clarifies that a product environmental footprint complements rather than replaces site-specific environmental impact assessments and chemical risk assessments. This comparison relies directly on openly verifiable texts of ILCD 2010, the EU Official Journal, and the UK and Danish government reports; the uniform verification boundary for the paywalled texts of ISO 14044:2006 and ISO/TS 14071:2014 is documented in the Reading Guide.
claims.scope: Boundary rules on traveling limitations and non-equivalence under ILCD 2010 Section 9.4 (Provisions II.a–II.d) and EU PEF Annex I Section 6.4, plus the verification boundary for paywalled ISO 14044:2006 and ISO/TS 14071:2014
caveats: ISO 14044:2006 and ISO/TS 14071:2014 are copyright-protected paywalled standards; verbatim clause-level verification awaits inspection of licensed texts.

claims.text: Taken together, the carrier-bag studies bind three layers of life cycle interpretation discipline into a single evidentiary chain. At the calculation layer, reuse thresholds shift by orders of magnitude with functional-unit framing, integer bag rounding, secondary waste-bag credits, and single- versus multi-indicator selection. At the evaluation layer, completeness, sensitivity, and consistency checks paired with transparent hotspot and negative-credit rules identify true drivers while segregating unmodeled effects such as littering outside LCA scores. At the governance layer, review structure determines whether findings serve internal decision support or public comparative assertions, and every public recommendation must carry its assumptions and limitations out of the report alongside it.
claims.scope: Synthesis of the calculation, evaluation, and governance layers of life cycle interpretation across the UK EA (2011), Danish EPA (2018), ILCD 2010, and EU PEF frameworks
caveats: These three layers govern retrospective and micro-level comparisons of existing commercial technologies; comparing emerging processes not yet at commercial scale additionally requires bounding scale-up assumptions, learning curves, and future background energy scenarios.

claims.text: Suppose a novel wall coating is still in laboratory trial synthesis. To ask whether it could eventually replace an incumbent paint, simply dividing trial electricity use by sample mass yields only today's unit electricity demand for producing laboratory samples. Arvidsson et al. (2018) describe prospective life cycle assessment (pLCA) as modeling the potential environmental impacts of an emerging technology at an early stage of development as it might perform in the future at a more mature, larger scale. Their study applies prospective attributional life cycle assessment (LCA) and draws recommendations from selected case studies that do not exhaust prior work; other prospective assessments may adopt different modeling structures.
claims.scope: Definition of prospective attributional LCA in Arvidsson et al. (2018, Chalmers repository text) paired with this monograph's hypothetical coating example.
caveats: Does not equate this usage with the classification in Ekvall et al. (2005) merely because both share the word "prospective."
The laboratory coating, trial electricity demand, and candidate incumbent paint are author-constructed illustrations, not original cases or empirical observations from Arvidsson et al. (2018).

claims.text: Scaling up a laboratory process begins by examining how individual inputs and outputs change with process configuration. In this hypothetical coating example, repeatedly heating small batches of raw materials in the laboratory differs from continuous industrial production: heat demand, material losses, and yields per unit of product need not preserve their laboratory proportions, because they vary with scale, time, and process state. Arvidsson et al. (2018) discuss how to represent such scale-dependent shifts. Subsequent critical work by van der Giesen et al. (2020) cautions that borrowing engineering scale-up heuristics or learning curves from incumbent technologies to parameterize a new technology requires explicit justification; whether those assumptions reflect future industrial operation still demands independent verification.
claims.scope: Explains scale-up assumptions from foreground modeling in Arvidsson et al. (2018) and methodological critique in van der Giesen et al. (2020); not a universal scale-up algorithm.
caveats: Engineering scale-up models require domain-specific applicability evidence; one cannot assume all scale changes follow the same functional relationship.
Repeated batch heating and continuous operation are qualitative pedagogical illustrations constructed for this book.

claims.text: Once larger-scale coating production has been estimated, the comparison still requires an alternative that delivers the same service. Following the approach in Wall Service Comparison, analysts first fix the substrate, hiding power, and service life before determining material quantities and coat counts for each option. As van der Giesen et al. (2020) note, a valid comparison must also specify the time period in which the emerging technology is assumed to reach its modeled scale and maturity, along with how competing technologies may evolve over the same period. If a candidate coating serves different substrates or provides different protective performance, the appropriate comparator can shift as well; today's incumbent cannot be assumed to remain the only product displaced in the future.
claims.scope: Time- and function-matched comparison guidance from van der Giesen et al. (2020), linked to Wall Service Comparison and the book's hypothetical coating example.
caveats: Competing alternatives under differing assumptions require case-specific evidence; methodological guidance alone does not establish a particular substitution relationship.
The substrate, hiding power, coating, and reference pathway are pedagogical framing and do not report real future materials or market displacement.

claims.text: Before building a systematic model, analysts must untangle future-oriented terms that are frequently conflated in the literature. Arvidsson et al. (2024) organize the field along two axes—temporal position and technological maturity. Temporal position separates future-oriented prospective LCA from past-oriented retrospective LCA, while technological maturity distinguishes pre-commercial ex-ante LCA, commercialized ex-post LCA, and unscaled laboratory-scale LCA. The authors recommend prospective LCA as the overarching umbrella term encompassing both emerging technologies and mature technologies evaluated under future background conditions. Ex-ante LCA necessarily involves upscaling in maturity; laboratory-scale LCA omits scale-up and is therefore suited only to early research-and-development hotspot screening rather than direct comparison with mature industrial technologies; anticipatory LCA emphasizes stakeholder participation in defining system boundaries, functional units, impact categories, and weighting; and dynamic LCA resolves emissions and characterization factors across time steps, occupying a distinct analytical dimension from point-in-time prospective studies that aggregate a system to a single future year.
claims.scope: Maps the temporal-position and technological-maturity axes in Arvidsson et al. (2024) to distinguish prospective, ex-ante, anticipatory, laboratory-scale, and dynamic LCA.
caveats: The terminology recommendations in Arvidsson et al. (2024) aim to standardize scope disclosure (explicitly reporting target year or period and technology readiness level) rather than prescribing a single modeling algorithm.

claims.text: With terminology clarified, the core engineering challenge lies in translating a laboratory recipe into an industrial life cycle inventory (LCI). Tsoy et al. (2020) systematically reviewed 18 ex-ante LCA upscaling studies—15 in chemical engineering and waste treatment, and 11 scaling directly from laboratory to industrial scale—and uncovered two stark empirical gaps: using the European Association of Research and Technology Organisations (EARTO) technology readiness level (TRL 1–9) scale, 0 of the 18 studies reported specific TRL values, and 0 performed post-commercialization empirical validation. Moreover, 15 studies did not document technical expert involvement, and 9 omitted complete process flowcharts. To structure practice, the authors distill a three-step framework—defining projected technology scenarios, drafting projected process flowcharts, and estimating inventory data—and rank four estimation methods in descending order of accuracy: process simulation (6 studies; highest accuracy but dependent on process conditions and software), manual calculations (10 studies; most common, including stoichiometry and scaling factors), molecular structure models (1 study; limited to chemical substances), and proxy data (7 studies; used when data are scarce).
claims.scope: Synthesizes the TRL-reporting and post-deployment validation gaps, three-step upscaling framework, and four-tier inventory estimation hierarchy from Tsoy et al. (2020)'s review of 18 ex-ante LCA studies.
caveats: The 18 studies reviewed by Tsoy et al. (2020) are heavily concentrated in chemicals and waste treatment, and the authors do not classify empirical learning curves as a standalone data-estimation category (learning curves are typically paired with macro-scale capacity projections).

claims.text: When strong grounds exist to expect a particular trajectory, analysts can construct predictive scenarios; when only several meaningful operating conditions can be bounded, scenario ranges test how conclusions respond across them. Arvidsson et al. (2018) also allow retaining status quo conditions where justified—for example, when evidence indicates that a process can reasonably be treated as unchanged over the target period—provided that rationale is documented. Enumerating multiple futures allows each case to be calculated, yet doing so neither reveals which future is more likely nor supports assigning occurrence probabilities.
claims.scope: Scenario distinctions from Arvidsson et al. (2018) and future-uncertainty discussion from van der Giesen et al. (2020); final sentence bounds probabilistic inference.
caveats: Learning curves and their parameters remain uncertain; no probabilities are assigned to any scenario here.

claims.text: Specifying a future production process also requires declaring which time period's electricity, materials, and transport data are paired with it. Holding today's electricity supply constant helps isolate the effect of changing the process alone, but using that result to represent future performance requires explaining why today's grid mix can stand in for the future scenario. Both Arvidsson et al. (2018) and van der Giesen et al. (2020) stress temporal alignment between foreground processes and background supply systems. Reporting the new process's direct input requirements separately from the selected background's contribution makes recalculation straightforward when the background changes, while full life cycle impact totals must still account for both.
claims.scope: Future background alignment and disaggregated reporting from Arvidsson et al. (2018) and van der Giesen et al. (2020); modular reuse does not substitute for full-system results.
caveats: Whether a status quo background suits a future scenario requires separate justification; historical methodological guidance does not validate the applicability of current background datasets.

claims.text: Holding the wall-service reference fixed, analysts should first compare the material and electricity demands of both coating processes under an identical electricity supply, then select a clearly defined future electricity scenario and recalculate both pathways with data from that same period.
