Updating electricity data for only one pathway obscures whether indicator differences stem from the process or from the power mix. If one pathway genuinely requires a distinct electricity source in the real scenario, however, the model should represent that difference explicitly. Structured this way, the matrix separates differences arising from the process itself, from a shift in shared power-supply conditions, or from genuinely distinct power sources.
claims.scope: Qualitative pedagogical comparison that does not alter the numerical figures in Wall Service Comparison.
caveats: Adds no new wall-case numerical values, makes no assumptions about real-world processes, and forecasts no electricity grid mix.

claims.text: Scaling a foreground process to 2030 or 2050 while leaving background electricity, steel, and cement anchored in today's databases creates a foreground–background temporal mismatch. The mainstream remedy integrates future pathways from integrated assessment models (IAMs, such as IMAGE 3.0) into background LCI databases (such as ecoinvent 3.7). Conventionally, however, each combination of climate scenario and target year spawns a separate database of roughly 15,000 processes, making manual relinking highly error-prone. Steubing and de Koning (2021) address this bottleneck with a "superstructure database + scenario difference file (SDF)" architecture: the superstructure stores the union of all processes and exchanges across scenarios, while the SDF records only values that vary across scenarios; at solve time, the matrix is built once in memory and overwritten scenario by scenario. In their electric-vehicle illustration, 8 separate databases spanning 2 pathways—Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 2 (SSP2) baseline and Representative Concentration Pathway 2.6 (RCP 2.6) mitigation—across 4 years (2020–2050) collapse into 1 superstructure plus 1 difference table, overwriting roughly 135,000 exchanges per scenario, completing all 16 calculations in under 5 seconds, and showing that background electricity decarbonization can exert greater emission-reduction leverage than a 40% foreground reduction in both energy consumption and battery inputs.
claims.scope: Explains IAM-coupled background scenario alignment and the superstructure + scenario difference file (SDF) architecture from Steubing and de Koning (2021).
caveats: The "40% reduction in both energy consumption and battery inputs" in the electric-vehicle illustration is a methodological demonstration assumption meant to show sensitivity to background decarbonization relative to foreground efficiency, not an empirical forecast for a specific vehicle model.

claims.text: Convenience in software and data architecture must never be mistaken for scientific validation of the underlying scenarios. Steubing and de Koning (2021) explicitly acknowledge that the superstructure + SDF approach is purely a technical implementation and offers no guarantee of scenario plausibility or quality. At the engineering level, when a process exists in only a subset of scenarios, preventing an all-zero matrix column—which would render the matrix singular—requires setting that process's diagonal output to 1, leaving disconnected "ghost processes" in scenarios where the process does not occur. In addition, current SDF implementations do not yet propagate parameter uncertainty during matrix overwriting, and standardized storage of scenario-level metadata remains unresolved. More broadly, sectoral and modeling-paradigm misalignments between IAMs and background LCI databases, commercial database licensing restrictions, and a lack of documentation meeting Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) principles remain practical barriers to widespread adoption of future background scenarios.
claims.scope: Defines the technical and methodological limits of superstructure scenario databases—scenario quality, ghost processes, uncertainty propagation, and licensing—from Steubing and de Koning (2021).
caveats: Even when software eliminates multi-database relinking errors, analysts must still independently scrutinize the macro-level assumptions and regional disaggregation conventions of IAM scenarios.

claims.text: Even when the emerging process, competing option, and background system are aligned to the same scenario, certain emissions may still lack suitable impact categories or characterization factors. Arvidsson et al. (2018) leave further development of life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) as an open research question, and van der Giesen et al. (2020) note that novel materials and technologies are especially prone to such coverage gaps. Dynamic climate calculations—examined in Climate Equivalence—address emission timing and response horizons, whereas other environmental consequences require their own characterization methods. Whenever an impact indicator is missing from a results table, the study should state clearly that those consequences remain unassessed.
claims.scope: Scope limits on temporal characterization and emerging-technology impact coverage across Arvidsson et al. (2018), van der Giesen et al. (2020), and Levasseur et al. (2010/2011); not a hazard judgment on any specific new material.
caveats: Identifies and quantifies no specific future damages; does not turn missing characterization factors into a uniform blocking rule.

claims.text: Estimating future technological states, tracking future emission timing, and assigning probabilities to alternative futures each require separate evidentiary justification. Prospective scenarios here indicate which inputs or emissions shift evaluated indicators under stipulated maturity, scale, function, comparator, and background conditions. Whether those conditions will materialize—and whether conclusions transfer to other scenarios—requires independent evidence. Although Ekvall et al. (2005) also use the term "prospective" in their taxonomy, sharing a word does not imply identical research purposes or modeling structures.
claims.scope: Analytical links among temporal response, future-technology scenarios, and comparison boundaries; not a new standard or real-world ranking.
caveats: Distinguishing two uses of "prospective" does not constitute a universal crosswalk across all contemporary methodological labels.
Methodological recommendations and cross-references across authors are not independent validation of future performance.

claims.text: Suppose a candidate coating achieves a lower indicator value only under a low-burden electricity scenario. The next step is to check how much electricity industrial production actually requires and whether defensible electricity scenarios can be constructed for both pathways. Even if the ranking across relevant indicators holds after switching to another well-supported background, that judgment still applies only within the conditions actually tested.
claims.scope: Illustration of conditional judgment; reports no empirical comparison results.
caveats: Hypothetical illustration; claims no advantage for any coating and reports no completed sensitivity calculation.

claims.text: Along the temporal dimension, point-in-time prospective snapshots of selected future years must be distinguished from dynamic modeling that tracks emission timing year by year. Lueddeckens et al. (2020) reviewed 60 studies on temporal issues in LCA; after setting aside rarely applied dynamic weighting and dynamic normalization, they identify four practical issues—time horizon, temporal discounting, dynamic inventory, and dynamic characterization—and draw a strict distinction among three time horizons: the goal-defined assessment time horizon, the inventory time horizon over which emissions are recorded, and the characterization time horizon embedded in impact factors. Multiplying a greenhouse gas (GHG) emission occurring in year 99 by a static 100-year global warming potential (GWP100) implicitly spans 199 years, violating an intended 100-year assessment boundary. Attaching timestamps to inventory flows while retaining static factors constitutes only a semi-dynamic LCA; only coupling a dynamic inventory with dynamic characterization factors that respond to changing background concentrations and receptor sensitivity constitutes a fully dynamic LCA.
claims.scope: Synthesizes the three time horizons, semi-dynamic versus fully dynamic LCA, and the static-GWP100 horizon conflict from Lueddeckens et al. (2020)'s 60-study systematic review.
caveats: Lueddeckens et al. (2020) classify consequential LCA and life cycle stage partitioning as indirect temporal issues and exclude them from their count of six direct temporal issues.

claims.text: Recognizing the strict requirements of fully dynamic LCA explains why practice usually pairs discrete future-year scenarios with sensitivity ranges. Lueddeckens et al. (2020) highlight two layers of constraint. On the data and tooling side, most impact categories lack consensus-tested dynamic characterization factors—existing ones cluster in a few categories such as global warming and photochemical ozone formation—and background supply chains rarely provide temporal scheduling data. On the value-judgment side, neither time horizons nor discounting commands scientific consensus: too short a horizon invites pushing emissions past the cutoff and undermines intergenerational equity, too long a horizon dilutes near-term action, and a discount rate of roughly 1% suffices to marginalize distant impacts over multi-decade scales. Dynamic normalization introduces a further counterintuitive pitfall, as assuming lower future background pollution can weaken incentives for near-term emission reductions. Future-oriented comparisons should therefore keep scenario assumptions, time horizons, and value choices visibly separate, using multi-scenario envelopes to show the exact conditions under which conclusions hold.
claims.scope: Summarizes dynamic characterization coverage, supply-chain data bottlenecks, time-horizon and discounting value choices, and the dynamic-normalization pitfall from Lueddeckens et al. (2020) to anchor conditional reporting discipline.
caveats: The availability of dynamic characterization factors expands as atmospheric and ecological models advance, but time-horizon truncation and intergenerational discounting remain normative value choices that higher model resolution alone cannot eliminate.

claims.text: If two inventories are both expressed "per kilogram," can they be compared directly? Kilograms convert to grams by a fixed ratio, yet comparing alternatives requires knowing what service each kilogram delivers. Databases exhibit an analogous distinction: multiple processes may reference the same flow record, while each exchange carries its own amount and role. Judging a real choice requires first identifying the activities each figure describes, then asking whether those activities fulfill the same service.
claims.scope: Connecting conditions linking flow objects, exchange relationships, and cross-option service comparison; author synthesis without claiming conceptual equivalence.
caveats: Flow records, exchanges, and functional units belong to different analytical levels; a shared analytical structure does not prove conceptual equivalence.
This connection is an analytical synthesis, not a new procedural phase in any standard.
This claim bounds cross-option comparative interpretation and does not make study goal a precondition for dimensional unit conversion.

claims.text: The beverage container studies at the start of this monograph show that shifting the research question can expand the required system boundary. The 1974 nine-container comparison scaled process outputs and inputs to a common beer-delivery task; the returnable pathway included replacement bottles, washing, and return transport, but excluded roadside litter. The 1972 Research Triangle Institute (RTI) policy report cited litter as one rationale for intervention and referenced estimates of potential energy savings from shifting to refillable bottles, while also asking how much additional energy demand would arise if consumers spent their monetary savings on other goods—an increment the report left unquantified. Delivery comparisons can estimate energy-saving potential within the delivery system, whereas policy judgment must also account for changes beyond it.
claims.scope: Comparative reading of the explicit questions and boundaries in the 1972 RTI container policy report (EPA-R2-72-059) and the 1974 SW-91c nine-beverage-container report.
caveats: The expenditure-shift mechanism in the RTI report is proposed as a possible channel without an empirical estimate of its net impact.
The 1973 printing is a reissue with an added cover and front matter; publication approval and policy adoption each require separate evidence.
Institutional relationships, intellectual influence, and historical priority between the two reports lie outside these excerpts.

claims.text: The research question determines which activities enter the calculation. In the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) hand-washing illustration, if users value and actually obtain moisturizing service, the bar-soap option may require adding hand lotion. Similarly, an emerging technology may serve multiple uses, so defining the target service comes before selecting an appropriate comparator. Adding lotion or changing the comparator alters the set of activities that must be modeled; merely changing the reporting unit cannot capture such structural shifts.
claims.scope: Activity boundaries and comparators when service conditions change; author synthesis providing no empirical substitution quantities.
caveats: The hand-washing passage is a pedagogical illustration and the emerging-technology passage is methodological guidance; neither supplies empirical substitution amounts.
Does not establish that functional matches transfer automatically across studies.

claims.text: When final demand changes while process coefficients stay constant, the existing inventory equations yield the new activity levels and corresponding emissions. When a laboratory process scales up to industrial production, however, material, energy, and performance coefficients may shift together. Certain social consequences likewise need not vary in direct proportion to product demand. If only demand changes, the original linear model can be reused; once process or social-impact relationships change, analysts must identify where they shift and substantiate the revised coefficients or evaluation relationships.
claims.scope: Distinguishes fixed-coefficient quantity scaling, industrial process scale-up, and social-consequence response; author synthesis.
caveats: Does not claim that linear models are universally invalid, nor does it supply replacement functions for emerging technologies or social consequences.
Industrial scale shifts and social thresholds serve solely as methodological conditions within their respective sources.
This three-way distinction is an analytical framework rather than a universal standard or empirical case validation.

claims.text: Analysts may also ask which activities a given action will change. Ekvall et al. (2005) distinguish burdens of an existing system from consequences of an action according to the information a study is meant to supply, whereas Arvidsson et al. (2018) apply attributional assessment to estimate potential environmental impacts of an early-stage process under a defined future maturity scenario. Both works use the word "prospective," yet their research questions differ. Addressing both an emerging technology and policy consequences requires specifying the future system's process, scale, and supply conditions as well as substantiating which supply activities the policy will alter; comparing two technologies inside a stipulated future scenario does not by itself show how actual markets will respond.
claims.scope: Distinguishes the 2005 information-orientation framing from the 2018 future-technology definition and outlines their conditional combination; author proposal, not a universal taxonomy crosswalk.
caveats: Does not establish a general mapping across the 2005, 2018, and all contemporary attributional/consequential LCA labels.
Combining future scenarios with change mechanisms is a conditional construction, not an empirical validation in a real case.

claims.text: Assessments invoke several distinct notions of time. An organization's reporting period defines which activities are included; assigning an operating year to a future process governs its technological maturity and supply background; and dynamic climate characterization must distinguish emission timing, response duration, and the evaluation endpoint. Even when these refer to the same calendar years, they perform different roles in calculation. Knowing how a given emission exerts impacts over time aids interpretation, but determining what a future process will emit still requires building the process model and scenario first.
claims.scope: Coordinates reporting period, technological operating scenario, and emission-response timing; author synthesis without proposing a universal time grid.
caveats: Proposes no cross-domain universal time grid and does not claim fixed time windows are unsuitable for all questions.
The dynamic climate excerpts remain confined to radiative-forcing-based methods.

claims.text: System boundaries and temporal settings must also account for cross-cycle circularity accounting and future-oriented scenario coupling. Partitioning parameters in the Circular Footprint Formula (CFF) do more than shift recycled-material burden attribution between upstream and downstream products: under differing market supply-demand constraints, they can cause product-level footprint signals to point in the opposite direction of system-wide net changes. Prospective life cycle assessment (LCA) must use the two-axis framework of temporal position and technological maturity to keep prospective, ex-ante, anticipatory, laboratory-scale, and dynamic LCA distinct, while confronting the empirical gap that industrial scale-up studies rarely report technology readiness levels (TRLs) or conduct post-commercialization empirical validation. Even when coupling integrated assessment models (IAMs) to background databases through superstructure and scenario difference file (SDF) architectures eliminates multi-database relinking errors, software architecture never guarantees the scientific quality of scenario assumptions. Meanwhile, both semi-dynamic modeling (timestamped inventories paired with static factors) and fully dynamic modeling (coupled dynamic characterization factors) remain bounded by characterization coverage and normative time-horizon choices, so future comparisons must disclose scale-up conditions, background decarbonization pathways, and temporal boundaries side by side.
claims.scope: Connects circular-footprint accounting with prospective, ex-ante, and dynamic LCA conclusions, defining revision boundaries for cross-cycle partitioning and future scenario coupling.
caveats: Both circular-partitioning parameters and future background scenarios are conditional modeling assumptions and cannot substitute for observed recycling-market responses or post-deployment empirical validation.

claims.text: The wall-coating calculation shows that even when the delivered service is identical, the initial substrate changes the operations required to deliver it. Both paints provide the same color and hiding service over the same period under a shared electricity emission intensity. On a smooth substrate, the difference swings positive or negative with electricity intensity yet stays within the preset pedagogical tolerance. On a rough substrate, under the case's assumptions, Paint B requires preparing the entire wall and consumes additional electricity; across the original parameter range, Paint A's indicator remains lower and the gap stays outside the tolerance. That added preparation step and its electricity demand explain why the outcome reverses. The conclusion covers only the specified activities, two greenhouse gases, and one climate indicator; no probabilities are assigned to the parameter range, and characterization-factor uncertainties are not propagated.
claims.scope: Comparison of two initial substrates in the author-constructed wall-service case under a fixed model and factors, restricted to the selected climate indicator.
caveats: Paint performance, activities, and emission values are pedagogical settings; the tolerance is author-defined, whereas real procurement thresholds and stakeholder acceptance require independent evidence.

Only the two modeled gases and one climate indicator enter the comparison; the shared parameter range carries no probability assignment, and source uncertainties in central characterization factors are not propagated.

claims.text: The wall-coating example can be recalculated because it publishes both its results and the exact step where each datum enters the model. Two methods can likewise share the same substance dataset while applying different models: the ReCiPe 2016 method paper notes that its toxicity calculations build on USES-LCA 2.0 using USEtox substance data rather than the USEtox model itself. Prospective technology studies that report foreground and background contributions separately similarly support downstream reuse. Recalculating with updated background data such as electricity still requires knowing how foreground processes use those inputs and what assumptions originally governed them.
claims.scope: Conditions for preserving usage and dependency relationships when reusing inputs or modules across models; author synthesis.
caveats: These two literature examples do not validate any specific factor release package, software implementation, or cross-database reuse result.
Disaggregated reporting alone does not guarantee that a full model can be reconstructed.

claims.text: Citing numbers from external studies requires preserving their provenance. A documented zero in an inventory differs fundamentally from a missing entry displayed as zero. The USEtox 2.0 documentation sets human effect factors to zero by convention when toxicological data are lacking, requiring users to disclose those missing data. A zero on a compliance scale, the relative worst end of a dashboard, and a net zero formed by offsetting positive and negative terms each carry distinct meanings. Before reusing a result, verify what data are absent, what reference is used, or which sub-terms cancel; identifying a gap shows what is unknown, not how large the missing quantity is.
claims.scope: Distinct meanings of zero across inventories, missing values, toxicity conventions, social scales, and offset totals; author documentation guidance.
caveats: Reporting information status alongside numerical values is a documentation recommendation and does not require uniform software encoding.
A true zero still requires measurement or model-applicability evidence; distinguishing information states does not verify any specific zero value.

claims.text: Even when a number is present, check what it can actually substantiate. Sector- or country-level data can flag labor-condition risks, whereas judging a specific factory's conduct requires site-specific data from that factory. Comparative toxicity potentials in USEtox derive from fate, exposure, and effect models and cannot be used directly to determine how many disease cases have been observed in a given locality. Answering the first question requires finer facility-level evidence; answering the second also requires checking model scope and assumptions alongside local exposure and health-outcome evidence.
claims.scope: Distinct inferential boundaries for social-risk proxies and comparative toxicity potentials; author synthesis establishing no numerical correspondence.
caveats: Does not test real factory conduct, causal identification, or site-level exposure.
Proposes no numerical correspondence between social risk and toxicity potential.

claims.text: When facility data include an interval, first establish which population the data represent, then check whether the interval reflects inter-facility spread or the estimation precision of the mean. Even highly representative data require knowing the sampling design to interpret estimation precision; a narrow interval never justifies transferring data to a different technology or time period. The cup-weight survey illustrates the same point: how much individual units vary and how precisely the mean is estimated are separate questions.
claims.scope: Link between data representativeness and statistical estimation targets; author synthesis not substituting for sample or distribution evidence.
caveats: Derives no statistical distributions from guideline quality dimensions and calibrates no empirical datasets.
Does not generalize the assumptions of the five-facility illustration to other samples.

claims.text: Data quality ratings can signal which records need strengthening. Ciroth et al. (2012) compared datasets grouped by quality characteristics against reference sets to empirically ground dispersion parameters, and Edelen and Ingwersen (2018) recommend pairing quality assessment with quantitative uncertainty analysis. Where empirical calibration exists, pedigree factors can parameterize a distribution's spread, yet neither work establishes consensus for deriving probabilities directly from quality scores. Parameter distributions propagate uncertainties already expressed in the model, whereas altering allocation rules or supply backgrounds tests sensitivity to those modeling assumptions. Adding more scenarios or simulations—or weighting scenarios equally—never by itself establishes the probability that any scenario will occur.
claims.scope: Evidentiary links among data quality descriptions, probability parameters, and future scenarios; author synthesis establishing no joint probability model.
caveats: Does not reject empirically grounded probabilistic forecasts; constructs and validates no joint distributions.
Retains the empirical limits and tabular caveats of the 2012 calibration study without introducing universal default factors.

claims.text: Combining multiple datasets also requires checking for double counting. Process data and economic-sector data in a hybrid inventory may cover the same activity, requiring identification of the specific activity and its quantitative basis. Environmental, social, and cost assessments may all address human health, requiring comparison of the affected populations, impact pathways, and counted consequences. Dropping items solely by heading risks omitting burdens that belong separately, whereas summing them directly risks double counting.
claims.scope: Distinct audit conditions for activity duplication and cross-pillar topic overlap; author synthesis providing no uniform deduction rule.
caveats: Performs no empirical overlap deduction on a hybrid inventory and establishes no common cross-pillar damage unit.
Does not claim that any health item across the three sustainability pillars should be deleted automatically.

claims.text: Once the research reference and activity inventory are aligned, analysts must recognize another source of variation frequently mistaken for a physical difference: the same inventory can yield different rankings under different life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) methods, spatial resolutions, or release packages. As verified across this monograph's impact assessment chapters—covering mineral and fossil resources, biogenic carbon, acidification and eutrophication, fine particulate matter, water use, ozone and radiation, and toxicity—divergences typically stem from four non-physical sources: evaluation cut-points and category boundaries (such as classifying uranium under mineral versus fossil resources, treating biogenic carbon as zero-net versus accounting for carbon storage and differing time windows, or deducting soil retention from agricultural phosphorus runoff), spatial and emission-compartment resolution (global averages versus watershed or urban-archetype factors), time-horizon settings, and errata in official method XML files or workbooks. Only by separating physical changes in the inventory from shifts in characterization models and package versions can one tell whether a ranking change reflects technological improvement or a switch in modeling conventions.
claims.scope: Synthesizes the monograph's impact assessment comparisons to separate physical inventory changes from four non-physical LCIA sources: category boundaries, spatial compartments, time windows, and official package errata.
caveats: Physical pathways and model maturity differ across impact categories; version-update sensitivity in one category cannot be generalized to assume all categories are equally robust or fragile.

claims.text: At the level of evidence coverage and numerical provenance, this book's cross-framework comparisons of data applicability, uncertainty, and quality scoring establish a boundary that must hold: geographic and market representativeness of background databases, data quality ratings (DQR), and statistical probability distributions are not interchangeable. Global averages and Rest-of-World (RoW) datasets drift as databases release new versions and add country-specific records, while standards diverge in their secondary-data fallback hierarchies and cut-off rules. Although pedigree matrices conveniently assign default dispersions across five dimensions when empirical variance is unavailable, those heuristic defaults and empirical sampling distributions are different mathematical objects; Monte Carlo intervals driven by pedigree factors cannot be presented as statistical proof of observational error. Likewise, ecoinvent pedigree variances, empirical error calibration, the ordinal quality ratings of the European Union (EU) Product Environmental Footprint (PEF), and the qualitative uncertainty disclosures of the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol each perform distinct roles; reports must separately document data-source tier, quality-rating convention, and observed variation range.
claims.scope: Synthesizes the data-applicability, uncertainty, and data-quality comparisons to demarcate geographic/market drift, pedigree Monte Carlo limits, and DQR roles across four frameworks.
caveats: A strong data quality rating indicates only that a record meets a specific framework's metadata and representativeness thresholds; it does not automatically eliminate system-boundary truncation or model-structure uncertainty.

claims.text: After quantifying activities and impacts, an assessment must still justify how trade-offs are weighed. Fairness rationales in joint production govern burden partitioning, cost evaluations must state who bears expenses, dynamic assessments require choosing an evaluation endpoint, and weights set each indicator's share in an aggregate judgment. Each choice needs its own justification—even assigning equal weights to all indicators imposes a specific relative weighting. Preserving disaggregated results and stating which conditions alter rankings lets readers see whether disagreement stems from the model or from value trade-offs.
claims.scope: Distinct justifications for fairness, cost-bearing actor, temporal endpoint, and weighting choices; author synthesis without treating them as interchangeable parameters.
caveats: Judges no single fairness view, actor perspective, time horizon, or weight set as universally correct.
Does not treat recommendations from different sources as a single mandatory rulebook.

claims.text: Monetary figures serve distinct roles across studies. Early beverage container policy research used expenditure flows to trace industrial demand, trade-model social assessments can use monetary outlays as a study reference, and life cycle costing (LCC) tracks who pays expenses and who receives revenues. Equal monetary amounts do not prove equivalent service, nor can expenditure-linked social risk indicators be treated as directly observed impacts. A single decision may draw on these separately to describe activity levels, risk exposure, and burden distribution, while unpriced damages still require separate reporting.
claims.scope: Distinguishes monetary figures as activity links, model references, and cost objects; author synthesis.
caveats: LCC boundaries remain at the level cited in the 2010 sustainability paper referencing the 2008 costing volume.
Distinguishing these roles establishes no cross-model monetary conversion or common monetary benchmark.

claims.text: Before adopting a study, check what reviewers actually verified. Reviewing a dataset against database-entry criteria examines a different object from critically reviewing a complete comparative study. Version updates, review criteria, and unmet conditions also limit which studies a review opinion can support. Citations enable readers to trace sources, while judgments synthesized from multiple sources must also lay out their reasoning chain. Whether primary texts support a claim, whether empirical evidence validates a modeled relationship, and whether domain review accepts a study must each be verified separately.
claims.scope: Applicability links among review criteria, reviewed objects, and version changes; author synthesis that does not transfer review verdicts through citation.
caveats: Reviews described in the 2011 database guidance do not constitute external certification of new citations or syntheses.
Does not infer current ISO or EU statutory compliance requirements from citations to database guidance.

claims.text: Even when a study cannot declare an overall winner, it can still show where burdens concentrate, which assumption most urgently needs evidence, or which impacts shift under specified future conditions. Turning those findings into procurement or policy recommendations still requires verifying that evidence covers the conditions the recommendation presupposes. When available data cannot resolve a difference, conclusions can report observed trade-offs alongside open questions; claiming that a difference is small enough to accept requires explicit criteria such as a tolerance threshold backed by commensurate evidence.
claims.scope: Evidentiary burden for conditional findings, recommendation scope, and equivalence assertions; author synthesis offering no specific procurement or policy verdict.
caveats: Offers no specific product-procurement or public-policy recommendation.
The 1972 container example is not an empirical proof of current net economic effects.

claims.text: Whether a recommendation holds up can be audited backward from the conclusion: which comparisons and checks support it, how models and data represent each option, and how each option delivers the studied service? When evidence supports a clearly scoped choice, a recommendation is warranted; when it establishes only where burdens shift, the conclusion should state that trade-off. Documenting data and reasoning transparently lets future analysts, once new evidence arrives, identify the exact step that requires recalculation.
claims.scope: Conditional links among function, model, and result interpretation; not a new external standard.

claims.text: When comparisons span multiple environmental categories, social dimensions, and financial perspectives, the aggregation rule itself often decides the ranking. As demonstrated across this book's valuation, regionalization, and integrated assessment chapters, normalization and weighting are never neutral rescalings: the geographic scope and estimation bias of external normalization denominators interact with weighting factors to amplify or suppress particular categories' relative contributions, while regionalized adjustments must check emission location, transport pathway, background load, and receptor sensitivity layer by layer so that local hotspots are not averaged away. Converting environmental externalities into monetary terms and accounting for corporate cash-flow LCC belong to incommensurable ledgers. Linear weighting in multi-criteria decision analysis implicitly permits full compensation across criteria; where worker safety, human-rights floors, or irreversible ecological thresholds are involved, non-compensatory outranking or veto thresholds are necessary. Even in planetary-boundary assessments aimed at absolute environmental sustainability, changing the sharing principle for allocating safe operating space suffices to reverse whether the same option complies.
claims.scope: Synthesizes normalization/weighting, regionalization, social assessment, monetization and LCC, multi-criteria decision analysis, and planetary-boundary comparisons to define incommensurability and veto boundaries.
caveats: Declining to collapse multidimensional results into a single score is not avoiding a decision; it moves value stances, compensation limits, and sharing principles out of hidden coefficients and into open scrutiny.

claims.text: Even when a comparison aligns functional service, system boundaries, and background pairing computationally, whether it may publicly assert that "Option A outperforms Option B" must pass institutional and review boundaries. The three major frameworks contrasted across this monograph draw clear dividing lines: the International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Handbook (2010) forbids weighting in comparative assertions disclosed to the public, prohibits basing comparative assertions on inventory results alone, and requires critical review by an independent expert panel; the EU PEF framework—alongside the EU Batteries Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2023/1542) and the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR, Regulation (EU) 2024/1781)—establishes comparability and compliance boundaries through named Product Environmental Footprint Category Rules (PEFCRs), quantitative hotspot thresholds, performance classes, and statutory verification pathways; and the GHG Protocol Product Standard explicitly states that it is not designed to support public comparative assertions of product superiority. For copyright-protected, paywalled international standards whose full texts were not audited clause by clause—such as ISO 14044, ISO 14067, and ISO/TS 14071 (uniform verification boundaries detailed in the Reading Guide)—this book preserves explicit silence, neither equating external guidelines with ISO text nor passing off secondary paraphrase as standard-level authority.
claims.scope: Synthesizes product-footprint rules and the wall-service and carrier-bag review comparisons to demarcate computational comparability from institutional boundaries across ILCD, EU PEF/regulations, and the GHG Protocol, alongside paywalled-ISO silence discipline.
caveats: A result verified under one regime cannot be transferred automatically to another jurisdiction or another public comparative assertion; cross-regime reuse requires re-checking functional unit, background database, and review scope.

claims.text: The supermarket carrier-bag report shows how critical review clarifies what a calculation can answer. Commissioned by the UK Environment Agency and dated February 2011 (referencing UK 2006/07 conditions), the report defined carrying one month's supermarket groceries home as the nominal shared service and derived initial bag counts from bag capacity and item count. The share of lightweight bags that replace purchased bin liners alters the total number of shopping trips—including the first trip—required for a thicker bag to break even. Under the baseline assumption that roughly 40.28% of lightweight high-density polyethylene (HDPE) bags displace purchased bin liners, a thicker low-density polyethylene (LDPE) bag used for five shopping trips in total achieves a lower climate indicator yet remains slightly higher than the lightweight bag on abiotic resource depletion. The critical review panel accepted the revised study while maintaining reservations over actual functionality, whether required reuse counts are achieved in practice, and land- and water-use concerns affecting mainly cotton and biopolymer bags. Calculation shows how many uses are needed; empirical observation is still required to establish how many uses actually occur.
claims.scope: UK Environment Agency report SC030148 (dated February 2011), covering its UK 2006/07 grocery-carrying service, modeled break-even thresholds, and final critical-review opinion.
caveats: The bin-liner substitution rate is a modeled study condition, and total shopping uses include the first trip; cross-category comparisons under the baseline preserve each indicator's own unit and meaning.

The final review opinion applies to that study edition; land- and water-use reservations primarily concern cotton and biopolymer bags, while actual reuse rates, contemporary bag designs, disposal conditions, and public recommendations each require separate evidence.

claims.text: When new data arrive, first identify which analytical step they alter. If a new survey finds different bag fill volumes, recalculate how many bags are required to deliver the same carrying service. If evidence shows that bin-liner purchases do not fall as assumed, re-examine the basis for the substitution credit. If a new model captures previously omitted impacts, return to the corresponding impact-assessment step. Pinpointing which link a change affects determines whether the original conclusion still stands, requires narrowing in scope, or must be rewritten.
claims.scope: Study-wide interpretation and iterative revision responsibilities.

claims.text: Other studies can be revised by the same logic. When the service changes, re-examine required processes and comparators; when a background database updates, check what the new release represents and which calculations are affected; when previously omitted flows are added, verify which impacts now have data coverage and whether indicators must be recalculated; and when governing rules undergo substantive revision, check whether the original calculation procedure still complies. Keeping steps whose basis remains sound while re-verifying only the affected links clarifies whether the next gap requires new observations, better explanation of modeled relationships, or explicit justification of value choices.
claims.scope: Targeted re-audit after service, data, coverage, or rule changes; author guidance, not an automated impact-detection algorithm.
caveats: Recorded dependencies may still be incomplete and cannot establish a blanket rule exempting steps from re-inspection.
This is a targeted review recommendation and provides no calculation, software, or regulatory-compliance verification.

claims.text: Returning to this book's opening question—when a product saves electricity in use yet consumes more energy in manufacturing, how do we judge whether switching pays off?—the answer starts with seeing the boundaries of the comparison clearly. The beverage container studies estimated energy-saving potential within the delivery system, whereas policy analysis also had to consider energy demand outside it; the wall-coating calculation showed that even for an identical service, adding one surface-preparation step can alter the comparison; and the carrier-bag study calculated how many trips a thicker bag requires, while empirical observation of whether shoppers meet that threshold remained absent. Precisely because every conclusion rests on specific service definitions, boundaries, data, and review premises, new evidence calls for targeted recalculation at the affected link—neither starting over from scratch nor retreating into blanket disclaimers.
claims.scope: Author synthesis across the two selected early container reports, the pedagogical wall-coating case, and the historical carrier-bag study.
caveats: Connections among these materials represent the monograph's analytical contrast; institutional lineage, discipline-wide progress, and historical priority each require independent historical evidence.
Traceable model links provide a starting point for re-audit; practical applicability to a real decision still depends on study evidence, scope, and supporting rationales.

claims.text: Following this layered architecture—in which conclusions rest sequentially on service requirements, system models, background data, impact assessment, value trade-offs, uncertainty, and review regimes—each class of new evidence maps to its own targeted revision entry point. Shifts in observed user behavior or secondary functions trigger recalculation of the functional unit, reference flows, and reuse thresholds without invalidating upstream process mass balances; background database updates or method-package errata point to inventory linking or characterization matrices and must not be misread as sudden deterioration in plant energy performance; shifts in normalization denominators, weights, or planetary-boundary sharing principles alter composite rankings and compliance criteria rather than underlying physical emission inventories; and updates to category rules or critical-review scope alter institutional eligibility for public claims rather than internal hotspot diagnostics. Routing revisions layer by layer lets both research teams and readers see immediately which step new evidence rewrites and which prior foundations remain valid.
claims.scope: Bridges the historical return to establish a book-wide targeted revision protocol mapping new evidence to affected steps, revised propositions, preserved foundations, and prohibited inferences.
caveats: When a single real-world change touches multiple layers simultaneously—for instance, a new process that alters both functional lifetime and upstream feedstock routes—analysts should apply the routing table row by row rather than revising only the most visible layer.

claims.text: Closing this monograph and looking back across its three recurring cases—beverage containers, wall coatings, and supermarket carrier bags—together with the methodological comparisons spanning all seven parts, what life cycle assessment can responsibly deliver is never a context-free "ultimate winner" label, but a traceable, recalculable, falsifiable structure of conditional judgment: laying bare how environmental, social, and cost burdens shift, marking the quantitative thresholds where conclusions flip, documenting model boundaries, data provenance, and review authority, and leaving precise revision entry points for future work. It can never replace political and ethical value choices, substitute for unobserved real-world usage, or let a single calculation automatically cross statutory compliance regimes across jurisdictions; yet precisely by acknowledging those boundaries and refusing to conceal assumptions inside a black box, life cycle assessment earns its place as a scientific instrument that grows with evidence and withstands public scrutiny.
claims.scope: Monograph closing statement synthesizing the three recurring cases and seven-part methodological comparisons to define the responsible deliverables and non-substitutable boundaries of revisable LCA judgment.
caveats: This closing synthesis draws on verified primary literature and open calculation cases across the monograph; it does not substitute for site-specific monitoring in a given engineering project or statutory conformity assessment in a given jurisdiction.

claims.text: In ecoinvent, the choice of system model governs which processes supply one another, how environmental burdens are assigned across functions, and under what conditions substitution is applied. Before using an inventory dataset, check which system model generated it and verify that its linking and attribution rules match the study's goal and system boundary.
claims.scope: Overview from the ecoinvent System Models documentation.

claims.text: Under ecoinvent's Allocation, cut-off by classification system model, primary production burdens remain with the primary user. Recyclable materials enter the subsequent product system at a designated handoff point free of primary production burdens, while still carrying the burdens associated with recycling activities. Tracing the complete inventory of a recycled product therefore requires following collection, transport, and reprocessing from that handoff point onward.
claims.scope: Overview of ecoinvent's Allocation, cut-off by classification system model.
caveats: Specific recycling chains involve exceptions and modeling details; this summary does not substitute for process-by-process inspection.

claims.text: ecoinvent classifies Allocation at the Point of Substitution (APOS) as an attributional system model in which waste generators and downstream users of treatment outputs share the associated burdens. When comparing APOS with the cut-off model, inspect which activities enter the shared-burden pool and at what point treated outputs enter the next product system.
claims.scope: Overview of ecoinvent's Allocation at the Point of Substitution (APOS) system model.

claims.text: ecoinvent's consequential system model resolves multifunctionality through substitution and selects suppliers according to marginal supply assumptions. Interpreting its results requires identifying which processes are substituted and which supply streams are constrained. This description applies specifically to ecoinvent's named consequential system model.
claims.scope: Overview of ecoinvent's Substitution, consequential, long-term system model.
caveats: This implementation should not be generalized as the sole approach to consequential life cycle assessment (LCA).

claims.text: According to ecoinvent's documentation, the system model now called Allocation at the Point of Substitution (APOS) was previously named Allocation, ecoinvent default and was renamed in ecoinvent 3.2.
claims.scope: Retrospective naming history reported on the official ecoinvent System Models page.
caveats: A change in model name does not by itself establish that the underlying algorithm or methodology changed.

claims.text: When comparing two allocation or recycling results, align their intended purpose, system boundary, and active system model before tracing process-to-process links. Even when exchange fields map one-to-one across data files, analysts must still verify whether burden attribution and substitution rules match.
claims.scope: Cross-layer comparison between ecoinvent system models and openLCA data representations.
caveats: This statement specifies conditions to verify during comparison and does not declare any system model universally superior.

claims.text: The 100-year Global Warming Potential (GWP100) interpretation used in this example follows Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) Working Group I (WGI) Chapter 7: relative emission metrics compare the physical effect of a given emission against that of a reference CO2 emission, and GWP evaluates integrated radiative forcing over a chosen time horizon. Here, kg CO2-eq preserves the mass-accounting basis rather than representing an actual mass of emitted CO2, a temperature at year 100, or observed climate damage.
claims.scope: Corresponding passages of IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 7 and the October 7, 2025 errata; factor interpretation is bounded to that edition and the stated accounting conditions.
caveats: Citations preserve the historical identity of the textual excerpts used in the original case; parallel excerpts from the primary report or errata listed in the same note do not constitute independent scientific validation.
The selected metric and characterization factors do not establish comparative conclusions for real-world coatings.
Characterization factors from this named edition do not automatically serve as default requirements across all reporting frameworks.

claims.text: In replacement Table 7.15 of the IPCC AR6 WGI errata (Version 7 October 2025), the GWP-100 value in the CO2 row is 1.000. Teaching calculations write this value as 1 while remaining anchored to that errata edition.

claims.text: In the same replacement table, the GWP-100 column for the CH4-fossil row reports 28.1 ± 10.4. This example uses the central value of 28.1 while preserving the fossil-origin species identity; the reported uncertainty is not propagated within the single-parameter range of this worked example, and arithmetic precision must not be mistaken for empirical certainty.
claims.scope: Corresponding passages of IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 7 and the October 7, 2025 errata; factor interpretation is bounded to that edition and the stated accounting conditions.

claims.text: The multi-model intercomparison by Joos et al. (2013) defines a shared reference experiment for the carbon dioxide (CO₂) impulse response function. Background atmospheric CO₂ is raised to 389 parts per million (ppm) and held constant. In paired emission-driven runs, researchers inject a 100 gigatonnes of carbon (GtC) pulse in 2015 and subtract a matching control run to isolate the pulse-induced perturbation. The reported "per-kilogram response" is therefore a normalized output of this prescribed experiment, with 2015 as the pulse year and 389 ppm as the background state. Because the reference response is conditional on that experimental protocol, it cannot be treated as a forecast for arbitrary future product emissions.
claims.scope: 100 GtC CO₂ pulse and control runs under the prescribed background protocol of Joos et al. (2013).
caveats: Several participating models did not submit full-length control or pulse runs, as documented separately in the paper and its supplementary protocol; only the published multi-model fit is used here.

claims.text: Because Joos et al. (2013) publish the fitted parameters explicitly, the reference response can be reconstructed directly. Letting R(t) denote the fraction of an emission pulse remaining in the atmosphere t years after release, the fitted function takes the form R(t) = a₀ + Σ aᵢ exp(−t/τᵢ). In the selected multi-model row of Table 5, the constant term is a₀ = 0.2173, and the three exponential weights 0.2240, 0.2824, and 0.2763 pair with time constants of 394.4, 36.54, and 4.304 years, respectively. The weights sum to 1, ensuring R(0) = 1, and the fit is defined over the paper's specified domain of 0 to 1,000 years after emission.
claims.scope: Multi-model CO₂ impulse response fit from Joos et al. (2013), Table 5, over the 0–1,000-year domain.
caveats: The constant term a₀ is a fitting component over this finite 1,000-year horizon and does not assert that a fixed fraction of emitted carbon remains permanently in the real atmosphere.

claims.text: Integrating this fitted function term by term yields I(H) = a₀H + Σ aᵢτᵢ[1 − exp(−H/τᵢ)]. Using the printed parameters, the remaining fraction at year 100 is R(100) = 0.409428, and the cumulative integral from 0 to 100 years is I(100) = ∫R(t)dt = 52.355389 years. In the companion figure in the main chapter, the upper curve tracks the instantaneous remaining fraction at each time point, while the shaded area beneath the curve up to that horizon represents the time integral of that fraction.
claims.scope: Instantaneous remaining fraction and analytical time integral reconstructed from the printed parameters of the Joos et al. (2013) fit.

claims.text: At time horizons of 20, 100, and 500 years, this fitted function integrates to approximately 14.242, 52.355, and 183.638 years, corresponding to the values of 14.2, 52.4, and 184 years displayed in Table 4 of Joos et al. (2013). This reconstruction verifies the published fit and its rounding alignment, but it does not regenerate the underlying trajectories of individual Earth system models. Likewise, inter-model spread cannot be transferred directly as a confidence interval for an arbitrary product inventory. The response-and-integral figure in the main chapter plots this fit so that the shaded area in the upper panel matches the corresponding horizon value in the lower panel.
claims.scope: Comparison of analytical integrals from the published fit against displayed values in Joos et al. (2013), Table 4.

claims.text: Recalculating the absolute global warming potential (AGWP) from the fitted integral tests how closely printed inputs reproduce published table entries. Multiplying the 100-year integral by the radiative efficiency of 1.77 × 10⁻¹⁵ W m⁻² kg⁻¹ given in the Joos et al. (2013) table footnote produces 92.669 × 10⁻¹⁵ W m⁻² yr kg⁻¹, whereas Table 4 reports a mean of 92.5 × 10⁻¹⁵ W m⁻² yr kg⁻¹. The two figures are close without matching to every digit, and the exact source of the small gap remains unidentified. Both the parameter-based recalculation and the authors' reported value should therefore be retained separately; even if an adjusted parameter can be back-solved to eliminate the difference, that does not establish it as the authors' undisclosed original input.
claims.scope: Recalculation from displayed parameters in Joos et al. (2013) versus Table 4 reported values, without back-solving undisclosed precision.
caveats: The exact source of this small discrepancy is unidentified; displayed parameter precision and physical uncertainty are distinct issues.

claims.text: Relative metrics can also fail to reproduce digit for digit from printed absolute values. In the corrected supplementary table of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) Working Group I (WGI), generic methane has an AGWP100 of 2.43 pW m⁻² yr kg⁻¹ and the CO₂ reference is 0.093 pW m⁻² yr kg⁻¹; their direct quotient is 26.129, yet the relative-metric column displays 26.2. If each printed entry is explicitly assumed to carry a rounding band of half a unit in the last displayed place, the columns are mutually consistent. This check diagnoses arithmetic compatibility among displayed numbers; it does not estimate a confidence interval for physical climate effects.
claims.scope: Displayed-precision check for the generic methane AGWP100 ratio in the corrected IPCC AR6 WGI supplementary table.

claims.text: Re-running historical author code verifies whether a specific source snapshot reproduces the values printed at the time. The 2021 Zenodo archive of the IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 7 author code and the later GitHub snapshot—which added the carbon-feedback functions and metric-generation workflow—contain different routines. On its 0.1-year time grid over the selected scope, the later snapshot yields a generic methane 100-year global warming potential (GWP100) of 27.859214 and a 100-year global temperature change potential (GTP100) of 5.377065, matching the pre-errata supplementary table. Because this run includes warming-driven carbon-cycle feedbacks but does not execute the fossil oxidation or biogenic uptake pathways for methane's own carbon, it reproduces neither the two main-table methane rows nor the 2025 errata.
claims.scope: Selected native routines (0–100 years) from the post-release IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 7 author-code snapshot for the historical generic methane column.
caveats: Only selected routines over 0–100 years were executed; this does not replay all original models, full notebooks, figures, other gases, or uncertainty ensembles.

claims.text: Refining the time step reveals how sensitive the numerical output is to discretization. Holding all physical parameters constant and halving the feedback-convolution step from 0.1 years to 0.05 years increases GWP100 by approximately 0.079728 and GTP100 by approximately 0.099951. Agreement on the original discrete grid confirms internal consistency for that code version, whereas establishing full numerical convergence requires testing progressively finer grids. Nor does the difference between these two step sizes explain the official errata or measure climate-parameter uncertainty. The value of numerical reconstruction lies in specifying exactly which object is reconstructed and keeping each diagnostic check within its own scope.
claims.scope: Numerical grid sensitivity between 0.1-year and 0.05-year time steps under fixed physical parameters.

claims.text: Start from the two balance equations in the 1992 Guide from the Center of Environmental Science at Leiden University (CML) aluminum-foil toy model, where x denotes the electricity activity level and y denotes the aluminum activity level. Substituting x = 50y + 0.1 into y = 0.01x + 0.1 gives y = 0.5y + 0.101, so 0.5y = 0.101 and y = 0.202. Direct substitution completes the solution without invoking matrix notation. The original Guide instead solves the system via Cramer's rule—computing intermediate determinants from the coefficient matrix and taking their ratios. On page 39, however, it prints the second column-substituted determinant (replacing the aluminum column with the demand vector) as 0.01 while still printing the aluminum activity level as 0.202. Recalculating from the equations on the same page yields 0.101; dividing the printed value 0.01 by the coefficient-matrix determinant of 0.5 would give only 0.02. Here the activity level is reconstructed from the explicit balance equations while preserving the original discrepancy, rather than treating one matching final value as proof that the entire page is arithmetically consistent.
claims.scope: Arithmetic discrepancy on page 39 of the CML 1992 Guide between the printed determinant, balance equations, and reported activity level.

claims.text: Comparing parameters with different physical units requires examining percentage responses. In the CML 1992 Guide aluminum-foil toy model, the normalized local response of total solid waste to the aluminum output coefficient recalculates to −1.973, matching the entry printed in the original table. Near the baseline state, holding per-unit inputs fixed, increasing the aluminum process output coefficient—the mass of aluminum produced per unit of activity—by a small percentage reduces total selected solid waste by approximately 1.973 times that percentage. Electricity generation remains the largest direct source of solid waste, yet the strongest parameter response occurs in aluminum production output. The two findings do not conflict: contribution analysis identifies where existing waste originates, whereas sensitivity analysis measures how the total responds to a parameter change.
claims.scope: Normalized local parameter response in the CML 1992 Guide aluminum-foil toy model with all other coefficients held fixed.

claims.text: Next, evaluate a finite parameter perturbation directly in the model. Keeping the final demand fixed at 10 aluminum-foil bags and all other coefficients unchanged in the CML 1992 Guide toy model, raising the aluminum output coefficient from 1 kg per unit activity to 1.01 kg per unit activity and re-solving yields approximately 22.084 kg of solid waste—a change of −1.935% from the baseline, compared with the local tangent approximation of −1.973%. The Guide subsequently refers to an approximate 1.9% reduction in the "total volume of waste," even though the model and its tables track waste mass in kilograms without providing a density or volume conversion, and the original sentence does not state its rounding convention. Finite recalculation and local tangent approximation are distinct operations and should not be conflated simply because their numerical outputs lie close together.
claims.scope: Finite perturbation versus local approximation for a single aluminum output coefficient at fixed service demand.
caveats: This recalculates the response of a selected parameter and does not claim that every entry in the original marginal matrix was rounded to the nearest displayed digit; original software was not executed.

The original text uses the phrase "total volume of waste," whereas the selected table and model are expressed in kilograms with no density or volume conversion provided; this recalculation tracks model mass while preserving the original wording separately.

claims.text: Whereas the main chapter checks US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) baseline screening scores against point values of photochemical ozone creation potential (POCP) from the CML 1992 Guide, comparing the same source's scenario ranges against the scoring bins shows what scenario information is lost in discretization. The 1992 Guide lists a POCP range of 0.410–0.830 for toluene: the lower end falls into bin 5, while the upper end falls into bin 3. A single fixed screening score therefore cannot represent the full scenario variation reported in the source table. At the same time, this span does not establish a probability distribution for the score, because the original scenario and multi-day trajectory ranges are not sampling probabilities or confidence intervals.
claims.scope: Comparison of CML 1992 Guide toluene POCP scenario range against EPA baseline scoring bins without probabilistic assumptions or site-specific modifiers.

claims.text: Begin with the glass-container manufacturing stage, where the denominator is 1 short ton of finished glass containers. Volume II, Table 22 of the 1974 study lists five energy inputs per short ton of glass containers: 1.2 gallons of distillate oil, 5.5 gallons of residual oil, 10,700 cubic feet of natural gas, 0.023 gallons of gasoline, and 263 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electricity. Interpreting any of these numbers requires stating both the energy carrier and the per-short-ton basis; applying the same figures directly on a "per bottle" or "per filling" basis alters their physical meaning.
claims.scope: Energy-input rows of Volume II, Table 22 of the 1974 EPA container study on the reported per-short-ton basis.
caveats: These five inputs do not constitute the complete glass-system inventory and do not imply identical energy demands across all glass plants.

claims.text: In the 1974 report, the total energy factors in Volume II, Table 1 are expressed in million British thermal units (Btu) per 1,000 gallons for liquid fuels and million Btu per 1,000 cubic feet for natural gas, while the electricity factor in Table 4 is expressed in million Btu per 1,000 kWh. Because the process inputs are tabulated in single gallons, cubic feet, or kWh, each input must first be divided by 1,000 to match the factor denominator. The five resulting contributions are 1.2 × 158.9 / 1,000, 5.5 × 169.9 / 1,000, 10,700 × 1.086 / 1,000, 0.023 × 144.9 / 1,000, and 263 × 11.1 / 1,000—all in million Btu per short ton of glass. Summing these five terms gives 15.6679627 million Btu per short ton, which rounds to 15.668 at three decimal places and matches the total glass-manufacturing energy of 15.668 reported in Table 14.
claims.scope: Selected verification of raw energy inputs multiplied by total energy factors (including upstream supply) in Volume II of the 1974 EPA container study.
caveats: Factor denominators are 1,000 gal, 1,000 ft³, and 1,000 kWh, respectively; calculated decimal places do not represent measurement precision, and matching total energy does not independently verify the separate process and transport columns.

claims.text: With glass-container manufacturing energy verified, Volume II, Table 8 can be used to account for glass manufacturing together with its upstream raw-material supply. Table 8 is normalized to 1 short ton of the one-way glass (OWG) container system, meaning every entry is already scaled to the material quantity required for that system rather than to 1 short ton of each individual upstream process. On this shared per-short-ton system basis, the eight stages—feldspar mining (0.100), glass sand mining (0.569), natural soda ash mining (0.040), soda ash manufacturing (1.851), lime manufacturing (0.215), limestone mining (0.031), salt mining (0.049), and glass-container manufacturing (15.668)—sum to 18.523 million Btu. Because this subtotal already includes glass-container manufacturing, the 15.668 term must not be added a second time.
claims.scope: Displayed coefficients for the eight glass-manufacturing and upstream inorganic raw-material stages in Volume II, Table 8 of the 1974 EPA container study.
caveats: Entries share the Table 8 common system basis rather than summing per-short-ton outputs of separate processes; this branch excludes full secondary packaging, closures, filling, disposal, and separately itemized system transport.

claims.text: Applying the same 18.523 million Btu per short ton branch coefficient to the new-glass mass (in short tons) required for each scenario yields 30.5 × 18.523 = 564.9515 million Btu for the 10-trip returnable glass scenario and 205 × 18.523 = 3,797.215 million Btu for the one-way glass scenario, both referenced to the same 1 million fillings. Because the two container systems differ in both bottle weight and trippage, this comparison does not isolate the effect of trippage alone. Moreover, the recalculation covers only glass manufacturing and upstream raw-material supply, not the full set of activities in either container system.
claims.scope: Conditional calculation combining disclosed new-glass tonnages with the Table 8 glass-branch coefficient.
caveats: The same scaling factor is not applied to filling, return packaging flows, or all transport stages.

claims.text: A third scenario provides an additional cross-check on this scaling rule. At 5 trips per bottle, new glass demand is 61 short tons; multiplying 61 × 18.523 gives 1,129.903 million Btu, which rounds to 1,130 and matches the "Bottle system" column total of 1,130 in Volume II, Table 9. This agreement verifies only the glass-manufacturing and raw-material supply branch; it does not validate the remaining columns of Table 9 or the entire 5-trip container system.
claims.scope: Numerical cross-check between the Volume II, Table 9 bottle-system column and the published Table 8 branch coefficient.
caveats: Internal consistency within a single report does not constitute independent empirical replication.

claims.text: Assembling the full table falls 70.09 million Btu short of the total reported in the 1974 study. To test how much of that gap could stem from displayed-digit rounding alone, suppose only the 13 three-decimal-place coefficients drawn from Table 8 each carry a rounding error of at most 0.0005, while the 205 short tons of glass are held strictly fixed. Under those conditions, the maximum possible cumulative rounding error is 13 × 0.0005 × 205 = 1.3325 million Btu—far smaller than 70.09 million Btu. This bound rules out the hypothesis that displayed rounding of the listed coefficients alone explains the gap under fixed tonnage, but it does not account for undisclosed precision in bottle weight and is not an empirical uncertainty interval.
claims.scope: Author-constructed conditional upper bound on coefficient-rounding error, not a statistical analysis from the 1974 report.
caveats: No probability distribution is assumed and the full cause of the discrepancy is not inferred; holding 205 short tons fixed is a prerequisite of this bound.

claims.text: Release height is also built into the Humbert et al. (2011) emission archetypes. For the urban archetype, published intake fractions for fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅) released from high stacks, low stacks, and ground-level sources are 11, 15, and 44 mg/kg, respectively; the corresponding urban values for coarse particulate matter are 8.8, 13, and 40 mg/kg. Here, "ground-level" refers to the method's near-ground release archetype. By embedding representative dispersion and population conditions, these figures demonstrate that equal emitted masses can produce markedly different population exposures, yet they neither predict intake for a specific real-world stack nor capture the full environmental consequences of altering stack height.
claims.scope: Urban fine and coarse particulate matter intake-fraction archetypes by high-stack, low-stack, and ground-level release height in Humbert et al. (2011).

claims.text: Comparing height-averaged intake fractions for mixed emission sources also requires the mass shares emitted from each height class. In the US inventory dataset used by Humbert et al. (2011) to construct height-weighted averages, fine particulate matter emissions split 0.41, 0.17, and 0.42 across high-stack, low-stack, and ground-level sources, whereas coarse particulate matter splits 0.08, 0.02, and 0.90. Coarse particles are heavily concentrated at ground level, with road dust accounting for a major share. Because this weighting dataset excludes wildfires and miscellaneous sources, any inventory that omits road dust requires re-weighting in line with the paper's stated conditions.
claims.scope: US mass shares by release height and exclusions used by Humbert et al. (2011) to construct height-weighted average intake fractions for fine and coarse particulate matter.

claims.text: Weighting the printed urban archetype values by these mass shares gives 0.41 × 11 + 0.17 × 15 + 0.42 × 44 = 25.54 mg/kg for fine particulate matter and 0.08 × 8.8 + 0.02 × 13 + 0.90 × 40 = 36.964 mg/kg for coarse particulate matter, matching the published table entries of 26 and 37 mg/kg. Even though fine particles have a higher intake fraction at every individual release height, the mixed-source ranking reverses because the two size fractions differ sharply in their height distribution. This calculation checks the arithmetic consistency of the height-weighting step; because the individual height factors themselves were derived from unknown-height anchor values and scaling ratios, agreement confirms internal weighting consistency rather than independent validation. Moreover, this comparison concerns intake fraction only and cannot show that coarse particles are more toxic to human health.
claims.scope: Height-weighted recalculation of mixed urban fine and coarse intake fractions and the arithmetic condition behind the ranking reversal.
caveats: This arithmetic check does not propagate parameter, structural, or input uncertainty from the original models; extra decimal places reflect exact arithmetic on the listed inputs rather than empirical precision.

claims.text: The recommended intake fractions in Humbert et al. (2011) draw on multiple underlying models and literature sources. Primary fine particulate matter relies mainly on re-parameterized USEtox archetype runs, height and size-fraction scaling ratios draw on RiskPoll, and secondary precursors rely on distinct literature models. Harmonizing breathing rates and population conditions enables cross-model consistency checks, but it does not substitute for independent empirical measurements across all scenarios. Because the authors explicitly distinguish inter-model spread, spatial variability, and unquantified uncertainties, a unified summary table should not be read as equally supported empirical evidence across every row.
claims.scope: Model lineage (USEtox, RiskPoll, and precursor literature models) and unquantified uncertainty behind the recommended intake fractions in Humbert et al. (2011).
caveats: Supplementary regressions and displayed population figures in Humbert et al. (2011) do not fully close every precursor entry in the main table; main-table values are retained as published without claiming full reconstruction of all recommendations.

claims.text: Multiplying published factors verifies unit consistency and reported arithmetic, but assessing whether intake estimates align with independent evidence requires comparing distinct estimation pathways. Gronlund et al. (2015) estimated US population intake from both the 2005 national emissions inventory and ambient concentration data, finding that the emissions-based total was roughly 2.2 times the concentration-based total. At the county level, the two approaches also have different spatial boundaries: one sums impacts across all receptors affected by emissions originating in a county, whereas the other sums exposure experienced by residents within that county. Because both pathways share the same health-response and severity derivations, their divergence highlights consistency limits in intake estimation; it neither validates the health-response function independently nor measures the outcome of an actual abatement intervention.
claims.scope: The 2.2-fold discrepancy and spatial boundary difference between emissions-based and concentration-based intake estimates for the 2005 US inventory in Gronlund et al. (2015).

claims.text: The 2017 multi-compartment model for primary particulate matter by Fantke et al. illustrates how emission rates translate into compartment concentrations. Under a continuous, constant emission rate, steady state requires inflows and outflows in every compartment to balance; the rate-constant matrix K records inter-compartment transfers and places total removal rates as negative entries on the diagonal. Defining the fate factor matrix as FF = −K⁻¹, FF carries units of days under the paper's daily time convention. Multiplying FF by an emission-rate vector e (in kg/day) yields the steady-state particulate mass in each compartment, and dividing by each compartment's air volume gives the source-attributable incremental concentration. Meteorology, ventilation, deposition, and compartment dimensions enter through the transfer coefficients and volumes, so numerical evaluation requires their concrete parameter values.
claims.scope: Symbolic steady-state mass-balance interpretation of the four-compartment primary particulate model in Fantke et al. (2017).
caveats: Expanding FF × e follows directly from mass balance and dimensional analysis; it does not imply access to the supplementary macro workbook or reconstruction of its numerical parameters.

claims.text: Next, the exposure factor (XF) specifies the fraction of each compartment's air volume inhaled per unit time by the corresponding exposed population. Multiplying XF by the compartment fate factor matrix (FF)—which retains residence times and multi-pass transfers—produces the intake fraction (iF). This decomposition allows analysts to trace atmospheric transport and residence separately from human inhalation across compartments. Although sharing a fate–exposure–effect structure helps readers bridge chemical toxicity models such as USEtox and particulate matter models, that shared architecture does not make their substance coverage, characterization factors, or health endpoints automatically equivalent.
claims.scope: Matrix decomposition of intake fraction into compartment fate factor matrix (FF) and exposure factor (XF) in Fantke et al. (2017).

claims.text: For indoor activities, emission duration and exposure duration need not coincide. The dynamic indoor model of Bhoonah et al. (2023) starts from the activity-induced incremental indoor concentration, multiplies by occupancy and breathing rate, and integrates over time, so inhalation continues after the emitting activity stops. Room volume, ventilation rate, occupancy, outdoor background concentration, and activity duration jointly govern the outcome. Consequently, intake or health damage calculated for a single reference activity cannot simply be scaled linearly with time while ignoring residual post-activity concentrations and overlapping activities.
claims.scope: Dynamic boundary conditions of time-integrated indoor incremental concentration and post-activity residual exposure in Bhoonah et al. (2023).

claims.text: The distinction between "marginal" and "average" effects also arises in Acidification and Eutrophication, where average ecosystem effects may be anchored to a policy target or an alternative ecological state.
