In Particulate Matter and Photochemical Ozone, by contrast, the integrated exposure-response (IER) counterfactual derives from epidemiological population-health risk models. Both domains distinguish a local slope near an operating point from an average slope between two states, yet each relies on its own reference state, response metric, and evidentiary base. An ecological guidance document's alternative operating point cannot be substituted directly as a concentration counterfactual for human health.
claims.scope: System boundary separating particulate-health counterfactual references from ecological target references in defining marginal versus average effect factors.

claims.text: For a reduced-form atmospheric model, a distinct diagnostic question is how accurately it approximates its full parent model. The TM5-FAst Scenario Screening Tool (TM5-FASST) study derives source–receptor relationships from emission perturbations and tests its linear approximation under selected scenarios; deviations emerge for certain large perturbations, and additive superposition is still assumed where systematic multi-precursor joint runs are unavailable. Such comparisons quantify model-simplification error, but they do not constitute independent empirical abatement tests and cannot replace locally constrained observational chemistry studies such as Cabauw. Both lines of evidence should be weighed according to the specific question each answers.
claims.scope: Simplification-error testing of TM5-FASST linear source–receptor approximations against the parent model versus local observational verification.

claims.text: Using published numerical factors reliably also requires distinguishing among the journal article, its supplementary tables, and subsequent errata. The formal 2019 correction to the global fine particulate matter effect-factor paper by Fantke et al. explicitly relabels columns F:P in the revised workbook as average effect factors and columns R:AB as marginal effect factors, fixing an earlier column-label swap. Such an error does not reveal itself automatically because both sets of columns share the same unit of disability-adjusted life years (DALY) per kg of inhaled PM₂.₅. A usable factor identity therefore requires specifying the release version, column definition, location, and scenario together.
claims.scope: Correction of swapped average (columns F:P) and marginal (columns R:AB) labels in the 2019 erratum to Fantke et al. (2019).

claims.text: While the erratum clarifies how to read the summary columns, whether the workbook's internal formulas reproduce the published values requires a separate audit. The operational sheet of the revised supplementary workbook computes effects from the difference in attributable deaths between two concentration points, yet the revision notes still point to operational columns that do not match the live formulas, and the default-location operational output differs from the published summary value for the same city. Citing published factors, interpreting the paper's analytical equations, and reproducing the workbook's operational formulas are therefore three distinct tasks. Because the exact calculation link between the operational sheet and the published summary remains unresolved, citations should state explicitly which layer a number comes from.
claims.scope: Unclosed discrepancy among the paper equations, two-point operational sheet, and published summary values in the Fantke et al. (2019) supplementary workbook.
caveats: This audit does not assign fault for the discrepancy or propose a single unique fix, and does not present operational-sheet recalculation as a full reproduction of the original paper.

claims.text: When applying Global Life Cycle Impact Assessment Method (GLAM) factors, users must keep publication dates and workbook release dates separate. The 2026 GLAM human-health journal article notes that version 1 was released publicly in late 2024; the particulate matter workbook inside the official V1.0.2024.10 archive should therefore be cited under its own release identity. The paper's publication year, the characterization-factor release version, and the reference year of the model's background data are three distinct dates and should be documented separately when citing results.
claims.scope: Distinction among the 2026 GLAM human-health paper publication date, the V1.0.2024.10 particulate workbook release, and the 2015 background-data year.

claims.text: The indoor indicators described in the GLAM human-health paper also include a midpoint indicator expressed in modeled deaths, which is not the same quantity as endpoint health damage in DALY; the paper derives this mortality midpoint by back-calculating from damage under a specified severity factor. Furthermore, expressing a factor per unit of activity duration links the impact to the emitting activity's length without truncating post-activity exposure when the activity ends. Finally, the fact that an indicator is discussed in the journal article does not by itself establish that it is included in the specific workbook release being used.
claims.scope: Relationship between indoor indicators described in the GLAM human-health paper and actual coverage in the published workbook.

claims.text: The GLAM outdoor framework computes impacts by source location, release height, receptor, and background state before aggregating to regional summaries. Its documentation specifies a 2015 background, a 2 m ground-level release height, and a simplified fate term paired with a global-average effect term beyond 250 km; spatial averages for regional factors are not weighted by population density or actual emission intensity, which the documentation lists as potential alternatives. Spatial averaging across grids, taking an average slope along an exposure-response curve, and weighting release heights by emission shares represent three distinct levels of averaging. Consequently, country and urban/rural entries in the factor table group emissions on the source side, whereas resulting health damage may occur across multiple receptor regions; matching a country name does not ensure that the factor reflects the spatial distribution of a particular stack or industrial sector.
claims.scope: Unweighted spatial averaging of GLAM outdoor regional factors and its distinction from exposure-response slope averaging and source-height weighting.
caveats: This notes only that the documentation explicitly omits population and emission weighting; it does not infer from "unweighted" that every regional mask, area calculation, or grid-generation script has been audited.

claims.text: For example, converting the Australian ground-level primary PM₂.₅ entries in the 2024 GLAM raw workbook into micro-DALY per kg emitted yields approximately 229.937 (marginal) and 205.604 (average) for the urban scenario, and approximately 7.611 (marginal) and 7.981 (average) for the rural scenario. One micro-DALY equals one-millionth of a DALY and is used here purely as a compact display unit, while the denominator remains 1 kg of the listed emission. Because these four characterization factors already express health damage per kilogram of emitted PM₂.₅, they must not be multiplied again by the historical effect factor of 78 from the earlier example.
claims.scope: Conversion of the Australian urban and rural ground-level primary PM₂.₅ marginal and average characterization factors in GLAM V1.0.2024.10 to micro-DALY/kg emitted.

claims.text: Computed from the unrounded workbook entries, the average-to-marginal ratio is approximately 0.894 in the Australian urban scenario and approximately 1.049 in the rural scenario—one below 1 and the other above 1. Although these two ratios alone do not isolate which background concentration or aggregation condition drives the difference, they are sufficient to refute any blanket claim that average factors are always larger than marginal factors. Comparing average and marginal factors always requires inspecting the underlying exposure-response curve, reference state, and regional aggregation procedure.
claims.scope: Australian urban (0.894) and rural (1.049) primary PM₂.₅ average-to-marginal ratios demonstrating bidirectional departure from 1.
caveats: This calculation does not propagate parameter, structural, or input uncertainty from the underlying models; displayed decimal places reflect arithmetic on the tabulated inputs rather than empirical precision.

claims.text: Part V closed by asking which factory, material, and time period a study's numbers actually represent. Part II (Goal and Scope Definition) already separated foreground and background systems from both the specificity and management perspectives; once modeling begins, no single team can measure hundreds of upstream supply chains—power generation, steelmaking, basic chemicals, shipping, and waste treatment—plant by plant, so studies rely on background life cycle inventory databases for upstream process matrices. Because background datasets often dominate a product's footprint, each library's lineage, modeling rules, and licensing boundaries shape reported results from the outset.
claims.scope: Division of labor between foreground and background systems and the methodological choices embedded inside background databases.
caveats: The boundary between foreground and background depends on decision control and data availability rather than a fixed industrial dividing line.

claims.text: Background databases evolved across four structural generations. In the 1970s and 1980s, early energy and packaging inventories compiled by the Midwest Research Institute (MRI), Franklin Associates, and the Boustead model existed as printed tables or closed spreadsheets with mutually incompatible units, boundaries, and flow names. During the 1990s, institutional inventories reusable across studies emerged in Europe—such as the Swiss BUWAL 132/250 series, ETH-ESU 96, and the Dutch IDEMAT and IVAM datasets—alongside engineering-oriented commercial libraries pioneered by PE International (later GaBi). In 2000, Swiss federal offices and research institutes of the ETH domain launched a harmonization effort that released ecoinvent v1 in 2003 (reaching more than 2,500 consistent, unit-process-transparent datasets by v1.1 in 2005). Over the same decade, NREL launched USLCI in the United States, the European Commission Joint Research Centre (JRC) released ELCD, Japan’s AIST initiated IDEA, and IKE and Sichuan University developed CLCD in China, marking the transition to systematic LCI databases.
claims.scope: Historical progression from 1970s hand-compiled inventory tables to the first systematic 2000s LCI databases.
caveats: Several 1970s–1990s archival print reports (such as original BUWAL and ETH-ESU volumes) were not inspected page by page; this summary captures recognized architectural milestones.

claims.text: ecoinvent version 3 (2013) inaugurated a third generation built on decoupled linking: instead of shipping one hard-wired static matrix, it separated unlinked raw unit-process datasets from system-model linking rules so the same underlying records could generate cut-off attributional, point-of-substitution, and long-term consequential databases while adding flow properties to support mass and elemental balance checks. In parallel, the European Union developed regulatory EF 2.0/3.0/3.1 reference packages and secondary datasets; specialized agri-food (AGRIBALYSE, Agri-footprint, WFLDB) and chemical (Carbon Minds) databases expanded; and multi-regional input-output models such as EXIOBASE 3 and USEEIO addressed process-level truncation gaps. In the 2020s, confronted with fragmented, mutually incompatible libraries, initiatives such as UNEP’s Global LCA Data Access network (GLAD), the U.S. Federal LCA Commons, the open-source BONSAI community, and the TianGong LCA Data System specification (TIDAS) shifted the frontier from sheer dataset volume toward metadata discovery, open schemas, and auditable mapping.
claims.scope: Decoupled multi-system-model linking and sectoral specialization in the 2010s, followed by federated discovery and open-schema interoperability in the 2020s.
caveats: Federated discovery networks such as GLAD improve metadata search and selected elementary-flow mappings, but do not automatically resolve underlying methodological conflicts across databases.

claims.text: Among comprehensive multi-sector databases, ecoinvent—maintained by the Swiss non-profit ecoinvent Association—stands as the flagship transparent unit-process library in academic and cross-industry LCA. Three design features define it: first, nearly all datasets are documented at the unit-process level, enabling users to inspect upstream supply chains, substitute local electricity grids, and propagate Monte Carlo uncertainty; second, since version 3 it strictly separates transforming activities from market activities (consumption mixes including average transport and losses) and derives multiple coherent system models—Cut-off by classification, Allocation at the Point of Substitution (APOS), and long-term Consequential substitution—from one unlinked master layer; third, it follows rolling annual sector updates. For example, version 3.11 (November 2024) added 136 Swiss agricultural datasets with Agroscope across mountain, hill, and plain subregions and introduced NMC532 and NMC622 lithium-ion battery chemistries for China and global geographies. While methodology documentation is public, full machine-readable access requires a tiered commercial or academic license.
claims.scope: Unit-process architecture, multiple system models, rolling updates, and licensing boundaries of ecoinvent.
caveats: This account rests on public methodology papers and the official v3.11 release page; machine-readable EcoSpold2 dataset values inside licensed ecoinvent v3.11 distributions were not inspected directly.

claims.text: A sharp structural contrast is provided by Sphera Managed LCA Content (MLC, formerly the GaBi databases, paired with Sphera LCA for Experts). According to public institutional documentation and literature overviews, MLC is built through top-down industrial engineering modeling in collaboration with global industry associations across energy, metals, chemicals, plastics, electronics, and automotive manufacturing, with core modeling principles and content undergoing regular third-party verification (such as by DEKRA) and annual updates to electricity grids and road-transport emissions. To protect industrial confidentiality, MLC delivers a large share of its background library as vertically or horizontally aggregated LCI results rather than open unit-process trees. Internal consistency within the library is high because one engineering team governs modeling conventions, but external analysts generally cannot unpack or swap embedded upstream electricity or sub-processes as transparently as in unit-process databases.
claims.scope: Engineering-led modeling, aggregated LCI delivery, third-party review, and proprietary access boundary of Sphera MLC (formerly GaBi).
caveats: Sphera MLC is a proprietary, license-restricted database; this assessment rests strictly on public institutional documentation and peer-reviewed metadata without inspecting internal commercial process tables.

claims.text: A third comprehensive category consists of policy- and regulator-mandated reference libraries, exemplified by the European Commission JRC’s historical European Reference Life Cycle Database (ELCD) and its successor Environmental Footprint (EF 3.0/3.1) reference packages and compliant secondary datasets. ELCD formerly offered free European baseline data for energy, transport, and core materials, but is no longer maintained and survives only as a historical archive rather than a current compliance baseline. The succeeding EF 2.0, 3.0, and 3.1 architecture is tightly bound to Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 for Product and Organisation Environmental Footprints (PEF/OEF): datasets use the ILCD-EF XML format with strict UUID identities, are typically released as partly terminated systems embedding Circular Footprint Formula (CFF) conventions and formal review rules, and carry use-restricted licenses tailored to PEF/OEF compliance rather than unrestricted redistribution. As the European Commission’s 2026 transition guidance notes regarding limited availability of EF-compliant datasets in certain sectors, regulatory databases prioritize uniform comparability under statutory rules over exhaustive coverage for exploratory research.
claims.scope: Historical archive status of ELCD and the statutory-compliance design, licensing limits, and availability constraints of EU EF 3.0/3.1 secondary datasets.
caveats: Exact free-access terms for EF secondary datasets evolve with European Commission data-node tenders and license agreements; statutory filings must check current European Platform on LCA (EPLCA) notices.

claims.text: Alongside commercial multi-sector libraries and regulatory secondary packages, national and regional programmes anchor domestic electricity, fuels, agriculture, and core industries under varied architectures. In the United States, NREL's USLCI and the interagency Federal LCA Commons publish public-domain unit processes alongside the Federal Elementary Flow List (FedEFL) and public APIs, though standalone USLCI retains unclosed upstream gaps in some industrial chains. Japan's AIST IDEA and China's CLCD (developed by IKE and Sichuan University) serve domestic industrial and energy chains, while France's AGRIBALYSE (ADEME/INRAE) opens aggregated agri-food results publicly yet relies on ecoinvent and WFLDB backbones for non-domestic and industrial unit processes. Complementing database repositories, the open-source TianGong specification (TIDAS) defines machine-validatable schemas that separate public semantic contracts from downstream policy rules. For licensed commercial distributions such as IDEA and CLCD, internal process tables were not directly inspected without a license.
claims.scope: Architectures and licensing boundaries of national/regional background libraries (USLCI/Federal LCA Commons, IDEA, CLCD, AGRIBALYSE) and open data specifications (TIDAS).
caveats: The Federal LCA Commons continually adds agency repositories, so upstream closure must be checked on the specific release snapshot; internal process tables of licensed distributions such as IDEA and CLCD were not directly inspected without a license and are scoped to public institutional documentation and bibliographic metadata.

claims.text: Two complementary library families cover sectoral depth and economy-wide closure. First, industry associations such as the World Steel Association (worldsteel), PlasticsEurope, and the International Aluminium Institute (IAI) pool member-plant inventories into aggregated cradle-to-gate profiles to protect confidentiality while embedding sector-specific recycling conventions, alongside commercial specialty libraries for agri-food allocation variants (Agri-footprint, WFLDB) and country- and route-specific chemicals (Carbon Minds). Second, environmentally extended and social input–output matrices couple monetary trade tables with satellite accounts: U.S. EPA's open-source reproducible USEEIO v2.0 (adding waste disaggregation, domestic-versus-foreign impact splits, and purchaser-price conversion) and research-open EXIOBASE 3 close economy-wide upstream truncation, while PSILCA and SHDB map country-sector monetary flows onto risk-weighted worker hours. Double-counting rules for hybrid process–IO closure are detailed in Hybrid Inventory Analysis (Part II), and social risk-hour scales and limits appear in Social Performance and Impacts (Part V).
claims.scope: Paradigm boundaries of industry-association averages (worldsteel, PlasticsEurope, IAI), agri-food and chemical specialty libraries (Agri-footprint, WFLDB, Carbon Minds), and EEIO/MRIO and social risk matrices (USEEIO v2.0, EXIOBASE 3, PSILCA, SHDB).
caveats: Plant-level unit processes behind industry-association averages and commercial specialty libraries remain confidential or licensed and cannot be inspected row by row; sector granularity and reference years for USEEIO, EXIOBASE 3, and social MRIO libraries vary across releases and must be verified before use.

claims.text: In applied LCA, evaluating the exact same product—such as 1 kg of packaging polymer, 1 kg of low-alloy steel, or 1 kWh of industrial electricity—with identical foreground activity data and the same impact-assessment method can still yield order-of-magnitude shifts or even rank reversals once the background library switches among ecoinvent, Sphera MLC (formerly GaBi), EU EF 3.1, USLCI, IDEA, CLCD, or EEIO models. Such divergences rarely reflect arithmetic mistakes; rather, major databases embed incompatible methodological choices across four foundational axes: system models, aggregation depth, geographic residual and market modeling, and capital-goods and cut-off conventions.
claims.scope: Four foundational methodological axes explaining why identical products yield systematically different results across background databases.
caveats: Database divergences often intertwine with software-implementation differences; diagnosing discrepancies requires first verifying identical LCIA methods and elementary-flow mappings.

claims.text: The first foundational divergence lies in system models and multifunctionality (whose conceptual rules and guardrails are developed in Part III, Joint Production and Market Response). Architecturally, ecoinvent v3 decouples unlinked raw unit processes (UPRs) from linking rules, generating four official system models from the same underlying data: Allocation, cut-off by classification (passing recyclates burden-free to the next life cycle), Cut-off EN 15804 for construction declarations, Allocation at the Point of Substitution (APOS, expanding wastes and by-products to shared allocation points), and Substitution, consequential, long-term (substituting by-products via unconstrained marginal suppliers). Official documentation notes that all models prioritize subdivision and that Cut-off versus APOS diverges specifically on wastes and recyclables; paired tests by Steubing et al. (2016) show that switching system models alone drives substantial shifts across GWP100a, ReCiPe endpoint, and ecological scarcity scores.
claims.scope: Structural roles of ecoinvent v3’s four official system models and documented multi-indicator divergences among them.
caveats: Analysts must never mix datasets from different system models within one product system (such as linking a Cut-off recycled input to a Consequential electricity grid), which violates mass/system consistency and attributional/consequential coherence.

claims.text: Across other major libraries, default multifunctionality rules are locked in incompatible ways. EU EF 3.0/3.1 secondary datasets bind mandatory compliance to the Circular Footprint Formula (CFF, whose A/B parameters and quality ratios are analyzed in Part III, Material Recycling Chains), diverging from both ecoinvent Cut-off's 100/0 rule and consequential marginal substitution. Sphera MLC (formerly GaBi) and industry-association libraries such as steel and aluminium rely on centralized engineering teams to fix sector-specific allocation or expansion defaults rather than offering library-wide model toggles. National libraries (USLCI, IDEA, CLCD) typically fix a single attributional convention, while EXIOBASE 3 and USEEIO project national supply-use tables via industry- or commodity-technology assumptions.
claims.scope: Cross-database divergences in multifunctionality and recycling rules across EU EF CFF, Sphera MLC, industry associations, national LCI libraries, and EEIO models.
caveats: Because Sphera MLC, CLCD, and several industry-association libraries are proprietary or request-gated, the exact physical or economic allocation rule for a given process must be verified in its accompanying dataset documentation.

claims.text: The second structural divergence concerns delivery granularity: transparent unit processes (UPR) versus aggregated LCI results or partly terminated systems. The ILCD Handbook strictly distinguishes single-operation unit processes, black-box unit processes, partly terminated systems, and aggregated LCI results. Transparent unit-process libraries (such as ecoinvent and core USLCI repositories) expose every direct material, energy input, and direct emission at each stage, enabling analysts to trace which upstream step drives an impact, substitute a regional average grid with site-specific renewable electricity, and propagate parameter uncertainty through the full matrix. By contrast, aggregated LCI results and partly terminated systems—predominant in Sphera MLC, EU EF 3.1 secondary datasets, and PlasticsEurope, worldsteel, and IAI profiles—pre-solve dozens or hundreds of upstream steps into a single cradle-to-gate exchange table.
claims.scope: Structural contrast between transparent unit processes (UPR) and aggregated LCI or partly terminated systems in auditability, grid substitution, and uncertainty propagation.
caveats: Some databases (including ecoinvent) distribute both unit-process (UPR) and pre-solved system-process (LCI) versions; selecting the pre-solved distribution likewise forfeits supply-chain disassembly and parameter uncertainty propagation.

claims.text: Aggregating a dataset is never mere file compression; it permanently freezes upstream modeling choices inside a black box. Once a steel or polymer profile is delivered as an aggregated LCI result, its embedded electricity reference year, upstream fuel leakage rates, co-product allocation shares, and emission sub-compartments are locked in: downstream analysts can neither verify whether internal energy assumptions conflict with foreground green-power contracts nor disaggregate total water consumption back to specific watersheds for regionalized scarcity assessment (such as AWARE). Yet vertical aggregation also serves a real institutional purpose: by shielding plant-level recipes and energy intensities, it persuades industry associations and companies to contribute recent operational averages that are often fresher than aging academic literature. Recognizing this trade-off between auditability and confidentiality-backed data freshness is essential when comparing libraries.
claims.scope: Trade-off between locked-in upstream assumptions (blocking grid swaps and regionalization) and confidentiality-enabled industrial representativeness in aggregated datasets.
caveats: When relying on aggregated datasets, analysts should inspect accompanying metadata reports to confirm embedded electricity mixes, geographic scope, and reference years rather than treating them as current local measurements.

claims.text: The third structural divergence lies in geographic aggregation, residual construction, and market modeling. ecoinvent version 3 enforces a strict non-overlapping geography rule for the same activity: when both Switzerland (CH) and Europe (RER) datasets exist, they cannot overlap spatially, so the database constructs “Europe without Switzerland” to prevent double representation; for large countries such as the United States, Brazil, China, and India, electricity systems are disaggregated into sub-national regional grids rather than collapsed into a single national average. Where a global (GLO) dataset coexists with country-specific datasets, all remaining geographies fall into a Rest-of-the-World (RoW) residual. Consequently, whenever a new release adds data for a major producing nation, the RoW residual automatically shifts—even though no new primary sampling occurred in the remaining countries.
claims.scope: Non-overlapping geography constraints, sub-national grid disaggregation, and dynamic GLO/RoW residual coupling in ecoinvent v3.
caveats: Using a RoW dataset as a proxy for a specific developing country can introduce substantial geographic bias because residual composition shifts across database versions.

claims.text: Databases also diverge sharply in how they model freight transport and electricity boundaries. ecoinvent separates transforming activities (factory-gate production) from market activities (consumption mixes that automatically embed average freight distances, import shares, and distribution losses); selecting a market activity therefore already includes transport and grid losses. By contrast, many engineering libraries and industry-association profiles deliver factory-gate production datasets that require modelers to add road, rail, or maritime transport explicitly in the foreground. On the electricity side, libraries differ on production versus consumption mixes (including cross-border imports), high-/medium-/low-voltage transformer losses, and residual grid mixes required under EU PEF after removing tracked renewable certificates. Switching databases without checking whether transport and transmission losses are already embedded readily causes transport double-counting or grid-loss omission.
claims.scope: Divergences between market-embedded transport/losses versus explicit gate-to-gate transport, and incompatible electricity mix/voltage boundaries.
caveats: Within the same country and reference year, busbar generation emission factors and low-voltage consumption-mix factors can differ appreciably due to transmission losses and inter-regional power trade; cross-database electricity comparisons must first align voltage and trade boundaries.

claims.text: The fourth structural divergence involves capital goods (infrastructure and equipment), cut-off rules, and temporal baselines. ecoinvent systematically includes factories, machinery, roads, ports, power-plant construction, and decommissioning across most unit processes, whereas many industrial engineering libraries, industry-association inventories, and product-carbon-footprint rules omit or selectively exclude capital goods based on the traditional assumption that amortized infrastructure contributes little. While that omission has limited leverage on fuel-dominated fossil generation or energy-intensive smelting, it is decisive for wind power, solar photovoltaics, hydropower, nuclear energy, and low-energy services whose burdens concentrate in equipment manufacturing and civil construction. Comparing wind power from a capital-goods-inclusive database against coal- or gas-fired power from a capital-goods-exclusive library introduces severe structural bias.
claims.scope: Asymmetric bias introduced by including versus excluding capital goods when comparing renewable energy and low-energy services against fossil systems.
caveats: Some Product Category Rules (PCRs) or carbon-footprint standards explicitly allow excluding capital goods; cross-database or cross-standard comparisons must verify that capital-goods switches match.

claims.text: Closely linked to capital goods are cut-off rules and temporal reference lags. Statutory cut-off thresholds across frameworks were compared in Goal and Scope Definition (Part II), yet background databases implement them unevenly: Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 caps cumulative exclusions below 3.0% across mass, energy, and every impact category, whereas process-based libraries inevitably truncate minor auxiliaries and services (and standalone USLCI historically retains unclosed upstream chains), while EEIO/MRIO matrices such as USEEIO v2.0 and EXIOBASE 3 eliminate economy-wide upstream truncation at the price of multi-year national-account publication lags. Meanwhile, fast-evolving sectors—photovoltaics, lithium-ion batteries, and decarbonizing grids—change faster than database update cycles, so mixing libraries anchored in different reference years quietly widens result divergence.
claims.scope: Process cut-off thresholds versus EEIO zero-truncation, and uneven intra-database temporal lag across sectors.
caveats: Assessing data currency requires checking each process’s valid-time metadata and primary sampling year rather than relying on the overall database release year.

claims.text: Selecting a background database therefore means adopting an entire bundle of embedded assumptions on system models, aggregation depth, geographic residuals, transport boundaries, capital goods, and reference years. Even when a study mixes only a few processes across libraries or applies one system's impact assessment method to another library's inventory, it immediately hits a deeper engineering barrier: why can neither elementary flows nor technosphere processes be mapped losslessly across databases? That question anchors the next chapter, Cross-Database Mapping of Flows and Processes.
claims.scope: Synthesis of the four methodological divergences and transition to elementary-flow and technosphere-process mapping limits.
caveats: The structural divergences summarized here govern cross-database comparability; actual numerical sensitivity always depends on the product’s process structure and dominant impact categories.

claims.text: Practitioners new to cross-database modeling often assume that because carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide, chromium, and freshwater are objective physical substances, a simple lookup table keyed by chemical name or CAS number should translate elementary flows losslessly between databases. That intuition mistakes an elementary-flow list for a neutral chemistry dictionary. In reality, every major elementary-flow system is shaped backwards by the underlying Life Cycle Impact Assessment (LCIA) models it serves: whatever receiving compartments, emission heights, population-density sub-compartments, water types, oxidation states, or spatial location codes those LCIA methods require dictate how the inventory database partitions its elementary flows.
claims.scope: Core principle that elementary-flow lists are not neutral chemical dictionaries, but are structurally shaped by underlying LCIA model requirements.
caveats: For globally well-mixed, single-species long-lived greenhouse gases such as fossil CO₂, cross-database mapping is nearly lossless; mapping failures concentrate in flows carrying compartment, speciation, spatial, or carbon-origin distinctions.

claims.text: Because their target LCIA methods differ, the three dominant elementary-flow nomenclature systems diverge in data architecture. ecoinvent organizes flows by a three-part tuple of name, category, and sub-category (such as air / urban air close to ground or water / surface water), supplemented by activity geography in regionalized workflows; the EU EF 3.0/3.1 reference package assigns strict UUIDs to each flow and binds country- or watershed-level factors directly via <location> tags inside LCIA method XMLs; and the U.S. Federal LCA Commons defines standardized FlowList and FlowMapping specifications through the open-source fedelemflowlist package to support interagency interoperability and software export. Precisely because these systems disagree on what constitutes a distinct elementary flow, UNEP launched the Global LCA Data Access (GLAD) network in June 2020 with a dedicated Working Group on Nomenclature (WG1) to maintain official cross-system mapping files.
claims.scope: Structural differences among ecoinvent, EU EF 3.1, and U.S. Federal LCA Commons (fedelemflowlist) elementary-flow architectures and the role of UNEP GLAD WG1.
caveats: Reference flow lists bundled inside software tools such as openLCA often blend multiple historical naming traditions; analysts should verify the active reference-list version before importing external databases.

claims.text: In practice, water and carbon flows are the first two structural mismatch zones to break cross-database mapping. For water—as verified earlier in Water Consumption and Scarcity Potential (Part IV)—EU EF 3.1’s AWARE method computes net water consumption by netting 7 positive-factor withdrawal flows against 4 negative-factor return flows across 209 country/regional location codes. Other databases may lump withdrawal, cooling return, and turbine water together, report mass (kg) instead of volume (m³), or omit watershed/country tags; naive mapping can turn 10 m³ of non-consumptive cooling water returned to the same river into 10 m³ of permanent water consumption, inflating water scarcity scores by an order of magnitude. For carbon, EF 3.1 splits 1,099 climate flows into separate fossil (1,074), biogenic (13), and land-use-change (12) tracks; mapping a dataset using −1/+1 biogenic uptake-and-release accounting onto a 0/0 biogenic-neutral target method creates spurious negative-carbon credits or double-counted emissions at the cradle-to-gate boundary.
claims.scope: Structural cross-database mismatches in water accounting (withdrawal/return netting and spatial tags) and carbon accounting (fossil/biogenic/dLUC and 0/0 vs. −1/+1).
caveats: Water-flow mapping must check not only substance identity and units (m³ vs. kg), but also exchange direction (resource input vs. emission output) and non-consumptive cooling or hydropower flows.

claims.text: Land use, heavy-metal speciation, and particulate size fractions form two further high-frequency mismatch zones. Land flows must separate occupation (area × time, m²·a) from transformation (converted area, m², distinguishing both “from” and “to” land classes), yet databases use incompatible land taxonomies (CORINE classes, biomes, or management intensities) that resist direct translation. For metals and particulates, toxicity models (USEtox, USES-LCA) assign vastly different characterization factors to trivalent versus hexavalent chromium or inorganic versus methyl mercury—information a mapping table cannot recover if the source library records only generic “Chromium.” Likewise, EF 3.1 assigns sharply different factors to fine PM2.5, coarse PM2.5–10 (no characterization factor entry), total PM10 (0.23× PM2.5 multiplier), and urban ground-level, rural, high-stack, or unspecified air; collapsing PM2.5–10 into PM10 or degrading high-stack emissions into unspecified air multiplies health-damage distortion.
claims.scope: Information loss and distortion in cross-database mapping of land occupation/transformation, metal oxidation states, and particulate size/compartment splits.
caveats: When source inventories lack valence or stack-height data, any automated mapping table must choose between conservative proxies and zeroing out—a methodological assumption that must never be mistaken for physical measurement.

claims.text: Mathematically, cross-database elementary-flow conversion almost never forms a one-to-one bijection; instead, it oscillates between many-to-one semantic collapse and one-to-many fabricated precision. Mapping a fine-grained source library (distinguishing urban ground-level, low-stack, and high-stack air emissions) into a coarse target library (holding only air, unspecified) causes many-to-one collapse: spatial exposure information is permanently erased. Conversely, mapping a coarse source flow (such as water, unspecified or generic Chromium) into a fine-grained LCIA method triggers a one-to-many dilemma: forcing it into a specific sub-compartment (such as urban air or freshwater) invents precision absent from the source data, whereas leaving it as unspecified causes LCIA methods lacking generic fallback factors to drop it altogether.
claims.scope: Non-bijective mapping dilemmas: many-to-one semantic collapse versus one-to-many fabricated precision.
caveats: Many-to-one mapping is irreversible on round-trip export: once sub-compartment or emission-height detail collapses to unspecified during conversion, exporting back to the original format cannot restore it.

claims.text: A closely related many-to-one hazard involves aggregate group flows such as NMVOC (non-methane volatile organic compounds), VOC, total PAHs, or generic pesticides. In older or entry-level inventories, a single coating or combustion process may list specific compounds (toluene, xylene, styrene) alongside an aggregate NMVOC flow. As examined in Data Applicability later in this Part for ecoinvent and ILCD rules, rigorous libraries require subtracting individually reported substances from group totals. Row-by-row cross-database mapping tables, however, lack process-level mass-balance context: they cannot verify whether a group flow was already net of speciated compounds and therefore cannot prevent double-counting in photochemical ozone or toxicity scores.
claims.scope: Double-counting and omission risks created by aggregate group flows (NMVOC, VOC, generic pesticides) under row-by-row flow mapping.
caveats: When auditing chemical, coating, printing, or agricultural pesticide processes, analysts should explicitly check whether speciated compounds and aggregate group flows coexist in the same exchange table.

claims.text: Even when substance and compartment align, three quantitative traps lurk in flow mapping: stoichiometric reference substances, unit bases, and sign/direction conventions. First, the same nutrient may be inventoried under different chemical reference species—phosphorus as elemental P, phosphate (PO₄³⁻), or phosphorus pentoxide (P₂O₅, whose elemental-P conversion factor is 0.436), and nitrogen as elemental N, nitrate (NO₃⁻), or ammonium (NH₄⁺); renaming a flow without applying the stoichiometric multiplier skews scores by more than a factor of two. Second, energy and biomass flows switch between lower and higher heating values (LHV vs. HHV), dry versus wet mass, and normal cubic meters (Nm³) versus kilograms. Third, software formats differ in waste and water sign/direction conventions—which is why the openLCA schema encodes FlowPropertyFactor and explicit conversion factors inside FlowMapEntry. Pure name-based mapping without unit, stoichiometric, and sign verification corrupts calculations directly.
claims.scope: Quantitative mapping traps: stoichiometric reference substances (e.g., P vs. P₂O₅ 0.436), heating-value/dry-wet units, and sign/direction conventions.
caveats: Converting gas volumes (m³ or Nm³) to mass (kg) requires verifying temperature, pressure, and gas-composition baselines rather than applying an arbitrary density constant.

claims.text: The most insidious error in cross-database LCA is not a software crash, but silent unmapped drop-to-zero. Flows, Exchanges, and Boundaries (Part II) already separated true measured zeros from missing characterization factors within a single model; cross-database imports amplify that risk dramatically. The ILCD Handbook (§8.2, pp. 276–281) warns explicitly that when an inventory elementary flow fails to match an LCIA characterization factor due to UUID, spelling, compartment-path, or language mismatches, solvers routinely proceed without halting and assign zero impact—disguising mapping failure as zero environmental burden and severely understating methane, heavy-metal, pesticide, or regionalized water impacts.
claims.scope: ILCD missing-factor verification rule and silent zero-characterization failure when unmapped elementary flows receive zero impact without error.
caveats: Because many tools relegate uncharacterized flows to secondary log tabs, silent flow drops are rarely visible from headline bar charts unless audited proactively.

claims.text: Although explicit FlowMap specifications in openLCA and cross-system elementary-flow mapping files maintained by UNEP GLAD Working Group 1 (WG1) substantially reduce repetitive translation work, automated mapping does not remove the need for underlying nomenclature verification. One engineering rule governs every workflow: every LCIA method must be co-validated with its native elementary-flow list. Consistent with the ILCD Handbook (§8.2, pp. 276–281) guidance on missing characterization factors, before trusting any cross-database score, analysts must run a zero-characterization audit across dominant mass- and impact-contributing uncharacterized flows (covering key climate, water, and toxicity emissions) to distinguish true scientific non-relevance from silent nomenclature drop-out.
claims.scope: Platform differences in handling unmapped flows and the mandatory engineering rule of co-validating LCIA methods with their native elementary-flow lists.
caveats: Even official mapping tables (such as GLAD or openLCA mapping packs) can acquire new unmapped flows after minor database or LCIA version updates; zero-characterization audits must be rerun on every version bump.

claims.text: Economic and product classification schemes across background LCA databases are inherently non-bijective: ecoinvent pairs ISIC activity classes with CPC product classes, EEIO models such as USEEIO follow BEA/NAICS economic-account sectors, trade statistics use HS codes, and legacy tools such as SimaPro rely heavily on free-text names, making cross-database process correspondence intrinsically many-to-many rather than one-to-one.
claims.scope: Non-bijective classification axes for processes and product flows
caveats: Even within a single classification standard, version transitions (such as ISIC Rev. 3 to Rev. 4 or CPC v2 to v2.1) introduce splits and mergers of their own.

claims.text: Because heterogeneous LCA databases and software platforms rarely share universal persistent process identifiers, migration tools must fall back on matching attributes such as name, reference product, location, and unit; minor naming drift, case changes, or legacy export constraints break exact linking and cannot be losslessly reverse-engineered from strings alone.
claims.scope: Fragility of cross-platform attribute-based linking
caveats: Even when UUIDs are used internally, UUIDs generated independently by different database publishers are not mutually interoperable without an explicit binding table.

claims.text: A technosphere process is never identified by product name alone, but by a four-tuple of reference product and technical specification, technology route, geography and supply-chain boundary, and market versus transforming role; changing any one dimension turns an identically named product into a materially different system node.
claims.scope: Four-dimensional identity criteria for technosphere processes
caveats: For time-sensitive or multi-output sectors such as agriculture, electricity, and metals, temporal representativeness and co-product allocation rules add further implicit dimensions.

claims.text: Even between consecutive releases of the same database family, a single technosphere activity can split into multiple routes: the randonneur migration rule from ecoinvent 3.9.1 to 3.10 disaggregates European xylene production into two distinct BTX routes (0.1176 from pyrolysis gas and 0.8824 from reformate), proving that even intra-database version updates are frequently one-to-many rather than simple renames.
claims.scope: Empirical one-to-many disaggregation in intra-database version migration
caveats: The 0.1176/0.8824 split reflects a specific version transition and European market backdrop and must not be transferred blindly to other regions or facility-specific routes.

claims.text: Substituting a gate-to-gate transforming activity directly for a market activity that embeds average transport, trade mixes, and losses—or swapping a dynamic Rest-of-World (RoW) residual for a national average process—silently alters transport boundaries, trade structure, and upstream electricity without triggering any software error.
claims.scope: Silent boundary shifts from market/transforming and RoW residual mismatches
caveats: If a foreground model already accounts for inbound raw-material transport, linking to a market activity that also includes average delivery double-counts transport.

claims.text: When unit processes from different databases are stitched into one product system, the two most common silent boundary distortions are double-counted or omitted transport and asymmetric capital-goods coverage—such as linking infrastructure-inclusive ecoinvent background modules into a sectoral or regulatory foreground that excludes capital goods.
claims.scope: Transport and capital-goods boundary traps in cross-database stitching
caveats: While capital goods may contribute modestly to energy-intensive primary smelting, they can substantially alter totals in solar PV, wind power, agriculture, and services.

claims.text: Stitching datasets built under incompatible system models (such as Cut-off recycled-content modules with Consequential marginal-substitution modules) or incompatible biogenic-carbon conventions (−1/+1 uptake-and-release tracking versus 0/0 carbon-neutral rules) violates mass, energy, and carbon conservation across the seam, manufacturing artificial credits or phantom emissions that exist in no real supply chain.
claims.scope: System-model clashes and biogenic-carbon conservation breaks across seams
caveats: In cradle-to-gate models combining biobased materials with fossil-based downstream steps, inconsistent biogenic-carbon conventions are especially deceptive and require an explicit elemental carbon balance check.

claims.text: When an upstream database supplies pre-aggregated cradle-to-gate system processes rather than transparent unit processes, downstream modelers cannot open and re-link embedded electricity grids, transport legs, co-product allocations, or elementary-flow versions to match the target background—permanently locking hidden methodological contradictions inside the hybrid result.
claims.scope: How pre-aggregated system processes block cross-database re-linking
caveats: Under commercial confidentiality or statutory single-package mandates, aggregated datasets may be legally required, but they must not be presented as transparently re-linkable unit processes.

claims.text: String similarity, vector semantic retrieval, and large language model assistants can dramatically accelerate candidate screening across tens of thousands of multilingual process names, but lexical or semantic proximity does not verify physical mass balance, technical grade, system-model compatibility, or hidden boundary assumptions; unsupervised auto-mapping merely dresses structural mismatches in plausible-looking numbers.
claims.scope: Real operational limits of automated semantic matching and LLM-assisted mapping
caveats: A defensible workflow restricts automated tools to candidate recall and metadata-diff highlighting, requiring human verification of the four-tuple identity, system model, and reference-flow unit before linking.

claims.text: Taken together, both the elementary-flow and technosphere-process analyses in this chapter show that no universal lossless auto-mapper exists across background databases; credible interoperability must shift toward explicit data-exchange schemas, auditable declarative migration recipes, and clear governance redlines, examined next in Data Formats, Mapping, and Conversion Disclosure.
claims.scope: Transition from technosphere mapping limits to exchange formats and governance redlines
caveats: Specific exchange-format capabilities, mapping infrastructure, and interoperability redlines are examined next in Data Formats, Mapping, and Conversion Disclosure and in Data Applicability later in Part VI.

claims.text: LCA data exchange formats are never neutral file wrappers; each embeds the data model of a particular era and software worldview—from parameter-less EcoSpold 1 and ecoinvent-coupled EcoSpold 2, to multi-file web-API-oriented ILCD/eILCD, name-linked proprietary SimaPro CSV, and typed entity trees in openLCA JSON-LD—making round-trip conversion across formats structurally lossy.
claims.scope: Underlying data models and structural lossiness across major LCA exchange formats
caveats: Lossless exchange holds only when source and target share the complete entity semantics, such as native openLCA exchanges in olca-schema.

claims.text: As documented in the openLCA schema specification, SimaPro CSV has no formal public specification and no independent product-system entity (hard-linking processes by name, which invites clashes in collaborative work), while ILCD lacks stand-alone global parameters and eILCD models product systems via process instances whose exchange linking cannot separate two exchanges of the same flow unless their locations differ.
claims.scope: Documented structural constraints of SimaPro CSV and ILCD/eILCD
caveats: These structural limits characterize the exchange formats rather than denying the ability of those platforms to execute standard models inside their native ecosystems.

claims.text: Modern open specifications—such as openLCA JSON-LD (olca-schema, pairing an Entity/RefEntity/RootEntity inheritance tree with JSON-LD @type/@id and an RDF ontology) and the TianGong LCA Data System specification (tidas-spec)—bring persistent references, parameterized formulas, multi-method allocation factors, results, and EPDs into machine-validatable schemas, moving away from fragile free-text names.
claims.scope: Design trajectory of modern open schemas such as openLCA JSON-LD and TianGong TIDAS
caveats: Open schemas eliminate syntactic and reference ambiguity, but cannot replace scientific judgment or erase underlying system-model conflicts.

claims.text: Public mapping infrastructures are emerging to curb duplicated manual reconciliation: UNEP GLAD (launched June 2020) hosts cross-system elementary flow lists and mapping files through Working Group 1 (WG1), while the U.S. Federal LCA Commons fedelemflowlist standardizes FlowList and FlowMapping tables with direct export to openLCA JSON-LD archives.
claims.scope: Public mapping infrastructures including UNEP GLAD and Federal LCA Commons
caveats: Public mapping hubs cut repetitive labor, yet practitioners must still audit many-to-one collapse, unmapped gaps, and LCIA method alignment as established in Cross-Database Mapping of Flows and Processes.

claims.text: For cross-version and cross-software migrations, declarative JSON transformation recipes such as randonneur (providing create, replace, update, delete, and disaggregate verbs, explicit conversion_factor values such as 0.599 from TiO₂ to elemental Titanium, and Brightcon 2022 release IDs) contrast sharply with imperative code tools such as wurst by turning every substitution and split into an auditable, versioned data artifact.
claims.scope: Governance contrast between declarative JSON migration recipes and imperative scripts
caveats: Declarative recipes can still carry non-conservative weights (randonneur explicitly notes disaggregation allocations need not sum to 1), so human review and validation tests remain mandatory.

claims.text: Sound cross-database engineering requires a three-tier interoperability boundary: Tier 1 permits automated lossless syntactic normalization (units, letter casing, verified persistent IDs); Tier 2 allows conditional proxy or disaggregation mapping only with explicit conversion factors, shares, and sensitivity disclosure; Tier 3 prohibits silent mixing of conflicting system models, incompatible biogenic-carbon conventions, or mismatched LCIA flow lists.
claims.scope: Three-tier governance boundary for cross-database interoperability
caveats: When statutory rules or client mandates force two disparate sources into one project, Tier 3 does not always forbid calculation outright, but strictly forbids silent mixing—requiring harmonized recomputation or explicit incomparability warnings.

claims.text: Any cross-database study claiming auditability should disclose at minimum four mapping records: exact release identifiers and system models for source databases, target databases, and LCIA methods (<database>-<version>-<modifier>); provenance and version of every mapping file applied alongside unmapped or uncharacterized flow shares; all stoichiometric conversion factors, dry-versus-wet basis adjustments, and one-to-many disaggregation shares; and whether pre-aggregated system processes prevented upstream re-linking along with their share of hotspot results.
claims.scope: Minimum transparent disclosure checklist for cross-database modeling
caveats: Even under commercial confidentiality agreements where raw unit-process matrices cannot be published, database versions, mapping provenance, and uncharacterized-flow shares can and should still be disclosed.

claims.text: Because proprietary formats (such as SimaPro CSV) and internal commercial database schemas lack formal open specifications, third-party converters and researchers can verify behavior only on inspected public specifications and export samples, and must treat undocumented proprietary edge cases as an explicit epistemic boundary rather than assuming round-trip fidelity.
claims.scope: Epistemic boundary regarding proprietary formats and internal commercial schemas
caveats: This same boundary governs this monograph: every format comparison is strictly confined to verified public technical documentation without speculating on undocumented proprietary internals.

claims.text: Long-term LCA interoperability will not be achieved by endlessly expanding static manual lookup tables; it requires moving governance upstream through versioned persistent identifiers, machine-readable system-model and boundary declarations, and schema-validated open specifications so incompatibilities are flagged automatically before matrix inversion.
claims.scope: Long-term interoperability trajectory from static translation to verifiable metadata
caveats: Widespread adoption of open schemas requires sustained coordination across industry, regulators, and open-source communities; in the interim, auditable declarative mapping tables remain vital bridging infrastructure.

claims.text: The opening three chapters of this Part examined background database lineages, methodological divergences, elementary-flow and technosphere mapping limits, and exchange-format governance redlines; yet choosing a library and policing conversions only keeps the calculation chain intact. Evaluating whether a dataset fits the study object, how uncertainty propagates, whether pedigree ratings map to valid probabilities, and how product footprint rules govern public claims are taken up across the next four chapters of Part VI, beginning with Data Applicability.
claims.scope: Transition from Part VI's opening database and interoperability chapters into Data Applicability, Uncertainty, Data Quality Scores, and Product Footprint Rules.
caveats: Readers should carry the opening chapters' insights on database versioning, system models, and mapping loss directly into the subsequent Part VI chapters on data quality ratings and version-upgrade redlines.

claims.text: Before tracing individual environmental pathways, it is essential to separate mandatory impact assessment calculations from optional post-processing. Across mainstream frameworks, selecting impact categories, assigning elementary flows to categories (classification), and multiplying by characterization factors to obtain category indicator results (characterization) form the mandatory core—as codified, for example, in Annex I §§5.1.1–5.1.2 of the EU Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) method across 16 fixed categories. Subsequent steps—normalization against a regional or global reference system, grouping, and cross-category weighting—are classified as optional in both the ILCD 2010 Handbook (cross-referencing ISO 14044:2006 §§4.4.3.2, 4.4.3.4, and 4.4.5) and the CML 2001 Part 2a Guide. CML 2001 strongly recommends normalization to reveal relative magnitudes while emphasizing that normalized scores do not by themselves rank alternatives; both CML 2001 and ILCD 2010 Provision 8.4 III explicitly prohibit numeric weighting in comparative assertions intended for public disclosure. EU PEF, by contrast, operationalizes normalized and weighted single scores for quantitative hotspot screening (identifying the most relevant categories accounting for at least 80% of the single score, with a minimum of three categories) while restricting public comparisons to compliant product category rules and verification. Readers should always inspect mandatory characterized profiles separately from optional normalized or weighted totals; normalization denominators and weighting rules are examined in full in Part V.
claims.scope: Division between mandatory LCIA elements (classification and characterization) and optional elements (normalization, grouping, weighting) across CML 2001, ILCD 2010, and EU PEF 2021.
caveats: This discussion rests on openly accessible CML 2001, ILCD 2010, and EU (EU) 2021/2279 texts; the paywalled full text of ISO 14044 was not directly inspected.

claims.text: Feeding the same life cycle inventory into different LCIA method families changes indicator architecture, spatial granularity, and temporal framing (Table 1). Leiden University's CML 2001/2002 stays strictly at baseline midpoints without endpoint aggregation, prioritizing transparency and minimal modeling assumptions. ReCiPe 2016 links 17 midpoints to three endpoints—human health, ecosystem quality, and resource scarcity—while varying time horizons and evidence thresholds through three cultural perspectives and stopping at those three areas of protection without releasing default cross-area weighting sets. EU EF 3.1 locks 16 midpoints to machine-readable reference packages designed for policy and product-footprint compliance. LC-IMPACT builds a globally regionalized endpoint-only framework (with no midpoint layer) at ecoregion and watershed resolution, explicitly separating 100-year core horizons from full long-term integrals. IMPACT World+ (Bulle et al. 2019), developed as a joint update to IMPACT 2002+, EDIP, and LUCAS, offers four hierarchical spatial resolutions (global default, continental, country, and native resolution) and four complementary viewpoints—midpoint, damage, three areas of protection (human health, ecosystem quality, and resources & ecosystem services), and water and carbon areas of concern—spanning 18 recommended (+1 interim) midpoints and 21 recommended (+23 interim) damage categories while splitting every long-term impact into shorter-term (0–100 yr) and long-term (>100 yr) damages. As Bulle et al. (2019), citing Verones et al. (2017), emphasize, once characterization factors become spatially explicit, local fate, exposure, and ecosystem sensitivity vary across locations, breaking the older assumption of a single global constant midpoint-to-damage conversion factor. Alongside these implementations, the UNEP Global Guidance for Life Cycle Impact Assessment Indicators (GLAM) synthesizes consensus models and links them to absolute ecological boundaries and multi-criteria trade-offs. Switching method families therefore alters the analytical skeleton itself, never merely decimal rounding.
claims.scope: Comparative architecture of six major LCIA method families (CML, ReCiPe 2016, EF 3.1, LC-IMPACT, IMPACT World+, and UNEP GLAM) and why spatial differentiation breaks global midpoint-to-damage constants.
caveats: Interim indicators in IMPACT World+ and subsequent minor revisions of each method family should be verified against their latest official release documentation.

claims.text: Stratospheric ozone depletion factors are not fixed physical constants; they evolve with each World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion, and operational LCIA factor packages typically lag current atmospheric science by eight to ten years (Table 1). Section A.2.4 of the WMO 2022 Annex retains the semi-empirical steady-state ODP formulation relative to CFC-11 (using a bromine efficiency factor of 60 relative to chlorine and roughly 250 for iodine), while Table A-5 updates steady-state ODPs and total lifetimes across key species: Halon-1301 rises to 17 (total lifetime 72 yr, up from roughly 65 yr), Halon-2402 stands at 15.6 (28 yr), Halon-1211 drops from 7.900 in WMO 2011 to 7.1 (16 yr), methyl bromide remains 0.57 (0.8 yr), CFC-115 adjusts to 0.45 (lifetime revised to 540 yr), HCFC-22 rises from 0.034 in WMO 2014 to 0.038 (11.6 yr), and nitrous oxide carries a steady-state ODP of 0.017 (lifetime revised from 123 yr in WMO 2018 to 109 yr, with Footnote O2 citing Ravishankara et al. 2009). Tracing Halon-1301 against Halon-2402 across three WMO assessments reveals a double ranking reversal: 15.900 > 13.000 in ReCiPe 2016 Egalitarian (WMO 2011), flipping to 15.2 < 15.7 in EF 3.1 (WMO 2014), and flipping back to 17 > 15.6 in WMO 2022. Comparing ozone depletion scores across studies therefore requires recording the WMO assessment edition alongside nitrous oxide inclusion and time-horizon choices.
claims.scope: WMO 2022 Annex Section A.2.4 and Table A-5 steady-state ODP updates, the double ranking reversal between Halon-1301 and Halon-2402, and the publication lag in operational LCIA packages.
caveats: WMO 2022 Annex Table A-5 publishes steady-state ODPs only and does not release updated 20-year or 100-year finite-horizon ReCiPe scaled tables.

claims.text: Published land-use, mineral, and fossil resource reports likewise contain verifiable internal table discrepancies that must be checked alongside methodological boundaries. In RIVM Report 2016-0104, the grassland/pasture and annual-crop recovery endpoint factors printed in Table S7.3 disagree with the main-text equation and midpoint table: recomputing from the printed occupation factors, mean recovery times, and conversion constant shows that the two rows are transposed to the reported precision. Similarly, page 96 and Table S9.2 label cumulative fossil extraction in kg or Nm³, yet substituting crude oil's 1.61 × 10¹⁴ kg directly into the printed log-linear cost equation yields a negative denominator of roughly −105.6 and no positive cost, whereas Figure 13.2 labels its horizontal axis in billion barrels of oil; without access to unpublished worksheets or underlying IEA curves, midpoint–endpoint checks must rely on published Tables 13.1 and 13.2 rather than inventing unit conversions to claim an independent recomputation. Taken together, reading any land, biodiversity, or resource score requires four checks: whether the midpoint tracks geological stock, future ore demand, heating value, or local relative species loss; whether heating values are net or higher and whether natural uranium is assigned to fossils or minerals; how recovery windows, reserve limits, and missing-data proxies are set; and remembering that species·yr and USD2013 represent model-conditioned ecological damage and future surplus extraction cost rather than observed extinction counts or current purchase prices. Having traced individual environmental pathways across Part IV, Part V turns to cross-category trade-offs across normalization, weighting, regionalized valuation, social impacts, and life cycle costing.
claims.scope: Verification of RIVM 2016-0104 land Table S7.3 and fossil page 96 discrepancies, four resource-and-land reading checks, and transition into Part V.
caveats: The documented RIVM Report 2016-0104 table discrepancies are verifiable internal inconsistencies rather than official errata; this chapter's biodiversity discussion focuses on land-use indicators in ReCiPe 2016 and LC-IMPACT rather than surveying all biodiversity assessment frameworks.

The check 40.0 − 4.45·ln(1.61 × 10¹⁴) ≈ −105.6 demonstrates only that the printed formula does not close directly under Table S9.2's kg unit; it does not invalidate Figure 13.2's original fit in billion barrels.

Additional RIVM 2016-0104 fossil-chapter citations and units: p. 96 miscites the higher-heating-value appendix as Table S9.2 (actually S9.1), miscites the crude-oil cost curve as Fig. 11.2 (actually Fig. 13.2), attributes C_x = 1/(a_x + b_x·ln CFE_x) to the mineral SOP paper (Vieira et al. 2016b), and cites endpoint factors as an unpublished "in preparation" manuscript; Table S9.2 lists crude oil a = 40.0, b = −4.45, CFE = 1.61 × 10¹⁴ kg, prints hard-coal cumulative extraction as n.a., and labels current costs USD2008 while the main endpoint table uses USD2013.

claims.text: A life cycle assessment does not begin by opening modeling software or pulling emission factors; it begins by stating unambiguously why the study is being conducted, who will read it, and what decision it is meant to support. Operational frameworks diverge immediately on what a goal statement must lock down (Table 1). The ISO 14044:2006 public preview (§4.2.2) mandates four items—intended application, reasons for carrying out the study, intended audience, and whether results are intended for comparative assertions disclosed to the public—while §4.1 bars life cycle inventory (LCI) studies alone from public comparative assertions and notes that no scientific basis exists for reducing LCA results to a single overall score. The ILCD 2010 Detailed Guidance (Ch. 5) expands this to six mandatory aspects, adding upfront disclosure of method, assumption, and impact-coverage limitations (§5.2.2) alongside the commissioner and influential actors (§5.2.6), and classifying audiences as internal, restricted external, or public as well as technical or non-technical (§5.2.4). EU Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) guidance (Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279, Annex I §3.1) mandates five items that anchor the verifier's identity right inside the goal definition; CML 2001/2002 (Part 2a, §§2.3.1–2.3.2) requires establishing process context and stakeholder supervision before scoping; and the GHG Protocol Product Standard (2011, Ch. 2) starts directly from corporate business goals such as climate-risk evaluation, longitudinal reduction tracking, and customer disclosure.
claims.scope: Cross-framework comparison of mandatory goal-definition items, audience classification, verifier anchoring, and business-goal framing across five open-access primary texts.
caveats: ISO 14044:2006 references rest strictly on the openly accessible preview pages 6–9 (§§4.1–4.2.3.5); the remaining four frameworks were verified directly against their open-access texts.

claims.text: Once the goal is stated, the decisive modeling fork is whether the study describes an existing supply chain's attributed share of burdens or evaluates which suppliers expand, contract, or exit because of a decision. ILCD 2010 (§5.3, Table 2) classifies studies upfront along two axes: first, whether the study supports a decision; and second, if it does, whether that decision triggers large-scale structural capacity changes in the background or other economic systems (such as building or retiring power plants or smelters) rather than merely adjusting utilization of installed equipment. That matrix produces three archetypes: micro-level decision support (Situation A, none or small-scale non-structural changes), meso/macro-level decision support (Situation B, large-scale structural changes), and descriptive accounting (Situation C, subdivided into C1 including cross-system interactions such as recycling or co-products and C2 excluding them). By contrast, the GHG Protocol Product Standard (§5.2) fixes all product inventories on an attributional path; EU PEF standardizes supply-chain accounting inside its PEFCR governance; and CML 2001 (Part 2a, §§2.2 and 3.2) adopts steady-state equilibrium modeling oriented toward long-term structural decisions. The context selected here governs how Part III handles co-product allocation, constrained markets, marginal electricity grids, and recycling loops.
claims.scope: Upfront decision-context classification (ILCD Situations A, B, C1, and C2 versus other frameworks' default orientations) and its control over downstream inventory and allocation rules.
caveats: ILCD decision contexts govern LCI modeling rules within the ILCD framework; other standards bind studies to their own database and category-rule conventions. The full mechanics of attributional versus consequential modeling are developed in Part III.

claims.text: Where the goal states why a study is undertaken, the scope lays out the full technical blueprint so analytical depth matches that purpose. The ISO 14044:2006 public preview (§4.2.3.1) enumerates fourteen scope items that must be considered and clearly described: the product system, its functions, functional unit, system boundary, allocation procedures, LCIA methodology and types of impacts, interpretation approach, data requirements, assumptions, value choices and optional elements, limitations, data quality requirements, type of critical review (if any), and report type and format. Operational guides package those items into distinct engineering checklists. EU PEF (Annex I §3.2) organizes them into five blocks, mandates all 16 EF impact categories without exclusion (Table 2), and requires intermediate products to disclose factory-gate biogenic carbon content, recycled content (R1), and relevant Circular Footprint Formula parameters as additional technical information (§3.2.4.2). CML 2001 (Part 2a, §2.3.3) foregrounds temporal, geographical, and technological coverage—defaulting to modal-modern technology currently installed in the target region—matched to simplified, detailed, or optional-extension tiers. The GHG Protocol Product Standard (Ch. 6–7) anchors scope in the unit of analysis, reference flow, five default life-cycle stages, and a mandatory process map.
claims.scope: Comparison of ISO 14044 public-preview fourteen scope elements against scope specifications in EU PEF, CML 2001, and the GHG Protocol Product Standard.
caveats: The ISO 14044 public preview covers §4.2.3.1, §§4.2.3.2–4.2.3.4, and the opening portion of §4.2.3.5 (terminating inside §4.2.3.5 on printed p. 9); the remainder of §4.2.3.5, §§4.2.3.6–4.2.3.8, and subsequent paywalled clauses fall outside the public preview and were not directly inspected.

claims.text: Although scope must be drafted before data collection starts, it is neither an immutable contract nor a license to shift goalposts once unfavorable numbers appear. The ISO 14044 public preview (§§4.2.1 and 4.2.3.1) emphasizes LCA's iterative nature: unforeseen constraints or new evidence may require refining the scope—or even the goal—provided every modification and its justification are documented. ILCD 2010 (Ch. 4) structures this iteration as multi-round refinement loops that screen hotspots first and then concentrate primary data collection on dominant processes through completeness, sensitivity, and consistency checks—while warning explicitly that high uncertainty can mask real differences, so shortages of data, time, or budget never justify concluding that "no significant difference" exists. EU PEF (Annex I §4.1) formalizes that opening loop as a dedicated screening step: it must run through impact assessment with zero cut-off allowed, using readily available primary or secondary data to identify hotspots before refining the initial scope and committing resources to company-specific data collection.
claims.scope: Legitimate boundaries for iterative scope refinement, ILCD's precision warning against false equivalence, and EU PEF's zero-cut-off screening step.
caveats: Legitimate iteration improves completeness and precision for the stated question; altering the functional unit or dropping inconvenient stages after viewing preliminary rankings violates documented goal-consistent revision.

claims.text: A single checkbox inside the goal statement—whether results are intended for comparative assertions disclosed to the public—simultaneously tightens scope, boundary, impact assessment, and verification requirements across the entire study. Under the ISO 14044 public preview, while every system comparison must already verify functional equivalence under the same functional unit and reference flows and document omitted additional functions (§4.2.3.2), declaring public comparative-assertion intent immediately triggers two additional hard gates: LCI studies alone are barred (§4.1), and the final sensitivity analysis must evaluate mass, energy, and environmental significance cut-off criteria together (§4.2.3.3.3). CML 2001 (Part 2a, §2.3.4) further requires demonstrating system equivalence across performance, boundaries, data quality, allocation, evaluation rules, and impact assessment, while commenting on relevant alternatives not covered. EU PEF (Annex I §§1 and 3.1) tightens the gate to dual category-rule and external-verification compliance: cross-product comparisons and comparative assertions are permitted only under an applicable PEFCR with mandatory independent verification. The GHG Protocol Product Standard (Appendix A) draws an explicit line: a single-indicator GHG inventory does not support ISO 14044 comparative assertions without separate harmonized product rules.
claims.scope: Cascading scope, cut-off sensitivity, equivalence-disclosure, and category-rule gates triggered by declaring an intent for public comparative assertions.
caveats: Detailed ISO 14044 clauses on panel critical review for comparative assertions lie outside the public preview and are not reconstructed here; only inspected preview clauses §§4.1, 4.2.3.2, and 4.2.3.3.3 are cited, and cross-framework review and verification regimes are examined in later chapters.

claims.text: Before assembling an inventory, the scope must also establish two foundational terms used throughout this book: the foreground system and the background system. Practitioners often equate "foreground" with a company's own factory and "background" with a commercial database, yet ILCD 2010 (§6.6.1 Box and Figure 13) shows that those labels actually conceal two distinct definitions serving different purposes whose boundaries do not coincide (Table 2). Under the specificity perspective—ILCD's default for data collection—the foreground system consists of processes specific to the studied product that cannot be replaced by market averages, covering not only the producer's facilities but also tier-1 suppliers and upstream links tied by specific contracts such as certified electricity or certified timber; the background system consists of processes supplied through homogeneous markets where average or generic data are appropriate (meaning generic use and end-of-life stages sit in the background unless specific scenarios are investigated). Under the management perspective—used in ecodesign—the foreground system consists of processes under the direct control or decisive influence of the producer, service operator, or user, including own operations, made-to-order tier-1 suppliers under attributional LCA, and design-governed use-phase efficiency or recyclability; tier-2+ suppliers and sole-source suppliers locked into unchangeable long-term contracts fall into the background. A locked-in specialized supplier is therefore foreground under specificity (requiring specific data) yet background under management (outside short-term decision control); without naming which perspective applies, foreground/background debates talk past one another.
claims.scope: Formal definition of foreground and background systems and the boundary divergence between ILCD 2010's specificity and management perspectives.
caveats: ILCD 2010 §6.6.1 stresses that both distinctions are indicative rather than rigid dichotomies: high-quality generic data can occasionally outperform poor site measurements in the foreground, and many supply-chain processes sit under only partial management influence.

claims.text: Once drawn, the foreground/background line translates directly into mandatory primary-versus-secondary data hierarchies and comparative-bias checks.
