EU PEF (Annex I Glossary and §§3.2.2, 4.6.1–4.6.3) defines primary data as synonymous with company-specific or supply-chain-specific data, requires the system boundary diagram to highlight where company-specific data are used, mandates company-specific data for the bill of materials (BoM) and main-product manufacturing, and enforces a strict four-tier secondary-data hierarchy: use EF-compliant secondary datasets first; if unavailable, use an EF-compliant proxy (including datasets converted from earlier EF versions) and report it under limitations; failing that, use an ILCD Entry-Level (ILCD-EL) proxy capped at 10% of the single overall score; if none exists, exclude the process as a documented data gap validated by the verifier. CML 2001 (Part 2a, §§3.3.4–3.3.5) guards against both format drift and comparison skew by applying a harmonized exchange format (SPOLD) to foreground collection while leaving background processes in database or literature formats, and explicitly warning analysts to check whether compared product systems differ sharply in their foreground-to-background data ratios. The GHG Protocol Product Standard (Ch. 7–8) similarly maps directly operated attributable processes to primary data and upstream/downstream links to secondary databases or spend-based factors. The global evolution, methodological divergences, and cross-database mapping limits of background databases themselves are examined in detail in Part VI (Data Infrastructure and Evidence).
claims.scope: EU PEF company-specific data mandates and four-tier secondary hierarchy, CML 2001 foreground-to-background ratio asymmetry warning, and GHG Protocol data alignment.
caveats: Detailed Data Quality Rating (DQR) matrices and pedigree-matrix variance rules are developed in Part VI (Data Applicability and Data Quality Scores and Probability); this section focuses on how foreground/background scoping sets data hierarchies.

claims.text: The system boundary determines which unit processes belong to the studied product system and where tracing stops. Structurally, every complete LCA model manages three nested interfaces: the technosphere–ecosphere boundary (where elementary flows enter from nature or leave as emissions), the boundary between the product system and the rest of the technosphere (where reference flows, co-products, recyclates, and waste treatments hand off), and the boundary between modeled and cut-off processes. By life-cycle coverage, studies adopt three standard archetypes (ILCD 2010, Figure 12): cradle-to-grave across the full life cycle, cradle-to-gate stopping at the factory gate (suited to multi-purpose intermediate products), and gate-to-gate covering site-internal operations as reusable modules. Both EU PEF (§4.2) and the GHG Protocol (§7.2, Figure 7.1) standardize five default life-cycle stages—raw material acquisition and pre-processing, manufacturing, distribution and storage, use, and end-of-life—with PEF excluding distribution, use, and end-of-life for intermediate products. Yet ILCD 2010 (§6.6.2) adds an essential technical boundary check: when a studied product is a component embedded in a larger system—such as a car starter battery, a water-saving showerhead, or window-frame materials—it cannot be compared in isolation whenever it alters how the host system operates; those technical interactions must sit inside the system boundary.
claims.scope: The three nested system-boundary interfaces, cradle-to-grave/gate/gate-to-gate archetypes, five default life-cycle stages, and component–host technical interactions.
caveats: ILCD 2010 §6.6 Provision I notes that standard LCA covers normal and abnormal operation while excluding accidents, spills, and direct human ingestion of products; where such risks are material to a decision, they must be addressed explicitly outside routine inventory boundaries.

claims.text: Because tracing raw materials, equipment, and services upstream quickly spans the entire global economy, every process inventory confronts cut-off rules specifying which minor flows may be omitted. Yet frameworks diverge sharply on thresholds, denominators, and the burden of proof for exclusion (Table 1). The ISO 14044 public preview (§§4.2.3.3.1 and 4.2.3.3.3) permits omissions only if they do not significantly alter overall conclusions and requires mass, energy, and environmental significance criteria together in final sensitivity analysis for public comparative assertions—precisely because a catalyst or precious metal under 0.1% by mass can dominate toxicity or resource depletion. ILCD 2010 (§6.6.3) therefore discards mass-only cut-offs in favor of environmental-impact completeness (such as covering 85% or 95% of each included impact category or of normalized-and-weighted total impact), warning that the "100% total" is itself an extrapolation whose uncertainty widens as more processes are excluded. EU PEF (§§4.1 and 4.6.4) imposes the strictest quantitative cap: zero cut-off during screening, and a cumulative limit of 3.0% across material, energy, single overall score, and every impact category in the main study—applied on top of cut-offs already embedded inside background datasets. The GHG Protocol Product Standard (§§7.2 and 7.3.4–7.3.5) instead partitions activities upfront into mandatory attributable processes and optional non-attributable processes (capital goods, facility overhead, corporate R&D, administration, and marketing, included when inseparable or relevant); attributable processes may be excluded only when all three conditions hold—a data gap exists, no proxy or extrapolation can fill it, and conservative upper-limit estimation demonstrates insignificance (illustrating a < 1% mass, energy, volume, and GHG rule of thumb)—with documented justification.
claims.scope: Substantive divergences across ISO 14044 public preview, ILCD 2010, EU PEF, and the GHG Protocol on attributable boundaries and quantitative cut-off rules.
caveats: Quantifying truncation error and closing upstream gaps via hybrid input–output models are examined in Hybrid Inventory Analysis at the close of Part II; this section compares scoping-stage exclusion gates.

claims.text: When designing or auditing any LCA study, four checks quickly test whether its goal and scope hold together. First, audit goal and comparative eligibility: verify that target audience, decision context, and comparative-assertion intent are stated explicitly and match the chosen framework (for instance, avoiding comparative superiority claims from a climate-only inventory or a PEF study without a PEFCR). Second, audit foreground and background boundaries: check whether the specificity or management perspective governs, whether custom tier-1 suppliers and design-driven use parameters carry primary data, and whether compared alternatives suffer from asymmetric foreground-to-background data ratios. Third, audit system boundaries and cumulative cut-offs: confirm that a process map aligns with report terminology, that component–host technical interactions are captured, and that cut-offs respect environmental significance rather than mass alone without double-ignoring background cut-offs. Fourth, audit iteration logs and standard-source boundaries: verify that scope revisions are justified and that uninspected paywalled clauses—such as ISO 14044:2006 §§4.2.3.6–4.2.3.8 and §§4.3–5.3 beyond public preview page 9—are candidly disclosed rather than reconstructed. With study goal, foreground boundaries, and system scope anchored, the next chapter (Functional Reference) turns to the core unit of comparison: fixing the service delivered as a measurable functional unit and reference flow.
claims.scope: Four-step goal-and-scope audit checklist, candid ISO 14044 public-preview boundary disclosure, and transition to Functional Reference.
caveats: This checklist synthesizes five openly accessible primary texts; statutory filings and third-party certifications require consulting the current authorized standard texts and applicable category rules.

claims.text: Before taking up co-production, markets, electricity, or recycling, Part III draws one foundational divide rooted directly in the Goal and Scope decision contexts established in Part II: whether a study performs attributional accounting or consequential system-response modeling. Foundational allocation literature (Ekvall and Tillman 1997; Ekvall, Tillman, and Molander 2005—whose original terminology and ethical arguments are unpacked in the Information Goals section below) already established that this divide turns on the type of question asked—describing the environmental flows linked to a defined product system versus estimating how a possible decision alters those flows—rather than calendar time. Contemporary frameworks diverge sharply along this divide: the GHG Protocol Product Standard (2011, Section 5.2 and Box 5.1) locks product inventories into attributional accounting and assigns consequential analysis to mitigation projects or public policy; the ILCD 2010 Handbook (Section 5.3 Table 2 and Sections 6.5.4.2–6.5.4.4) classifies studies by decision-support role and whether large-scale structural capacity changes occur in background markets, separating pure accounting (Situation C, with C2 excluding cross-system crediting), micro-level decision support using existing capacity and average market mixes as a practical simplification (Situation A), and meso/macro structural changes (Situation B); while Weidema et al. (2013) position the ecoinvent v3 consequential system model for small-scale long-term decisions, arguing that individual purchases cumulatively steer capital investment and therefore linking directly to unconstrained marginal suppliers instead of average mixes.
claims.scope: Conceptual divide opening Part III between attributional accounting and consequential system response, linked to Part II decision contexts and primary texts from Ekvall/Tillman, ILCD, GHG Protocol, and ecoinvent v3.
caveats: Retrospective versus prospective and attributional versus consequential are not identical across every paper; the chapters below preserve each source's own terminology and scope conditions rather than collapsing four frameworks into one binary label.

claims.text: This single divide recurs across all four domains of Part III, changing both the equations and the empirical proof required in each chapter (Table 1). In Joint Production, an attributional account partitions a batch's emissions across outputs by physical or economic shares, whereas a system-response route adds missing functions or subtracts a displaced reference supply under system expansion to compare route differences (ILCD Section 6.5.3); even inside its attributional framework, EU PEF Annex I Section 4.5 distinguishes Step 1 subdivision or whole-system expansion from Step 2 direct substitution requiring dual proof. In Market Response, attributional models link to historical average consumption mixes or contractual supplier hierarchies (such as EU PEF Annex I Section 4.4.2's four-tier electricity hierarchy and residual-mix fallback when a country's untracked consumption exceeds 95%), whereas consequential models must verify capacity, by-product, and regulatory constraints to identify unconstrained marginal suppliers. In Electricity Systems, annual regional plant averages (such as eGRID2023 Revision 2 over annual net generation) serve attribution, whereas short-run dispatch models (such as AVERT 4.3.0 for existing fossil fleets within roughly five years of the base year) and long-run capacity-expansion perturbations (such as Cambium 2024 Long-Run Marginal Emission Rates, LRMER, pairing national baseline and perturbed runs) model physical grid responses across distinct time horizons—and comparing across datasets always requires checking busbar-generation versus end-use distribution-loss denominators. In Material Recycling Chains, cut-off rules or the EU PEF Annex I Section 4.4.8 Circular Footprint Formula (CFF) allocate recycling burdens and credits across life cycles via fixed factor A, quality ratios, and factor B (default 0), whereas consequential counterfactuals (such as Ekvall et al., 2021) ask whether diverting an extra tonne of waste plastics to recycling under fixed local incineration capacity actually cuts local heat and power generation or simply frees capacity that draws in imported combustible waste treated elsewhere.
claims.scope: Propagation of the attributional-versus-consequential divide across Joint Production, Market Response, Electricity Systems, and Material Recycling Chains, summarized in Table 1.
caveats: This paragraph and Table 1 synthesize the shared analytical scaffold across Part III; worked numbers, reproduction conditions, and model-specific limits are developed in each of the four chapters that follow.

claims.text: Because attributional accounting and consequential modeling answer different questions, neither is universally more accurate—and the sharpest pitfall is mixing them without declaring the question. Ekvall, Tillman, and Molander (2005) review each orientation's criticisms of the other regarding causal coverage, modeling uncertainty, and value judgments, concluding that neither universally dominates. Frischknecht (1998) likewise separates mathematical uniqueness, additive consistency across partitioned outputs, and the substantive defense of a rule as three distinct obligations. Mixing attributional foreground accounts with unverified market substitution credits breaks additivity and invites double counting—for instance, when two linked producers both claim substitution credit for the same recyclate or low-carbon electricity. Major frameworks therefore enforce strict cross-boundary guardrails: ILCD 2010 (Section 6.5.4 Provision I.a) restricts Situation A substitution with average market mixes to cases with verified equivalence and sufficient market absorption (checking broader equivalent functions or shifting to Situation B when scale falls short, and falling back to allocation under Provision I.a.iv.4 only when substitution modeling is infeasible and generic data are not sufficiently accurate); EU PEF (Annex I, Section 4.5) demands dual evidence of direct market effect and a directly representative inventory before permitting direct substitution inside its attributional account; and the GHG Protocol Product Standard (Sections 9.3.2 and 11.3.2) allows attributional system expansion only when by-product fate is known and supplier-specific or average factors are used, while barring market avoided emissions from being subtracted from the product inventory total. With these boundaries and guardrails in view, the next section turns to the foundational information goals of joint production before working through partitioning and reference-supply examples.
claims.scope: Why neither attributional nor consequential modeling is universally superior, how unstated mixing causes double counting, and the cross-boundary guardrails in ILCD, EU PEF, and the GHG Protocol.
caveats: The guardrails summarized here reflect the verified open-access texts cited above; statutory disclosures and sector-specific product category rules (PCR/PEFCR) require checking the current enforceable edition.
